| Hexokinase | Rare hemolytic anemia | First step of glycolysis

| Phosphofructokinase (Tarui disease) | Exercise intolerance + hemolysis | Muscle glycogenosis (GSD VII)

| Succinate dehydrogenase | Mitochondrial disorders/tumors | Not relevant in RBCs

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 12-year-old girl suffers from an inadequately treated type 1 diabetes mellitus. She is currently hyperglycemic. Which of the following is most likely to occur?
options: Increased conversion of fatty acids to acetyl-CoA
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increased conversion of fatty acids to acetyl-CoA

In poorly controlled type 1 diabetes mellitus, insulin deficiency causes a catabolic state. Low insulin and high glucagon activate hormone-sensitive lipase, increasing lipolysis. Released fatty acids are transported to the liver and undergo β-oxidation, producing large amounts of acetyl-CoA, which contributes to ketone body formation during hyperglycemia.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Glycogenesis in muscle: Requires insulin; it is decreased in insulin deficiency.

B. Increased protein synthesis: Insulin is anabolic; protein breakdown predominates instead.

D. Decreased cholesterol synthesis: Cholesterol synthesis is actually reduced due to low insulin, but the dominant metabolic change here is increased fatty acid oxidation

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 14-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department due to excessive urination and thirst. He has lost 4.5 kg in the last 3 weeks. Physical examination shows dry mucous membranes. Laboratory studies reveal blood glucose of 455 mg/dl, normal anion gap, and hemoglobin A1 c of 11.3%. The patient is diagnosed with type 1 diabetes, and treatment with insulin is initiated. In addition to lowering blood glucose, insulin increases glycogen synthesis in hepatocytes. Activation of which of the following molecules most likely promotes this metabolic effect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Protein phosphatase

Insulin promotes glycogen synthesis in hepatocytes by activating protein phosphatases, particularly protein phosphatase 1 (PP1). PP1 dephosphorylates and activates glycogen synthase while inactivating glycogen phosphorylase, shifting metabolism toward glycogen storage. This effect complements insulin’s role in lowering blood glucose.

Why the others are incorrect:

A. Janus kinase (JAK): Mediates cytokine and growth hormone signaling, not insulin’s glycogen effects.

B. Phospholipase C: Part of Gq-coupled receptor pathways, involved in IP3/DAG signaling, not glycogen synthesis.

C. Protein kinase A: Activated by cAMP in response to glucagon/epinephrine; phosphorylates glycogen synthase to inhibit glycogen formation, opposite of insulin’s action.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 19-year-old man presents with progressive shortness of breath and recurrent lower respiratory tract infections. Genetic analysis reveals a mutation causing misfolding of a protein that is normally synthesized in the rough endoplasmic reticulum. Instead of being transported to the Golgi apparatus, the misfolded protein is retro-translocated to the cytosol and degraded by proteasomes. Which cellular quality-control mechanism is responsible for this process?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Endoplasmic reticulum–associated degradation (ERAD)

• ERAD removes misfolded proteins from ER
• Proteins are retro-translocated to cytosol
• Tagged with ubiquitin
• Degraded by 26S proteasome
• Classic example: ΔF508 CFTR in cystic fibrosis
• Misfolded ER protein → cytosol → ubiquitin → proteasome = ERAD.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 19-year-old man presents with sudden chest pain and is found to have aortic root dilatation on echocardiography. Ophthalmologic exam reveals lens dislocation. He has normal cognitive function. Which direction of lens dislocation would be expected, and which connective tissue protein is primarily defective?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Upward/temporal; fibrillin-1

Normal intellect + aortic root dilatation = Marfan syndrome (vs homocystinuria, which causes decreased intellect and thrombosis rather than aortic dilatation). Marfan lens dislocation is upward/temporal (mnemonic: "Marfan fans out"), caused by defective fibrillin-1 (FBN1 mutation), which normally sequesters TGF-β and forms a sheath around elastin.

| Feature | Marfan syndrome | Homocystinuria

| ------- | --------------- | --------------

| Inheritance | Autosomal dominant | Autosomal recessive

| Intellect | Normal | Decreased

| Vascular complication | Aortic root dilatation | Thrombosis

| Lens dislocation | Upward/temporal | Downward/nasal

| Defective protein | Fibrillin-1 | Cystathionine synthase

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with fever, vomiting, and sleepiness. Since the newborn period, the parents say that the patient has had multiple similar episodes. Lab results revealed increased blood ammonia levels during these episodes and markedly increased orotic acid excretion in the urine. Physical examination shows a tachypneic boy who is unresponsive to all stimuli. Which of the following enzymes is most likely to be deficient in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ornithine transcarbamylase

This patient presents with hyperammonemia and markedly increased urinary orotic acid, which are hallmark features of ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, an X-linked urea cycle disorder. OTC deficiency leads to accumulation of carbamoyl phosphate, which is shunted into pyrimidine synthesis, producing excess orotic acid. Clinical presentation includes recurrent vomiting, lethargy, and tachypnea in early childhood.

Why the others are incorrect:

A. Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I: Deficiency also causes hyperammonemia but orotic acid is low, not elevated.

B. Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT): Deficiency causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome (hyperuricemia, self-mutilation), not hyperammonemia.

D. Uridine monophosphate synthetase: Deficiency leads to orotic aciduria without hyperammonemia; differs from OTC deficiency.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 2-year-old child is evaluated for developmental delay and recurrent seizures. The pediatric neurologist suspects a hereditary disorder caused by a mutation in a specific gene. To confirm the diagnosis, DNA extracted from the child's blood is analyzed using a technique in which DNA fragments are separated by electrophoresis, transferred to a membrane, and hybridized with a labeled complementary probe. This technique is primarily used to detect:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Specific DNA sequence

Southern blotting is a molecular biology technique used to detect specific DNA sequences within a complex mixture of DNA. The procedure involves:

1. Digestion of DNA with restriction endonucleases.
2. Separation of DNA fragments by agarose gel electrophoresis.
3. Transfer (blotting) of DNA onto a nitrocellulose or nylon membrane.
4. Hybridization with a labeled complementary DNA probe.
5. Detection of the hybridized DNA, identifying the presence of the target DNA sequence.

Southern blotting is widely used to detect gene mutations, gene rearrangements, deletions, insertions, restriction fragment length polymorphisms (RFLPs), and DNA fingerprinting.

Other Options:

• Option A. Specific protein: Incorrect. Western blotting is used to detect specific proteins using antibodies directed against the target protein.
• Option C. Specific RNA sequence: Incorrect. Northern blotting detects RNA molecules and is commonly used to study gene expression.
• Option D. Protein-binding site in DNA: Incorrect. Southwestern blotting is used to identify DNA-binding proteins and study protein-DNA interactions.

High-yield blotting techniques:

| Technique | Detects | Probe/Detection Method

| --------- | ------- | ----------------------

| Southern blot | DNA | Labeled DNA probe

| Northern blot | RNA | Labeled DNA/RNA probe

| Western blot | Protein | Specific antibodies

| Southwestern blot | DNA-binding proteins | Labeled DNA probe

| Eastern blot | Post-translational modifications of proteins (e.g., glycosylation, lipids) | Specific ligands/antibodies

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 2-year-old girl who had normal development until 14 months now shows regression of previously acquired motor and verbal skills, along with stereotypic hand-wringing movements and new-onset seizures. Genetic testing reveals a de novo mutation. Which gene is implicated, and why is this condition seen almost exclusively in females?
options: FMR1; embryonically lethal in males due to X-inactivation skewing
MECP2; embryonically lethal in males since they lack a second X chromosome to compensate
DMPK; autosomal dominant, equal sex distribution expected but rare in males due to anticipation
UBE3A; paternal allele silencing makes males asymptomatic carriers only
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. MECP2; embryonically lethal in males since they lack a second X chromosome to compensate

Rett syndrome: de novo MECP2 mutation on the X chromosome. Since males have only one X chromosome (hemizygous), a MECP2 mutation is embryonically lethal — there is no second, potentially normal X copy to provide partial compensation as occurs in heterozygous females (who survive due to mosaic expression from X-inactivation, with the unaffected X-bearing cells providing some normal MECP2 function). This explains why Rett syndrome is seen almost exclusively in females.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 21-year-old female is evaluated for progressive gait instability and slurred speech. DNA analysis shows GAA repeat expansion causing decreased expression of a mitochondrial protein due to heterochromatin formation. What is the underlying mechanism?
options: Anticipation due to gain-of-function in a cytoplasmic protein
Transcriptional repression due to gene silencing
mRNA instability due to nonsense-mediated decay
Toxic RNA aggregation in neuronal nuclei
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Transcriptional repression due to gene silencing

This describes Friedreich ataxia, caused by GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FXN gene. The expanded repeats induce heterochromatin formation, leading to epigenetic gene silencing and reduced transcription of frataxin, a mitochondrial protein involved in iron–sulfur cluster formation. The disease results from loss of function due to decreased gene expression, not from a toxic protein or RNA effect.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Anticipation due to gain-of-function in a cytoplasmic protein: Friedreich ataxia is a loss-of-function disorder, not gain-of-function.

C. mRNA instability due to nonsense-mediated decay: There is no premature stop codon causing mRNA degradation.

D. Toxic RNA aggregation in neuronal nuclei: Toxic RNA aggregation occurs in disorders like myotonic dystrophy, not here.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 22-year-old woman presents to the dermatology clinic with brittle hair and fragile nails. The keratin in the skin is normally much softer and more flexible than that in the nails. Keratin in the skin is softer than keratin in the nails because skin keratin has:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fewer disulfide bonds

The hardness and tensile strength of keratin are primarily determined by the number of disulfide (S–S) bonds formed between cysteine residues in adjacent keratin molecules. These covalent cross-links stabilize the keratin network and increase its rigidity.

• Soft keratin, found in the epidermis (skin), contains fewer disulfide bonds, making it more flexible.
• Hard keratin, found in the nails and hair, contains a much higher concentration of cysteine residues, resulting in more disulfide cross-links and greater mechanical strength.

Other Options:

• B. Fewer salt bridges: Incorrect. Salt bridges contribute to protein stability but are not the major determinant of the difference in hardness between skin and nail keratin.
• C. Higher sodium content: Incorrect. Sodium concentration has no significant role in determining the structural rigidity of keratin.
• D. Different water affinity: Incorrect. Hydration may influence flexibility to some extent, but the primary determinant of keratin hardness is the number of disulfide bonds.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 24-month-old boy is brought to the physician for the evaluation of intellectual and behavioral abnormalities and abnormal movements of his extremities. His mother reports that he often hits his head and limbs against furniture. He is unable to walk without support and speaks in unclear 2-word phrases. Examination shows multiple bruises on the forehead and several healing wounds over the fingers. There is increased muscle tone in all extremities. Laboratory studies show an increased serum uric acid concentration. The serum concentration of which of the following substances is most likely to also be increased in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate

This child has Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, caused by deficiency of hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT). HGPRT normally salvages hypoxanthine and guanine to IMP and GMP. Its deficiency leads to:

• Hyperuricemia (excess purine degradation)
• Self-mutilation, intellectual disability, dystonia, spasticity

The lack of purine salvage causes PRPP accumulation, because it is not being used in the salvage pathway. Elevated PRPP stimulates de novo purine synthesis, further increasing uric acid production.

Why other options are incorrect:

• A. HGPRT: This enzyme is deficient, not increased.
• C. dATP (deoxyadenosine triphosphate): Increased dATP occurs in ADA deficiency, not Lesch-Nyhan.
• D. Branched-chain amino acids: Not related to HGPRT deficiency; elevated in maple syrup urine disease.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 25-year-old patient presented with dark urine, which further blackens on exposure to air. What’s the enzyme defect in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Di Hydroxy Phenyl Acetate Dioxygenase

The patient’s dark urine that blackens on standing is a classic sign of alkaptonuria, which results from a block in the tyrosine degradation pathway. The enzyme homogentisate dioxygenase (also called dihydroxyphenylacetate dioxygenase in some texts) is deficient. This leads to accumulation of homogentisic acid, which is excreted in urine and oxidizes to a dark pigment on exposure to air.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase: Deficiency causes tyrosinemia type I with liver and kidney failure, not darkening urine.

C. Homogentisate dehydrogenase: TRAPPER ALERT! It's Homogentisate oxidase, not dehydrogenase! This option was created as a distractor.

D. Phenylalanine hydroxylase: Deficiency causes phenylketonuria, not urine darkening.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 25-year-old patient with Type 1 diabetes mellitus is started on recombinant human insulin produced using genetically engineered bacteria. During the manufacturing process, scientists need to obtain the correct genetic template to synthesize insulin in bacteria. Which of the following is the most appropriate starting material for this purpose?
options: Genomic DNA from human pancreatic beta cells
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. mRNA from pancreatic beta cells

Production of recombinant human insulin requires a gene template without introns, because bacteria cannot process introns (no splicing machinery).

• Best starting material:

• mRNA from pancreatic β-cells
• Contains only exons (coding sequence)
• Converted to cDNA using reverse transcriptase → inserted into bacterial plasmid

• Why not genomic DNA:

• Contains introns + exons
• Bacteria cannot remove introns → nonfunctional protein

• Why pancreatic β-cells specifically:

• Actively express insulin mRNA
• Lymphocytes do not produce insulin

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 27-year-old man is brought to the emergency department due to confusion. His roommate says that he has been binge drinking for the last 5 days and probably has had very little to eat. The patient's medical history is significant for alcohol-related seizures 1 year ago. He had been sober until 2 weeks ago, when he started drinking again. The patient's past medical history is otherwise unremarkable. On examination, he responds to voice but does not follow commands. Fingerstick glucose is 35 mg/dL and urine is strongly positive for ketones. Suppression of which of the following is the primary cause of this patient's hypoglycemia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gluconeogenesis

In chronic alcohol use with fasting, hypoglycemia occurs primarily due to inhibition of gluconeogenesis.

• Mechanism:

• Ethanol metabolism (via alcohol dehydrogenase) → ↑ NADH/NAD⁺ ratio
• This shifts key reactions:

• Pyruvate → lactate
• Oxaloacetate → malate

• Result → depletion of substrates required for gluconeogenesis

• Why hypoglycemia occurs:

• Glycogen stores are already depleted (prolonged fasting)
• Body depends on gluconeogenesis, which is now suppressed

→ Leads to severe hypoglycemia

• Associated findings:

• Ketosis (starvation + alcohol)
• Possible lactic acidosis

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 28-year-old man presents with fatigue, pallor, and ringed sideroblasts on bone marrow biopsy. Lab findings show increased serum iron and decreased hemoglobin. Which statement correctly differentiates ALA synthase I (ALAS-1) and ALA synthase II (ALAS-2) regulation in this patient?
options: ALAS-1 is expressed in erythroid cells and activated by iron availability.
ALAS-2 is expressed in the liver and inhibited by heme accumulation.
ALAS-2 is erythroid-specific and requires pyridoxal phosphate.
ALAS-1 is regulated by iron through iron-responsive elements.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. ALAS-2 is erythroid-specific and requires pyridoxal phosphate.

Aminolevulinic acid (ALA) synthase

ALA synthase is a mitochondrial enzyme. Two isoforms:

ALA-S1

• Located mostly in liver cells and to a smaller extent in other cells in the body
• Heme production for the liver cytochrome P450 mono-oxygenase system
• Gene is located on chromosome-3
• Loss-of-function mutation in the ALA-S1 gene causes impaired metabolism of xenobiotics

ALA-S2

• Produced in erythroid tissue
• Heme production for RBC hemoglobin
• Gene is located on the X-chromosome
• Loss-of-function mutations in ALA-S2 result in anemia

Porphyrin biosynthesis is primarily regulated via ALA-S regulation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 3-month-old infant presents with liver failure, bleeding, garlic-like odor, hypophosphatemic rickets, and renal Fanconi syndrome. Which amino acid’s catabolic pathway is blocked?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tyrosine

• Defect: Fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase.
• This presentation is classic for Tyrosinemia type I, caused by deficiency of fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase, the final enzyme in tyrosine catabolism.
• Accumulation of toxic metabolites (fumarylacetoacetate, succinylacetone) leads to acute liver failure, bleeding diathesis, renal Fanconi syndrome, hypophosphatemic rickets, and a characteristic of garlic-like odor.
• The disease presents in infancy and is life-threatening without treatment (nitisinone, liver transplant).

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Methionine: Causes homocystinuria, not liver failure with Fanconi syndrome.

B. Phenylalanine: PKU causes neurodevelopmental delay, not hepatic failure.

D. Tryptophan: Associated with Hartnup disease, mainly neurologic and skin findings.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 3-month-old male infant presents with sparse, brittle, hypopigmented hair, hypotonia, and seizures. Skeletal survey shows metaphyseal spurring and wormian bones resembling changes seen in a nutritional deficiency of vitamin C. Serum copper and ceruloplasmin are low. Deficient activity of which enzyme best explains the connective tissue findings in this infant?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lysyl oxidase

| Point | Fact

| ----- | ----

| Diagnosis (inferred) | Menkes disease (kinky/steely hair disease)

| Defective enzyme | Lysyl oxidase — Cu-dependent, cross-links collagen/elastin → connective tissue fragility, vascular tortuosity

| Why X-ray mimics scurvy | Both scurvy (vit C, prolyl/lysyl hydroxylase) and Menkes (Cu, lysyl oxidase) impair collagen cross-linking/maturation → similar metaphyseal changes

| Other Cu-dependent enzymes affected | Cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV), dopamine β-hydroxylase, tyrosinase, SOD1

| Cytochrome c oxidase | Explains neurodegeneration, not the connective tissue defect specifically

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his parents because he has not yet begun to walk or speak. Assessment of his developmental milestones shows severe intellectual disability. He dies 6 months later from refractory seizures resulting in respiratory failure. Autopsy shows pallor of the substantia nigra, locus ceruleus, and vagal nucleus dorsalis. The underlying condition responsible for this patient's death is most likely caused by a deficiency of which of the following enzymes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Phenylalanine hydroxylase

This child’s presentation is classic for untreated phenylketonuria (PKU): severe intellectual disability, developmental delay, seizures, and early death if untreated. PKU is caused by a deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase, which converts phenylalanine → tyrosine. Accumulation of phenylalanine and its metabolites leads to neurotoxicity, affecting brain development and function, including catecholaminergic regions like the substantia nigra and locus ceruleus, as seen on autopsy.

Why the others are incorrect:

A. Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase: Causes maple syrup urine disease with metabolic acidosis and odor, not this neurologic pattern.

B. Dopamine hydroxylase: Deficiency causes autonomic dysfunction, hypotension, and low norepinephrine, but not severe intellectual disability from birth.

C. Homogentisic acid oxidase: Causes alkaptonuria with dark urine and connective tissue pigmentation; neurologic deficits are not typical.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 3-year-old boy is evaluated for recurrent episodes of vomiting, developmental delay, and failure to thrive. Metabolic screening suggests an inborn error of metabolism, and genetic testing identifies a missense mutation resulting in the substitution of a single amino acid in a metabolic enzyme. The altered enzyme is unstable and has markedly reduced catalytic activity. The primary structural defect responsible for most inborn errors of metabolism occurs at which level of protein structure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Primary structure

Most inborn errors of metabolism (IEMs) are caused by mutations in genes encoding metabolic enzymes, leading to alterations in the primary structure of proteins—the linear sequence of amino acids. Even a single amino acid substitution can impair protein folding, stability, or catalytic activity, resulting in enzyme deficiency and accumulation of toxic metabolites or deficiency of essential metabolic products.

The altered primary structure may subsequently affect the protein's secondary, tertiary, or quaternary structure, but the initial defect lies in the amino acid sequence.

Other Options:

• B. Secondary structure: Incorrect. Secondary structure refers to local protein folding into α-helices and β-pleated sheets through hydrogen bonding. These changes are usually secondary to alterations in the primary structure.
• C. Tertiary structure: Incorrect. Tertiary structure is the three-dimensional conformation of a single polypeptide chain formed by interactions among amino acid side chains. Although often disrupted in IEMs, the primary genetic defect usually affects the amino acid sequence first.
• D. Quaternary structure: Incorrect. Quaternary structure is the arrangement of multiple polypeptide subunits. While some inherited disorders affect multimeric proteins, this is not the most common structural defect in inborn errors of metabolism.

High-yield:

• Primary structure: Amino acid sequence (determined by DNA sequence)
• Secondary structure: α-Helices and β-sheets
• Tertiary structure: Three-dimensional folding of a single polypeptide
• Quaternary structure: Association of two or more polypeptide chains
• Most inborn errors of metabolism: Caused by mutations altering the primary structure of metabolic enzymes, leading to loss or reduction of enzyme function.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 3-year-old child presents with acute onset fever, cough, and respiratory distress. The clinician suspects multiple possible viral etiologies (influenza, RSV, adenovirus) and orders a single molecular test that can simultaneously detect all these pathogens from one sample. Which of the following techniques is most appropriate for this purpose?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Multiplex PCR

🔥 Key Points (exam-focused)

• Detects multiple targets in one reaction
• Uses multiple primer sets
• Saves time and sample volume
• Common in respiratory panels, sepsis panels

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 3-year-old child presents with painful, non-pruritic, thickened plaques on the palms and soles, along with photophobia, excessive tearing, and bilateral corneal ulcers. On slit-lamp examination with fluorescein staining, the corneal lesions take up dye poorly. Mild developmental delay is also noted. Plasma amino acid analysis reveals elevated tyrosine. Deficiency of which enzyme best explains this presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tyrosine transaminase

| Point | Fact

| ----- | ----

| Diagnosis (inferred) | Type 2 Tyrosinemia: Richner-Hanhart syndrome (oculocutaneous tyrosinemia)

| Enzyme defect | Tyrosine transaminase (cytosolic, hepatic)

| Elevated amino acid | Tyrosine (plasma and urine)

| Skin finding | Non-pruritic, painful hyperkeratotic plaques on palms and soles

| Ocular finding | Pseudodendritic corneal ulcers from intracellular tyrosine crystal deposition — a key clinical pearl is poor fluorescein uptake, since these are not true epithelial defects (unlike herpetic dendritic keratitis, which stains brightly) — this distinction prevents misdiagnosis and inappropriate antiviral therapy

| Why not A | Fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency causes Type 1 (hepatorenal) tyrosinemia — presents with liver failure, renal Fanconi syndrome, cabbage-like odor, not this cutaneous-ocular picture

| Why not C | Homogentisate oxidase deficiency causes alkaptonuria — dark urine on standing, ochronosis, arthropathy — unrelated presentation

| Why not D | Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency causes PKU — mousy odor, hypopigmentation, intellectual disability, not corneal/skin findings

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 30-year-old man is being evaluated for lipoprotein lipase deficiency. Which of the following lipoproteins will be elevated in this patient's plasma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chylomicron and Triglycerides

Lipoprotein lipase (LPL) hydrolyzes triglycerides in chylomicrons and VLDL into free fatty acids for uptake by tissues. In LPL deficiency, this step is impaired, leading to accumulation of chylomicrons in plasma and marked hypertriglyceridemia. Patients classically present with milky plasma, pancreatitis, eruptive xanthomas, and lipemia retinalis, while cholesterol-rich lipoproteins are less affected.

Why other options are incorrect:

B. LDL and HDL: These are not substrates for LPL.

C. HDL and VLDL: VLDL rises, but HDL typically decreases.

D. Chylomicron and LDL: LDL metabolism is not directly dependent on LPL.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 30-year-old man is brought with hyperthermia, tachycardia, and profuse sweating after ingestion of a weight-loss drug. Laboratory evaluation shows increased oxygen consumption with decreased ATP production. Mitochondrial studies reveal dissipation of proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane without inhibition of electron transport. Which of the following agents most likely produced this effect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2, 4-dinitrophenol

This describes uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation:

•          Electron transport continues → ↑ oxygen consumption

•          Proton gradient dissipated → ↓ ATP production

•          Energy released as heat → hyperthermia

2,4-DNP acts as a proton carrier, collapsing the proton gradient.

Other options:

Option A. Rotenone → inhibits Complex I

Option B. Cyanide → inhibits Complex IV

Option D. Oligomycin → inhibits ATP synthase (blocks proton flow)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 32-year-old previously healthy man comes to the emergency department due to a 3-hour history of chest pain, diaphoresis, and dyspnea. He does not smoke, exercises regularly, and eats a balanced diet. His father died at age 56 from a myocardial infarction. His blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg and pulse is 110/min and regular. ECG shows ST elevation in the anterolateral leads. Coronary angiogram reveals proximal left anterior descending artery stenosis and thrombosis, which is treated with angioplasty and stent placement. Laboratory results are as follows: • Total cholesterol: 160 mg/dL • Low-density lipoprotein: 90 mg/dL • Glucose, serum: 98 mg/dL • Homocysteine, plasma: 21.5 µmol/L (normal: 4-14 µmol/L) Further testing reveals a homozygous mutation in the methylene tetrahydrofolate reductase gene that leads to decreased enzymatic activity. Due to this defect, the patient most likely has impairment converting homocysteine to which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Methionine

This patient has elevated homocysteine and a homozygous MTHFR mutation, which reduces activity of methylene tetrahydrofolate reductase. MTHFR generates 5-methyltetrahydrofolate, the methyl donor required by methionine synthase to convert homocysteine → methionine. Deficiency leads to hyperhomocysteinemia, a risk factor for premature atherosclerosis and thrombosis, as seen in this patient with early-onset MI.

Why other options are incorrect:

• A. Cystathionine: Formed from homocysteine via cystathionine β-synthase, which requires vitamin B₆; not directly affected by MTHFR.
• B. Cysteine: Downstream product of the transsulfuration pathway; secondary to cystathionine.
• D. Methylmalonyl-CoA: Formed from propionyl-CoA; requires vitamin B₁₂ but unrelated to homocysteine metabolism.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 34-year-old man undergoes strenuous aerobic exercise. During this period, there is increased production of cytosolic NADH due to enhanced metabolic activity. For continued ATP generation, these reducing equivalents must be transferred into the mitochondria for oxidative phosphorylation. The malate–aspartate shuttle is required most for which of the following metabolic pathways?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glycolysis

The malate–aspartate shuttle is essential for transferring cytosolic NADH into mitochondria, since NADH itself cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane.

• Key role: Regenerates NAD⁺ in cytosol to allow glycolysis to continue
• During aerobic glycolysis, NADH is produced in the cytosol (at glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase step)
• These electrons must enter mitochondria for oxidative phosphorylation → ATP generation
• Glycolysis depends on continuous availability of NAD⁺
• Without shuttles (malate–aspartate or glycerol-3-phosphate), glycolysis would halt

Why others are wrong:

• A. Glycogenolysis: does not produce NADH
• C. HMP shunt: produces NADPH, not NADH
• D. Gluconeogenesis: uses NADH but is not the primary source of cytosolic NADH needing shuttle

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 34-year-old woman comes to the OPD after her sister was diagnosed with breast cancer. Her sister was found to have a multiple base pair insertion affecting exon 11 of the BRCA 1 gene that leads to a frameshift mutation. A screening test to evaluate for a similar insertion mutation in the patient's BRCA 1 gene is performed. The test uses polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to amplify the target exon and gel electrophoresis to assess the size of the exon compared to the wild-type allele. Which of the following must be known to perform the amplification part of this analysis?
options: Restriction enzyme susceptibility sites within the target exon
The amino acid sequence of the abnormal BRCA 1 protein
The complete nucleotide sequence of the target exon
The nucleotide sequence of the regions flanking the target exon.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. The nucleotide sequence of the regions flanking the target exon.

PCR amplification requires primers that bind to sequences flanking the target exon. Knowing these flanking sequences allows the primers to anneal specifically, enabling amplification of the exon containing the potential insertion mutation. After amplification, gel electrophoresis can detect size changes indicative of insertions or deletions.

Why the others are incorrect:

A. Restriction enzyme sites: Only needed for restriction fragment analysis, not standard PCR.

B. Amino acid sequence: Protein sequence cannot be used to design DNA primers; DNA sequence is needed.

C. Complete nucleotide sequence of exon: Knowing the exon alone is insufficient; primers must bind to flanking regions for PCR amplification.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 35-year-old female is hospitalized with headaches and vomiting. She has a long history of psychiatric illness and is known to practice eccentric. dietary habits. Physical findings include papilledema, dry skin, and hepatosplenomegaly. Head CT scan is ordered immediately but is negative for intracranial mass. Which of the following is a likely cause of this patient's condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vitamin A overuse

This patient has hypervitaminosis A, suggested by headaches, vomiting, papilledema (pseudotumor cerebri), hepatosplenomegaly, dry skin, and psychiatric issues with eccentric diet. Excess vitamin A leads to increased intracranial pressure and systemic toxicity affecting the skin and liver. Head CT is normal, which is typical for pseudotumor cerebri caused by vitamin A toxicity.

Why the others are incorrect:

A. Thiamine deficiency: Causes Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome or beriberi; does not produce papilledema or hepatosplenomegaly.

B. Riboflavin deficiency: Leads to cheilitis, glossitis, dermatitis, not intracranial hypertension.

C. Vitamin C overuse: Can cause kidney stones or GI upset, not pseudotumor cerebri.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 4-month-old breastfed infant develops failure to thrive, jaundice, and hepatomegaly. Slit-lamp examination reveals bilateral cataracts. Urine testing shows a reducing substance that is non-glucose. Which enzyme deficiency explains this presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency

Classic galactosemia (galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency) causes accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate AND upstream galactose, which is shunted via aldose reductase to galactitol — this alcohol sugar deposits in the lens, causing infantile cataracts. This is distinct from isolated galactokinase deficiency, which also causes galactitol-mediated cataracts but with a comparatively milder overall systemic presentation (no hepatomegaly, failure to thrive, or E. coli sepsis risk), since galactose-1-phosphate itself does not accumulate to toxic levels in galactokinase deficiency.

| Feature | Classic galactosemia

| ------- | --------------------

| Enzyme deficient | Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase

| Toxic accumulation | Galactose-1-phosphate, galactitol

| Cataract mechanism | Galactose → galactitol (via aldose reductase) → lens deposition

| Additional risks | Failure to thrive, jaundice, hepatomegaly, intellectual disability, E. coli sepsis

| Treatment | Exclude galactose AND lactose from diet

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 4-month-old infant who appeared healthy at birth is brought for evaluation of recurrent episodes of fasting hypoglycemia and progressive muscle weakness. The parents report that symptoms are most prominent after prolonged fasting, such as overnight. Physical examination reveals hepatomegaly. Laboratory investigations demonstrate elevated AST and ALT levels along with ketoacidosis (arterial pH 7.25). Liver biopsy shows excessive glycogen accumulation, accounting for approximately 8% of liver weight. A glucagon stimulation test is performed: • After a carbohydrate-rich meal: Blood glucose rises appropriately. • After an overnight fast: No significant increase in blood glucose is observed. Which enzyme deficiency best explains these findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Debranching enzyme

This infant most likely has glycogen storage disease type III (Cori/Forbes disease), caused by deficiency of the glycogen debranching enzyme.

The key findings are:

• Fasting hypoglycemia
• Hepatomegaly
• Elevated AST and ALT
• Ketosis/ketoacidosis
• Progressive muscle weakness
• Excess accumulation of structurally abnormal glycogen in the liver

Glucagon stimulation test

• After a carbohydrate-rich meal: Blood glucose rises because recently synthesized glycogen has relatively long outer chains. Glycogen phosphorylase can initially break these α-1,4 bonds and release glucose-1-phosphate.
• After an overnight fast: The outer glycogen chains have already been shortened to within four glucose residues of the branch points. Without the debranching enzyme, further glycogen breakdown cannot occur, so glucagon produces little or no rise in blood glucose.

This characteristic response supports debranching enzyme deficiency.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• B. Muscle glycogen phosphorylase: Causes McArdle disease, presenting with exercise intolerance, muscle cramps, and myoglobinuria. It does not cause hepatomegaly or fasting hypoglycemia.
• C. Glucose-6-phosphatase: Causes von Gierke disease. It produces severe fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, and hyperlipidemia, but muscle weakness is not a prominent feature. Glucagon fails to raise blood glucose in both fed and fasting states.
• D. Liver glycogen phosphorylase: Causes Hers disease. It leads to mild fasting hypoglycemia, ketosis, and hepatomegaly but generally does not cause progressive muscle weakness.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the pediatric neurology clinic because of developmental delay, recurrent episodes of painful swelling in the joints, and a history of biting his lips and fingers until they bleed. His parents report frequent aggressive outbursts and involuntary movements. Laboratory investigations reveal markedly elevated serum uric acid levels. The pediatrician suspects Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is incorrect?
options: It is caused by a mutation in the HPRT gene on chromosome 6
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. It is caused by a mutation in the HPRT gene on chromosome 6

Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by mutations in the HPRT1 (HGPRT) gene located on the X chromosome (Xq26–q27), not chromosome 6. Deficiency of hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT) impairs the purine salvage pathway, leading to increased degradation of purines into uric acid, resulting in hyperuricemia. Excess PRPP also stimulates de novo purine synthesis, further worsening uric acid overproduction.

The syndrome is characterized by a triad of:

• Hyperuricemia (gout, nephrolithiasis, orange "sand" crystals in diapers)
• Neurological dysfunction (dystonia, choreoathetosis, spasticity)
• Behavioral abnormalities, especially self-mutilation and compulsive aggressive behavior.

Other Options:

• A. Hyperuricemia: Correct. Excess uric acid production leads to gout, uric acid nephrolithiasis, and urate crystal deposition.
• B. Self-mutilative behavior: Correct. Self-biting of the lips, tongue, and fingers is a hallmark feature of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.
• C. Compulsive aggression: Correct. Behavioral disturbances, including compulsive aggression and self-injurious behavior, are common neurological manifestations.

High-yield:

• Inheritance: X-linked recessive
• Enzyme deficiency: HGPRT (Hypoxanthine-Guanine Phosphoribosyltransferase)
• Pathway affected: Purine salvage pathway
• Biochemical findings: ↑ PRPP, ↓ IMP/GMP, ↑ de novo purine synthesis, ↑ uric acid
• Classic presentation: Hyperuricemia + dystonia/choreoathetosis + self-mutilation
• Treatment: Allopurinol or febuxostat lowers uric acid but does not improve the neurological manifestations.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 45-year-old homeless man comes to the emergency department due to a "pins-and-needles" sensation in his legs. He also has painful lesions on his lips and corners of his mouth. Abdominal examination reveals hepatomegaly. Laboratory evaluation shows very low urinary riboflavin excretion. Activity of which of the following enzymes is most likely directly impaired in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Succinate dehydrogenase

Riboflavin (vitamin B₂) is the precursor for FAD and FMN, which are essential cofactors for flavoproteins. Succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II of the ETC) is an FAD-dependent enzyme, and its activity is directly impaired in riboflavin deficiency. This leads to defects in oxidative phosphorylation and energy metabolism, which contributes to neuropathy and muscle weakness seen in this patient.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase: NADP⁺-dependent; indirectly affected by riboflavin deficiency but not directly FAD-dependent.

B. HMG-CoA reductase: Requires NADPH, not FAD/FMN.

C. Isocitrate dehydrogenase: Uses NAD⁺ or NADP⁺, not FAD/FMN.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 45-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus is advised micronutrient supplementation to improve insulin action. Which of the following trace elements enhances insulin sensitivity by potentiating insulin receptor activity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chromium

Chromium is an essential trace element that forms part of the Glucose Tolerance Factor (GTF).

• It potentiates insulin action by enhancing insulin receptor tyrosine kinase activity.
• This leads to ↑ glucose uptake in peripheral tissues and improved glycemic control.
• Deficiency is associated with insulin resistance, impaired glucose tolerance, and hyperglycemia.
• Hence, chromium supplementation can improve insulin sensitivity, especially in deficient states.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 45-year-old obese man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes undergoes abdominal ultrasound for unrelated reasons, which reveals hepatic steatosis. Fasting insulin levels are markedly elevated, yet peripheral tissue glucose uptake remains impaired. Which of the following best explains the mechanism underlying the hepatic steatosis in this patient?
options: Decreased hormone-sensitive lipase activity in adipose tissue, reducing free fatty acid flux to the liver
Impaired insulin-mediated inhibition of hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue, increasing free fatty acid delivery to the liver
Increased GLUT-4-mediated glucose uptake in adipose tissue, promoting triglyceride synthesis
Decreased hepatic VLDL synthesis, causing triglyceride accumulation within hepatocytes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Impaired insulin-mediated inhibition of hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue, increasing free fatty acid delivery to the liver

| Point | Fact

| ----- | ----

| Normal physiology | In the well-fed state, insulin inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) in adipose tissue, suppressing lipolysis

| Pathophysiology here | Insulin resistance → target tissues (adipose, muscle) fail to respond to insulin despite hyperinsulinemia → HSL inhibition lost → unchecked lipolysis continues

| Consequence | ↑ Release of free fatty acids into circulation → increased hepatic FFA uptake → re-esterified to triglycerides within hepatocytes → hepatic steatosis (non-alcoholic fatty liver disease)

| Why not A | Opposite of the actual defect — HSL activity is increased, not decreased, due to failed insulin inhibition

| Why not C | GLUT-4-mediated glucose uptake is impaired (insulin resistance), not increased

| Why not D | Insulin resistance is typically associated with increased, not decreased, hepatic VLDL synthesis (as the liver attempts to export excess triglyceride); impaired export capacity relative to FFA influx contributes to steatosis, but the primary driver here is ↑ FFA delivery

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman undergoes routine health screening, including a lipid profile, while fasting. Her results show a total cholesterol of 300 mg/dL, HDL cholesterol of 25 mg/dL, and triglycerides of 150 mg/dL. Utilizing the Friedewald equation to assess her cardiovascular risk, what is the LDL cholesterol level in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 245 mg/dl

Use the Friedewald equation (valid when TG < 400 mg/dL and patient is fasting):

Given values

• Total cholesterol (TC) = 300 mg/dL
• HDL = 25 mg/dL
• Triglycerides (TG) = 150 mg/dL

Step 1: Calculate VLDL

Step 2: Calculate LDL

Correct answer: a) 245 mg/dL

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 46-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals. Ultrasonography reveals multiple cholesterol gallstones. During counseling, the gastroenterologist explains that bile acids are normally conjugated with specific amino acids before being secreted into bile, a process that increases their water solubility and facilitates fat digestion. Which of the following amino acids are conjugated to the steroid nucleus of bile acids?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Glycine and taurine

Primary bile acids (cholic acid and chenodeoxycholic acid) are synthesized in the liver from cholesterol and are conjugated with either glycine or taurine before being secreted into bile. This conjugation forms glycocholic acid and taurocholic acid (and their corresponding chenodeoxycholic acid derivatives), increasing the water solubility of bile acids and lowering their pKa. These changes enhance their ability to emulsify dietary fats and facilitate the absorption of lipids and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K).

Other Options:

• B. Glycine and alanine: Incorrect. Alanine is not involved in bile acid conjugation.
• C. Histidine and glycine: Incorrect. Histidine does not conjugate with bile acids.
• D. Glutamic acid and valine: Incorrect. Neither glutamic acid nor valine participates in bile acid conjugation.

High-yield:

• Primary bile acids: Cholic acid, Chenodeoxycholic acid (synthesized in the liver)
• Conjugating amino acids: Glycine and Taurine
• Conjugated bile salts: Glycocholate, Taurocholate
• Function: Increase bile acid solubility, promote fat emulsification, and aid absorption of fat-soluble vitamins.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 48-year-old man is infused with glucagon. Hepatic glycolysis decreases due to inhibition of phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1). This effect is mediated by which of the following changes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Decreased fructose-2,6-bisphosphate levels

Glucagon inhibits hepatic glycolysis by lowering levels of fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (F-2,6-BP), the most important regulator of PFK-1.

• Mechanism:

• Glucagon → ↑ cAMP → PKA activation
• PKA phosphorylates PFK-2/FBPase-2 enzyme
• Shifts activity toward FBPase-2 → ↓ F-2,6-BP

• Effect of ↓ F-2,6-BP:

• ↓ PFK-1 activity → ↓ glycolysis
• ↑ fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase → ↑ gluconeogenesis

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy is being evaluated for progressive muscle weakness that has resulted in numerous recent falls. There is no family history of muscle disorders. Physical examination reveals bilateral calf enlargement. When the patient is asked to stand, he uses his hands and arms to help push himself to an upright position. Serum creatine kinase is 12,600 U/L (normal: 30-170 U/L). Molecular tests reveal a large muscle protein that is defective due to the loss of 508 amino acid residues. Genetic analysis reveals a single base substitution within exon 48 of the gene encoding this muscle protein. This patient's gene mutation has most likely resulted in which of the following mRNA codon changes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. UCA → UGA

This vignette describes Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) due to a mutation in the dystrophin gene, leading to a truncated, nonfunctional protein.

• A single base substitution creating a premature stop codon (nonsense mutation)
• Example: UCA (Ser) → UGA (STOP)

→ Results in early termination of translation

• Produces a shortened dystrophin protein → unstable muscle cell membrane
• Leads to muscle fiber damage → high CK → progressive weakness
• Clinical clues:

• Gowers’ sign (using hands to stand)
• Calf pseudohypertrophy
• Markedly elevated CK

Nonsense mutation = introduction of stop codon → truncated protein

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy with developmental delay is brought to the OPD due to difficulty "seeing the board" at school. Examination shows a tall, thin habitus with elongated limbs. Funduscopy shows bilateral lens subluxation. Four years later, the patient dies suddenly of a massive cerebrovascular accident. Autopsy shows middle cerebral artery thrombosis and old renal infarcts. His parents wish to know if anything could have been done to have prevented his death. Which of the following would have been the most appropriate supplementation for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pyridoxine

This child has homocystinuria, suggested by tall stature, lens subluxation, developmental delay, and premature thromboembolic events. The most common form is due to cystathionine β-synthase deficiency, which leads to elevated homocysteine and methionine. Supplementation with pyridoxine, a cofactor for CBS, can lower homocysteine levels in responsive patients and reduce the risk of thrombosis, potentially preventing early death.

Why the others are incorrect:

A. Ascorbic acid: Used for collagen hydroxylation defects (e.g., scurvy), not homocystinuria.

B. Carnitine: Helps with fatty acid metabolism; not effective in CBS deficiency.

D. Thiamine: Coenzyme for pyruvate dehydrogenase; unrelated to homocysteine metabolism.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 5-year-old child presents with progressively unsteady gait since age 2, along with recurrent sinopulmonary infections. Examination reveals telangiectatic vessels over the conjunctivae and skin. Serum alpha-fetoprotein is markedly elevated, and the child shows an exaggerated tissue reaction following a diagnostic chest X-ray. A defect in which DNA repair pathway is most likely responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. dsDNA break repair

• This presentation is classic for Ataxia telangiectasia, caused by mutation of the ATM gene, a key sensor and signaling kinase in the homologous recombination pathway that repairs double-strand DNA breaks.
• Because ionizing radiation predominantly causes double-strand breaks, defective homologous recombination explains the child's exaggerated, radiosensitive reaction to a routine chest X-ray, along with the progressive cerebellar ataxia, oculocutaneous telangiectasia, recurrent sinopulmonary infections (from combined immunodeficiency), and elevated alpha-fetoprotein that together characterize this disorder.
• A. Nucleotide excision repair defects instead cause disorders of UV-induced bulky adduct/pyrimidine dimer repair (xeroderma pigmentosum, Cockayne syndrome), presenting with photosensitivity rather than radiosensitivity or ataxia.
• B. Base excision repair defects cause MUTYH-associated polyposis (colorectal polyps/cancer), and C. mismatch repair defects cause HNPCC with microsatellite instability — neither fits this neurological and immunological picture.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 50-year-old obese man with type 2 diabetes mellitus is started on lifestyle modification. After a few weeks, his insulin sensitivity improves, leading to increased glucose uptake in peripheral tissues. Which of the following transporters is primarily responsible for this insulin-mediated glucose uptake?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. GLUT4 in skeletal muscle

Insulin-mediated glucose uptake in peripheral tissues is primarily via GLUT4.

• GLUT4:

• Found in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue
• Insulin-dependent transporter
• Insulin → translocation of GLUT4 from intracellular vesicles to cell membrane → ↑ glucose uptake

• Other GLUTs (important contrasts):

• GLUT1 → RBCs, basal uptake (insulin-independent)
• GLUT2 → liver, pancreas (high Km, bidirectional)
• GLUT3 → neurons (high affinity, insulin-independent)

• Clinical relevance:

• In type 2 diabetes, insulin resistance → ↓ GLUT4 translocation
• Exercise and lifestyle changes improve GLUT4 activity → ↑ insulin sensitivity

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 55-year-old woman is diagnosed with chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). Molecular analysis demonstrates a constitutively active tyrosine kinase due to the BCR-ABL fusion gene. The oncologist explains that protein kinases regulate numerous cellular processes by transferring phosphate groups to specific amino acid residues in target proteins. Which of the following amino acids is not phosphorylated by protein kinases in eukaryotic cells?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Asparagine

Protein kinases catalyze the transfer of the γ-phosphate group of ATP to the hydroxyl (-OH) group of specific amino acid residues in proteins. In eukaryotic cells, the three amino acids that undergo phosphorylation are:

• Serine
• Threonine
• Tyrosine

Phosphorylation is a reversible post-translational modification that regulates enzyme activity, signal transduction, cell growth, metabolism, and gene expression.

Asparagine cannot be phosphorylated by protein kinases because its side chain contains an amide (-CONH₂) group rather than a hydroxyl group, making it unsuitable for phosphate transfer.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 56-year-old man suffering from uncontrolled diabetes mellitus came for a routine checkup. His lipid profile revealed increased TG (triacylglycerol) and VLDL (very low-density lipoprotein). What is the cause of this abnormal lipid profile?
options: Increased activity of lipoprotein lipase and decreased activity of hormone sensitive lipase
Increased activity of hormone sensitive lipase and decreased lipoprotein lipase activity
Increase in peripheral function of LDL receptors
Increased in activity of hepatic lipase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increased activity of hormone sensitive lipase and decreased lipoprotein lipase activity

• Hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL): Breaks down stored triglycerides in adipose tissue into free fatty acids, which are transported to the liver. Increased HSL activity leads to more fatty acids reaching the liver, increasing VLDL synthesis.
• Lipoprotein lipase (LPL): Hydrolyzes circulating triglycerides in VLDL and chylomicrons. Decreased LPL activity impairs VLDL clearance, resulting in hypertriglyceridemia.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Increased LPL & decreased HSL: Would lower triglycerides and VLDL, opposite effect.

C. Increase in LDL receptor function: Lowers LDL cholesterol, not VLDL or TG.

D. Increased hepatic lipase: Mainly affects HDL and IDL metabolism, not primary VLDL/TG elevation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 58-year-old man with chronic liver disease presents with progressive abdominal distension and bilateral pedal edema. Laboratory evaluation is requested to assess his nutritional status and liver synthetic function. The clinician orders serum total protein and serum albumin levels. Which of the following assays is not typically used for the estimation of total serum protein?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Bromocresol green assay

Bromocresol green (BCG) is not used for estimating total serum protein. It is a dye-binding assay that specifically measures serum albumin. At an acidic pH, bromocresol green binds selectively to albumin, producing a green-colored complex whose intensity is proportional to the albumin concentration.

In contrast, total serum protein includes albumin as well as globulins, and is commonly measured using assays that detect peptide bonds or protein-dye interactions.

Other Options:

• Option A. Biuret assay: Incorrect. The Biuret method is the reference method for estimating total serum protein. Copper ions react with peptide bonds in an alkaline medium to produce a violet-colored complex.
• Option B. Bradford assay: Incorrect. The Bradford assay uses Coomassie Brilliant Blue G-250 dye, which binds to proteins and is widely used for total protein estimation, especially in research laboratories.
• Option C. Lowry's assay: Incorrect. The Lowry method combines the Biuret reaction with the reduction of the Folin-Ciocalteu reagent, making it a highly sensitive method for total protein estimation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 6-month-old girl is brought to the OPD by her mother for a check-up appointment. The mother states, "My baby doesn't seem to be growing much despite feeding as often as my previous children I'm worried that something is wrong with her." Height and weight are below the 10th percentile. Physical examination shows hepatomegaly and hypotonia. Laboratory results show hypoglycemia and ketoacidosis. Liver biopsy shows hepatic fibrosis without fat accumulation. Further analysis reveals excessive amounts of limit dextrins within the cytosol of the hepatocytes. Which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Glycogen debrancher enzyme

This 6-month-old has Cori disease (glycogen storage disease type III), suggested by hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, hypotonia, growth delay, and ketoacidosis. The liver biopsy shows excess limit dextrins—short outer branches of glycogen—because the glycogen debranching enzyme is deficient. Debranching enzyme normally allows complete glycogen breakdown by removing α-1,6-linked branches.

Why the others are incorrect:

A. Acid α-glucosidase: Deficiency causes Pompe disease, leading to lysosomal glycogen accumulation and cardiomyopathy, not cytosolic limit dextrins.

B. Glucose-6-phosphatase: Deficiency causes Von Gierke disease, with severe fasting hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, and lactic acidosis; glycogen is structurally normal.

D. Liver glycogen phosphorylase: Deficiency causes GSD type VI (Hers disease); glycogen accumulates, but limit dextrins do not.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 6-month-old infant is brought for evaluation of global developmental delay, recurrent seizures, marked hypotonia, poor visual tracking, and feeding difficulties. Physical examination reveals hepatomegaly, hyporeflexia, and characteristic craniofacial abnormalities. Laboratory and genetic testing suggest a peroxisome biogenesis disorder, resulting in defective extramitochondrial lipid metabolism. Which of the following metabolic processes is most likely impaired?
options: β-Oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids within peroxisomes
Mitochondrial β-oxidation of long-chain fatty acids via the carnitine shuttle
Oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA in mitochondria
Cytosolic synthesis of fatty acids from acetyl-CoA
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. β-Oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids within peroxisomes

This infant has features suggestive of Zellweger syndrome, the prototype peroxisome biogenesis disorder.

Key clinical clues

• Severe hypotonia ("floppy infant")
• Developmental delay
• Seizures
• Dysmorphic facial features
• Hepatomegaly
• Hyporeflexia
• Defective extramitochondrial lipid metabolism

The defect lies in the PEX genes, which are responsible for the formation and function of peroxisomes.

What do peroxisomes do?

Peroxisomes are responsible for:

• β-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs; ≥22 carbons)
• α-Oxidation of branched-chain fatty acids (e.g., phytanic acid)
• Synthesis of plasmalogens (important for myelin)
• Detoxification of hydrogen peroxide by catalase

Because VLCFAs cannot initially be degraded in mitochondria, they must first undergo β-oxidation in peroxisomes.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 6-month-old infant presents with fair skin, light-colored hair, developmental delay, and a musty odor of urine. Laboratory evaluation reveals markedly elevated phenylalanine levels. This defective enzyme is best classified as which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Monooxygenase

Phenylketonuria (PKU) is caused by deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH), an enzyme that converts phenylalanine → tyrosine.

• PAH is a monooxygenase

• It incorporates one atom of oxygen into the substrate and reduces the other to water
• Requires tetrahydrobiopterin (BH₄) as a cofactor

Clinical correlation:

• ↑ Phenylalanine → toxic to brain → developmental delay
• ↓ Tyrosine → ↓ melanin → fair skin, light hair
• Musty (mousy) odor due to phenylacetate

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 6-year-old presents with recurrent abdominal pain, hepatosplenomegaly, and eruptive xanthomas. Blood drawn after a 12-hour fast shows a creamy supernatant layer. Lipid panel shows minimal cardiovascular risk despite the severity of the lipid abnormality. Which enzyme or cofactor defect is responsible?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lipoprotein lipase or apo CII

Creamy supernatant + pancreatitis-type presentation + no increased atherosclerosis risk = Type I (hyperchylomicronemia), caused by lipoprotein lipase or apo CII deficiency, preventing chylomicron/VLDL triglyceride hydrolysis.

| Type | Defect | Atherosclerosis risk

| ---- | ------ | --------------------

| I | LPL or apo CII | No

| II | LDL receptor or apo B100 | Yes (severe)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 62-year-old man comes to the OPD due to an enlarging mole on his right forearm. Excisional biopsy is performed and histopathology reveals malignant melanoma. Immunohistochemical analysis indicates that the malignant cells have decreased integrin expression. These cells are most likely to exhibit poor adhesion to which of the following components of the extracellular matrix?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Fibronectin

Integrins are transmembrane receptors that mediate cell adhesion to extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins such as fibronectin, laminin, and collagen. Decreased integrin expression in melanoma cells reduces adhesion to fibronectin, facilitating detachment, invasion, and metastasis.

Why the others are incorrect:

A. Actin: Cytoskeletal protein inside the cell; integrins connect to actin, but actin itself is not an ECM component.

C. Hyaluronic acid: A glycosaminoglycan in ECM; adhesion involves CD44, not integrins.

D. Keratan sulfate: ECM proteoglycan; not a primary ligand for integrins in melanoma cell adhesion.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 65-year-old man presents with persistent back pain, fatigue, and recurrent respiratory infections. Laboratory investigations reveal normocytic anemia, hypercalcemia, and elevated serum creatinine. Serum protein electrophoresis shows a monoclonal spike, and urine analysis is performed to detect monoclonal light chains. On heating the urine sample, a precipitate forms at 50°C, but it disappears on further heating to 100°C and reappears upon cooling. The protein responsible for this characteristic finding is most likely:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bence Jones protein

Bence Jones proteins are free monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains (κ or λ) produced in excess by malignant plasma cells in disorders such as multiple myeloma and light-chain amyloidosis. These proteins are filtered by the kidneys and can be detected in urine.

A classic laboratory feature is their thermoreversible precipitation:

• Precipitate at 40–60°C
• Redissolve on boiling (≈100°C)
• Reprecipitate on cooling

Although this historical heat test has largely been replaced by urine immunofixation electrophoresis and serum free light-chain assays, it remains an important classic examination finding.

Other Options:

• B. Cryoglobulins: Incorrect. Cryoglobulins precipitate at low temperatures (<37°C) and dissolve on warming. They are associated with hepatitis C infection, autoimmune diseases, and lymphoproliferative disorders.
• C. Complement: Incorrect. Complement proteins are heat-labile and become irreversibly inactivated at approximately 56°C for 30 minutes. They do not show reversible precipitation.
• D. Alpha-2 macroglobulins: Incorrect. Alpha-2 macroglobulin is a large plasma protease inhibitor that does not exhibit thermoreversible precipitation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 7-year-old child was evaluated for night blindness. Ophthalmoscopy showed atrophic changes in the choroid, retina, and pigment epithelium. Urine and plasma ornithine levels were elevated. Defective catabolism of which of the following amino acids led to this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Arginine

This child has gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina, a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency of ornithine aminotransferase (OAT).

• OAT normally converts ornithine → glutamate semialdehyde (P5C).
• Deficiency of OAT leads to hyperornithinemia (high plasma and urinary ornithine).
• Excess ornithine is toxic to the retina, resulting in:

• Progressive night blindness
• Chorioretinal degeneration
• Peripheral visual field loss
• Eventual blindness if untreated

Why is Arginine the correct answer?

• Ornithine is produced from arginine in the urea cycle by the enzyme arginase.
• Therefore, defective ornithine metabolism represents impaired catabolism of arginine, since ornithine is an intermediate in arginine degradation.

Pathway:

Arginine ──(Arginase)──► Ornithine ──(Ornithine aminotransferase)──► Glutamate semialdehyde → Glutamate/Proline

When OAT is deficient, ornithine accumulates.

Why the other options are incorrect

• A. Histidine: Catabolized to glutamate; not associated with hyperornithinemia or gyrate atrophy.
• B. Glycine: Metabolized via the glycine cleavage system; defects cause nonketotic hyperglycinemia.
• C. Serine: Converted to glycine or pyruvate; not related to ornithine metabolism.

High-yield pearl

• Enzyme deficiency: Ornithine aminotransferase (OAT)
• Accumulated metabolite: Ornithine
• Clinical hallmark: Gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina with night blindness
• Treatment: Arginine-restricted diet (reduces ornithine production) and high-dose vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) in B6-responsive patients, as OAT is a pyridoxal phosphate (PLP)-dependent enzyme.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 8-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department due to vomiting and lethargy. He hasn’t eaten anything for 24 hours. On examination, the patient appears listless. Mild hepatomegaly is noted. Laboratory results are as follows: Glucose- 22mg/dl Acetoacetate – Undetected ALT-47 IU AST-50 IU Patient began seizing in the emergency. The likely deficient enzyme is ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase

This child has severe hypoglycemia with absent ketone bodies after fasting, along with vomiting, lethargy, seizures, and mild hepatomegaly—classic for fatty acid oxidation defect, most commonly medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency. In fasting states, inability to perform β-oxidation leads to failure of ketogenesis and inadequate energy production, causing hypoketotic hypoglycemia and neurologic symptoms.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase: Involved in fatty acid synthesis, not fasting metabolism.

B. Glycogen phosphorylase: Deficiency causes ketotic hypoglycemia with normal FA oxidation.

D. Glucose-6-phosphatase: Von Gierke disease shows lactic acidosis and ketosis, not absent ketones.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 9-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department with recurrent episodes of vomiting, poor feeding, increasing irritability, and intermittent lethargy. Laboratory investigations reveal marked hyperammonemia with normal blood glucose levels. Further metabolic evaluation confirms a urea cycle defect that follows an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hyperammonemia Type II

• The key clue is the inheritance pattern.
• Among the urea cycle disorders, only Ornithine Transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency is inherited as an X-linked recessive disorder.
• OTC deficiency is also known as: Hyperammonemia Type II

Why does OTC deficiency cause hyperammonemia?

OTC catalyzes the reaction: Carbamoyl phosphate + Ornithine → Citrulline

When OTC is deficient:

• Carbamoyl phosphate accumulates in mitochondria.
• Ammonia cannot be incorporated into the urea cycle.
• Blood ammonia levels rise, causing hyperammonemic encephalopathy.
• Excess carbamoyl phosphate enters the pyrimidine synthesis pathway, producing increased orotic acid in urine.

| Disorder | Enzyme Defect | Inheritance | Orotic Acid | Key Feature

| -------- | ------------- | ----------- | ----------- | -----------

| Hyperammonemia Type I | Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I | Autosomal recessive | Normal/↓ | Severe neonatal hyperammonemia

| Hyperammonemia Type II ✅ | Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) | X-linked recessive | ↑ Increased | Most common urea cycle disorder

| Citrullinemia | Argininosuccinate synthetase | Autosomal recessive | Normal | ↑ Citrulline

| Argininosuccinic aciduria | Argininosuccinate lyase | Autosomal recessive | Normal | ↑ Argininosuccinate, brittle hair

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A bacterial culture produces β-galactosidase even in absence of lactose. Which mutation is most likely?
options: Mutation in promoter region reducing RNA polymerase binding
Mutation in CAP binding site preventing cAMP activation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mutation in lacI

The lacI gene encodes the lac repressor, which normally binds the operator and prevents transcription of lac operon genes in the absence of lactose. A mutation in lacI produces a nonfunctional repressor that cannot bind the operator, resulting in constitutive expression of β-galactosidase, even without lactose.

Why other options are incorrect:

A.  Mutation in lacZ: Would reduce or abolish β-galactosidase production, not increase it.

C. Mutation in promoter region: Decreased RNA polymerase binding would reduce transcription.

D. Mutation in CAP binding site: Prevents cAMP–CAP activation, lowering transcription, especially in low glucose.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A biochemist compares elastin and collagen at the amino acid level. Which compositional feature distinguishes elastin from collagen, and what is the functional consequence of this difference?
options: Elastin is rich in hydroxylated proline and lysine, conferring rigidity; collagen lacks hydroxylation, conferring elasticity
Elastin is rich in nonhydroxylated proline, glycine, and lysine, conferring elastic stretch; collagen's hydroxylated residues support its structural/tensile rigidity
Both proteins have identical hydroxylation patterns; elasticity depends solely on cross-linking density
Elastin lacks glycine entirely, while collagen is one-third glycine by composition
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Elastin is rich in nonhydroxylated proline, glycine, and lysine, conferring elastic stretch; collagen's hydroxylated residues support its structural/tensile rigidity

Elastin is rich in nonhydroxylated proline, glycine, and lysine — contrasting with collagen's hydroxylated proline and lysine residues (hydroxylation requires vitamin C, a collagen-specific step). This compositional difference underlies elastin's stretch/recoil property versus collagen's tensile/structural strength. Cross-linking in elastin still occurs via lysyl oxidase (shared mechanism with collagen), but the absence of hydroxylation allows greater conformational flexibility.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A biochemist isolates a nascent lipoprotein particle secreted by both the liver and intestine, which subsequently acquires cholesteryl esters through the action of an enzyme requiring a cofactor found exclusively on this same particle type. Which enzyme-cofactor pairing correctly completes this maturation step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. LCAT activated by apoAI

Nascent HDL matures via LCAT, which esterifies free cholesterol to cholesteryl esters; LCAT requires apoAI as its activating cofactor, and apoAI is found exclusively on HDL particles among all the lipoproteins listed.

| Enzyme | Activating apolipoprotein | Particle specificity

| ------ | ------------------------- | --------------------

| LCAT | ApoAI | HDL only

| Lipoprotein lipase | ApoCII | Chylomicrons, VLDL

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A boy presents with intellectual disability, large ears, and macro-orchidism. CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion is found in the FMR1 gene. The transcriptional silencing results primarily from which epigenetic mechanism?
options: Loss-of-function mutation in histone acetyltransferase gene
Hypermethylation of the FMR1 promoter CpG island secondary to CGG expansion
Gain-of-function of histone deacetylase at the FMR1 locus
Deletion of H1 binding sites causing unregulated transcription
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypermethylation of the FMR1 promoter CpG island secondary to CGG expansion

200 CGG repeats in 5'-UTR of FMR1 → hypermethylation of the adjacent CpG island promoter → transcriptional silencing → loss of FMRP. This is NOT a mutation in enzymatic machinery — it is aberrant CpG methylation triggered by repeat expansion. Dysregulated DNA methylation is implicated in Fragile X syndrome.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A cancer cell line shows markedly extended survival through unlimited replication cycles without progressive shortening of chromosome ends. Expression analysis reveals upregulation of a reverse transcriptase that uses an internal RNA template. Which of the following best describes the normal regulation of this enzyme in somatic cells?
options: It is constitutively active in all somatic cells to maintain chromosomal integrity during every S phase
It is downregulated in differentiated somatic cells and upregulated in progenitor cells and cancers, adding TTAGGG repeats to 3' chromosome ends
It functions only on the leading strand, adding telomeric repeats to prevent loss from continuous 5'→3' synthesis
It is activated by DNA topoisomerase II to relieve telomeric supercoiling during end-replication
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It is downregulated in differentiated somatic cells and upregulated in progenitor cells and cancers, adding TTAGGG repeats to 3' chromosome ends

Telomerase is upregulated in progenitor cells and cancers; downregulated in aging and progeria. It is an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase (reverse transcriptase) that adds TTAGGG repeats to 3' chromosome ends — compensating for the end-replication problem (lagging strand cannot fully replicate chromosome ends). Its suppression in somatic cells = progressive telomere shortening = cellular aging.

| Context | Telomerase activity | Consequence

| ------- | ------------------- | -----------

| Progenitor/stem cells | High | Telomere length maintained

| Differentiated somatic cells | Low/absent | Progressive shortening → senescence

| Cancer cells | Upregulated | Unlimited replication — immortality

| Aging/progeria | Downregulated | Accelerated telomere loss

| Repeat added | TTAGGG (3' end) | Protects coding DNA

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A chemotherapy drug blocks de novo pyrimidine synthesis by inhibiting carbamoyl phosphate incorporation. Which observation about pyrimidine ring construction, as distinct from purine ring synthesis, makes this a plausible mechanism?
options: Pyrimidines use Glycine and Glutamine as precursors, which are blocked by the drug
The pyrimidine ring is built on ribose-5-phosphate first, then the ring is assembled on the sugar
Carbamoyl phosphate and aspartate contribute directly to the pyrimidine ring, which is assembled before attachment to ribose
Purines and pyrimidines share an identical biosynthetic pathway, making the drug non-selective
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Carbamoyl phosphate and aspartate contribute directly to the pyrimidine ring, which is assembled before attachment to ribose

Key distinction:

• Purines are built directly on ribose-5-phosphate (base assembled on sugar).
• Pyrimidines — the ring is assembled first (carbamoyl phosphate + aspartate form the ring), then attached to ribose-5-phosphate.
• Carbamoyl phosphate contributes C2 and N3 of the pyrimidine ring.
• Blocking this step prevents all pyrimidine synthesis (C, U, T).

| Feature | Purine synthesis | Pyrimidine synthesis

| ------- | ---------------- | --------------------

| Ring assembly | On ribose-5-P (base built on sugar) | Ring built first, then attached to sugar

| Key precursors | Gly, Asp, Gln, CO₂, THF | Carbamoyl phosphate, Aspartate

| First committed product | IMP | UMP

| Thymine synthesis | — | Methylation of dUMP → dTMP (by thymidylate synthase)

| Drug targets | PRPP amidotransferase (azathioprine) | Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (leflunomide)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child presents with coarse facial features, gingival hyperplasia, corneal clouding, and claw hand deformities. Laboratory analysis shows markedly elevated plasma lysosomal enzyme levels but enzyme deficiency within fibroblast lysosomes. Which step in the protein trafficking pathway is most directly defective?
options: COPII-mediated transport from ER to cis-Golgi
Phosphorylation of mannose residues on glycoproteins in the Golgi
SRP-mediated targeting of the polypeptide-ribosome complex to RER
Clathrin-mediated transport from trans-Golgi to lysosomes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Phosphorylation of mannose residues on glycoproteins in the Golgi
