I-cell disease: defect in N-acetylglucosaminyl-1-phosphotransferase → failure to phosphorylate mannose residues → ↓ mannose-6-phosphate tag → lysosomal enzymes are not recognized for lysosomal delivery → secreted extracellularly instead → ↑ plasma lysosomal enzyme levels (paradoxically) while lysosomes themselves are enzyme-deficient → cellular debris accumulates (inclusion bodies).

| Step | Normal | I-cell disease

| ---- | ------ | --------------

| Mannose phosphorylation | Occurs in Golgi | Absent

| Mannose-6-phosphate tag | Present | Absent

| Enzyme destination | Lysosome | Secreted extracellularly

| Plasma enzyme levels | Normal | ↑↑

| Lysosomal enzyme content | Normal | Deficient

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child presents with hepatomegaly, severe fasting hypoglycemia, and lactic acidosis. Enzyme assay shows absent glucose-6-phosphatase activity. Which two separate metabolic processes converge at this single enzymatic step, both becoming nonfunctional as a source of free glucose?
options: The urea cycle and heme synthesis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis

Glucose-6-phosphatase (deficient in von Gierke disease) sits at the convergence point where glycogenolysis (breakdown of glycogen → glucose-1-phosphate → glucose-6-phosphate) and gluconeogenesis (synthesis from non-carbohydrate precursors, ultimately producing glucose-6-phosphate) both require this single enzyme to release free glucose into circulation. Its absence means neither stored glycogen nor newly synthesized glucose-6-phosphate can be converted to usable free glucose — explaining the severe fasting hypoglycemia despite intact upstream pathways, along with secondary lactic acidosis from accumulated glycolytic intermediates being shunted elsewhere.

| Pathway | Product requiring glucose-6-phosphatase

| ------- | ---------------------------------------

| Glycogenolysis | Glucose-6-phosphate → free glucose

| Gluconeogenesis | Glucose-6-phosphate → free glucose

| Deficiency | Von Gierke disease (Type I glycogen storage disease)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child presents with hyperphagia, obesity, hypogonadism, and intellectual disability. Genetic testing shows that the paternal copy of a specific region on chromosome 15 has been deleted. Which mechanism explains why deletion of the paternal (rather than maternal) copy causes disease in this specific condition?
options: The maternal copy of this region is normally silenced by imprinting, so the paternal copy is the only one normally expressed
The maternal copy is deleted in this condition, not the paternal copy, making this scenario inconsistent with Prader-Willi syndrome
Both maternal and paternal copies are normally expressed equally, so either deletion would cause identical disease severity
The paternal copy is normally silenced, so its deletion has no clinical consequence
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. The maternal copy of this region is normally silenced by imprinting, so the paternal copy is the only one normally expressed

In Prader-Willi syndrome, maternally derived genes at this locus are normally silenced by imprinting — only the paternal copy is normally expressed. Therefore, deletion or mutation of the paternal allele leaves no functional gene product at all (since the maternal copy was never going to be expressed regardless), causing the disease phenotype (mnemonic: POP — Prader-Willi, Obesity, Paternal allele deleted).

| Feature | Prader-Willi syndrome

| ------- | ---------------------

| Silenced parental copy | Maternal

| Expressed parental copy | Paternal

| Disease-causing event | Paternal allele deleted/mutated

| UPD contribution | 25% of cases — maternal uniparental disomy

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child presents with thinning of hair and scaling of the scalp. On taking further history, it is found that she consumes raw eggs in her diet regularly. The given manifestations are due to the defect in which of the following reactions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pyruvate carboxylase

This child is likely suffering from biotin deficiency due to avidin in raw egg whites binding biotin. Biotin is a cofactor for carboxylase enzymes, including pyruvate carboxylase, which catalyzes pyruvate → oxaloacetate in gluconeogenesis. Deficiency leads to impaired gluconeogenesis, metabolic acidosis, thinning hair, and dermatitis (scaling of scalp).

Why other options are incorrect:

B. Pyruvate dehydrogenase: Thiamine and lipoic acid–dependent; not affected by biotin.

C. Glycogen phosphorylase: Vitamin B6–dependent; unrelated to biotin deficiency.

D. Glutathione reductase: FAD-dependent; not affected by biotin deficiency.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child with autosomal recessive impairment of neutral amino acid transport in proximal renal tubular cells and enterocytes develops a photosensitive rash, diarrhea, and dementia. Direct supplementation with the deficient vitamin is initiated as treatment. Which vitamin is this, and why does dietary protein alone fail to fully correct the deficiency in this specific disorder?
options: Vitamin B2; riboflavin absorption is independently impaired by the same transporter defect

Vitamin B3; tryptophan (its precursor) cannot be adequately absorbed from the gut or reabsorbed renally due to the transporter defect, limiting endogenous niacin synthesis regardless of dietary protein intake
Vitamin B6; pyridoxine absorption requires the same transporter affected in this disease
Vitamin B5; pantothenic acid synthesis depends on tryptophan transport in enterocytes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin B3; tryptophan (its precursor) cannot be adequately absorbed from the gut or reabsorbed renally due to the transporter defect, limiting endogenous niacin synthesis regardless of dietary protein intake

This describes Hartnup disease — autosomal recessive deficiency of neutral amino acid transporters (including tryptophan) in proximal renal tubules and enterocytes → neutral aminoaciduria and ↓gut absorption → ↓tryptophan available for niacin (B3) synthesis → pellagra-like symptoms despite adequate dietary protein, because the defect is in transport, not digestion — so increasing dietary protein doesn't bypass the transporter defect; direct nicotinic acid (B3) supplementation is required.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A chronic alcoholic patient initially presents with confusion, nystagmus, and ataxia, treated successfully with thiamine. Months later, he develops permanent memory loss with confabulation and personality changes, though his acute neurologic symptoms have resolved. Which anatomic structures were damaged to produce this delayed presentation, and what is this specific permanent disorder called?
options: Mammillary bodies and medial dorsal thalamic nucleus; Korsakoff syndrome
Mammillary bodies only; reversible Wernicke encephalopathy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mammillary bodies and medial dorsal thalamic nucleus; Korsakoff syndrome

Korsakoff syndrome = amnestic disorder from chronic alcohol overuse, caused by damage to the medial dorsal nucleus of the thalamus and mammillary bodies — presenting with confabulation, personality changes, and permanent memory loss. This is distinct from the acute, reversible Wernicke encephalopathy (confusion, ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus, ataxia) that may precede it; together they form Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome when both components are present.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A coding DNA triplet GAG is altered by a single nucleotide substitution at the second position, changing G to T, producing GTG. The mRNA codon becomes GUG, coding for valine instead of glutamic acid. Which classification of point mutation does this represent, and what type of base change occurred?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Missense mutation; transversion (purine to pyrimidine)

• GAG → GTG: amino acid changes from Glu to Val = missense.
• Base change: G (purine) → T (pyrimidine) = transversion.
• This is the exact molecular lesion of sickle cell disease (β-globin gene, codon 6).

| Mutation type | Definition | Example

| ------------- | ---------- | -------

| Silent | Same amino acid encoded | GAG→GAA (both Glu)

| Missense | Different amino acid | GAG→GTG (Glu→Val) — sickle cell

| Nonsense | Premature stop codon | GAG→TAG (Glu→Stop)

| Transition | Purine↔purine or pyrimidine↔pyrimidine | A↔G, C↔T

| Transversion | Purine↔pyrimidine | A↔T, A↔C, G↔T, G↔C

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A codon in an mRNA reads 5'-CCU-3' specifying proline. A point mutation changes position 3 from U to C, producing 5'-CCC-3'. Which property of the genetic code explains why this mutation produces no change in the encoded protein?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. The code is degenerate

Degeneracy + wobble hypothesis: first 2 positions essential; 3rd position (wobble) can vary. CCU and CCC both encode proline. The mutation is synonymous/silent. Methionine (AUG) and tryptophan (UGG) are the only amino acids with a single codon — no wobble flexibility.

| Code property | Definition | Exception

| ------------- | ---------- | ---------

| Unambiguous | 1 codon → 1 amino acid only | None

| Degenerate | 1 amino acid → multiple codons | Met, Trp (1 codon each)

| Wobble | Position 3 variability tolerated | Met (AUG), Trp (UGG)

| Commaless | Read continuously, no punctuation | Some viruses

| Universal | Same code across species | Human mitochondria

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A dermatology researcher is studying the role of different amino acids in wound healing. She cultures mature dermal fibroblasts in growth media. After several days, the fibroblasts begin synthesizing polypeptide chains that assemble into triple helical structures, followed by fibrils. The fibrillar proteins are hydrolyzed and separated into their constituent amino acids via paper chromatography. Which of the following amino acids is most likely to be found in the highest quantity in these proteins?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. GIycine

The question describes collagen synthesis (triple helix → fibrils), the main protein produced by dermal fibroblasts during wound healing.

• Collagen structure:

• Repeating sequence: Gly–X–Y
• X and Y are often proline and hydroxyproline

• Why glycine is highest:

• Present at every third position
• Smallest amino acid → allows tight packing of triple helix
• Accounts for \~33% of collagen amino acids

• Other important components:

• Proline & hydroxyproline → provide structural stability
• Vitamin C required for hydroxylation (deficiency → scurvy)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A diabetic man takes his insulin bolus and then takes his meal. This would cause activation of all of the following enzymes, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase

After insulin bolus and a meal, the body is in a fed state, promoting anabolic pathways:

• Phosphofructokinase: Activated by insulin → stimulates glycolysis.
• Glycogen synthase: Activated by insulin → promotes glycogen synthesis.
• Acetyl-CoA carboxylase: Activated by insulin → promotes fatty acid synthesis.
• PEPCK: A key gluconeogenic enzyme, which is inhibited by insulin because gluconeogenesis is suppressed in the fed state.

Why other options are incorrect:

• PFK, glycogen synthase, and ACC are all upregulated/activated by insulin to store glucose and energy.
• Only PEPCK is downregulated to prevent glucose production when exogenous glucose is available.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A drug developer wants to lower serum LDL by preventing a specific receptor from being degraded after it has delivered its cargo into the hepatocyte. Which target should the drug inhibit?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. PCSK9

PCSK9 normally degrades the LDL receptor after it has been internalized, preventing its recycling back to the cell surface. Inhibiting PCSK9 increases LDL receptor recycling, enhancing hepatic LDL clearance and lowering serum LDL.

| Enzyme | Effect | Therapeutic relevance

| ------ | ------ | ---------------------

| PCSK9 | Degrades LDL receptor | Inhibition → ↓serum LDL

| CETP | Transfers cholesteryl esters between particles | Different mechanism

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A eukaryotic cell is exposed to a toxin that selectively inhibits a nuclear enzyme without directly affecting ribosomal activity, peptide bond formation, or tRNA charging. Protein synthesis is secondarily affected due to lack of mRNA production. Which of the following enzymes is most likely inhibited?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. RNA polymerase

Protein synthesis depends on mRNA production (transcription) before translation can occur.

• RNA polymerase (in nucleus):

• Synthesizes mRNA from DNA template
• In eukaryotes:

• RNA Pol II → mRNA

• Inhibition → no mRNA → translation cannot proceed

• Key concept in the question:

• Ribosomes, peptide bond formation, and tRNA charging are intact
• Therefore, defect must be upstream → transcription

• Why others are incorrect:

• Peptidyl transferase → translation step (ribosome)
• Aminoacyl tRNA synthetase → tRNA charging
• rRNA → structural component, not enzyme inhibited here

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A gene-rich region with repeated CG dinucleotide sequences adopts an alternating purine–pyrimidine structure. This form of DNA is often associated with transcriptional regulation and is stabilized during negative supercoiling. Which DNA form is this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Z-DNA

Z-DNA is a left-handed DNA helix formed in gene-rich regions containing alternating purine–pyrimidine sequences, classically CG repeats. It is stabilized by negative supercoiling and is often found near actively transcribed genes, where it plays a role in transcriptional regulation and chromatin remodeling. Its zig-zag sugar-phosphate backbone gives it the characteristic “Z” shape.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. A-DNA: Right-handed helix seen in dehydrated DNA and RNA–DNA hybrids.

B. B-DNA: Normal right-handed DNA form, lacks alternating CG zig-zag structure.

D. C-DNA: Not a biologically relevant or well-defined DNA conformation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A geneticist analyzes a Southern blot pedigree showing two unaffected heterozygous parents, one affected homozygous mutant child, one heterozygous unaffected child, and one homozygous normal child. Which inheritance pattern is most consistent with this pattern, and what molecular principle does the Southern blot directly visualize to determine each individual's genotype?
options: Autosomal dominant; blot visualizes RNA splicing patterns
Autosomal recessive; blot visualizes DNA fragment size via labeled probe hybridization to complementary sequences
X-linked recessive; blot visualizes protein quantity via antibody binding
Autosomal recessive; blot visualizes mRNA expression levels reflecting gene activity
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Autosomal recessive; blot visualizes DNA fragment size via labeled probe hybridization to complementary sequences

Two unaffected heterozygous parents (Aa × Aa) producing an affected homozygous child (aa) = classic autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. Southern blot specifically visualizes DNA — cleaved fragments separated by electrophoresis, transferred to a membrane, and detected via a labeled probe that hybridizes to its complementary DNA sequence — distinguishing genotypes (AA, Aa, aa) by fragment size/banding pattern.

| Blot type | Sample analyzed | Detection method | Use

| --------- | --------------- | ---------------- | ---

| Southern | DNA | Labeled DNA probe (complementary hybridization) | Genotyping, FMR1 CGG repeat count

| Northern | RNA | Similar probe hybridization | mRNA levels, splicing errors

| Western | Protein | Labeled antibody | Protein identification/quantity

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A geneticist studies two mature mRNAs derived from the same heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA). Both encode different proteins despite originating from an identical primary transcript. Which mechanism best explains this observation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Alternative splicing

Alternative splicing is a post-transcriptional process in which different combinations of exons from the same pre-mRNA (hnRNA) are joined together to generate multiple mature mRNA transcripts. As a result, a single gene can produce multiple protein isoforms, significantly increasing protein diversity without increasing the number of genes.

This mechanism is especially common in eukaryotes and is regulated in a tissue-specific and developmental stage-specific manner.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Promoter mutation: Alters the rate or site of transcription initiation but does not produce multiple mRNAs from the same hnRNA.
• C. DNA methylation: An epigenetic modification that regulates gene expression by affecting transcription, not mRNA splicing.
• D. Polyadenylation: Adds a poly(A) tail to the 3′ end of mRNA, improving stability and translation efficiency. It does not typically generate different protein products from the same transcript.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A group of investigators are studying the regulation of catecholamine synthesis in response to severe stress. In the experiments, subject rats are randomly assigned to either an experimental or a control group. The experimental rats undergo resection of the pituitary gland, and the control rats undergo craniotomy without pituitary resection. The experimental animals are subsequently found to have decreased production of epinephrine by the adrenal medulla and cortisol from the adrenal cortex compared with the control animals. Decrease d activity of which of the following enzymes is most likely responsible for the lower epinephrine in the experimental animals?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Phenyl ethanolamine-N-methyltransferase

The pituitary gland produces ACTH, which stimulates the adrenal cortex to release cortisol. Cortisol, in turn, enters the adrenal medulla and induces PNMT, the enzyme that converts norepinephrine to epinephrine. Pituitary resection reduces ACTH → lower cortisol → decreased PNMT activity → reduced epinephrine synthesis.

Why the others are incorrect:

A. Catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT): Inactivates catecholamines by methylation; not involved in epinephrine synthesis.

C. Dopamine β-hydroxylase: Converts dopamine to norepinephrine; norepinephrine can still be made, but conversion to epinephrine is impaired in this experiment.

D. Monoamine oxidase (MAO): Degrades catecholamines; its activity does not regulate synthesis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A man is rescued from a house fire, unconscious, with cherry-red skin discoloration, severe lactic acidosis, and a faint bitter-almond odor on his breath despite a normal arterial oxygen saturation. Biochemical studies show blockade of electron transfer at the terminal enzyme of the electron transport chain, with the offending agent(s) binding at a site distinct from the enzyme's natural substrate-binding site. If the kinetics of this enzyme were plotted as a Lineweaver–Burk plot in the presence versus absence of the offending agent(s), which of the following would be observed?
options: Lines intersect on the y-axis, with a common y-intercept but different x-intercepts
Lines intersect on the x-axis, with a common x-intercept but different y-intercepts
Lines are parallel, with both intercepts shifted proportionally
Lines intersect at the origin, with unchanged Vmax and Km
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lines intersect on the x-axis, with a common x-intercept but different y-intercepts

| Step | Reasoning

| ---- | ---------

| Clinical inference | Smoke inhalation → combined CO and cyanide toxicity (synthetic material combustion releases cyanide); cherry-red skin + lactic acidosis + bitter-almond odor + normal SaO2 (tissue hypoxia despite adequate oxygenation)

| Enzyme targeted | Cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV) — terminal enzyme of ETC

| Type of inhibition | Noncompetitive — inhibitor binds a site other than the substrate (O2/electron)-binding site; does not compete with substrate

| Effect on Km | Unchanged — inhibitor does not affect substrate affinity → x-intercept (−1/Km) stays the same

| Effect on Vmax | Decreased — fewer active enzyme molecules functionally available → y-intercept (1/Vmax) increases

| LB plot pattern | Lines share the same x-intercept but diverge in y-intercept → intersect on the x-axis

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A marathon runner is performing prolonged, high-intensity exercise. Skeletal muscle cells exhibit accelerated glycolysis, low intracellular ATP levels, and increased production of alanine, which is released into the bloodstream. Which of the following best describes the regulation of pyruvate kinase under these conditions, and what is the significance of alanine release?
options: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate inhibits pyruvate kinase; alanine release indicates pyruvate is being preferentially shunted into the TCA cycle

Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate stimulates pyruvate kinase (feedforward activation); concurrently, alanine (itself an inhibitor of pyruvate kinase under different conditions) is being generated from pyruvate via transamination, contributing to the Cori cycle
ATP depletion alone activates pyruvate kinase regardless of fructose-1,6-bisphosphate levels
Glucagon and epinephrine directly activate pyruvate kinase during anaerobic exercise, overriding all other regulatory inputs
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate stimulates pyruvate kinase (feedforward activation); concurrently, alanine (itself an inhibitor of pyruvate kinase under different conditions) is being generated from pyruvate via transamination, contributing to the Cori cycle

Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate stimulates pyruvate kinase (feedforward activation, ensuring downstream glycolytic flux keeps pace with upstream flux during high glycolytic demand). Separately, alanine is a known inhibitor of pyruvate kinase under different physiologic conditions (e.g., fasting, where alanine signals amino acid-derived gluconeogenic substrate availability) — but here, alanine is being actively generated from pyruvate via transamination in muscle, exported to the liver as part of the alanine cycle (analogous to the Cori cycle with lactate), supporting hepatic gluconeogenesis during intense exercise.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A microbiologist performs a genetic experiment in which cultures of Escherichia coli are treated with a chemical that induces a high frequency of mutations. Individual bacterial colonies are isolated to identify a mutant strain that lacks a specific enzyme involved in DNA replication. This specific enzyme is responsible for removing short fragments of RNA that are base paired to the DNA template. Which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient in this strain of E coli?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. DNA polymerase I

In E. coli, DNA polymerase I has both polymerase and 5′→3′ exonuclease activity, allowing it to remove RNA primers from Okazaki fragments and replace them with DNA during replication. A deficiency in this enzyme prevents proper removal of RNA primers, leading to incomplete lagging-strand synthesis.

Why the others are incorrect:

B. DNA polymerase III: Main enzyme for DNA elongation but cannot remove RNA primers.

C. Gyrase: Relieves supercoiling ahead of the replication fork; unrelated to primer removal.

D. Primase: Synthesizes RNA primers but does not remove them.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A molecular biologist is investigating whether a specific transcription factor binds to the promoter region of a target gene in living cells. The researcher uses a technique that cross-links proteins to DNA, immunoprecipitates the protein of interest with a specific antibody, and then identifies the associated DNA sequences. This technique is primarily used to study which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Protein–DNA interactions

Chromatin Immunoprecipitation (ChIP) is a molecular biology technique used to determine whether a specific protein is bound to a particular region of DNA inside living cells.

It is widely used to study:

• Transcription factor binding
• Histone modifications
• Chromatin remodeling proteins
• Epigenetic regulation of gene expression

| Technique | Studies

| --------- | -------

| ChIP | Protein–DNA interactions ✅

| ChIP-seq | Genome-wide protein-binding sites

| RIP | RNA–protein interactions

| CLIP | RNA–protein interactions with nucleotide-level resolution

| DRIP | DNA–RNA hybrids (R-loops)

| 3C / Hi-C | DNA–DNA interactions (chromatin architecture)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A molecular biologist is preparing to amplify a specific DNA segment using an enzyme catalysed thermocycler-based reaction. Which of the following components if not included in reaction mixture will not affect the amplification process?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. DNA ligase

In PCR (polymerase chain reaction), amplification requires Taq polymerase, DNA primers, Mg²⁺ ions, and dNTPs. DNA ligase is not required, because PCR synthesizes new DNA strands without joining separate DNA fragments; ligase only seals nicks in DNA, which is unnecessary for standard PCR amplification.

Why the others are incorrect:

B.Taq polymerase: Catalyzes DNA synthesis; without it, no amplification occurs.

C. DNA primers & Mg²⁺ ions: Primers provide initiation sites for polymerase; Mg²⁺ is a cofactor essential for enzyme activity.

D. dNTPs: Serve as building blocks for new DNA strands; omission halts synthesis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A molecular biologist is working on isolating a specific gene within a large DNA fragment ranging from 50 to 100 kilobases (KB) in length. Which technique is most suitable for this purpose?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Chromosome walking

Chromosome walking is a technique used to isolate and sequence a gene within large DNA fragments (tens to hundreds of kilobases). It involves progressive cloning and sequencing of overlapping DNA fragments starting from a known marker or sequence, allowing researchers to “walk” along the chromosome to reach the gene of interest.

Why the others are incorrect:

A. Notch: Not a DNA isolation method; it refers to a signaling pathway or gene.

B. RFLP (Restriction Fragment Length Polymorphism): Detects DNA polymorphisms but is not a method for isolating large genes.

C. SSLP (Simple Sequence Length Polymorphism): Used for genetic mapping; it does not help clone long DNA sequences.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A molecular biology lab synthesizes an oligonucleotide in which uracil replaces thymine throughout. In which of the following clinical/biological contexts would this substitution be least disruptive to function?
options: As a template strand for DNA replication in a mammalian cell
As an mRNA molecule to be translated at the ribosome
As a primer for DNA polymerase in PCR amplification
As a component of a nucleosome-associated chromatin fiber
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. As an mRNA molecule to be translated at the ribosome

Uracil is the normal base in RNA — mRNA uses U instead of T. Translation at the ribosome reads codons on mRNA; ribosomes recognize U-containing codons perfectly (UUU = Phe, etc.). In DNA contexts (options A, C, D), uracil is aberrant — uracil-DNA glycosylase would flag and excise it (option A/C), and nucleosomal DNA is double-stranded DNA requiring thymine (option D). Mitochondrial DNA uses standard bases but does not use histones.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A mutation from GCCACCATGG to GCCACCCTGG leads to decreased protein translation without affecting mRNA level. Which step is impaired?
options: Ribosome scanning and start codon recognition
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ribosome scanning and start codon recognition

(Kozak sequence → important for AUG recognition)

The sequence GCCACCATGG represents the Kozak consensus sequence, which is critical for efficient ribosomal recognition of the AUG start codon during translation initiation. The mutation to GCCACCCTGG disrupts the AUG start codon context, impairing ribosome scanning and start codon recognition. As a result, translation efficiency decreases, even though mRNA levels remain normal, indicating a post-transcriptional defect.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. RNA polymerase binding: Would affect transcription and mRNA levels, not translation alone.

C. 5’ capping: Required for mRNA stability and ribosome binding; defects reduce mRNA levels.

D. Polyadenylation: Affects mRNA stability and nuclear export, also reducing mRNA levels

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A mutation in a non-coding DNA sequence is believed to affect expression of the gene coding for a specific fetal enzyme. Liver and bone marrow cells from the fetus and his parents are obtained. Which of the following is the best method to determine if this gene is being transcribed in cultures of the isolated cells?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Northern blot

Northern blotting detects specific RNA transcripts, allowing measurement of gene expression at the transcriptional level. In this case, it can determine whether the fetal enzyme gene is being transcribed in liver or bone marrow cells. It distinguishes mRNA presence, size, and relative abundance.

Why other options are incorrect:

B. Western blot: Detects protein, not transcription; post-transcriptional or translational changes could confound results.

C. Southern blot: Detects DNA sequences, used for identifying gene presence or mutations, not transcription.

D. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA): Measures protein concentration, not RNA expression.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A neonate is found to have severe combined immunodeficiency. Genetic workup reveals autosomal recessive inheritance. Metabolic analysis shows accumulation of a deoxyribonucleoside that halts DNA synthesis in lymphocytes. Which sequence of events is directly responsible?
options: Absent HGPRT → ↑ PRPP → ↑ IMP → ↑ AMP → ↑ dATP → ribonucleotide reductase inhibited
Absent ADA → deoxyadenosine accumulates → ↑ dATP → ribonucleotide reductase inhibited → ↓ DNA precursors → lymphocyte death
Absent APRT → adenine accumulates → converted to 2,8-dihydroxyadenine → toxic to lymphocyte nuclei
Absent adenosine kinase → adenosine cannot be phosphorylated → ATP pool depleted → lymphocyte apoptosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Absent ADA → deoxyadenosine accumulates → ↑ dATP → ribonucleotide reductase inhibited → ↓ DNA precursors → lymphocyte death

↓ADA → ↑dATP → ↓ribonucleotide reductase → ↓DNA precursors → ↓lymphocytes — Autosomal recessive SCID.

| Step | Consequence

| ---- | -----------

| ADA absent | Adenosine/deoxyadenosine not degraded

| deoxyadenosine → dATP | Phosphorylated in lymphocytes

| dATP ↑ | Inhibits ribonucleotide reductase

| All dNTPs ↓ | DNA synthesis halted

| Lymphocyte outcome | Apoptosis → SCID

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A neonate presents with hyperammonemia, and metabolic workup shows elevated orotic acid in the urine alongside low blood urea nitrogen. Which urea cycle enzyme deficiency is most consistent with this combination, and what is the precise biochemical link explaining the orotic aciduria in this specific context?
options: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I deficiency; excess carbamoyl phosphate is shunted to cytosolic pyrimidine synthesis, elevating orotic acid
Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency; carbamoyl phosphate accumulates in mitochondria and leaks into cytosol, entering the pyrimidine synthesis pathway and elevating orotic acid
Argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency; citrulline accumulation directly converts to orotic acid via an alternate pathway
Arginase deficiency; excess arginine is directly converted to orotic acid in the cytosol
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency; carbamoyl phosphate accumulates in mitochondria and leaks into cytosol, entering the pyrimidine synthesis pathway and elevating orotic acid

Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency (X-linked) blocks the conversion of carbamoyl phosphate to citrulline within mitochondria, causing carbamoyl phosphate to accumulate and leak into the cytosol, where it enters the pyrimidine synthesis pathway (via CPS II-independent carbamoyl phosphate availability), producing excess orotic acid. This is the key distinguishing feature from CPS I deficiency, which would NOT cause orotic aciduria, since CPS I deficiency means no excess carbamoyl phosphate is generated in the first place — there is nothing to leak into the cytosol.

| Urea cycle defect | Orotic aciduria? | Reasoning

| ----------------- | ---------------- | ---------

| CPS I deficiency | No | No excess carbamoyl phosphate produced

| OTC deficiency | Yes | Excess carbamoyl phosphate leaks to cytosol → pyrimidine pathway

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A neonate with poor feeding, lethargy, seizures, and a burnt-sugar odor in urine is diagnosed with Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD). Plasma amino acid profile shows markedly elevated leucine, valine, and isoleucine. Which amino acid is primarily responsible for the severe neurologic manifestations and cerebral edema seen in MSUD?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Leucine

• Leucine is the most neurotoxic branched-chain amino acid.
• Rapidly crosses BBB via LAT1 transporter.
• Inhibits oxidative phosphorylation → ↓ ATP → Na⁺/K⁺ pump failure → cytotoxic edema.
• Correlates directly with seizures, coma, and brain damage in MSUD.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A neutrophil undergoing a respiratory burst to kill phagocytosed bacteria requires a continuous supply of reducing equivalents for NADPH oxidase activity. Which metabolic pathway directly regenerates this NADPH, and which of the listed processes shares this same cofactor dependency despite serving an entirely different physiologic purpose?
options: Glycolysis regenerates NADPH; shared by the citric acid cycle
HMP shunt regenerates NADPH; shared by the cytochrome P-450 detoxification system and glutathione reductase
Beta-oxidation regenerates NADPH; shared by oxidative phosphorylation
Gluconeogenesis regenerates NADPH; shared by ketogenesis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. HMP shunt regenerates NADPH; shared by the cytochrome P-450 detoxification system and glutathione reductase

NADPH is a direct product of the HMP shunt. Beyond respiratory burst (NADPH oxidase in phagocytes), NADPH is also required by the cytochrome P-450 system (drug/toxin metabolism) and glutathione reductase (regenerating reduced glutathione for antioxidant defense) — three mechanistically unrelated physiologic functions unified by their shared dependence on this single reducing cofactor pool.

| NADPH-dependent process | Physiologic role

| ----------------------- | ----------------

| Anabolic processes (steroid/fatty acid synthesis) | Biosynthesis

| Respiratory burst | Microbial killing (NADPH oxidase)

| Cytochrome P-450 system | Drug/toxin detoxification

| Glutathione reductase | Antioxidant defense (regenerates GSH)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A newborn presents with dysmorphic facial features, hypotonia, and developmental delay. A chromosomal abnormality is suspected, and the clinician plans appropriate genetic investigations. Which of the following techniques is most appropriate for detecting this abnormality?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Karyotyping

Suspected chromosomal abnormalities (e.g., aneuploidy, large deletions/duplications) are best detected by karyotyping.

• Karyotyping:

• Visualizes entire chromosomes under microscopy
• Detects numerical abnormalities (e.g., trisomy 21)
• Detects large structural changes (translocations, inversions)

• Clinical clues for chromosomal disorders:

• Dysmorphic features
• Hypotonia
• Developmental delay

• Why other techniques are incorrect:

• DGGE / SSCP → detect small mutations (point mutations)
• Sanger sequencing → detects base-level changes, not large chromosomal abnormalities

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A newborn presents with hypotonia, seizures, jaundice, and craniofacial dysmorphism. Biochemical analysis reveals accumulation of pipecolic acid. Which organelle's biogenesis defect explains this presentation, and what is the inheritance pattern?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Peroxisome; autosomal recessive

Zellweger syndrome = autosomal recessive disorder of peroxisome biogenesis due to mutated PEX genes → accumulation of pipecolic acid. Distinguished from adrenoleukodystrophy (X-linked recessive, ABCD1 mutation, VLCFA accumulation specifically) and Refsum disease (autosomal recessive but specifically affects α-oxidation, causing phytanic acid buildup).

| Disorder | Defect | Inheritance | Accumulated substance

| -------- | ------ | ----------- | ---------------------

| Zellweger syndrome | Peroxisome biogenesis (PEX genes) | Autosomal recessive | Pipecolic acid

| Refsum disease | α-oxidation | Autosomal recessive | Phytanic acid

| Adrenoleukodystrophy | β-oxidation (ABCD1) | X-linked recessive | VLCFA

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A newborn presents with intractable seizures, severe neurological deterioration, and elevated sulfite levels in urine. Xanthine and hypoxanthine are also markedly increased. Deficiency of which metal-dependent enzyme MOST likely explains the findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Molybdenum-dependent sulfite oxidase

This presentation fits molybdenum cofactor deficiency, causing combined deficiency of sulfite oxidase and xanthine oxidase.

Sulfite oxidase failure → ↑ urinary sulfite with severe neonatal encephalopathy, intractable seizures, and rapid neurodegeneration.

Xanthine oxidase failure → ↑ xanthine and hypoxanthine (often with low uric acid). Thus the key impaired metal-dependent enzyme is molybdenum-dependent sulfite oxidase.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Iron-dependent succinate dehydrogenase: SDH defect causes mitochondrial myopathy/lactic acidosis, not sulfite/xanthine rise.

B. Copper-dependent cytochrome oxidase: Cytochrome oxidase defects cause oxidative phosphorylation failure, not sulfite.

D. Manganese-dependent enolase: Enolase issues affect glycolysis, not these metabolites.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient develops a disease due to defective assembly of small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs). Which step of gene expression is directly affected first?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pre-mRNA processing

• snRNPs combine with proteins to form the spliceosome, whose function is removal of introns from pre-mRNA.
• Therefore the earliest affected step is: Pre-mRNA → Mature mRNA

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient has a rare congenital defect affecting the enzyme responsible for matching amino acids to their correct tRNA. Which structural feature of tRNA is recognized by this enzyme for proper identification?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. D-arm

D-arm contains dihydrouridine residues necessary for recognition by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase ("D-arm allows Detection"). T-arm is for ribosome binding; CCA tail is the amino acid attachment site; anticodon loop pairs with mRNA codon, not synthetase recognition.

| tRNA region | Function

| ----------- | --------

| D-arm | Synthetase recognition

| T-arm | Ribosome binding (TΨC)

| Anticodon loop | Codon pairing

| CCA (3') | Amino acid attachment

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient in severe DKA has a strongly positive urine ketone dipstick and a fruity breath odor, yet his serum β-hydroxybutyrate (measured by a separate lab assay) is far higher than the dipstick result would suggest. Which pairing of facts about ketone body chemistry explains both observations?
options: The dipstick reaction specifically detects acetoacetate and underrepresents β-hydroxybutyrate, the fruity odor comes from acetone
The dipstick detects β-hydroxybutyrate exclusively, and the fruity odor is caused by acetoacetate crossing into exhaled breath
Both ketone bodies are detected equally by dipstick; the fruity odor is unrelated to ketone chemistry and instead reflects co-existing fasting halitosis
The dipstick measures total serum pH rather than any specific ketone, explaining the discrepancy with the serum β-hydroxybutyrate assay
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. The dipstick reaction specifically detects acetoacetate and underrepresents β-hydroxybutyrate, the fruity odor comes from acetone

This is a frequently missed clinical pitfall: a "mild" urine ketone result on dipstick can coexist with severe ketoacidosis if β-hydroxybutyrate (not measured by standard dipstick) predominates. The fruity odor is from acetone, a true volatile ketone (not a ketoacid like the other two), explaining why it's detected by smell/breath rather than urine testing.

| Ketone body | Class | Detected by urine dipstick | Detected by breath

| ----------- | ----- | -------------------------- | ------------------

| Acetoacetate | Ketoacid | Yes | No

| β-hydroxybutyrate | Ketoacid | No | No

| Acetone | Ketone | No | Yes (fruity odor)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient is evaluated for megaloblastic anemia caused by impaired one-carbon (folate-dependent) metabolism. Biochemical analysis reveals defective transfer of a one-carbon unit required for nucleotide synthesis. The affected reaction involves the interconversion of two amino acids through a tetrahydrofolate (THF)-dependent methyl group transfer. Which of the following reactions is most likely impaired?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Conversion of glycine to serine

The clue is defective one-carbon metabolism.

One-carbon metabolism is mediated by tetrahydrofolate (THF), which carries one-carbon units in different oxidation states. These one-carbon units are essential for:

• Purine synthesis
• Thymidylate (dTMP) synthesis
• Methionine synthesis
• Interconversion of serine and glycine

The reaction: Glycine + N⁵,N¹⁰-methylene THF ⇌ Serine + THF is catalyzed by serine hydroxymethyltransferase (SHMT) and requires:

• Tetrahydrofolate (THF)
• Pyridoxal phosphate (Vitamin B₆)

This is one of the most important THF-dependent one-carbon transfer reactions in amino acid metabolism.

Why this reaction is important

The serine–glycine interconversion:

• Generates N⁵,N¹⁰-methylene THF, the one-carbon donor required for:

• dTMP synthesis (thymidylate synthase)
• Purine synthesis

• Links amino acid metabolism with DNA synthesis.

Defects in folate metabolism impair this reaction, leading to reduced DNA synthesis and megaloblastic anemia.

Why the other options are incorrect?

B. Conversion of tyrosine to DOPA

• Catalyzed by tyrosine hydroxylase.
• Requires tetrahydrobiopterin (BH₄), not THF.
• First step in catecholamine synthesis.

C. Conversion of glutamate to GABA

• Catalyzed by glutamate decarboxylase.
• Requires pyridoxal phosphate (Vitamin B₆).
• No one-carbon transfer occurs.

D. Conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine

• Catalyzed by phenylalanine hydroxylase.
• Requires BH₄, not THF.
• Defective in phenylketonuria (PKU).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient on prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy develops dermatitis, alopecia, and enteritis. Laboratory workup shows normal anion gap but impaired conversion of propionyl-CoA to its downstream product. Which vitamin deficiency explains this, and what is the precise carbon count change in the affected carboxylation reaction?
options: Vitamin B9 deficiency; THF-mediated one-carbon transfer impaired, no change in carbon count
Vitamin B7 deficiency; propionyl-CoA carboxylase impaired, converting a 3-carbon substrate to a 4-carbon product
Vitamin B7 deficiency; pyruvate carboxylase impaired, converting a 4-carbon substrate to a 3-carbon product
Vitamin B6 deficiency; impaired transamination unrelated to carboxylation reactions
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin B7 deficiency; propionyl-CoA carboxylase impaired, converting a 3-carbon substrate to a 4-carbon product

Long-term antibiotic use disrupts gut microbiota that normally produce biotin (B7), and biotin is the cofactor for carboxylation enzymes. Propionyl-CoA carboxylase converts propionyl-CoA (3C) → methylmalonyl-CoA (4C) — a carboxylation reaction adding one carbon group, consistent with biotin's general function across all three carboxylase reactions (pyruvate carboxylase, acetyl-CoA carboxylase, propionyl-CoA carboxylase), each adding a single carbon to its substrate.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient overdoses on a heavy metal. The toxin binds to an enzyme at a site distinct from the active site, producing a noncompetitive inhibition pattern. Which treatment is most appropriate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Add a chelating agent

Heavy metals (e.g., lead, mercury) often cause noncompetitive inhibition by binding to an allosteric site or sulfhydryl groups on enzymes, reducing Vmax without changing Km. Because the inhibitor does not compete with the substrate at the active site, increasing substrate concentration does not overcome inhibition. The most effective treatment is a chelating agent (e.g., EDTA, dimercaprol), which binds the heavy metal and facilitates its removal, restoring enzyme activity.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Increase substrate concentration: Increasing substrate cannot overcome noncompetitive inhibition.

C. Administer substrate analog: Substrate analogs act as competitive inhibitors, worsening inhibition.

D. Give excess cofactor: Excess cofactor does not displace heavy metals from allosteric binding sites.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient with celiac disease presents with peripheral neuropathy and decreased vibration and position sense. Investigations show hemolytic anemia and normal methylmalonic acid levels. Which of the following is most likely deficient in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vitamin E

This patient has peripheral neuropathy with loss of vibration and position sense, along with hemolytic anemia but normal methylmalonic acid, which points toward vitamin E deficiency. Vitamin E (α-tocopherol) is a lipid-soluble antioxidant, and its deficiency—commonly seen in fat malabsorption disorders like celiac disease—leads to:

• Hemolytic anemia due to oxidative damage to RBC membranes.
• Neurologic symptoms (spinocerebellar and posterior column dysfunction) causing loss of vibration and proprioception.

Why other options are incorrect:

• A. Pyridoxine (B₆): Causes neuropathy but usually without hemolytic anemia.
• B. Folate: Causes megaloblastic anemia, not hemolytic anemia or posterior column neuropathy.
• C. Vitamin B₁₂: Deficiency elevates MMA, which is normal here, ruling it out.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient with chronic alcohol use disorder is admitted with confusion, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia. Before thiamine levels are confirmed, the emergency physician administers IV dextrose for hypoglycemia, then thiamine afterward. Which physiological consequence may result from this sequence, and what should have been the correct order of administration?
options: Glucose administration without prior thiamine may worsen ATP depletion in highly aerobic tissues, precipitating or worsening Wernicke encephalopathy; thiamine should be given before dextrose
No consequence results, as thiamine and dextrose can be administered in either order without clinical impact
Dextrose administration corrects thiamine deficiency directly, making thiamine administration afterward redundant
Glucose administration before thiamine causes irreversible Korsakoff syndrome immediately, regardless of subsequent thiamine therapy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Glucose administration without prior thiamine may worsen ATP depletion in highly aerobic tissues, precipitating or worsening Wernicke encephalopathy; thiamine should be given before dextrose

In thiamine-deficient patients (chronic alcohol use, malnutrition), glucose infusion without prior thiamine can worsen ATP depletion in highly aerobic, thiamine-dependent tissues (brain, heart) by increasing metabolic demand on an already-impaired pyruvate dehydrogenase/TCA cycle pathway — precipitating or worsening Wernicke encephalopathy. The correct clinical sequence is thiamine before dextrose specifically to prevent this.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient with chronic alcohol use disorder presents in a fasted state with hypoglycemia. Laboratory testing shows a markedly elevated NADH/NAD+ ratio, and despite high fatty acid availability, ketone body production is suboptimal relative to expected starvation physiology. Which biochemical explanation accounts for this finding, tracing the fate of a specific TCA cycle intermediate?
options: High NADH state shifts oxaloacetate toward malate, depleting oxaloacetate available for gluconeogenesis, but this has no effect on ketogenesis since ketogenesis does not require oxaloacetate
High NADH state downregulates the TCA cycle, shunting oxaloacetate to malate; while ketogenesis itself does not require oxaloacetate directly
High NADH directly inhibits HMG-CoA lyase, the rate-limiting enzyme of ketogenesis, fully explaining the suboptimal ketone production
High NADH state has no relationship to oxaloacetate or malate; ketogenesis failure is entirely attributable to alcohol's direct toxic effect on adipose tissue lipolysis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. High NADH state downregulates the TCA cycle, shunting oxaloacetate to malate; while ketogenesis itself does not require oxaloacetate directly

Chronic alcohol overuse produces a high NADH state, which downregulates the TCA cycle and shunts oxaloacetate to malate. While ketogenesis (via HMG-CoA lyase) does not directly require oxaloacetate, the broader hepatic metabolic derangement (impaired TCA cycle flux, depleted gluconeogenic capacity) disrupts the liver's overall capacity to coordinate the fasting response, contributing to the clinical picture of hypoglycemia with disrupted, rather than appropriately compensatory, ketone production — distinguishing this from a primary defect in the ketogenic pathway itself.

| Condition | Oxaloacetate fate | Mechanism

| --------- | ----------------- | ---------

| Prolonged starvation/DKA | Depleted for gluconeogenesis | Used in gluconeogenesis itself

| Chronic alcohol overuse | Shunted to malate | High NADH downregulates TCA cycle

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient with chronic liver disease develops hyperammonemia, presenting with asterixis and somnolence. Brain imaging reveals cerebral edema. Which sequence of biochemical events directly links elevated ammonia to both the cerebral edema and the disruption of cerebral energy metabolism, tracing through two distinct downstream pathways from a single shared precursor?
options: NH3 directly damages the blood-brain barrier, causing edema; separately, NH3 inhibits glycolysis directly, causing energy failure — two unrelated mechanisms

NH3 combines with α-ketoglutarate to form glutamate, then glutamine; glutamine causes osmotic cerebral edema, while the consumption of α-ketoglutarate for this reaction depletes the TCA cycle intermediate, impairing oxidative energy metabolism
NH3 directly forms urea in the brain, and urea accumulation causes both osmotic edema and TCA cycle inhibition simultaneously
NH3 is converted to GABA directly without intermediate steps, causing both sedation and cerebral edema through GABA receptor overactivation alone
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. NH3 combines with α-ketoglutarate to form glutamate, then glutamine; glutamine causes osmotic cerebral edema, while the consumption of α-ketoglutarate for this reaction depletes the TCA cycle intermediate, impairing oxidative energy metabolism

Excess NH3 combines with α-ketoglutarate (forming glutamate, then glutamine via glutamine synthetase) — this serves two simultaneous pathologic purposes: (1) glutamine accumulation causes osmotic cerebral edema (glutamine draws water into astrocytes), and (2) the consumption of α-ketoglutarate for this detoxification reaction depletes a critical TCA cycle intermediate, inhibiting the TCA cycle and impairing cellular energy metabolism in the brain — both consequences trace back to the same nitrogen-disposal reaction, explaining the dual toxicity from a single shared precursor.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient with familial hypercholesterolemia has defective LDL receptor internalization. Which vesicular coat protein's normal function is most directly impaired in receptor-mediated endocytosis of LDL particles?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Clathrin

Clathrin mediates transport from plasma membrane → endosomes, specifically exemplified by receptor-mediated endocytosis (LDL receptor activity). Defective LDL receptor function/internalization in familial hypercholesterolemia directly implicates clathrin-coated pit formation and internalization.

| Coat protein | Pathway | Example

| ------------ | ------- | -------

| Clathrin | Plasma membrane → endosome | LDL receptor-mediated endocytosis

| Clathrin | trans-Golgi → lysosomes | Lysosomal enzyme delivery

| COPI | Retrograde Golgi/ER | —

| COPII | Anterograde ER → Golgi | —

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient with gout is found to have a defect in purine salvage pathway. His physician explains that de novo purine synthesis requires specific amino acid precursors. Which set of atoms contributed by amino acids forms the purine ring?
options: Glutamine, Alanine, Glycine — contribute nitrogen atoms only
Glycine, Aspartate, Glutamine — contribute carbons and nitrogens to the purine ring
Aspartate, Glutamate, Asparagine — contribute the complete purine ring scaffold
Glycine, Serine, Glutamine — with THF providing the nitrogen atoms
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glycine, Aspartate, Glutamine — contribute carbons and nitrogens to the purine ring

Mnemonic: "cats purr until they GAG": Glycine, Aspartate, Glutamine are the amino acids contributing to purine ring synthesis.

• Glycine contributes C4, C5, N7.
• Aspartate contributes N1.
• Glutamine contributes N3 and N9.
• CO₂ and THF (tetrahydrofolate) also contribute carbons, but the amino acid contributors are specifically these three.

| Contributor | Atoms donated | Position in ring

| ----------- | ------------- | ----------------

| Glycine | C4, C5, N7 | Core scaffold

| Aspartate | N1 | Amino group

| Glutamine | N3, N9 | Amide nitrogen

| CO₂ | C6 | Carbonyl carbon

| THF (N10-formyl) | C2, C8 | One-carbon units

| Carbamoyl phosphate | — | Pyrimidine only

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient with megaloblastic anemia is found to have impaired DNA synthesis due to a defect in one-carbon group transfer for purine and thymidine synthesis. Which activated carrier molecule is responsible for transferring these one-carbon units, and which vitamin is required for its activated form?
options: Coenzyme A; derived from vitamin B5
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tetrahydrofolate; derived from vitamin B9 (folate)

Tetrahydrofolate (THF), the activated form of folate (vitamin B9), carries one-carbon units — essential for purine ring synthesis (C2, C8 contributions) and thymidylate synthesis (dUMP → dTMP). Deficiency impairs DNA synthesis broadly, producing megaloblastic anemia. This is distinct from SAM (carries CH3 groups specifically, for methylation reactions) and biotin (carries CO2 for carboxylation reactions) — each activated carrier has a specific, non-overlapping cargo.

| Activated carrier | Cargo | Source vitamin

| ----------------- | ----- | --------------

| Tetrahydrofolate | 1-carbon units | B9 (folate)

| SAM | CH3 groups | Derived from methionine (B12/B9-dependent regeneration)

| Biotin | CO2 | B7

| TPP | Aldehydes | B1

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis is started on methotrexate. Six weeks later he develops oral ulcers and macrocytic anemia. His physician adds leucovorin (folinic acid) rescue. Which enzymatic step, when inhibited by methotrexate, most directly explains why both purine and pyrimidine synthesis are simultaneously impaired?
options: Thymidylate synthase inhibition, reducing dTMP and depleting the THF pool
Ribonucleotide reductase inhibition, blocking dNTP production at the dUDP and dADP step
Dihydrofolate reductase inhibition, preventing DHF → THF regeneration, starving both pathways of one-carbon units
IMP dehydrogenase inhibition, halting the IMP → GMP conversion and feedback-inhibiting CPS2
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dihydrofolate reductase inhibition, preventing DHF → THF regeneration, starving both pathways of one-carbon units

MTX inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) → DHF cannot be reduced to THF → THF pool depleted → N⁵N¹⁰-methylene THF unavailable for thymidylate synthase (dUMP→dTMP) → N¹⁰-formyl THF unavailable for purine ring synthesis (C2, C8). Both pathways simultaneously starved. Leucovorin (5-formyl THF) bypasses DHFR entirely, rescuing normal cells. Thymidylate synthase inhibition (5-FU) depletes THF secondarily but only affects pyrimidines primarily.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient with severe malnutrition presents with muscle pain, proximal muscle weakness, and cardiomyopathy. Labs show markedly decreased activity of an enzyme that converts H₂O₂ → H₂O using glutathione as a cofactor. Which trace element deficiency is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Selenium

The enzyme converting H₂O₂ → H₂O using glutathione is glutathione peroxidase, a selenium-dependent enzyme. Selenium deficiency leads to impaired detoxification of reactive oxygen species, causing oxidative muscle damage, proximal myopathy, and dilated cardiomyopathy (classically seen in severe malnutrition, e.g., Keshan disease). Reduced glutathione peroxidase activity explains the accumulation of hydrogen peroxide and resultant tissue injury.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Zinc: Required for many enzymes and transcription factors, not glutathione peroxidase.

B. Copper: Cofactor for cytochrome c oxidase and SOD, not H₂O₂ detoxification via glutathione.

D. Manganese: Cofactor for mitochondrial superoxide dismutase, not glutathione peroxidase.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A pediatric infectious disease specialist suspects herpes encephalitis in a neonate with seizures and lethargy. CSF PCR is ordered. During the PCR reaction, the sample is heated to separate the double-stranded viral DNA template into single strands. Which specific step of the PCR cycle does this represent, and what happens immediately afterward?
options: Annealing — Sample is heated further to allow primer binding
Elongation — DNA polymerase begins adding dNTPs immediately after heating
Denaturation — Sample is then cooled to allow primer annealing to the template
Denaturation — Temperature is immediately increased further for elongation without an intermediate cooling step
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Denaturation — Sample is then cooled to allow primer annealing to the template

Denaturation = heating to separate DNA strands (using template, primers, heat-stable polymerase, and dNTPs all present). This is immediately followed by annealing — cooling the sample so DNA primers can bind their specific complementary sequence on the template. Elongation (temperature increased again) occurs only after annealing, when DNA polymerase extends the primer using dNTPs.

| Step | Temperature change | Event

| ---- | ------------------ | -----

| 1. Denaturation | Heat | Strands separate

| 2. Annealing | Cool | Primers bind template

| 3. Elongation | Heat (increased) | Polymerase extends primer with dNTPs

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A pharmacology student is studying drug metabolism. A hepatocyte is found to have a selective defect affecting steroid synthesis and detoxification of poisons, but protein synthesis for export remains unaffected. Which organelle is most likely deficient, and which surface marker confirms this distinction from the unaffected organelle?
options: Rough ER; presence of surface ribosomes
Smooth ER; absence of surface ribosomes
Free ribosomes; absence of membrane attachment
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Smooth ER; absence of surface ribosomes

Smooth ER is the site of steroid synthesis and drug/poison detoxification, and lacks surface ribosomes — distinguishing it from RER (which has surface ribosomes and is responsible for secretory protein synthesis, unaffected in this scenario). SER also contains glucose-6-phosphatase (final step of glycogenolysis/gluconeogenesis). Rich in hepatocytes and steroid-producing cells of adrenal cortex/gonads.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A pregnant patient at advanced maternal age undergoes amniocentesis. The cytogenetics report identifies an extra copy of chromosome 21 using a technique that requires arresting cells in metaphase and visually ordering chromosomes by banding pattern. Which technique was used, and what general category of disorder does this finding represent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Karyotyping; numerical chromosomal abnormality (autosomal trisomy)

Karyotyping requires colchicine-induced metaphase arrest and visual ordering of chromosomes by morphology, size, and banding pattern — explicitly used to diagnose autosomal trisomies (numerical abnormality, e.g., trisomy 21/Down syndrome) and sex chromosome disorders. This is distinct from FISH, which is typically used for more targeted, gene-specific structural abnormalities (microdeletions, translocations, duplications) rather than whole-chromosome numerical counting, though FISH can also detect trisomies via signal counting.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A prokaryotic mRNA has a mutation in a specific sequence required for ribosomal binding, located upstream of the start codon. Translation initiation fails despite a normal AUG start codon. Which sequence is mutated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Shine-Dalgarno sequence

Shine-Dalgarno sequence is the prokaryotic ribosomal binding site, recognized by 16S rRNA of the small subunit — aligns the ribosome with the start codon for correct reading frame initiation. Kozak sequence is the eukaryotic equivalent.

| Feature | Prokaryotes | Eukaryotes

| ------- | ----------- | ----------

| Ribosome-binding sequence | Shine-Dalgarno | Kozak

| Recognized by | 16S rRNA | Small ribosomal subunit (40S) scanning

| Location | Upstream of start codon | Around start codon

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A research scientist is studying biochemical reactions that take place in the liver. He cultures hepatocytes in a growth media enriched with glutamate labelled with nitrogen isotopes. After some time, he finds that the nitrogen isotopes are transferred to oxaloacetate, forming aspartate in the process. Which of the following substances is most likely involved in this reaction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pyridoxine

The reaction described is a transamination, where an amino group from glutamate is transferred to oxaloacetate to form aspartate. This process is catalyzed by aminotransferases, which require pyridoxal phosphate (the active form of pyridoxine) as a cofactor. Pyridoxine is essential for all amino acid metabolism involving transamination.

Why the others are incorrect:

A. Biotin: Cofactor for carboxylation reactions (e.g., pyruvate → oxaloacetate), not transamination.

B. Folic acid: Involved in one-carbon transfers, nucleotide synthesis, and methylation reactions; not directly in amino group transfer.

C. Niacin: Precursor for NAD⁺/NADP⁺, used in redox reactions, not in nitrogen transfer.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A researcher adds oligomycin to isolated mitochondria during an experiment studying ATP production. Which of the following best describes the immediate effect of this inhibitor?
options: Inhibits electron transport at Complex I
Inhibits ATP synthase by blocking proton channel
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Inhibits ATP synthase by blocking proton channel

• Oligomycin binds to Fo subunit of ATP synthase (Complex V).
• It blocks proton (H⁺) flow back into the mitochondrial matrix.
• This stops ATP synthesis despite an intact electron transport chain initially.
•

Proton gradient builds up → eventually electron transport slows ↓ and O₂ consumption decreases.

•

OTHER INHIBITORS:

• Rotenone → Complex I inhibitor
• Cyanide/CO → Complex IV inhibitor
• 2,4-DNP → uncoupler (↑ O₂ consumption, ↓ ATP)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A researcher compares glucose-phosphorylating enzymes in hepatocytes and skeletal muscle. The hepatic enzyme shows high Km and high Vmax, and is not inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate. Which of the following best identifies this enzyme?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hexokinase IV

The hepatic glucose-phosphorylating enzyme with high Km, high Vmax, and no inhibition by glucose-6-phosphate is glucokinase (Hexokinase IV).

• Glucokinase (Hexokinase IV):

• Found in liver and pancreatic β-cells
• High Km → low affinity → active only at high glucose levels (postprandial)
• High Vmax → handles large glucose loads
• Not inhibited by G6P → continues glucose uptake/storage in liver

• Other hexokinases (I–III):

• Low Km (high affinity) → active even at low glucose
• Low Vmax
• Inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate

• Physiological role:

• Promotes glycogen synthesis and glycolysis in liver after meals
• Acts as a glucose sensor in β-cells → insulin secretion

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A researcher inserts a regulatory DNA sequence into the first intron of a eukaryotic gene. The sequence increases transcription only when specific activator proteins are present. Removal of this sequence markedly decreases gene expression, although the promoter remains completely normal. The inserted sequence is best classified as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Enhancer

•

Enhancers may be located close to, far from, or even within an intron of the gene they regulate.

•

Their function is to bind activator proteins, increasing transcription.

Comparison

| Feature | Promoter | Enhancer | Silencer

| ------- | -------- | -------- | --------

| Binds | RNA polymerase II & TFs | Activators | Repressors

| Function | Initiates transcription | Increases expression | Decreases expression

| Position | Upstream | Upstream, downstream or intronic | Upstream, downstream or intronic

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A researcher observes that certain cells are unable to synthesize glucose from pyruvate despite normal functioning of downstream gluconeogenic enzymes. Which of the following enzyme deficiencies most directly explains the loss of glucogenic capability from pyruvate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pyruvate carboxylase

Conversion of pyruvate → glucose (gluconeogenesis) requires the initial step catalyzed by pyruvate carboxylase:

• Pyruvate carboxylase:

• Converts pyruvate → oxaloacetate (OAA) in mitochondria
• Requires biotin as a cofactor
• This is the first and essential step of gluconeogenesis from pyruvate

• Why deficiency blocks gluconeogenesis:

• Without OAA, pathway cannot proceed → no substrate for PEPCK
• Leads to impaired glucose production → hypoglycemia

• Clinical correlation:

• ↑ Pyruvate → converted to lactate → lactic acidosis
• Energy deficit due to impaired TCA cycle entry

• Why other options are incorrect:

• PEPCK → acts after OAA is formed
• Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase & G6-phosphatase → later steps

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A researcher studies a patient with a rare enzyme deficiency in fatty acid oxidation, presenting with hypoketotic hypoglycemia during fasting. Genetic analysis reveals a mutation in carnitine acyltransferase I. Which physiologic regulator, when elevated due to active fatty acid synthesis, would normally inhibit this same enzyme — explaining why fatty acid oxidation and fatty acid synthesis are reciprocally regulated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Malonyl-CoA

Malonyl-CoA (the product of acetyl-CoA carboxylase, the rate-determining step of fatty acid synthesis) inhibits carnitine acyltransferase I (the rate-determining enzyme of fatty acid oxidation). This reciprocal regulation prevents simultaneous synthesis and oxidation of fatty acids — when the cell is actively synthesizing fatty acids (high malonyl-CoA), it makes biochemical sense to suppress the competing oxidative pathway, avoiding a futile cycle.

| Pathway | Rate-determining enzyme | Key inhibitor

| ------- | ----------------------- | -------------

| Fatty acid synthesis | Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) | Glucagon, palmitoyl-CoA

| Fatty acid oxidation | Carnitine acyltransferase I | Malonyl-CoA (product of ACC)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A researcher treats a prokaryotic cell-free replication system with a drug that causes accumulation of positively supercoiled DNA ahead of the replication fork, completely stalling synthesis. Which enzyme is directly inhibited, and what is its normal mechanistic role?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. DNA topoisomerase II (gyrase)

Topoisomerase II creates a double-stranded break to add/remove supercoils. In prokaryotes, TOP II = DNA gyrase. As helicase unwinds DNA, positive supercoils accumulate ahead — gyrase relieves this by introducing negative supercoils. Fluoroquinolones inhibit prokaryotic gyrase/TOP IV specifically. Without gyrase, torsional stress accumulates → replication fork physically cannot advance.

| Enzyme | Break type | Function | Inhibitor

| ------ | ---------- | -------- | ---------

| TOP I (eukaryotes) | Single-strand | Relieves supercoils | Irinotecan, topotecan

| TOP II/gyrase (prokaryotes) | Double-strand | Relieves + introduces supercoils | Fluoroquinolones

| TOP II (eukaryotes) | Double-strand | Relieves supercoils | Etoposide, teniposide

| TOP IV (prokaryotes) | Double-strand | Decatenation | Fluoroquinolones

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A sailor on a long voyage with a diet limited to tea and toast develops swollen, bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhages, and poor wound healing. Skin biopsy reveals a defect in post-translational collagen modification. Which two specific amino acid residues fail to undergo proper modification, and what is the direct biochemical consequence for collagen structure?
options: Glycine and alanine; failure prevents triple helix formation entirely, with no collagen produced at all
Hydroxylysine and hydroxyproline degradation is accelerated, paradoxically increasing collagen turnover
Lysine and arginine fail to undergo methylation, weakening cross-link formation via lysyl oxidase
Proline and lysine fail to undergo hydroxylation, producing unstable collagen with impaired structural integrity due to deficient hydrogen bonding within the triple helix
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Proline and lysine fail to undergo hydroxylation, producing unstable collagen with impaired structural integrity due to deficient hydrogen bonding within the triple helix

Vitamin C is required for hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues during collagen synthesis. Without hydroxylation, the resulting hydroxyproline/hydroxylysine residues (needed for stabilizing hydrogen bonds within the triple helix) are absent, producing structurally unstable collagen — explaining bleeding gums, poor wound healing, and perifollicular hemorrhages in scurvy. This is distinct from cross-linking (lysyl oxidase, copper-dependent — Menkes disease) or triple helix assembly itself (a downstream step that still initiates but produces unstable product).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A sprinter performs a 6-second maximal effort, recovers briefly, then performs a 50-second near-maximal effort, then later completes a 2-hour endurance event. Based on the relative timing of different energy systems' peak contribution, which sequence of dominant fuel systems correctly matches these three efforts?
options: Stored ATP → creatine phosphate → aerobic glycolysis
Creatine phosphate → stored ATP → aerobic metabolism
Anaerobic glycolysis → aerobic metabolism → stored ATP
Aerobic metabolism → anaerobic glycolysis → creatine phosphate
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Stored ATP → creatine phosphate → aerobic glycolysis

Stored ATP dominates only the first couple of seconds, creatine phosphate covers efforts up to roughly 10 seconds, anaerobic glycolysis dominates efforts up to about a minute, and aerobic metabolism sustains everything beyond that. The overall performance curve declines progressively across this range because each successive system sacrifices peak power output in exchange for being sustainable over a longer duration — explaining why no one can sprint at top speed for an hour, nor jog at marathon pace for a 100m dash with maximal output.

| Duration | Dominant system

| -------- | ---------------

| \~2 sec | Stored ATP

| \~10 sec | Creatine phosphate

| \~1 min | Anaerobic glycolysis

| Hours | Aerobic metabolism

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A strict vegan patient who also frequently consumes raw egg whites as a protein source presents with dermatitis, alopecia, and paresthesias. Which two vitamin deficiencies are most directly explained by these dietary patterns, and what is the specific molecular mechanism linking raw egg white consumption to one of these deficiencies?
options: Vitamin B12 (vegan diet, no animal source) and vitamin B7 (avidin in raw egg whites binds biotin, preventing absorption)
Vitamin B9 (vegan diet) and vitamin B3 (raw egg whites destroy niacin enzymatically)
Vitamin B2 (vegan diet) and vitamin B7 (raw egg whites contain excess biotin, causing competitive inhibition)
Vitamin B12 (vegan diet) and vitamin B6 (raw egg whites bind pyridoxal phosphate directly)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vitamin B12 (vegan diet, no animal source) and vitamin B7 (avidin in raw egg whites binds biotin, preventing absorption)

Vegan diets lack animal-source B12, requiring supplementation. Raw egg white consumption introduces avidin, which binds biotin (B7) and prevents its intestinal absorption — a well-described mechanism distinct from any enzymatic destruction or competitive inhibition. This combination (vegan diet + raw egg whites) creates dual risk for both B12 and B7 deficiency, each through entirely separate mechanisms (absence of dietary source vs. binding-mediated malabsorption).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A vegan patient with mild B12 deficiency is empirically given high-dose folate supplementation by a well-meaning but uninformed clinician. Several months later, her macrocytic anemia has resolved on repeat CBC, but she develops new-onset paresthesias and gait instability. Which explanation accounts for this clinical course?
options: Folate supplementation directly worsens B12-related neurologic damage through competitive inhibition of methylmalonyl-CoA mutase

Folate corrected the hematologic abnormality by bypassing the methionine synthase step, but did not address the methylmalonyl-CoA mutase defect responsible for the neurologic findings, allowing irreversible nerve damage to progress
The patient developed a new, unrelated deficiency in vitamin B6, explaining the neurologic findings independent of B12 status
Folate supplementation has no effect on B12 deficiency hematology or neurology, and the anemia resolved spontaneously
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Folate corrected the hematologic abnormality by bypassing the methionine synthase step, but did not address the methylmalonyl-CoA mutase defect responsible for the neurologic findings, allowing irreversible nerve damage to progress

Folate can mask the hematologic symptoms of B12 deficiency (by supplying THF for DNA synthesis pathways independent of B12-dependent methionine synthase) but does not correct the neurologic symptoms, since those arise from impaired methylmalonyl-CoA mutase activity (a B12-dependent, folate-independent enzyme). Untreated, this allows progression to irreversible nerve damage (subacute combined degeneration) while the blood count appears falsely reassuring.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A young male presents with progressive behavioral changes, vision loss, and adrenal insufficiency. MRI shows white matter demyelination. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in ABCD1. Which fatty acid species accumulates, and in which organelle does the defective oxidation normally occur?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Very-long-chain fatty acids; peroxisome (β-oxidation)

Adrenoleukodystrophy: ABCD1 mutation → defective peroxisomal β-oxidation of VLCFA → accumulation in adrenal glands, white matter (leuko), and testes.

Note: VLCFA β-oxidation is strictly peroxisomal — distinguishing it from standard fatty acid β-oxidation, which is mitochondrial.

| Process | Location | Substrate | Disorder if defective

| ------- | -------- | --------- | ---------------------

| VLCFA β-oxidation | Peroxisome (strictly) | VLCFA | Adrenoleukodystrophy

| Branched-chain α-oxidation | Peroxisome (strictly) | Phytanic acid | Refsum disease

| Standard fatty acid β-oxidation | Mitochondria | Long-chain fatty acids | —

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A young woman with hyperextensible skin and joint hypermobility presents to the emergency department with sudden abdominal pain. CT reveals a ruptured visceral artery. Which collagen type is most likely deficient, and which tissue distribution explains both her skin findings and the vascular catastrophe?
options: Type III — blood vessels, skin (early wound repair)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Type III — blood vessels, skin (early wound repair)

Vascular type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome = Type III collagen deficiency ("threE D" mnemonic). Type III collagen (reticulin) is found in skin, blood vessels, uterus, and fetal tissue, and is responsible for early wound repair. Deficiency explains both the hyperextensible skin (skin distribution) and the catastrophic arterial rupture (vascular distribution) — a single collagen defect manifesting at two anatomically distinct sites.

| Collagen type | Tissue (mnemonic: SCAB) | Disease if deficient

| ------------- | ----------------------- | --------------------

| I | Skeleton (bone, tendon, skin) | Osteogenesis imperfecta type I

| II | Cartilage | —

| III | Arteries (also skin, uterus) | Vascular EDS
