| IV | Basement membrane | Alport syndrome, Goodpasture target

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: All are tests for bile pigment except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hay’s sulfur test

Bile pigments (bilirubin) in urine are detected by the following tests:

• Fouchet’s test: bilirubin is oxidized → biliverdin (green color) → positive.
• Gmelin’s test: nitric acid oxidation → play of colors (green, blue, violet, etc.).
• Harrison’s test
• Hammarsten test
• Presence of bile pigments indicates conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (e.g., obstructive jaundice).

Bile salts:

• Principle: bile salts reduce surface tension of urine.
• Method: sprinkle sulfur powder on urine surface.
• Positive Hay’s test: sulfur sinks (↓ surface tension).
• Negative: sulfur floats.
• Bile salts appear in urine mainly in obstructive jaundice.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: All of the following are NADPH generating reactions except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ketoacyl-ACP dehydrogenase

Ketoacyl-ACP dehydrogenase is part of fatty acid synthesis, catalyzing the reduction of β-ketoacyl-ACP to β-hydroxyacyl-ACP using NADPH, but it consumes NADPH rather than generating it.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase: Generates NADPH in the pentose phosphate pathway.

B. Cytoplasmic isocitrate dehydrogenase: Produces NADPH by converting isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate in the cytosol.

C. Malic enzyme: Converts malate → pyruvate, generating NADPH for fatty acid synthesis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: All of the following reactions may be inhibited in an alcoholic except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lactic acid production

In chronic alcohol consumption, ethanol is metabolized to acetaldehyde and then acetate, producing excess NADH in the liver. This high NADH/NAD⁺ ratio inhibits:

• Gluconeogenesis ↓ (inhibited)

• Pyruvate → Lactate
• Oxaloacetate → Malate

• TCA cycle: High NADH inhibits key dehydrogenases (isocitrate, α-ketoglutarate, malate).
• Fatty acid oxidation: Requires NAD⁺; high NADH inhibits β-oxidation, promoting fatty liver.

Lactic acid production, however, is increased rather than inhibited, because excess NADH drives pyruvate → lactate via lactate dehydrogenase, often causing lactic acidosis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: An 18-year-old man comes to the office due to a progressive skin rash over the past year. He also has a long-standing history of an intermittent burning sensation in his palms and soles that is exacerbated by stress and fatigue. The burning sensation is particularly severe after exercise, during which the patient notes that he sweats minimally. Laboratory evaluation reveals an undetectable level of a-galactosidase A. Which of the following conditions is this patient at greatest risk for developing?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Renal failure

This patient has Fabry disease, an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by α-galactosidase A deficiency, leading to accumulation of globotriaosylceramide in various tissues. Early symptoms include angiokeratomas, acroparesthesias (burning in hands/feet), and hypohidrosis. Over time, deposition in renal vasculature and glomeruli causes progressive renal insufficiency and eventual renal failure if untreated.

Why the others are incorrect:

A. Ataxia: Not a primary feature of Fabry disease; neurologic involvement is mainly neuropathic pain.

B. Hepatomegaly: Liver enlargement is uncommon in Fabry disease.

C. Optic atrophy: Ocular manifestations usually involve cornea verticillata, not optic nerve degeneration.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: An 8-month-old boy is evaluated for poor weight gain, delayed developmental milestones, and recurrent lower respiratory tract infections. He was born after an uncomplicated pregnancy to healthy, unrelated parents. On examination, he has coarse facial features, gingival hypertrophy, macroglossia, an umbilical hernia, and hepatosplenomegaly. Ophthalmologic examination shows no corneal clouding. Skeletal radiographs reveal dysostosis multiplex with hypoplasia of the odontoid process. A skin fibroblast biopsy demonstrates numerous membrane-bound cytoplasmic inclusion bodies containing undegraded lysosomal material. Which of the following is the most likely underlying defect?
options: Failure of mannose-6-phosphate tagging of lysosomal enzymes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Failure of mannose-6-phosphate tagging of lysosomal enzymes

• The infant has I-cell disease (Mucolipidosis II).
• Unlike lysosomal storage disorders caused by deficiency of a single lysosomal enzyme, I-cell disease results from defective targeting of multiple lysosomal enzymes.
• The primary defect is: ↓ N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase (GlcNAc phosphotransferase)
• This enzyme normally adds mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) to newly synthesized lysosomal enzymes in the Golgi apparatus.

Without the M6P tag:

• Lysosomal enzymes are secreted outside the cell instead of being delivered to lysosomes.
• Lysosomes become filled with undegraded substrates, producing characteristic inclusion cells (I-cells).

| Disorder | Defect | Corneal Clouding | Characteristic Finding

| -------- | ------ | ---------------- | ----------------------

| I-cell disease (Mucolipidosis II) | Defective mannose-6-phosphate tagging (GlcNAc phosphotransferase deficiency) | Usually absent | Inclusion bodies in fibroblasts; ↑ lysosomal enzymes in plasma

| Hurler syndrome (MPS I) | α-L-iduronidase deficiency | Present | Dermatan & heparan sulfate accumulation

| Hunter syndrome (MPS II) | Iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency | Absent | X-linked; dermatan & heparan sulfate accumulation

| GM1 gangliosidosis | β-Galactosidase deficiency | Variable | GM1 ganglioside accumulation

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: An 8-month-old infant is brought to the pediatrician for evaluation of multiple episodes of seizures and hypoglycemia. A liver biopsy demonstrates hepatocytes with large glycogen stores. Biochemical analysis reveals glycogen with short outer chains. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cori disease

Cori disease (Glycogen storage disease type III) is caused by deficiency of the debranching enzyme, leading to accumulation of abnormally structured glycogen with short outer chains. Affected infants present with hepatomegaly, hypoglycemia, seizures, and excess glycogen in hepatocytes. Unlike Von Gierke disease, gluconeogenesis is intact, so hypoglycemia is less severe.

Why other options are incorrect:

B. Anderson disease: Defect in branching enzyme → long, poorly branched glycogen causing liver cirrhosis.

C. Von-Gierke disease: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency; glycogen structure is normal.

D. Pompe disease: Lysosomal acid maltase deficiency with cardiomegaly, not hypoglycemia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: An enzymologist is comparing catalytic mechanisms used by different enzymes. One mechanism, known as the ping-pong (double-displacement) mechanism, involves the enzyme reacting with the first substrate to form a modified enzyme intermediate before the second substrate binds. Which of the following enzymes does not utilize a ping-pong (double-displacement) reaction mechanism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate aldolase

What is a ping-pong (double-displacement) reaction?

In a ping-pong mechanism, the reaction occurs in two sequential steps:

1. First substrate binds to the enzyme.
2. The enzyme is chemically modified, and the first product is released.
3. Second substrate binds to the modified enzyme.
4. The enzyme transfers the intermediate to the second substrate, forming the second product, and the enzyme returns to its original state.

Key feature: The two substrates are never bound to the enzyme at the same time.

| Enzyme | Ping-Pong Mechanism? | Intermediate Formed

| ------ | -------------------- | -------------------

| Serine proteases | ✅ Yes | Acyl-enzyme intermediate

| Aminotransferases (ALT/AST) | ✅ Yes | PLP ⇌ PMP intermediate

| Pyruvate carboxylase | ✅ Yes | Carboxybiotin intermediate

| Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate aldolase | ❌ No | No ping-pong mechanism

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: An infant boy presents with neurologic regression, lactic acidosis, and elevated serum alanine. Genetic testing confirms an X-linked enzyme deficiency. Treatment includes a high-fat diet and supplementation with lysine and leucine. Which biochemical rationale explains why increasing ketogenic amino acids specifically benefits this condition, given the enzyme's normal role?
options: Lysine and leucine are converted to glucose via gluconeogenesis, bypassing the defective enzyme entirely
Lysine and leucine are purely ketogenic amino acids, providing acetyl-CoA directly without requiring pyruvate dehydrogenase, bypassing the blocked conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA
Lysine and leucine stimulate residual pyruvate dehydrogenase activity through allosteric activation
Lysine and leucine inhibit lactate dehydrogenase, redirecting pyruvate toward the TCA cycle directly
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lysine and leucine are purely ketogenic amino acids, providing acetyl-CoA directly without requiring pyruvate dehydrogenase, bypassing the blocked conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA

Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency (X-linked) blocks pyruvate → acetyl-CoA conversion, causing pyruvate buildup shunted to lactate (via LDH) and alanine (via ALT). Since lysine and leucine are purely ketogenic amino acids, they can be catabolized directly to acetyl-CoA without requiring pyruvate dehydrogenase — providing an alternative entry point into the TCA cycle that bypasses the defective enzyme entirely, explaining the therapeutic rationale for their supplementation alongside a high-fat (ketogenic) diet.

| Feature | PDH complex deficiency

| ------- | ----------------------

| Inheritance | X-linked

| Buildup | Pyruvate → shunted to lactate (LDH) and alanine (ALT)

| Treatment rationale | Ketogenic nutrients (fat, lysine, leucine) bypass PDH, supply acetyl-CoA directly

| Additional treatment | B1 (thiamine), lipoic acid — PDH complex cofactors

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: An infant has severe steatorrhea, failure to thrive, and acanthocytes on peripheral smear. Intestinal biopsy shows lipid-laden enterocytes. Genetic testing reveals a defect in a gene required to load triglycerides onto a specific apolipoprotein within the enterocyte. Which apolipoprotein-containing particle would be undetectable in this patient's serum?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Both chylomicrons and VLDL

Abetalipoproteinemia = MTP mutation, preventing apo B48 and apo B100 lipidation → both chylomicrons (apo B48) and VLDL/LDL (apo B100) are absent. HDL is unaffected since it doesn't depend on apo B.

| Particle | Apolipoprotein | Present in abetalipoproteinemia?

| -------- | -------------- | --------------------------------

| Chylomicron | B48 | No

| VLDL/LDL | B100 | No

| HDL | A1 | Yes

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: An investigator is studying the genotypes of fire-flies using full exome sequencing. They are found to have a point mutation in the gene encoding wing bud formation during embryogenesis. The point mutation in the gene causes the mRNA transcript to have a "UUG" segment instead of an "AUG" segment. Which of the following processes is most likely affected by this mutation?
options: Dissociation of mRNA from ribosome complex
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Binding of met-tRNA to 60S complex

The point mutation changes the start codon from AUG → UUG. AUG is the canonical start codon that recruits initiator methionine tRNA (Met-tRNAᵢ) to the small ribosomal subunit (40S in eukaryotes) and subsequently forms the 60S/40S initiation complex. A non-AUG codon prevents proper Met-tRNA binding, inhibiting translation initiation of the mRNA.

Why the others are incorrect:

A. Cleavage of 5' intron: This occurs during mRNA splicing, which is upstream of translation and unaffected by start codon mutation.

B. Catalyzation of peptide bond formation: This occurs at the ribosome during elongation; the start codon mutation prevents initiation, so elongation never occurs.

D. Dissociation of mRNA from ribosome complex: Happens during translation termination, which is downstream of initiation and unaffected by the start codon mutation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Arrange the enzymes of fatty acid synthase complex in the correct order: 1. Ketoacyl synthase 2. Enoyl reductase 3. Acetyl transferase 4. Malonyl transacyclase 5. Hydratase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3, 4, 5, 2

Order:

1. Ketoacyl synthase (KS)
2. Acetyl transferase (AT)
3. Malonyl transacylase (MT/MAT)
4. Hydratase (Dehydratase)
5. Enoyl reductase (ER)

In the fatty acid synthase (FAS) complex, the catalytic domains are arranged in a specific sequence. Simplifying to the enzymes listed in the question, the order is: Ketoacyl synthase → Acetyl transferase → Malonyl transacylase → Hydratase (Dehydratase) → Enoyl reductase

Hence: 1 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 2

High-yield note:

The complete domain order of the mammalian fatty acid synthase is: KS → MAT (acetyl/malonyl transferase) → DH (dehydratase) → ER (enoyl reductase) → KR (β-ketoacyl reductase) → ACP → TE (thioesterase)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Arrange the following steps of base excision repair in order: 1. Endonuclease excises the sugar backbone 2. Glycosylase removes the altered base 3. DNA-polymerase adds a nucleotide 4. Creation of apurinic/apyrimidinic site
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2 → 4 → 1 → 3

Base excision repair (BER) proceeds in the following order:

1.  Glycosylase removes the altered base (2): Recognizes and excises the damaged base, leaving an apurinic/apyrimidinic (AP) site.

2.  Creation of AP site (4): The sugar-phosphate backbone remains intact, now missing the base.

3.  Endonuclease excises the sugar backbone (1): AP endonuclease cleaves the phosphodiester bond at the AP site.

4.  DNA polymerase adds a nucleotide (3): Fills in the gap using the complementary strand as a template.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: As part of a research study hepatocytes are isolated from biopsy samples. The cells are homogenized and centrifuged to remove membrane components and organelles. Following subsequent rounds of centrifugation, the remaining supernatant contains only cytosol and cytosolic proteins. Activity of which of the following enzymes will most likely be detectable in the supernatant of healthy liver cells?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Glycogen synthase

The question asks which enzyme would be found in the cytosolic fraction after all membranes and organelles have been removed by differential centrifugation.

The remaining supernatant contains:

• Cytosol
• Cytosolic proteins

Therefore, only enzymes that normally reside in the cytosol will be detected.

Option Analysis

A. Ornithine transcarbamylase ❌

• Location: Mitochondrial matrix
• Function: Catalyzes the formation of citrulline in the urea cycle.
• Removed with mitochondria during centrifugation.

B. Pyruvate carboxylase ❌

• Location: Mitochondrial matrix
• Biotin-dependent enzyme that converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate in gluconeogenesis.
• Removed with mitochondria.

C. Succinate dehydrogenase ❌

• Location: Inner mitochondrial membrane (Complex II of the ETC)
• Participates in both the TCA cycle and electron transport chain.
• Removed with mitochondrial membranes.

D. Glycogen synthase ✅

• Location: Cytosol
• Catalyzes glycogen synthesis by adding glucose residues from UDP-glucose to glycogen.
• Remains in the cytosolic supernatant after centrifugation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: As part of an experiment, healthy volunteers undergo a 12-hour fast and then drink a solution containing radiolabeled alanine. Consecutive blood samples are drawn every 15 minutes for the next 3 hours. Initial blood samples detect the radiolabeled alanine, but analysis of later samples shows that the radiotracer is present in blood primarily in the form of glucose. Before alanine can be converted to glucose, its amino group is transferred to which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. α- Ketoglutarate

Alanine undergoes transamination in the liver as the first step of gluconeogenesis. Its amino group is transferred to α-ketoglutarate, forming glutamate and leaving behind pyruvate, which can then enter gluconeogenesis to produce glucose (as observed in the radiolabel experiment). This process is catalyzed by alanine aminotransferase (ALT).

Why other options are incorrect:

L-citrulline: Intermediate in the urea cycle; not directly involved in alanine transamination.

Malate & Citrate: Intermediates in the TCA cycle, not amino group acceptors for alanine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Azathioprine dose must be reduced by 75% when co-prescribed with allopurinol. A rheumatologist unfamiliar with this interaction prescribes standard-dose azathioprine with allopurinol for gout. The patient develops severe pancytopenia. The toxic metabolite that accumulates is:
options: Orotic acid, due to pyrimidine pathway overflow
Xanthine, due to upstream purine degradation block
6-thioguanine nucleotides, due to shunting of 6-MP away from xanthine oxidase inactivation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 6-thioguanine nucleotides, due to shunting of 6-MP away from xanthine oxidase inactivation

Azathioprine → 6-MP → normally inactivated by xanthine oxidase → 6-thiouric acid (excreted). Allopurinol inhibits XO → 6-MP cannot be inactivated → shunted to 6-thioguanine nucleotides (6-TGN) → incorporated into DNA/RNA of bone marrow cells → myelosuppression. 6-TGN are the toxic effectors.

| Metabolic step | Normal | + Allopurinol

| -------------- | ------ | -------------

| 6-MP → 6-thiouric acid (via XO) | Major inactivation route | Blocked

| 6-MP → 6-TGN (via TPMT/HGPRT) | Minor route | Becomes dominant

| 6-TGN accumulation | Low | ↑↑ toxic levels

| Bone marrow | Spared | Myelosuppression

| Action required | — | Reduce AZA by 75%

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Cells that are exposed to longer ischemic periods are found to have reduced numbers of ribosomes attached to the endoplasmic reticulum. This structural change is most likely to impair which of the following cellular functions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Synthesis of cell membrane proteins

Ribosomes attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER) synthesize secretory and membrane-bound proteins. Reduced ribosome attachment during ischemia impairs the production of integral membrane proteins and secreted proteins, disrupting normal cellular function and signaling.

Why the others are incorrect:

• A. Drug detoxification: Mainly occurs via smooth ER enzymes (e.g., cytochrome P450), independent of ribosome attachment.
• C. Synthesis of cytosolic proteins: Carried out by free ribosomes in the cytosol, not affected by RER ribosome reduction.
• D. Synthesis of steroid hormones: Occurs in the smooth ER, which does not require ribosome attachment.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Choose the correct statements about glucokinase. 1. Located in β cells of the pancreas. 2. Has a lower affinity for glucose. 3. Is induced by insulin. 4. Inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate 5. Mutations can lead to MODY.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2, 3, 5

Glucokinase:

• Located in β cells of the pancreas (1): True; glucokinase acts as a glucose sensor in pancreatic β cells and also in hepatocytes.
• Has a lower affinity for glucose (2): True; it has a high Km (\~10 mM), allowing it to respond to high glucose concentrations.
• Is induced by insulin (3): True; insulin upregulates hepatic glucokinase expression.
• Inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate: False; unlike hexokinase, glucokinase is not inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate.
• Mutations can lead to MODY (5): True; GCK mutations cause MODY2, a mild form of diabetes.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Choose the right sequence of steps in the conversion of cholesterol to testosterone:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 20, 22 desmolase, 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase 17 alpha hydroxylase, 17, 20 lyase

The conversion of cholesterol to testosterone occurs in the steroidogenic pathway as follows:

1.  Cholesterol → Pregnenolone by 20, 22 desmolase (cholesterol side-chain cleavage enzyme)

2.  Pregnenolone → Progesterone (Δ⁵ → Δ⁴ isomerization) by 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase

3.  Progesterone → 17-hydroxyprogesterone by 17α-hydroxylase

4.  17-hydroxyprogesterone → Androstenedione/testosterone by 17, 20 lyase

This sequence ensures proper hydroxylation and side-chain cleavage to form C19 androgens like testosterone.

Why other options are incorrect:

B. 3β-HSD before desmolase: Impossible; cholesterol must first be converted to pregnenolone.

D. 17α-hydroxylase before 3β-HSD: The Δ⁵ → Δ⁴ conversion occurs first for proper substrate formation.

Any other sequence: Does not follow the enzymatic order of the steroid biosynthesis pathway

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Chromosome painting is particularly useful for:
options: Identifying cryptic translocations and complex chromosomal rearrangements
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Identifying cryptic translocations and complex chromosomal rearrangements

Chromosome painting uses fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) with chromosome-specific probes to visualize entire chromosomes. It is particularly useful for detecting cryptic translocations, marker chromosomes, and complex structural rearrangements that may be missed on routine karyotyping, especially in cancers and congenital abnormalities.

Why other options are incorrect:

A.  Detecting point mutations in oncogenes: Requires sequencing techniques, not chromosome painting.

C.  Measuring telomerase activity: Assessed by TRAP assay or molecular methods.

D.  Quantifying gene expression levels: Performed using RT-PCR or microarray/RNA-seq techniques.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: CPS1 deficiency presents with hyperammonemia after high-protein intake but without orotic aciduria. OTC deficiency also causes hyperammonemia but with orotic aciduria. Which mechanistic difference directly explains this distinction?
options: CPS1 deficiency increases cytosolic carbamoyl phosphate, flooding pyrimidine synthesis
OTC deficiency causes mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate accumulation that leaks into cytosol, entering the pyrimidine pathway via CPS2
CPS2 is upregulated in CPS1 deficiency, producing excess orotic acid independently
OTC deficiency blocks the urea cycle at argininosuccinate, diverting intermediates to pyrimidine synthesis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. OTC deficiency causes mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate accumulation that leaks into cytosol, entering the pyrimidine pathway via CPS2

In OTC deficiency, carbamoyl phosphate accumulates in mitochondria → leaks into cytosol → enters pyrimidine pathway → excess orotic acid produced → orotic aciduria. In CPS1 deficiency, carbamoyl phosphate is never produced in excess — so nothing leaks. CPS2 (cytosolic) is entirely separate and unaffected.

| Condition | Carbamoyl phosphate | Orotic acid | Ammonia

| --------- | ------------------- | ----------- | -------

| CPS1 deficiency | Not produced (CPS1 absent) | Normal | ↑↑

| OTC deficiency | Accumulates → leaks to cytosol | ↑↑ | ↑↑

| Orotic aciduria (UMP synthase defect) | Normal | ↑↑ | Normal

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Deamination is a spontaneous DNA mutation mechanism. A G-C base pair undergoes deamination of 5-methylcytosine. What is the direct mutagenic consequence if unrepaired before replication?
options: G-C → G-U transition, corrected by uracil-DNA glycosylase
G-C → A-T transition, because 5-methylcytosine deaminates to thymine
G-C → G-C transversion, as methylation protects against deamination products
G-C → C-G inversion, due to strand switching during repair
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. G-C → A-T transition, because 5-methylcytosine deaminates to thymine

• 5-methylcytosine → thymine (via deamination).
• Unlike cytosine → uracil (which is recognized as foreign and removed by UNG), thymine is a normal DNA base — repair machinery does not flag it.
• Thymine pairs with adenine → after replication: original G-C becomes A-T.
• This is the most common point mutation in human cancer (CpG hotspots) and is clinically relevant in p53 mutations in skin cancers (UV-independent pathway).

| Deamination | Product | Repaired? | Mutation if unrepaired

| ----------- | ------- | --------- | ----------------------

| Cytosine → Uracil | Uracil (foreign in DNA) | Yes — UNG removes it | G-C → A-T if missed

| Adenine → Hypoxanthine | Hypoxanthine | Yes — removed | A-T → G-C

| Guanine → Xanthine | Xanthine | Yes — removed | G-C → A-T

| 5-methylcytosine → Thymine | Thymine (normal base) | NOT recognized | G-C → A-T (transition)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: DICER1 mutation-associated tumor syndrome commonly includes all of the following expect:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Retinoblastoma

DICER1 mutation–associated tumor syndrome predisposes to tumors related to abnormal microRNA processing. Common manifestations include Wilms tumor, Sertoli–Leydig cell tumors of the ovary, and multinodular goiter. Retinoblastoma, however, is caused by mutations in the RB1 tumor suppressor gene and is not associated with DICER1 mutations.

Why other options are incorrect:

• A.Wilms tumor: Well-recognized association with DICER1 syndrome.
• B. Sertoli–Leydig cell tumor: Characteristic ovarian tumor in DICER1 mutation carriers.
• C. Multinodular goiter: Common endocrine manifestation of DICER1 syndrome.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: During a cardiovascular physiology experiment, acetylcholine is infused into the coronary circulation of a healthy volunteer. Coronary angiography demonstrates marked dilation of the epicardial coronary arteries. The vasodilatory response is mediated by endothelial release of nitric oxide (NO). Nitric oxide is synthesized from which of the following amino acids?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Arginine

Acetylcholine binds to M3 muscarinic receptors on vascular endothelial cells, stimulating endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS).

eNOS catalyzes the conversion of:

• L-Arginine → Nitric oxide (NO) + L-Citrulline

Nitric oxide then diffuses into adjacent vascular smooth muscle cells, where it:

• Activates guanylyl cyclase
• Increases cyclic GMP (cGMP)
• Reduces intracellular calcium
• Produces vascular smooth muscle relaxation and vasodilation

In individuals with intact endothelium, acetylcholine causes vasodilation. In contrast, in endothelial dysfunction (e.g., atherosclerosis), acetylcholine may paradoxically produce vasoconstriction because NO production is impaired.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• B. Aspartate: Participates in the urea cycle and nucleotide synthesis; it is not a precursor of nitric oxide.
• C. Glutamate: An excitatory neurotransmitter and precursor of GABA; it has no role in NO synthesis in vascular endothelium.
• D. Tryptophan: Precursor of serotonin, melatonin, and niacin, but not nitric oxide.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: During forensic DNA analysis, a double-stranded DNA sample from an unknown source has a melting temperature (Tm) significantly higher than a reference sample of equal length. Which of the following nucleotide-level explanations best accounts for this finding?
options: The unknown sample has a higher A-T content, providing more hydrogen bonds per base pair
The unknown sample has a higher C-G content, as each C-G pair contributes 3 hydrogen bonds versus 2 in A-T pairs
The unknown sample underwent deamination of cytosine to uracil, strengthening base pairing
The unknown sample contains more phosphodiester bonds at the 3'-5' linkage, increasing backbone rigidity
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. The unknown sample has a higher C-G content, as each C-G pair contributes 3 hydrogen bonds versus 2 in A-T pairs

Melting temperature (Tm) = temperature at which 50% of dsDNA is single-stranded. C-G pairs have 3 hydrogen bonds vs A-T pairs with 2. Higher C-G content → more energy required to denature → higher Tm. Deamination of cytosine → uracil actually destabilizes pairing (uracil pairs with A, not G). Phosphodiester bond number is constant per nucleotide regardless of base composition.

| Base pair | H-bonds | Effect on Tm

| --------- | ------- | ------------

| A-T | 2 | Lower Tm

| C-G | 3 | Higher Tm

| ↑ C-G content | More H-bonds | ↑ Tm

| ↑ A-T content | Fewer H-bonds | ↓ Tm

| Deamination C→U | Mismatch risk | Destabilizing

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: During spontaneous DNA damage, 5-methylcytosine can undergo deamination. The resulting base is responsible for one of the most common point mutations in the human genome because it closely resembles a normal DNA base. Which of the following is produced by deamination of 5-methylcytosine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Thymine

Deamination of cytosine vs. 5-methylcytosine

1. Cytosine

• Deamination → Uracil
• Uracil is not a normal DNA base, so it is easily recognized and removed by uracil-DNA glycosylase through the base excision repair (BER) pathway.
• Reaction: Cytosine → Uracil

2. 5-Methylcytosine

• Deamination → Thymine
• Thymine is a normal DNA base, making the mismatch (T–G) much more difficult for the repair machinery to detect.
• If unrepaired, DNA replication converts this mismatch into a C:G → T:A transition mutation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: E. coli colonies grown on a lactose-containing medium up-regulate the production of the enzymes 13-galactosidase and galactoside permease. Which of the following best explains the synchronous production of both enzymes in response to lactose?
options: There are two activator binding sites for one activator protein.
There are two repressors for one inducer.
There are two promoters near each other.
There is one mRNA coding for both enzymes.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. There is one mRNA coding for both enzymes.

The lac operon is a classic example of polycistronic mRNA, where a single mRNA transcript encodes multiple enzymes, including β-galactosidase and galactoside permease. This allows synchronous expression of all enzymes needed to metabolize lactose in response to the inducer.

Why the others are incorrect:

A. Two activator binding sites: Not required; regulation is mainly via the lac repressor and CAP.

B. Two repressors for one inducer: Only the lac repressor regulates operon induction.

C. Two promoters: There is a single promoter driving the polycistronic transcript; multiple promoters are unnecessary for synchronized expression.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Enzyme used in recombinant DNA technology are: 1. Isomerase 2. Phosphatase 3. Terminal transferase 4. Crispr Cas 9
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2, 3, 4

Recombinant DNA (rDNA) technology uses several enzymes to cut, modify, join, and amplify DNA molecules. Among the given options:

• 1. Isomerase ❌

• Isomerases catalyze the rearrangement of molecules within the same compound.
• They do not play a routine role in recombinant DNA technology.

• 2. Phosphatase ✅

• Alkaline phosphatase removes the 5′ phosphate group from vector DNA.
• This prevents the vector from self-ligating, thereby increasing the efficiency of recombinant DNA formation.

• 3. Terminal transferase ✅

• Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) adds nucleotides to the 3′ end of DNA without requiring a template.
• It is used for homopolymer tailing and DNA labeling in molecular biology.

• 4. CRISPR-Cas9 ✅

• Cas9 is an RNA-guided endonuclease that introduces site-specific double-stranded DNA breaks.
• It is widely used for precise genome editing.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Gel filtration chromatography separates molecules mainly based on:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Size

• Large molecules elute first.
• Gel filtration chromatography (also called Size Exclusion Chromatography) separates molecules purely based on molecular size, not charge or polarity.
•

The column contains porous beads:

•

Large molecules cannot enter the pores → they take a shorter path → elute first.

• Small molecules enter deep into the pores → get delayed → elute last.

→ Separation = inverse of size

→ Big = fast

→ Small = slow

Why other options are incorrect:

• A. Polarity: Separation by polarity is characteristic of normal-phase chromatography.
• B. Charge: Ion-exchange chromatography separates molecules based on charge.
• D. pKa: pKa influences ionization, not size-exclusion separation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Gene repair by CRISPR-Cas9 can occur by all of the following methods except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mismatch repair

CRISPR-Cas9 introduces double-strand breaks (DSBs) in DNA. The cell repairs these DSBs via:

• Non-homologous end joining (NHEJ): Direct ligation of DNA ends; often error-prone.
• Microhomology-mediated end joining (MMEJ): Uses short homologous sequences to repair DSBs.
• Single-strand annealing (SSA): Uses repeated sequences flanking the break to repair.

Mismatch repair (MMR), on the other hand, corrects base mispairings after DNA replication and does not repair DSBs, so it is not used in CRISPR-Cas9–mediated gene editing.

Why other options are incorrect:

• A. NHEJ, B. MMEJ, D. SSA: All are DSB repair pathways actively exploited in CRISPR gene editing.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Identify the correct statements 1. Urinary levels of 3-methylhistidine are high in patients with Wilson disease. 2. Hyaluronic acid is the longest GAG 3. Keratan sulfate is the only GAG without uronic acid 4. Heparan sulfate is a major component of the glomerular basement membrane (GBM).
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2, 3, 4

• Hyaluronic acid is the longest GAG (2): True; it is a non-sulfated glycosaminoglycan with very high molecular weight.

• Keratan sulfate is the only GAG without uronic acid (3): True; its repeating units contain galactose and N-acetylglucosamine instead of uronic acids.

• Heparan sulfate is a major component of GBM (4): True; it contributes to the negative charge and selective filtration in the glomerular basement membrane.

Why the other option is incorrect:

Urinary 3-methylhistidine in Wilson disease (1): False; elevated urinary 3-methylhistidine indicates muscle protein breakdown, the levels are decreased in Wilson disease.This specific reduction, noted alongside other amino acids like 1-methylhistidine and taurine, generally stems from the broader metabolic alterations and generalized aminoaciduria that commonly present in Wilson disease.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Identify the correct statements: 1. Glucagon challenge test can be used to distinguish Von Gierke’s disease and Cori’s disease. 2. Choline should be avoided by patients with trimethylaminuria. 3. Oculocutaneous albinism type 1 (tyrosinase deficiency) is AR. 4. Creatine is synthesized from glycine, arginine and methionine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3, 4

• Glucagon challenge test: True; it distinguishes Von Gierke’s disease (G6Pase deficiency, impaired response) from Cori’s disease (debranching enzyme deficiency, normal response).

• Choline in trimethylaminuria: True; dietary choline increases trimethylamine production and should be limited.

• Oculocutaneous albinism type 1: True; caused by tyrosinase deficiency and inherited in an autosomal recessive manner.

• Creatine synthesis: True; creatine is synthesized from glycine, arginine, and methionine (methionine provides methyl group via SAM).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Identify the incorrect pair of UV absorption wavelength with respective compound:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Porphyrins - 200 nm

Porphyrins have a strong Soret band around 400–420 nm, not 200 nm. This allows their detection and quantification in biochemical assays.

Why other options are correct:

A. Tryptophan – 280 nm: True; aromatic amino acids absorb strongly around 280 nm.

B. Nucleic acids – 260 nm: True; nucleobases absorb UV light maximally at 260 nm.

C. NADH/NADPH – 340 nm: True; reduced forms of nicotinamide coenzymes absorb at 340 nm.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: If there are 4 consecutive nucleotides code for an amino acid. Then how many amino acid can be coded by nucleic acid?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 256

Each nucleotide in DNA or RNA can be one of 4 bases (A, T/U, G, C). If 4 consecutive nucleotides code for one amino acid, the total number of possible combinations is: 4⁴ = 256 different codons can theoretically code for amino acids.

Why the others are incorrect:

B. 64: This is the number of codons if 3 nucleotides per amino acid (standard genetic code: 4³ = 64).

C. 16: Would be 2 nucleotides per amino acid (4² = 16).

D. 4: Only 1 nucleotide per amino acid (4¹ = 4).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In an animal experiment, mice proerythroblasts are cultured in 2 different growth media; the first medium is folate deficient, whereas the second (control) is supplemented with folic acid. Both media contain high concentrations of erythropoietin. Over 48 hours, cells in the control media proliferate and differentiate into reticulocytes, whereas in the folate-deficient media, cell proliferation is minimal, with most cells undergoing apoptosis. In another experiment, a substance is added to the folate-deficient media, which prevents apoptosis and permits proliferation of the proerythroblasts. Which of the following is the most likely substance added to the growth medium?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Thymidine

Folate deficiency impairs thymidylate (dTMP) synthesis, leading to inability to synthesize DNA, cell cycle arrest, and apoptosis in rapidly dividing proerythroblasts. Supplementing thymidine, a pyrimidine nucleoside, bypasses the block in DNA synthesis, allowing DNA replication and proliferation even without folate.

Why the others are incorrect:

A. Cobalamin (Vitamin B12): Required for folate recycling, but supplementation alone cannot bypass dTMP deficiency.

B. Cytosine: A nucleobase that cannot be directly incorporated into DNA; does not rescue proliferation.

C. Homocysteine: Accumulates in folate deficiency; adding it does not restore DNA synthesis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In an electron transport system, which part will be the last to get electrons?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. O2

In the electron transport chain (ETC), electrons flow from NADH and FADH₂ → Complex I/II → Coenzyme Q → Complex III → Cytochrome C → Complex IV and finally to molecular oxygen (O₂), which acts as the terminal electron acceptor. Oxygen is reduced to water, completing the chain.

Why other options are incorrect:

• A. Coenzyme Q: Accepts electrons early from Complex I and II, not last.
• B. FADH₂: Donates electrons to Complex II, entering the chain before CoQ.
• D. Cytochrome C: Transfers electrons from Complex III to Complex IV; still before O₂.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In Lyonization (X-inactivation), which combination of chromatin-level events maintains the transcriptionally silent X chromosome as a Barr body?
options: Histone deacetylation + CpG island methylation + H3K27 trimethylation
H1 removal + histone acetylation + euchromatin formation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Histone deacetylation + CpG island methylation + H3K27 trimethylation

• Barr body = heterochromatin.
•

Maintained by:

•

CpG hypermethylation silencing promoters

• Histone deacetylation → condensation
•

H3K27me3 via PRC2/EZH2 — repressive Polycomb mark.

•

XIST RNA coats the inactive X and recruits these silencing complexes.

• H3K4me3 and acetylation are active/euchromatin marks — the exact opposite.

| Feature | Active X | Inactive X (Barr body)

| ------- | -------- | ----------------------

| DNA methylation | Low | High (CpG methylated)

| Histone acetylation | High | Low

| H3K4me3 | Present | Absent

| H3K27me3 | Absent | Present (PRC2)

| XIST RNA | Absent | Coats chromosome

| Chromatin type | Euchromatin | Heterochromatin

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Lorenzo oil is used in the treatment of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Adrenoleukodystrophy

Lorenzo’s oil is a mixture of oleic acid and erucic acid used to treat X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD). It works by inhibiting the synthesis of very long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs), which accumulate in ALD and cause demyelination of the CNS and adrenal insufficiency. Early use can slow disease progression in asymptomatic patients.

Why the others are incorrect:

A. Fabry’s disease: Treated with enzyme replacement therapy for α-galactosidase A deficiency.

C. Hurler’s disease: Managed with enzyme replacement or hematopoietic stem cell transplant for α-L-iduronidase deficiency.

D. Gaucher disease: Treated with glucocerebrosidase enzyme replacement or substrate reduction therapy

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Nutrition researchers investigating the relationship between fructose consumption and cardiovascular disease conduct a prospective cohortstudy on a population of randomly selected young adults. Study participants undergo semi-annual measurement of waist circumference, blood pressure, and serum cholesterol and triglyceride concentrations. Dietary fructose consumption is assessed through the use of questionnaires and by measuring urinary fructose excretion. A 23-year-old man enrolled in the study is found to excrete large amounts of fructose in his urine compared to other study participants despite maintaining a moderate fructose intake. Further evaluation shows a hereditary defect in fructose metabolism, but he is asymptomatic and has no other medical problems. This patient most likely remains able to metabolize fructose due to the compensatory activity of which of the following enzymes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hexokinase

This question describes essential fructosuria, a benign condition due to fructokinase deficiency.

• Normal fructose metabolism:

• Fructose → (fructokinase) → fructose-1-phosphate → (aldolase B) → glycolytic intermediates

• In fructokinase deficiency:

• Fructose is not trapped in liver cells → spills into blood → fructosuria
• Patient remains asymptomatic

• Why hexokinase compensates:

• Hexokinase can phosphorylate fructose → fructose-6-phosphate
• Enters glycolysis directly
• Though low affinity, it is sufficient to prevent toxicity

• Key differentiation:

• Essential fructosuria (fructokinase deficiency) → benign
• Hereditary fructose intolerance (aldolase B deficiency) → severe, hypoglycemia, liver damage

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Regarding alternative splicing of pre-mRNA, consider the following statements: 1. It allows a single gene to give rise to multiple protein isoforms. 2. The calcitonin/CGRP gene is a classic example, producing calcitonin in thyroid C-cells and CGRP in neurons. 3. It occurs in the nucleus and is carried out by the spliceosome. 4. It increases the coding capacity of the genome without increasing the number of genes. Which of the above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, 3 and 4

Distractor-by-distractor analysis:

• Statement 1. It allows a single gene to give rise to multiple protein isoforms: True. Different combinations of exons are retained or excluded, so one gene → several mRNAs → several protein isoforms. This is the core definition.
• Statement 2. The calcitonin/CGRP gene is a classic example, producing calcitonin in thyroid C-cells and CGRP in neurons: True. The single CALC I gene is the textbook example. Tissue-specific splicing yields calcitonin in thyroid parafollicular (C) cells and CGRP (calcitonin gene-related peptide) in neural tissue. This exact example is the most frequently tested instance in PG entrances — worth memorizing as the go-to answer.
• Statement 3. It occurs in the nucleus and is carried out by the spliceosome: True. Splicing is a nuclear, co-/post-transcriptional event performed by the spliceosome (snRNPs: U1, U2, U4, U5, U6). Regulation is via cis elements (splice enhancers/silencers) and trans factors (SR proteins, hnRNPs).
• Statement 4. It increases the coding capacity of the genome without increasing the number of genes: True. This explains the "proteome > genome" paradox — humans have \~20,000 genes but a far larger proteome, largely because of alternative splicing.

High-yield pearls to attach in the bank:

• Other classic examples: tropomyosin, immunoglobulin heavy chain (membrane-bound vs secreted forms), and Dscam (extreme diversity).
• Disease link — splice-site mutations cause β-thalassemia; SMN1/SMN2 splicing underlies spinal muscular atrophy (basis of nusinersen therapy).
• Common trap: alternative splicing is distinct from RNA editing (e.g., apolipoprotein B — C→U deamination creating a stop codon). Examiners love pairing these two as distractors.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Researchers are working to identify new targets for drug development to treat idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. After obtaining lung tissue samples from affected patients, they conduct a series of experiments to measure the expression and activity of various profibrotic proteins. The results for one such protein, galectin-3, are as follows: mRNA concentration: Normal Protein concentration: Increased Protein activity: Intact Which of the following processes best explains these findings?
options: Mutation in the Galectin-3 promoter region
Decreased methylation of the Galectin-3 gene
Shortening of the Galectin-3 mRNA poly-(A) tail
Decreased ubiquitination of the Galectin-3 protein
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Decreased ubiquitination of the Galectin-3 protein

The patient’s lung tissue shows normal galectin-3 mRNA but increased protein levels with intact activity, indicating that transcription is normal but protein degradation is reduced. Ubiquitination tags proteins for proteasomal degradation, so decreased ubiquitination stabilizes galectin-3, leading to higher protein levels without changing mRNA or activity.

Why the others are incorrect:

A. Mutation in the Galectin-3 promoter region: Would increase mRNA expression, which is normal here.

B. Decreased methylation of the Galectin-3 gene: Typically increases transcription, raising mRNA levels, not observed.

C. Shortening of the Galectin-3 mRNA poly-(A) tail: Usually reduces mRNA stability, leading to lower protein, opposite of what is seen.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: RNA produced from a fragment of DNA has the sequence of UAAGGC. The sequence of the non-template strand in the DNA that gave rise to this sequence is which one of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. TAAGGC

During transcription:

• RNA is synthesized complementary to the DNA template strand.
• The non-template (coding) strand has the same sequence as the RNA, except T replaces U.
• Given RNA: UAAGGC
• Replace U → T for DNA: TAAGGC

This corresponds to the non-template (coding) strand.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. CGGAAT: Complement of RNA; this is the template strand, not the coding strand.

B. UAAGGC: This is RNA, not DNA.

D. ATTCCG: Incorrect; the first base should be T → matches U in RNA.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: SARS CoV-2 diagnosis is done by all except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Southern blotting

SARS-CoV-2 diagnosis relies on detection of viral RNA or viral antigens/antibodies:

• RT-PCR / Real-time PCR: Detect viral RNA with high sensitivity; gold standard for diagnosis.
• Immunoassays: Detect viral antigens (rapid tests) or host antibodies against the virus.
• Southern blotting, however, detects DNA sequences and is not used for RNA viruses like SARS-CoV-2.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. RT-PCR & B. Real-time PCR: Standard methods for RNA detection.

D. Immunoassays: Widely used for serological testing or rapid antigen detection.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Selenocysteine is present in which of the following enzymes? 1. Glutathione reductase 2. Glutathione peroxidase 3. Thioredoxine peroxidase 4. Thioredoxine reductase 5. Iodothyronine deiodinase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2, 4, 5

Selenocysteine is the 21st amino acid, incorporated into enzymes that require selenium for redox activity. Among the listed enzymes:

• Glutathione peroxidase (2): Contains selenocysteine at the active site, catalyzing reduction of peroxides.
• Thioredoxin reductase (4): Uses selenocysteine to maintain redox homeostasis.
• Iodothyronine deiodinase (5): Contains selenocysteine for thyroid hormone activation/inactivation.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Glutathione reductase (1): Uses FAD, does not contain selenocysteine.
• Thioredoxin peroxidase (3): Typically uses cysteine, not selenocysteine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Serotonin production involves:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hydroxylation -> Decarboxylation of tryptophan

Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine, 5-HT) is synthesized from tryptophan in two main steps:

1.  Hydroxylation: Tryptophan is converted to 5-hydroxytryptophan by tryptophan hydroxylase (rate-limiting step; requires tetrahydrobiopterin as a cofactor).

2.  Decarboxylation: 5-hydroxytryptophan is then decarboxylated by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase to form serotonin.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Carboxylation → Hydroxylation / B. Hydroxylation → Carboxylation / D. Decarboxylation → Hydroxylation: These sequences are biochemically incorrect; serotonin biosynthesis does not involve carboxylation of tryptophan.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The 5’ cap of eukaryotic mRNA consists of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 7-methylguanosine linked via 5’→5’ triphosphate bond

The 5’ cap of eukaryotic mRNA is formed by addition of 7-methylguanosine to the 5’ end of the transcript through an unusual 5’→5’ triphosphate linkage. This cap protects mRNA from exonuclease degradation, facilitates nuclear export, and is essential for ribosome binding and translation initiation via cap-binding proteins.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. 3-methyladenosine: 3-methyladenosine is not a component of the mRNA cap.

C. 7-methyladenosine linked via 3’→5’ bond: The cap is guanosine, not adenosine, and linkage is not 3’→5’.

D. 3-methyluridine: 3-methyluridine is unrelated to mRNA capping.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The attachment of Eukaryotic mRNA to the ribosome initiation factor is mediated through:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 5’methylGuanyl Cap

In eukaryotes, the 5′ cap (7-methylguanosine) of mRNA is recognized by eukaryotic initiation factors (eIFs), which mediate the attachment of the mRNA to the ribosome. This cap-dependent mechanism ensures proper ribosome binding and scanning for the start codon (AUG).

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Poly-A tail: Stabilizes mRNA and aids in nuclear export but does not directly mediate ribosome attachment.

B. tRNA: Delivers amino acids during elongation, not involved in ribosome binding of mRNA.

D. Shine-Dalgarno sequence: Found in prokaryotic mRNA, aligns ribosome with start codon; absent in eukaryotes.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The base sequence of the strand of DNA used as the template for transcription has the base sequence GATCTAC. What is the base sequence of RNA product?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. GUAGAUC

During transcription, RNA is synthesized complementary to the DNA template strand and in the 5′ → 3′ direction.

• DNA template strand: GATCTAC (5′ → 3′)
• RNA transcript: GAUCUAC (5′ → 3′), complementary to the DNA template (A → U, T → A, G → C, C → G).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The enzyme that is not used in cholesterol synthesis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. HMG CoA lyase

Cholesterol synthesis occurs in the cytosol and ER and proceeds via formation of HMG-CoA, which is then reduced to mevalonate. HMG-CoA lyase is not involved in cholesterol synthesis; instead, it functions in ketone body synthesis, where it cleaves HMG-CoA to acetoacetate and acetyl-CoA in liver mitochondria.

Why other options are incorrect:

• A. Thiolase: Catalyzes condensation of acetyl-CoA molecules in early cholesterol synthesis.
• B. HMG-CoA reductase: Rate-limiting enzyme converting HMG-CoA to mevalonate.
• C. HMG-CoA synthase: Required to form HMG-CoA from acetyl-CoA and acetoacetyl-CoA.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The sequence of vitamin D synthesis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Skin - Liver - Kidney

The synthesis of vitamin D follows the sequence of Skin → Liver → Kidney, with each organ playing a critical role in converting the precursor to its active form.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: This tissue has the highest concentration of lipoprotein lipase. Identify this tissue:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cardiac muscle

During prolonged fasting, cardiac muscle preferentially uses fatty acids for energy because it has high concentrations of lipoprotein lipase (LPL), which hydrolyzes circulating triglycerides into free fatty acids for uptake. Fatty acids are an efficient fuel for the heart, providing sustained energy without relying on glucose.

Why the others are incorrect:

A. Adipose tissue: Mainly stores fat; it releases fatty acids during fasting but does not use them preferentially for energy.

B. Skeletal muscle: Uses both glucose and fatty acids, but cardiac muscle oxidizes fatty acids more efficiently.

C. Liver: Primarily performs gluconeogenesis and ketone body production; it does not rely on fatty acid oxidation for its own energy.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is allosteric activator of Pyruvate carboxylase?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acetyl CoA

Pyruvate carboxylase is a biotin-dependent mitochondrial enzyme that catalyzes the first committed step of gluconeogenesis:

Reaction:

Pyruvate + CO₂ + ATP → Oxaloacetate + ADP + Pi

The enzyme is allosterically activated by acetyl-CoA.

Why Acetyl-CoA?

• High levels of acetyl-CoA indicate that fatty acid β-oxidation is active.
• This signals that energy is abundant and that pyruvate should be diverted toward gluconeogenesis rather than entering the TCA cycle.
• Acetyl-CoA therefore activates pyruvate carboxylase, increasing the formation of oxaloacetate (OAA).

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Insulin ❌

• Insulin promotes glycolysis and glycogen synthesis while inhibiting gluconeogenesis.
• It does not allosterically activate pyruvate carboxylase.

• C. AMP ❌

• AMP is a marker of low cellular energy.
• It inhibits gluconeogenesis (notably fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase) and stimulates glycolysis.

• D. ADP ❌

• ADP also reflects a low-energy state.
• It inhibits several ATP-dependent steps of gluconeogenesis, including pyruvate carboxylase activity indirectly by signaling energy deficiency.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: When pKa = pH
options: Conc. Of drug is 50% ionic and 50% non ionic
Absorption of drug is 50% in ionic form and 50% non ionic
Conc. of drug is 75% ionic and 25% non ionic
Conc. of drug is 25% ionic and 75% non ionic
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Conc. Of drug is 50% ionic and 50% non ionic

According to the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation, when pH = pKa, the ratio of ionized to unionized drug is 1:1. This means 50% of the drug exists in its ionic form and 50% in its non-ionic (unionized) form, which is critical for drug absorption since unionized drugs cross membranes more easily.

Why the others are incorrect:

B. 50% absorption in ionic and non-ionic form: Absorption depends on unionized fraction, not directly 50/50.

C. 75% ionic / 25% non-ionic or D. 25% ionic / 75% non-ionic: These occur only when pH differs from pKa by ±0.5–1 units, not when pH = pKa.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which among the following are appropriate techniques for chromosomal aneuploidy? A. Fluorescence In Situ hybridization B. Conventional Cytogenetics C. PCR D. Sanger sequence
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A, B

Chromosomal aneuploidy refers to an abnormal number of chromosomes (e.g., trisomy 21, trisomy 18, trisomy 13, monosomy X). Techniques used to detect aneuploidy assess chromosome number or large chromosomal abnormalities.

• Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) is a rapid technique that uses fluorescent DNA probes to detect specific chromosomes or chromosomal regions. It is commonly used for the rapid diagnosis of common aneuploidies (13, 18, 21, X, and Y).
• Conventional cytogenetics (karyotyping) remains the gold standard for detecting whole-chromosome aneuploidies and large structural chromosomal abnormalities.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• C. PCR: Conventional PCR amplifies DNA sequences but does not determine chromosome number. (Specialized quantitative PCR-based methods exist, but routine PCR is not used for aneuploidy detection.)
• D. Sanger sequencing: Detects nucleotide sequence changes (point mutations and small insertions/deletions), not changes in chromosome number.

High-yield comparison

| Technique | Detects aneuploidy? | Primary use

| --------- | ------------------- | -----------

| FISH | ✅ Yes | Rapid detection of common aneuploidies and selected microdeletions

| Conventional cytogenetics (Karyotyping) | ✅ Yes | Aneuploidy and large structural chromosomal abnormalities

| PCR | ❌ No | Detection of specific gene mutations or pathogens

| Sanger sequencing | ❌ No | Single-gene disorders, point mutations, and small indels

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which clinical feature helps distinguish Refsum disease from Zellweger syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Retinitis pigmentosa

Refsum disease classically presents with retinitis pigmentosa, peripheral neuropathy, cerebellar ataxia, and hearing loss due to phytanic acid accumulation, while neonatal presentation is absent. In contrast, Zellweger syndrome presents in the neonatal period with hypotonia, seizures, craniofacial dysmorphism, and early death, and retinal changes are not a defining early feature. Thus, retinitis pigmentosa helps distinguish Refsum disease from Zellweger syndrome.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Hearing loss: Seen in Refsum disease but not exclusive.

C. Neonatal hypotonia: Typical of Zellweger, not Refsum.

D. Craniofacial dysmorphism: Characteristic of Zellweger syndrome.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which component of fiber delays gastric emptying and reduces cholesterol absorption?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pectin

Pectin is a soluble dietary fiber that forms a viscous gel in the gastrointestinal tract. This gel delays gastric emptying, slows intestinal transit, and binds bile acids, leading to increased bile excretion and reduced cholesterol absorption. These properties help lower LDL cholesterol and improve postprandial glycemic control.

Why other options are incorrect:

B. Cellulose: An insoluble fiber that mainly increases stool bulk without affecting cholesterol absorption.

C. Hemicellulose: Primarily insoluble with limited effect on gastric emptying or bile binding.

D. Lignin: Insoluble and non-fermentable; does not significantly reduce cholesterol absorption.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which end product/intermediate of the citric acid cycle is utilized in the detoxification of ammonia in the brain?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. α-Ketoglutarate

In the brain, detoxification of ammonia occurs primarily via conversion of glutamate to glutamine, a reaction catalyzed by glutamine synthetase.

• α-Ketoglutarate (TCA cycle intermediate) plays a central role:

• It is transaminated to form glutamate
• Glutamate then combines with ammonia → glutamine (non-toxic form)

• Thus, α-ketoglutarate acts as the key acceptor of ammonia, indirectly facilitating its detoxification

Pathophysiological relevance:

• Excess ammonia → drives conversion of α-ketoglutarate → glutamate → glutamine
• This depletes α-ketoglutarate, impairing the TCA cycle and ATP production in neurons
• Leads to cerebral edema and encephalopathy

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which gene is not involved in double strand DNA break repair mechanism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. MuTL

Double-strand DNA break (DSB) repair is mediated by homologous recombination (HR) and non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) pathways. MRE11 is part of the MRN complex involved in sensing and processing DSBs. BRCA1 plays a crucial role in homologous recombination repair by facilitating end resection. KU80 is a key component of the NHEJ pathway, binding DNA ends. MutL, however, is involved in DNA mismatch repair, not in double-strand break repair.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. MRE11: Essential for DSB recognition and end processing.

B. BRCA1: Central to homologous recombination repair.

C. KU80: Required for non-homologous end joining.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which is correct about isoenzymes?
options: Cannot be separated from each other on Electrophoresis.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Catalyse the same reaction.

Isoenzymes (isozymes) are different molecular forms of an enzyme that catalyze the same chemical reaction but may differ in amino acid sequence, kinetic properties, regulatory features, or tissue distribution. This allows fine-tuning of metabolism in different tissues or under different physiological conditions.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Same action with similar kinetics: False; isoenzymes often have different Km, Vmax, or regulatory properties.

B. Same quaternary structure: False; isoenzymes may have different subunit composition.

D. Cannot be separated on electrophoresis: False; isoenzymes can often be separated based on charge or size using electrophoresis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which methods among the following can identify changes in the DNA sequence? 1.Restriction fragment length analysis 2.Flow cytometry 3.Pyrosequencing 4.FISH
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 and 3

Changes in the DNA sequence can be detected by:

• Restriction fragment length analysis, which identifies sequence variations that create or abolish restriction sites.
• Pyrosequencing, a DNA sequencing method that directly determines the nucleotide sequence, allowing mutation detection.

Why the others are incorrect:

2. Flow cytometry: Analyzes cell size, granularity, and protein expression; it does not detect DNA sequence changes.

4. FISH (Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization): Detects large chromosomal abnormalities or specific DNA regions but cannot identify small sequence changes.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following acts as an RNA-directed nuclease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. CRISPR-Cas9

The CRISPR-Cas9 system uses a guide RNA to direct the Cas9 nuclease to a specific DNA sequence, allowing targeted cleavage. Although Cas9 itself is a DNA endonuclease, its activity is RNA-directed, meaning the RNA sequence determines where the nuclease cuts. This mechanism underlies gene editing and genome engineering applications.

Why the others are incorrect:

B. S1 nuclease: Cleaves single-stranded DNA or RNA but is not guided by RNA.

C. Primase: Synthesizes RNA primers for DNA replication; it does not cleave nucleic acids.

D. Telomerase: Adds repetitive DNA sequences to chromosome ends using its RNA template, but it functions as a reverse transcriptase, not an RNA-directed nuclease.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following are vitamin B12-dependent enzymes? 1. Methyl malonyl CoA mutase 2. Homocysteine synthase 3. Propionyl CoA carboxylase 4. Methionine synthase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 and 4 only

Vitamin B₁₂ (cobalamin) is required as a cofactor for two key enzymes in human metabolism. Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA in odd-chain fatty acid and amino acid metabolism. Methionine synthase catalyzes the remethylation of homocysteine to methionine, linking B₁₂ deficiency to hyperhomocysteinemia and megaloblastic anemia.

Why other options are incorrect:

2. Homocysteine synthase: Not a human enzyme; homocysteine is remethylated by methionine synthase.

3. Propionyl-CoA carboxylase: Biotin-dependent, not B₁₂-dependent.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the amphibolic nature of the citric acid cycle?
options: It generates ATP and produces citrate for fatty acid synthesis.
It exclusively produces NADH for oxidative phosphorylation.
It breaks down fatty acids and synthesises only cholesterol.
It provides intermediates solely for glucose synthesis.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It generates ATP and produces citrate for fatty acid synthesis.

The citric acid (TCA) cycle is amphibolic because it serves both catabolic and anabolic roles. Catabolically, it oxidizes acetyl-CoA to generate NADH, FADH₂, and GTP (ATP equivalent) for energy production. Anabolically, intermediates are withdrawn for biosynthesis—most notably citrate, which is exported to the cytosol and used for fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis.

Why other options are incorrect:

B. It exclusively produces NADH for oxidative phosphorylation: The TCA cycle does more than produce NADH; it also supplies anabolic intermediates.

C. It breaks down fatty acids and synthesises only cholesterol: Fatty acid breakdown occurs via β-oxidation, not the TCA cycle.

D. It provides intermediates solely for glucose synthesis: TCA intermediates contribute to multiple pathways, not only gluconeogenesis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following causes the inactivation of acetyl-CoA carboxylase?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Phosphorylation

Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) is the rate-limiting enzyme of fatty acid synthesis, converting acetyl-CoA → malonyl-CoA. Phosphorylation by AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) inactivates ACC, decreasing fatty acid synthesis during low-energy states.

Why other options are incorrect:

• B. Insulin: Activates ACC by stimulating dephosphorylation, promoting fatty acid synthesis.
• C. High levels of citrate: Allosterically activate ACC, counteracting phosphorylation.
• D. Dephosphorylation: Activates ACC, not inactivates it.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following does not happen in 5' to 3' direction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. RNA editing

RNA editing refers to post-transcriptional modification of RNA bases (e.g., A→I or C→U changes) and does not involve directional chain synthesis. Therefore, it does not proceed in a defined 5′→3′ direction like nucleic acid synthesis processes.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Transcription: RNA is synthesized 5′→3′ by RNA polymerase.

B. DNA replication: DNA polymerases add nucleotides only in the 5′→3′ direction.

C. DNA repair: Although excision occurs first, the resynthesis step by DNA polymerase still proceeds 5′→3′.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following does not require 5' capping?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. tRNA of Alanine

5′ capping (addition of 7-methylguanosine) occurs on RNA polymerase II transcripts, mainly mRNA and some small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs) like U1, U2, U4, U5, to:

• Protect RNA from degradation
• Facilitate nuclear export
• Promote translation initiation

tRNAs are transcribed by RNA polymerase III and instead undergo processing and modification at their ends, not 5′ capping. Similarly, siRNAs are processed from double-stranded RNA and do not require 5′ caps. Histone mRNAs are an exception; they have a special 3′ stem-loop instead of a poly-A tail, but still receive a 5′ cap.

Why other options are incorrect:

B. U6 snRNA: Does not get a 7-methylguanosine cap, but it is transcribed by RNA polymerase III; still small nuclear RNA function.

C. mRNA for histone/any protein, including ApoB-100: 5′ capping occurs even for histone mRNAs..

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following enzymes is produced in increased amounts than normal in the liver of a patient with lead toxicity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. ALA synthase

In lead poisoning, lead inhibits ferrochelatase and ALA dehydratase, leading to a decreased production of heme. As a compensatory response, the liver upregulates ALA synthase, the rate-limiting enzyme of heme synthesis, to try to restore heme levels. This results in accumulation of ALA and protoporphyrin, causing the biochemical and clinical manifestations of lead toxicity.

Why other options are incorrect?

• B. Heme oxygenase: Breaks down heme; not induced by lead toxicity.
• C. Ferrochelatase: Directly inhibited by lead, so activity decreases.
• D. Porphobilinogen deaminase: Activity is not increased in lead poisoning; defects in this enzyme cause acute intermittent porphyria, not lead toxicity.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following enzymes will show reduced activity in a person who is fasting?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Phosphofructokinase-2

During fasting, glucagon signaling leads to activation of cAMP-dependent protein kinase, which phosphorylates PFK-2, converting it into a fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase-active form. This reduces PFK-2 activity, lowering fructose-2,6-bisphosphate levels. Since fructose-2,6-bisphosphate is an allosteric activator of PFK-1, glycolysis is suppressed and gluconeogenesis is favored.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase: Activity actually increases during fasting to promote gluconeogenesis.

B. Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase: Activity increases during fasting to drive gluconeogenesis.

C. Pyruvate carboxylase: Activity increases to supply oxaloacetate for gluconeogenesis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is correct about monoclonal antibody production by hybridoma technique? 1. Antibody-producing B-lymphocytes are fused with immortal myeloma cell lines from mice 2. HAT medium contains Hypoxanthine-Aminopterin-Thymidine 3. HAT medium inhibits conversion of T->U 4. HGPRT is deficient is myeloma cells
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2, 4

In the hybridoma technique, antibody-producing B lymphocytes from an immunized mouse are fused with immortal myeloma cells to form hybridomas (Statement 1 true). Selection is done using HAT medium (Hypoxanthine-Aminopterin-Thymidine) (Statement 2 true). Myeloma cells are HGPRT-deficient, so they cannot survive in HAT medium unless fused with B cells (Statement 4 true).

Why other options are incorrect:

Statement 3: Aminopterin blocks U -> T, not otherwise.

Options including statement 3 are therefore incorrect.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is false regarding eukaryotic initiation?
options: Kozak sequence assists ribosomal scanning for AUG.
eIF4A helicase unwinds secondary RNA structures.
43S complex interacts with 5’ cap through eIF4E.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Formyl-methionine initiates protein synthesis

In eukaryotic initiation, translation begins with methionine, not formyl-methionine (fMet). fMet is a characteristic feature of prokaryotic translation, where it is used to initiate protein synthesis on bacterial ribosomes. Eukaryotes rely on a cap-dependent scanning mechanism and multiple initiation factors, without formylation of the initiator methionine.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Kozak sequence assists ribosomal scanning for AUG: True; it helps identify the AUG start codon.

B. eIF4A helicase unwinds secondary RNA structures: True; it removes secondary structures in 5′ UTR.

C. 43S complex interacts with 5′ cap via eIF4E: True; eIF4E binds the cap to recruit ribosomes.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is false regarding jaundice?
options: Urobilinogen is usually increased in hemolytic jaundice
Urine bilirubin is absent in hemolytic jaundice.
Crigler-Najjar syndrome presents with unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia
Obstructive jaundice shows a negative Van der Bergh reaction
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Obstructive jaundice shows a negative Van der Bergh reaction

The Van der Bergh reaction detects conjugated bilirubin. In obstructive (post-hepatic) jaundice, conjugated bilirubin accumulates in blood and urine, giving a positive Van der Bergh reaction. A negative reaction would be incorrect.

Why the others are correct:

A. Urobilinogen increased in hemolytic jaundice: Hemolysis increases unconjugated bilirubin, which is partially converted to urobilinogen in the intestine.

B. Urine bilirubin absent in hemolytic jaundice: Unconjugated bilirubin is not water-soluble, so it is not excreted in urine.

C. Crigler-Najjar syndrome: Causes unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia due to UDP-glucuronyl transferase deficiency.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is most directly responsible for triplex DNA formation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hoogsteen pairing

Triplex DNA forms when a third strand of DNA binds to the major groove of a double-stranded DNA through Hoogsteen hydrogen bonds. This usually occurs in polypurine–polypyrimidine regions, allowing the third strand to bind parallel or antiparallel to the purine-rich strand. Hoogsteen pairing is the specific hydrogen-bonding mechanism that stabilizes triplex formation.

Why the others are incorrect:

B. Palindromic sequences: Facilitate hairpin or cruciform structures, not triplex DNA.

C. Large number of guanosine repeats: Can form G-quadruplexes, not classical triplex DNA.

D. Polypyrimidine tracts: Often present in triplex-prone regions but do not directly cause triplex formation; Hoogsteen pairing is required for stabilization.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is not an amino acid-derived neurotransmitter?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Creatine

Creatine is not a neurotransmitter; it is a molecule involved in energy storage in muscles and the brain (as phosphocreatine) and does not act as a signaling molecule.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Melatonin: Derived from tryptophan (amino acid) and acts as a neurohormone/neurotransmitter regulating circadian rhythms.

B. Serotonin: Synthesized from tryptophan and functions as a classical neurotransmitter.

C. GABA: Synthesized from glutamate (an amino acid) and is the major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is not used for protein precipitation?
options: Change in pH other than isoelectric pH
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Change in pH other than isoelectric pH

Protein precipitation occurs most efficiently at the isoelectric pH (pI), where the net charge on the protein is zero, minimizing electrostatic repulsion and promoting aggregation. Changing the pH away from the isoelectric point increases the net charge on proteins, enhancing solubility rather than causing precipitation. Hence, pH changes other than pI are not useful for protein precipitation.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Heavy metals: Form insoluble complexes with proteins, causing precipitation.

B. Organic solvents: Reduce hydration shell and dielectric constant, leading to precipitation.

D. Trichloroacetic acid: A strong acid commonly used to precipitate proteins by denaturation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is the earliest sign of riboflavin deficiency?
options: Proliferation of the bulbar conjunctival capillaries
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Proliferation of the bulbar conjunctival capillaries

Riboflavin (vitamin B₂) deficiency initially affects rapidly dividing epithelial tissues and the eyes. The earliest clinical sign is dilatation and proliferation of bulbar conjunctival capillaries, giving a bloodshot appearance. This occurs before more obvious mucocutaneous manifestations and reflects impaired flavoprotein-dependent oxidative reactions.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Cheilosis: Occurs later as part of angular stomatitis.

B. Glossitis: A later mucosal manifestation of riboflavin deficiency.

C. Seborrheic dermatitis: Develops in more advanced deficiency, not an early sign.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is true about Hemochromatosis?
options: The mRNA for Transferrin receptor is stabilised by binding of IRP to 3’ stem-loop structures known as IRE.
The mRNA for the Transferrin receptor is not bound by IRP and is rapidly degraded.
The mRNA for apoferritin is not bound by IRP at 5’ stem loop IRE and is rapidly degraded.
The mRNA for apoferritin is bound by IRP and is not translated.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. The mRNA for the Transferrin receptor is not bound by IRP and is rapidly degraded.

In hemochromatosis, there is iron overload, so cellular iron levels are high. Under these conditions, apo-ferritin amounts need to be increased (to detoxify iron) while transferrin amount needs to decrease (to decrease total iron binding capacity-TIBC);

Mechanism: Iron regulatory proteins (IRPs) cannot bind to the iron-responsive elements (IREs) on the 3′ UTR of transferrin receptor mRNA, leading to rapid degradation. This decreases transferrin receptor synthesis, reducing iron uptake—a protective response to high intracellular iron.

Why other options are incorrect?

• A. The mRNA for Transferrin receptor is stabilised by binding of IRP to 3’ stem-loop structures known as IRE: Occurs only during iron deficiency, not overload.
• C. The mRNA for apoferritin is not bound by IRP at 5’ stem loop IRE and is rapidly degraded and D. The mRNA for apoferritin is bound by IRP and is not translated: IRP binds the 5′ IRE of ferritin mRNA when iron is low to block translation; during iron overload, ferritin is translated, so these statements are false.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following metabolic processes is not directly supported by vitamin B6 in its active form, pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Conversion of glucose to glycogen

• Vitamin B6 in its active form, pyridoxal 5′-phosphate (PLP), serves as a coenzyme in multiple amino acid metabolism reactions and in glycogenolysis.
• PLP is essential for transamination and decarboxylation reactions, facilitating amino acid interconversion and neurotransmitter synthesis. It also acts as a cofactor for glycogen phosphorylase, which breaks glycogen into glucose-1-phosphate.
