They accumulate C26—C38 polyenoic acids in brain tissue and also exhibit a generalized loss of peroxisomal functions. The disease causes severe neurologic symptoms, and most patients die in the first year of life.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 32-year-old male presents to OPD with eruptive xanthomas and a deranged lipid profile showing high TAG and VLDL; however, the cholesterol level was normal. The plasma sample was lipemic secondary to raised chylomicron levels. Which of the following points towards the metabolic defect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lipoprotein lipase deficiency

In the given clinical vignette, the most probable diagnosis is type I hyperlipoproteinemia, which is caused by lipoprotein lipase deficiency.

Type I Hyperlipoproteinemia: Deficiency in lipoprotein lipase (LPL) leads to hyperchylomicronemia (Type I Hyperlipoproteinemia). This condition results from defects in LPL or apo C-II, causing elevated levels of chylomicrons and VLDL, with decreased levels of LDL and HDL. Patients often develop eruptive xanthomas but are not at risk for coronary artery disease. However, they are at an increased risk of acute pancreatitis due to extremely high triglyceride levels, which can also cause a milky appearance in the plasma.

Type IIa Hyperlipoproteinemia: Defective LDL receptor points to a diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolaemia (type IIa hyperlipoproteinemia). This defect causes a decrease in the uptake of LDL and cholesterol. As a result, the blood levels of both LDL and cholesterol are elevated. Such patients are at increased risk of developing atherosclerosis and coronary artery disease.

Type III Hyperlipoproteinemia: It is also known as broad β-disease, remnant removal disease, or familial dysbetalipoproteinemia. Type III hyperlipoproteinemia is caused by a defective ApoE that mediates the removal of lipoprotein remnants. Clinical features include hypercholesterolaemia, xanthomas, and atherosclerosis. There is an increase in remnant chylomicrons, remnant VLDL (i.e., intermediate-density lipoprotein), cholesterol, and triglyceride levels. Fibrates are effective in treating patients with type III hyperlipoproteinaemia.

Type IV Hyperlipoproteinemia: It is also known as familial hypertriacylglycerolemia. It is caused by overproduction of VLDL. Cholesterol levels rise with the VLDL concentration  , and it is commonly associated with coronary heart disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity, alcoholism, and administration of progestational hormones.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 46-year-old male was recently diagnosed with colorectal cancer after presenting with multiple polyps in his colon during a colonoscopy. There is a strong family history of non-polyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC). Which of the following DNA repair mechanisms is most likely to be dysfunctional in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mismatch repair

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Lynch syndrome or hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC) and is due to defective DNA mismatch repair.

HNPCC is an autosomal dominant genetic condition that is associated with a high risk of colon cancer as well as other cancers, including endometrial cancer (the second most common), cancers of the stomach, ovary, ureters, etc. It is the most common cause of the syndromic form of colon cancer. Colon cancers are seen at younger ages and usually on the right side.

DNA mismatch repair proteins function as spell checkers during DNA replication by correcting the incorrect pairing. In HNPCC, the proofreading function of the mismatch repair systems (majorly MLH1 and MSH2) is lost, leading to the accumulation of errors throughout the genome. The genomes of these patients show microsatellite instability, which is characterised by changes in the length of short repeats.

Other options:

Option A: Defects in the nucleotide excision repair pathway are seen in patients with xeroderma pigmentosum.

Option B: Defects in non-homologous end-joining are seen in patients with subacute combined immunodeficiency syndrome (SCID).

Option C: Defects in DNA base excision repair are seen in patients with MUTYH-associated polyposis (MAP) syndromes.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 6-year-old child with a history of repeated, multiple, long bone fractures is diagnosed with osteogenesis imperfecta. Which of the following structures contains the type of collagen that is defective in this disease? * Tendon * Basement membrane * Elastic cartilage * Skin * Sclera
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 4, 5

Osteogenesis imperfecta(OI) is a connective tissue disorder that occurs due to abnormal type 1 collagen production. Type 1 collagen is also present in the skin, tendons, and sclera (1, 4, 5) apart from bones.

OI also called brittle bone disease, is an autosomal dominant disorder. There are 8 types of osteogenesis imperfecta. It occurs most commonly due to mutation in the COL1A and COL2A genes. These mutations lead to the replacement of glycine amino acid with another amino acid resulting in an abnormal triple helix of collagen. This results in the abnormal formation of type 1 collagen.

The defining clinical features of OI include:

* Osteopenia

* Recurrent Fractures

* Laxity of Ligaments

* Bluish Discoloration of The Sclerae

* Dentinogenesis Imperfecta ("Crumbling Teeth")

Note:

* Type I collagen is seen in the bone, dermis, tendon, ligaments, fibrocartilage, and sclera of the eyeball.

* Type II collagen is seen in hyaline and elastic cartilage (Option 3) and the vitreous body of the eye.

* Type III collagen is seen in reticulin fibers, smooth muscle, endoneurium, arteries, uterus, kidney, spleen, and liver.

* Type IV collagen is seen in epithelial and endothelial basal laminae and basement membranes. (Option 2)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A neonate was brought with features of lethargy, and poor oral intake. On examination, a cataract was seen. Urine Benedict's test was positive but negative for Glucose. What will be the enzyme deficiency in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase

The given clinical scenario of a neonate presenting with lethargy, and poor oral intake, with examination revealing a cataract and urine benedict's test was positive but negative for glucose, is suggestive of classical galactosemia and enzyme deficient is galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase.

Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase deficiency leads to classical galactosemia. It is an autosomal recessive disorder. Normally, newborns receive up to 40% of their intake as lactose (glucose + galactose). The deficiency of this enzyme leads to an inability to convert galactose-1-phosphate to uridine diphosphate galactose. This leads to the accumulation of galactose 1-phosphate and causes injury to the kidney, liver, and brain.

Clinical features:

* Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in the liver causes liver damage & leads to hepatomegaly, vomiting, and convulsions.

* Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate depletes the liver of inorganic phosphate leading to diminished ATP synthesis which affects gluconeogenesis resulting in hypoglycemia.

* Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in the nerves causes intellectual disability.

* Accumulation of galactitol in the lens causes oil-drop cataracts.

* Patients with galactosemia are at an increased risk of developing Escherichia coli neonatal sepsis.

In uridyl transferase deficiency, the epimerase is present in adequate amounts, so that the galactosemic individual can still form UDPGal from glucose. This explains how normal growth and development of affected children can occur despite the galactose-free diets.

Urinary reducing sugar (Benedict's test) and mucic acid test are positive. Direct enzyme assay using erythrocytes establishes the diagnosis.

Treatment is a galactose-free diet.

Other options:

Option A: Hexokinase is a glycolytic enzyme, involved in maintaining intracellular glucose concentration by catalysing the first step in glucose metabolism, i.e., phosphorylation of intracellular glucose.  Its deficiency leads to hemolytic anaemia. Splenomegaly may be another presenting feature.

Option B: Galactokinase is the enzyme responsible for the conversion of galactose to galactose 1-phosphate. Only cataract is seen in the deficiency of this enzyme because galactose-1-phosphate is not formed. Hence no toxic effects of this compound are manifested.

Option D: Phosphofructokinase is a key regulatory enzyme of glycolysis and is necessary for the ATP-dependent conversion of fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-diphosphate. Tauri's disease is type VII glycogen storage disorder that results due to the deficiency of phosphofructokinase.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A tall male patient, age 22, arrives at OPD for a standard physical examination. He has long legs, arachnodactyly, hypermobile joints, a wide arm span, and a high-arched palate. Which of the following gene mutations is the most likely to be responsible?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fibrillin

The given clinical vignette suggests a probable diagnosis of Marfan syndrome, which is caused by a mutation in a gene that codes for an extracellular matrix protein fibrillin-1 (FBN1).

Marfan's syndrome is an inherited connective tissue disorder. The FBN1 locus is on the long arm of chromosome 15. It is a clinical diagnosis based on skeletal, cardiovascular, and ocular manifestations. The Ghent criteria are used for diagnosing Marfan syndrome. The main features are tall stature, ectopia lentis, and aortic root dilatation.

Features of Marfan's syndrome (Mnemonic: MARFAN’S)

* Mitral valve prolapse

* Myopia due to upward dislocation of the lens (bilateral ectopic lentis)

* Aortic root dilatation, Aortic regurgitation

* Retinal detachment

* Fibrillin 1 gene defect: Reduced fibrillin 1 production, causing joint laxity

* Fifteen (Chromosome 15 is involved)

* Flat feet

* Arachnodactyly, Astigmatism, Air in lungs (Pneumothorax)

* Nearsightedness

* Subluxation of lens, Scoliosis, Speech disorders, Sleep apnea

Skeletal manifestations:

* Overgrowth of long bones (dolichostenomelia) with an arm span to height ratio of more than 1.05

* Pectus carinatum or pectus excavatum

* Long and slender fingers (arachnodactyly) and contracture of fingers (camptodactyly)

* Malar hypoplasia

* Joint laxity

Cardiovascular manifestations:

* Thickened atrioventricular valves, valvular prolapse (mitral regurgitation)

* Aortic valve dysfunction due to an aortic root aneurysm

* Aortic dissection and rupture due to cystic medial necrosis of the aorta

Ocular manifestations:

* ectopia lentis

* myopia

* flat cornea

* retinal detachments

* early cataracts and glaucoma

Other systemic manifestations:

* thoracic scoliosis

* spontaneous pneumothorax

* striae atrophicae in the skin

Other options:

Option B: Elastin is a crucial protein found in connective tissue. Williams-Beuren syndrome is an associated developmental disorder (deletions of the elastin gene) affecting connective tissue and the central nervous system. Fragmentation or a decrease of elastin is found in conditions such as pulmonary emphysema, cutis laxa, and ageing of the skin. Copper deficiency can also affect the formation of crucial cross-linking in elastin.

Option C: Collagen is a connective tissue. Defects in collagen lead to conditions like osteogenesis imperfecta, Stickler syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and Alport syndrome.

Option D: Laminin is a component of the basement membrane, providing structural support and anchoring the epidermis to the dermis. Mutations in its genes cause epidermolysis bullosa junctionale.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A two-month-old infant presents with difficulty feeding, vomiting, and lethargy. Laboratory tests reveal hyperammonemia and high levels of orotic acid in the urine. Which of the following is the most probable enzyme deficiency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency

The clinical scenario of a child with recurrent vomiting and failure to thrive, hyperammonemia and increased urinary excretion of orotic acid is indicative of Type 2 Hyperammonemia or ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency (OTC deficiency).

Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency leads to lethargy progressing to coma, protein aversion, intellectual disability, and hyperammonemia.

Type II hyperammonemia results from a deficiency of ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC). In the urea cycle, the enzyme ornithine transcarbamoylase catalyses the condensation of carbamoyl phosphate with ornithine to form citrulline. The deficiency of this enzyme leads to the accumulation of carbamoyl phosphate, which is channelled to pyrimidine synthesis, leading to increased excretion of orotic acid.

Clinical symptoms include vomiting, irritability and severe mental retardation. Mild forms show episodes of hyperammonemia, manifested by vomiting and neurologic abnormalities (e.g., ataxia, mental confusion, agitation). These episodes usually occur after ingestion of a high-protein diet or as a result of a catabolic state such as infection.

The laboratory findings during the acute attack are hyperammonemia accompanied by marked elevations of plasma concentrations of glutamine and alanine with low levels of citrulline and arginine. The blood level of urea is usually low. There is a marked increase in the urinary excretion of orotic acid. Diagnosis is confirmed by gene analysis.

Management includes treatment of acute hyperammonemia attacks. For enteral use, citrulline is used in place of arginine in patients with OTC deficiency. Liver transplantation is a successful treatment for patients with severe OTC deficiency. Long-term treatment consists of a protein-restricted diet.

Other options:

Option A: In Type 1 Hyperammonemia (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I deficiency), the symptoms appear during the first few days or even hours of life, and the baby presents with the signs and symptoms of hyperammonemia (refusal to eat, vomiting, lethargy, convulsion, and coma). Increased intracranial pressure is frequent. The child will show low levels of citrulline and orotic acid in the blood.

Option C: Argininosuccinate lyase enzyme splits argininosuccinate into arginine and fumarate. When deficient, argininosuccinate accumulates, leading to argininosuccinic aciduria, often presenting with brittle hair (trichorrhexis nodosa).

Option D: Orotic aciduria is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a defect in uridine monophosphate (UMP) synthase. This enzyme contains two activities, orotate phosphoribosyltransferase and orotidine decarboxylase. The lack of pyrimidines impairs nucleic acid synthesis needed for haematopoiesis, would result in megaloblastic anaemia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: An 8-year-old boy presented with tremors, slurred speech, hyperammonemia, and elevated levels of homocitrulline and ornithine in his urine. Which of the following transporter defects is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ornithine transporter

The HHH (Hyperornithinemia, Hyperammonemia, and Homocitrullinemia) syndrome is caused by a defect in the ornithine transporter.

HHH syndrome is caused by a defect in the transport system of ornithine from the cytosol into the mitochondria (ORNT1 gene), resulting in the accumulation of ornithine in the cytosol and a deficiency of this amino acid in mitochondria. The accumulation of cytosolic ornithine leads to hyperammonemia and hyperornithinemia. Homocitrulline is formed from the reaction of mitochondrial carbamyl phosphate with lysine. When ornithine is deficient, it leads to homocitrullinuria.

Components of HHH syndrome:

* Hyperammonemia

* Hyperornithinaemia

* Homocitrullinuria

In the urea cycle, the enzyme ornithine transcarbamoylase catalyses the condensation of carbamoyl phosphate with ornithine to form citrulline. The deficiency of this enzyme leads to the accumulation of carbamoyl phosphate, leading to elevated levels of glutamine in the blood, urine, and cerebrospinal fluid. Infants present with vomiting, irritability, lethargy, hypothermia, and apnoea due to high ammonia levels in the plasma. Mothers also have an aversion to protein-rich foods.

Urea cycle disorders are all characterised by hyperammonemia, encephalopathy, and respiratory alkalosis. This is due to an accumulation of the precursors of urea, namely ammonia and glutamine. Clinical features of urea cycle disorders are common to all and include vomiting, avoidance of high-protein foods, intermittent ataxia, irritability, lethargy, and severe mental retardation. Long-term treatment consists of a protein-restricted diet.

The enzymes involved in the urea cycle with their related disorders are given below:

* Carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase (CPS) 1 deficiency (hyperammonemia type 1) is rare and characterised by severe hyperammonemia.

* Ornithine transporter deficiency (HHH syndrome) is characterised by hyperornithinemia, hyperammonemia, and homocitrullinuria.

* Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency (hyperammonemia type 2) is inherited as an X-linked trait. Characterised by hyperammonemia and elevated glutamine levels in blood and CSF.

* Argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency is characterised by increased citrulline, citrullinuria, and hyperammonemia.

* Argininosuccinate lyase deficiency leads to argininosuccinic acidemia and metabolic acidosis. Hyperammonemia is less severe, and argininosuccinate is found in urine and CSF.

* Arginase deficiency is of the mild variety and is characterised by hyperargininaemia and argininuria.

Other options:

Option A: Citrin Transporter (Citrin Deficiency) – A defect in the citrin transporter leads to citrullinemia type 2, which has elevated citrulline levels.

Option C: Cystinuria: A type of aminoaciduria characterised by impaired reabsorption of positively charged amino acids: Cystine, Ornithine, Lysine and Arginine (COLA).

Option D: Deutetrabenazine is a vesicular monoamine transporter-2 (VMAT-2) inhibitor by which it decreases the uptake of monoamines into synaptic vesicles and depletes monoamine stores from nerve terminals. This drug is indicated for use in the presence of chorea associated with Huntington’s disease.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: How can one measure an enzyme's catalytic activity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vmax/[sₜ]

A homogeneous enzyme's catalytic activity is best described by its catalytic constant, kcat (Vmax divided by the number of active sites, sₜ).

kcat = Vmax/[sₜ]

While an enzyme's maximum capacity to convert substrate to product is important, the benefits of a high kcat can only be realised when Km is low enough. Thus, the catalytic efficiency of enzymes is best expressed as the ratio of these two kinetic constants, kcat/Km.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following can act as a major intracellular antioxidant, aiding in the elimination of reactive oxygen species (ROS)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glutathione

Glutathione is a major intracellular antioxidant and plays a crucial role in protecting cells from oxidative damage by directly neutralizing harmful ROS, such as free radicals and peroxides.

Glutathione is a tripeptide composed of glutamate, cysteine, and glycine. The cysteine component is crucial because it contains a thiol (-SH) group, which is responsible for the antioxidant properties of glutathione. Cysteine is the reduced form of cystine.

NADPH is utilised for the reduction of oxidised glutathione. Reduced glutathione removes H₂O₂, thereby preventing oxidative damage to RBCs and haemolysis. Thus, deficiency of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase results in haemolytic anaemia.

Selenium is an essential component of glutathione peroxidase, an antioxidant found in red blood cells and various tissues. It also plays a vital role in regulating normal immune function. Dietary sources of selenium include whole grains, meat, eggs, seafood, garlic, and mushrooms.

Ferroptosis is triggered when there are low levels of reduced glutathione. During oxidative stress, it gets used up, and there is unchecked lipid peroxidation of the membrane. This causes ferroptosis.

Ferroptosis is a form of cell death that is triggered because of excessive levels of intracellular iron deposition or when oxidative stress overwhelms the glutathione antioxidant system. Reactive oxygen species thus formed cause lipid peroxidation of the cell membrane. The cell membrane loses its selective permeability, and therefore cell death resembles necrosis. Caspases are not involved in ferroptosis. The most prominent ultrastructural feature is the loss of mitochondrial cristae and the rupture of the outer mitochondrial membrane.

Other options:

Option A and D: Copper (Cu) and zinc (Zn) are essential cofactors for the antioxidant enzyme superoxide dismutase (SOD), which converts the superoxide radical into hydrogen peroxide. While they are important for antioxidant defence, they are not major antioxidants themselves.

Option C: Peroxidase is an enzyme, not a direct antioxidant. It works with antioxidants, like glutathione, to facilitate the removal of ROS. While it is essential for the antioxidant defense system, it doesn't function as an antioxidant itself.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following vitamin deficiency is most likely to cause lactic acidosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Thiamine

Among the given options, thiamine is the most likely to cause lactic acidosis.

Thiamine is an essential cofactor for the enzyme pyruvate dehydrogenase, a key component of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex that converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA. This conversion is critical for linking glycolysis to the citric acid cycle, thereby facilitating energy production in the body.

Without sufficient thiamine, the activity of pyruvate dehydrogenase is severely impaired, leading to an accumulation of pyruvate and lactate in the blood, causing lactic acidosis. This biochemical disturbance contributes to the neurological symptoms observed. Immediate administration of thiamine is crucial in treating Wernicke's encephalopathy. If left untreated, the condition can progress to Korsakoff syndrome, a chronic and debilitating memory disorder. Thus, recognising the signs and symptoms early and providing thiamine supplementation can lead to rapid improvement and prevent long-term complications.

Gingelly (sesame) seeds have the highest content of thiamine. Thiamine is lost from rice during the process of milling. As it is a water-soluble vitamin, washing and cooking rice cause further losses. Hence, it is advisable to avoid highly polished rice and eat parboiled or under-milled rice.

Thiamine's active form, thiamine diphosphate, acts as a coenzyme for three critical enzyme complexes: pyruvate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and branched-chain keto acid dehydrogenase. This coenzyme facilitates oxidative decarboxylation by forming a reactive carbanion that attaches to carbonyl groups like those in pyruvate, leading to the release of CO₂. Thiamine diphosphate is also vital for transketolase in the pentose phosphate pathway.

Thiamine triphosphate, another form of thiamin, helps regulate nerve function by activating chloride channels in nerve membranes.

A thiamine deficiency can cause several conditions such as beriberi, characterised by peripheral neuritis, which can also involve heart failure and oedema. Additionally, thiamine deficiency can lead to Wernicke's encephalopathy and Korsakoff's psychosis, commonly associated with alcohol or drug abuse. The lack of thiamine impairs the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, leading to increased levels of lactate and pyruvate in the blood, which can result in dangerous lactic acidosis, especially in those consuming high-carbohydrate diets.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 21-year-old chronic alcoholic is brought to the emergency with confustion and tremors.On examination there is ataxia and ophthalmoplegia. Deficiency of which of the following is responsible for the condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vitamin B1

This patients clinical features are suggestive of Wernicke's encephalopathy. It is seen due to the deficiency of Thiamine/Vitamin B1. Thiamine is a cofactor for several important enzymes and also involved in the conduction of the axon potential and synaptic transmission.

Wernicke's encephalopathy/alcoholic encephalopathy is an acute neurological disorder. Glucose infusions may precipitate Wernicke’s disease in a previously unaffected patient or cause a rapid worsening of an early form of the disease (as in this patient). For this reason, thiamine should be administered to all alcoholic patients requiring parenteral glucose.

The triad is (GOA):

* Global Confusion

* Ophthalmoplegia (first symptom to improve with thiamine +dextrose infusion)

* Ataxia

Alcohol abuse leads to thiamine deficiency by the following mechanisms:

* Poor nutritional habits

* Folate deficiency which reduces thiamine absorption from the gastrointestinal tract

* Direct damage of the intestinal mucosa

Treatment:

It is a medical emergency and requires immediate administration of thiamine 100 mg IV or IM for 3 days followed by two to three times a day orally for 1 to 2 weeks.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 4-year-old child presents with a habit of biting his lips and fingers and you observe missing portions of fingers on his left hand. A detailed evaluation reveals delayed developmental milestone.On inquiry, the parents say that two male cousins on the mother's side have similar complaints and have been diagnosed with a genetic disorder. Lab reports reveal hyperuricemia. Which enzyme is most likely deficient in this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase

The given clinical scenario of self-mutilating behavior, delayed developmental milestones, positive family history and hyperuricemia is highly suggestive of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. It occurs due to the complete deficiency of the enzyme hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT).

Purines can be converted to nucleoside triphosphates to be reused by the body. This pathway is called the salvage pathway for purines.

Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder due to a complete deficiency of the HGPRT enzyme. This deficiency results in an inability to salvage hypoxanthine or guanine resulting in increased levels of phospho-ribosyl pyrophosphate (PRPP) and decreased levels of inosine monophosphate (IMP) and guanosine monophosphate (GMP). This causes increased de novo purine synthesis and excessive amounts of uric acid.

The clinical features include compulsive self-mutilation, intellectual disability, delayed milestones, dystonic movements, and hyperuricemia.

Diagnosis is made by deficient HGPRT enzyme activity in the erythrocyte.

The treatment of this condition includes:

* Allopurinol for hyperuricemia

* Behavioral management using restraints for self-mutilation

Partial deficiency of HGPRT leads to Kelley-Seegmiller syndrome.

Other options:

Option A:  Purine nucleoside phosphorylase deficiency results in decreased function of T cells but B cells are normal. This leads to multiple infections, neurologic abnormalities, and autoimmune diseases.

Option C: Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase deficiency results in the accumulation of adenine. This is oxidized to 2,8-dihydroxyadenine which is insoluble. This leads to urinary calculus formation with crystalluria, urinary tract infections, hematuria, and renal failure.

Option D: Adenosine deaminase deficiency is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner and is one of the major causes of severe combined immunodeficiency.

Pearl PF1567: Purine salvage deficiencies: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome and Adenosine deaminase deficiency(SCID)

Severe Combined Immunodeficiency(SCID):

Adenosine deaminase enzyme deficiency is one of the major cause of SCID. It is also called as Glanzmann–Riniker syndrome.

SCID patients are usually affected by severe bacterial, viral, or fungal infections early in life and often present with interstitial lung disease, chronic diarrhea, and failure to thrive.

Lesch-Nyhan syndrome:

It is due to deficiency of the enzyme Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase(HGPRT). It is an X-linked recessive disease.

Clinical features:

* Intellectual disability

* Self-mutilation

* Aggression

* Hyperuricemia

* Gout

Treatment:

* Allopurinol

* Febuxostat

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Maple syrup urine disease is due to a defect in which enzyme?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase

Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) is due to deficiency of branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase (BCKDH).

Leucine, isoleucine, and valine are the 3 essential amino acids, which are branched-chain amino acids. Their decarboxylation is accomplished by BCKDH using thiamine (vitamin B1) pyrophosphate as a coenzyme.

Leucine is metabolized by BCAA aminotransferase to α-ketoisocaproic acid, which leads to the disrupted metabolism of neurotransmitters and amino acids (glutamate, GABA, glutamine, alanine, and aspartate). α-Ketoisocaproic acid can reversibly inhibit oxidative phosphorylation and result in cerebral lactic acidosis. Collectively, these processes are detrimental to the normal function of neurons and glia, clinically manifesting as encephalopathy and brain edema and referred to as leucinosis.

Treatment options include hemodialysis, restricting dietary substances, thiamine for milder forms, and orthotopic liver transplant.

Other options:

B. Isovaleryl CoA dehydrogenase: Isovaleryl CoA dehydrogenase is involved in the breakdown of isovaleryl-CoA, a compound derived from the metabolism of the amino acid leucine. Deficiency of isovaleryl CoA dehydrogenase is associated with a different metabolic disorder called isovaleric acidemia, but not maple syrup urine disease.

C. Pyruvate carboxylase: Pyruvate carboxylase is an enzyme involved in gluconeogenesis, a process by which glucose is synthesized from non-carbohydrate sources. Deficiency of pyruvate carboxylase results in a different metabolic disorder known as pyruvate carboxylase deficiency, but it is not associated with maple syrup urine disease.

D. Acetyl CoA carboxylase: Acetyl CoA carboxylase is an enzyme involved in fatty acid synthesis. Deficiency of acetyl CoA carboxylase can lead to a different condition called malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency, but it is not related to maple syrup urine disease.

Pearl PF0080: Maple syrup urine disease(MSUD)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The co-factor for glutathione peroxidase is __?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Selenium

Selenium act as a cofactor for glutathione peroxidase.

Glutathione peroxidases:

* Also known as selenoproteins

* Selenium-containing glutathione peroxidases help transform hydrogen peroxide to harmless water (anti–oxidant action)

* Selenium deficiency results in Impaired function of glutathione peroxidases. As a result, destructive hydrogen peroxide breaks down into even more dangerous hydroxyl radical which damages cell membranes and cell DNA leading to serious disease

Selenium:

Selenium is an important trace element that is a part of the 21st amino acid selenocysteine.

There are many selenium-containing enzymes such as :

* Glutathione peroxidase

* De-iodinase

* Thioredoxin reductase

Selenium is also an intracellular antioxidant that complements the role of Vitamin E. Dietary sources of selenium include seafood, muscle meat, and some cereals.

Note:

Keshan Disease: Endemic cardiomyopathy.
Population affected: Primarily children and young women.
Location: Occurs in areas of China with low dietary selenium intake.
Cause: Linked to selenium deficiency in the diet.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The enzyme deficient in Von Gierke's disease is ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Glucose 6-phosphatase

Von Gierke disease is due to the deficiency of glucose 6-phosphatase.

Signs and symptoms of von Gierke disease are

* Seizures

* Doll-like facies (fat cheeks and relatively thin extremities)

* Hepatomegaly

* Growth retardation

* Hypoglycemia (blood glucose <60 mg/dL)

* Blood uric acid levels >5 mg/dL

* Lactic acidosis

* Elevated cholesterol and triglycerides

* Neutropenia (specific to Ib)

Treatment of von Gierke includes

* Maintenance of glucose levels by infusion of glucose or the use of uncooked cornstarch (as this is catabolized also by the debranching enzyme).

* Mild to moderate restriction of lactose, fructose, and sucrose.

* Ensure adequate intake of vitamins and minerals.

* Nicotinic acid, fibrates therapy should be started if triglyceride levels are >900 mg/dL, despite dietary therapy.

* Allopurinol (10 mg/kg/day) should be started for hyperuricemia if uncontrolled on dietary therapy.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following substance, facilitate the absorption of dietary iron?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin C

Vitamin C reduces the ferric iron to its ferrous form, thereby helping in the process of absorption of dietary iron from the intestine.

Vitamin C deficiency causes microcytic-hypochromic anemia due to

* Decreased absorption of iron

* Decreased hydroxylation of proline and lysine, which results in defective collagen synthesis and bleeding manifestations.

Note:

Alcohol and fructose also enhance iron absorption.

However, the absorption of both inorganic and heme iron is impaired by calcium. So, a glass of milk with a meal significantly reduces iron availability.

Vitamin C toxicity (>2000 mg/ day): Iron overload can be seen.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 34-year-old male was on maize as a staple diet for a prolonged period. He presented with diarrhoea and lesion over his neck as shown in the image below. The condition occurs due to deficiency of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Niacin

The above history and clinical features suggest niacin/vitamin B3 deficiency.

Excessive consumption of maize-based diets can cause pellagra. Corn/Maize has low levels of niacin and tryptophan. Jowar has high leucine content which inhibits QPRTase, an enzyme in the synthesis of Niacin.

Niacin deficiency leads to a disease called pellagra which is characterized by

* Diarrhea

* Dermatitis

* Dementia

The lesion in the neck is characteristic Casal’s necklace pattern, seen in pellagra. The Casal collar or Casal necklace is a clinical sign in which there is an erythematous pigmented skin rash in the distribution of a broad collar (dermatomes C3 and C4).

Other options:

B. Zinc: Zinc deficiency can cause various symptoms, but it does not typically present with the specific symptoms described in the case.

C. Thiamine (Vitamin B1): Thiamine deficiency can lead to a condition called beriberi, which primarily affects the nervous system and cardiovascular system. It does not typically present with skin lesions or diarrhea as described in the case.

D. Iron: Iron deficiency can result in anemia and other symptoms, but it does not cause the specific symptoms described, including skin lesions and diarrhea.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child on workup is found to be suffering from a rare form of pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency for which he has developed high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Which of the following is the best dietary advice for the patient?
options: High protein and low carbohydrate intake
High carbohydrate and low fat intake
High fat and low carbohydrate intake
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. High fat and low carbohydrate intake

Pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency(PDH) can be due to a defect in any one/more of the components of the PDH enzyme complex. Patients are advised to follow a high fat and low carbohydrate intake.

In pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency, there is a defect in the pyruvate dehydrogenase enzyme complex, leading to impaired conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA. This results in the accumulation of pyruvate and subsequent conversion to lactate, causing lactic acidosis and high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

To provide an alternative fuel source for the body, patients with pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency are often advised to follow a high-fat and low-carbohydrate diet. By reducing the intake of carbohydrates, which are metabolized to pyruvate, and increasing the intake of fats, which can be metabolized via alternative pathways, the reliance on the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex can be minimized.

Therefore, option C (High fat and low carbohydrate intake) is the most appropriate dietary advice for a patient with pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency and high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

Other options:

Option A: High protein and low carbohydrate intake - This option is incorrect because a high protein intake would still involve the metabolism of amino acids, which can contribute to the production of pyruvate and further exacerbate the metabolic acidosis in pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency.

Option B: High carbohydrate and low-fat intake - This option is incorrect because pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency impairs the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, resulting in the accumulation of pyruvate and subsequent lactic acidosis.

Option D: Only carbohydrate intake henceforth - This option is incorrect because pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency specifically affects the metabolism of carbohydrates, leading to the accumulation of pyruvate. Relying solely on carbohydrate intake would exacerbate the metabolic acidosis by increasing pyruvate levels.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presented to the OPD with complaints of abdominal pain and diarrhea. On further evaluation, the patient was found to have cutaneous flushing, extensive wheeze, and tricuspid insufficiency. Contrast enhanced-MRI revealed the presence of endocardial fibrosis. Which of the following substances will be excreted excessively in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 5-Hydroxy indole acetic acid

5-hydroxy indole acetic acid (5-HIAA) will be excreted excessively in the above given clinical scenario, as this is a case of carcinoid syndrome.

Carcinoid syndrome is due to excessive production of serotonin, a specialized product of tryptophan metabolism. It is then metabolized and excreted in urine as 5-HIAA. It is characterized by cutaneous flushing, abdominal cramps, and diarrhoea.

Note:

5-HIAA testing is a 24-hour urine test that is specific to carcinoid tumours. This test is the most common biochemical test for carcinoid tumours associated with carcinoid syndrome.

Pearl PF0663: Carcinoid syndrome

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A tall obese person, who is a known hypertensive was recently diagnosed with metabolic syndrome on routine workup. Which of the following is most likely to be found in this patient?
options: Increase in uric acid and insulin
Increase in triglycerides and total cholesterol
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increase in triglycerides and total cholesterol

Increase in triglycerides and total cholesterol is seen in patients with metabolic syndrome.

Metabolic syndrome is present if three or more of the following five criteria are met, which is given by NCEP-ATP III (National Cholesterol Education program and adult treatment panel III). It includes-

* Central obesity: waist circumference >102 cm (M), >88 cm (F)

* Hypertriglyceridemia: triglyceride level ≥ 150 mg/dL

* Low HDL cholesterol: <40 mg/dL and <50 mg/dL for men and women, respectively.

* Hypertension: blood pressure ≥130 mmHg systolic or ≥ 85 mmHg diastolic.

* Fasting plasma glucose level ≥100 mg/dL or specific medication or previously diagnosed type 2 diabetes mellitus.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In a fasting state, glucagon promotes the production of glucose by which of the following pathways?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis

The source of blood glucose in a fasting state is Gluconeogenesis and Glycogenolysis. It is promoted by glucagon.

The first stage of fasting: The fasting state begins two to four hours after the absorptive/well-fed state. In early fasting i.e; 4-18 hours after the well-fed state, the blood glucose level is maintained by hepatic glycogenolysis. The glycogen stores are sufficient for around 18 hours after a meal following which they start to deplete. So the source of blood glucose in a person fasting for 11 hours will be liver glycogenolysis.

Second stage of fasting: Gluconeogenesis begins 4–6 hours after the last meal but becomes fully active only after stores of liver glycogen are depleted (after 18 hours). They can serve as a source of glucose for up to 2 days.

Substrates for gluconeogenesis are:

* Glucogenic amino acids ( mainly alanine) from the muscle and

* Glycerol from adipose tissue

During fasting, the glucogenic amino acids are transported to the liver, transaminated into pyruvate, and converted to glucose.

Third stage of fasting:

* Lipolysis occurs in the adipose tissue due to the activity of hormone-sensitive lipase, stimulated by increased glucagon: insulin ratio.

* Free fatty acids are the source of energy in this stage and not glucose. Triacylglycerols will be hydrolyzed to fatty acids and glycerol.

* Beta oxidation of fatty acids takes place which provides acetyl CoA.

* In prolonged starvation (>3 days), acetyl CoA is converted to ketone bodies in the liver which will act as the main fuel source for skeletal and heart muscle and can meet up to 20% of the brain’s energy needs.

Final stage of fasting: After several weeks of starvation, ketone body synthesis will not take place due to depleted triacylglycerol stores. Proteins remain the only source of fuel. Protein degradation increases, and death results from a loss of heart, liver, or kidney function.

Role of insulin and glucagon:

When blood glucose falls during fasting, there is increased secretion of glucagon and decreased release of insulin. Hence glucagon: insulin ratio is increased.

Effects of increased glucagon: insulin ratio on enzymes of glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis:

* It activates glycogen phosphorylase, the key enzyme of glycogenolysis, and deactivates glycogen synthase. This causes a rapid mobilization of liver glycogen stores to be utilized as fuel.

* It favors the synthesis of glucose-6-phosphatase which converts glucose-6-phosphate to glucose. The resulting glucose is used by red blood cells (lack mitochondria) and the brain as they are largely dependent on glucose in the fasting state.

* Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase and fructose-1, 6-bisphosphatase are induced, leading to increased gluconeogenesis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Revised Which of the following is most likely to be released from the hypothalamus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hexokinase IV

Hexokinase type IV/ glucokinase is most likely to be released from the hypothalamus (ventromedial hypothalamus)

Glucokinase, also known as hexokinase IV, catalyses the conversion of glucose to glucose-6-phosphate, which constitutes the first step of glycolysis.

The hypothalamus is an important centre for the regulation of glucose homeostasis. It contains glucokinase/hexokinase IV which plays a central role in the counterregulatory response, which is a feedback system to counteract hypoglycemia by increasing the production of glucose and limiting its utilization.

There are four isoforms of hexokinase:

* Hexokinase type I: major isoform in the brain but also ubiquitously expressed

* Hexokinase type II: predominant in insulin-sensitive tissues such as adipose tissue, skeletal muscle, and cardiac muscle.

* Hexokinase type III: not predominant in any tissue.

* Hexokinase type IV: primarily in the liver, pancreas, hypothalamus, small intestine and other neuroendocrine tissue.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Testosterone is converted to which of the following hormone by aromatase enzyme?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Estradiol

Aromatase (CYP19) converts testosterone to estradiol.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The lab technician notices a urine sample from a 4-year-old male that was normal on collection but turns into the colour shown in the image after a few hours. It further darkened over the next few hours. Deficiency of which of the following can cause this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Homogentisic acid oxidase

Urine turning dark in colour on long-standing is a characteristic feature of alkaptonuria caused by the deficiency of homogentisic acid oxidase.

The dark colour of the urine on standing is due to the oxidation and polymerization of homogentisic acid.

Features of alkaptonuria:

* Uncommon autosomal recessive disorder

* Occurs due to the deficiency of homogentisic acid oxidase.

* This results in the accumulation of high amounts of homogentisic acid.

* The formed homogentisic acid is deposited in tissues or is excreted in urine.

* Clinical manifestations of alkaptonuria consist of ochronosis and arthritis in adulthood. Arthritis predominantly involves the spine, hip, and knee. Radiologically, it is characterized by intervertebral calcifications.

Ochronosis : Bluish black discoloration of sclera and ear cartilage due to deposition of homogentisic acid, beginning in late adolescence.

Other options:

A. Beta-carotene: Beta-carotene is a pigment that can give a yellow or orange color to certain foods and, to some extent, can affect the color of urine. However, beta-carotene deficiency is not associated with the darkening of urine on long-standing. It is not a characteristic feature of beta-carotene deficiency.

B. Tyrosine aminotransferase: Tyrosine aminotransferase is an enzyme involved in the metabolism of the amino acid tyrosine. However, deficiency of tyrosine aminotransferase is not known to cause darkening of urine on long-standing. Tyrosine aminotransferase deficiency is a very rare condition and is associated with symptoms related to impaired tyrosine metabolism, such as neurological and developmental issues.

C. L-ascorbic acid: L-ascorbic acid, also known as vitamin C, is an antioxidant and plays a role in various metabolic processes. While high doses of vitamin C supplements can sometimes cause changes in urine color, such as a more yellow or orange hue, deficiency of L-ascorbic acid is not associated with darkening of urine on long-standing. Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) is characterized by symptoms such as fatigue, joint pain, and skin changes.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is the most abundant plasma protein?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Albumin

Albumin is the most abundant protein in the blood and accounts for about 50% of all plasma proteins.

Serum protein electrophoresis is a method of separation and identification of proteins based on their net charge, size, and shape. The largest peak that lies closest to the positive electrode (left corner) is that of albumin since it is present in the largest proportion in the plasma.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding the Michaelis-Menten graph?
options: Km is directly proportional to substrate concentration
Km is directly proportional to enzyme concentration
Km is indirectly proportional to substrate concentration
Km has no relation to substrate concentration
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Km is directly proportional to substrate concentration

The Michaelis-Menten equation/graph represents the enzymatic rate (Km) at different substrate concentrations i.e Km is directly proportional to substrate concentration

For a typical enzyme, as the substrate concentration increases, initial velocity (Vi) increases until it reaches a maximum value Vmax. With further increase in the substrate concentration, the enzyme is said to be “saturated” with the substrate and the velocity remains the same. Hence, the shape of the curve that relates to the velocity of the reaction to substrate concentration is hyperbolic.

The Michaelis-Menten equation illustrates mathematically the relationship between Vi and [S] i.e,

Vi = Vmax ×[S]/Km+[S]

The Michaelis constant (Km) is the substrate concentration at which Vi is half the maximal velocity (Vmax/2).

The plot of initial reaction velocity against substrate concentration is hyperbolic.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient with thiamine deficiency develops lactic acidosis. Which of the following enzymes is affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pyruvate dehydrogenase

Pyruvate dehydrogenase is the enzyme affected in a patient with thiamine deficiency who develops lactic acidosis.

Pyruvate is transported from the cytosol into the mitochondria, where undergoes oxidative decarboxylation to form acetyl CoA in the presence of the multi-enzyme pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDHC) in the mitochondrial matrix.

The PDHC primarily consists of three enzymes: Pyruvate decarboxylase (also called Pyruvate dehydrogenase), dihydrolipoyl transacetylase, and dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase. It also requires the following co-enzymes:

1. Thiamine pyrophosphate, essential for pyruvate decarboxylase and is tightly bound to it
2. Lipoic acid and coenzyme A, essential for dihydrolipoyl transacetylase
3. FAD and NAD+, essential for dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase.

In a patient with thiamine deficiency, due to the inactive thiamine pyrophosphate, the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex is unable to act on pyruvate, which begins to accumulate on the body and is then shunted towards lactic acid formation by the enzyme lactate dehydrogenase.

This results in lactic acid accumulation and subsequent lactic acidosis in the patient.

Wernicke–Korsakoff, an encephalopathy-psychosis syndrome due to thiamine deficiency, may be seen in chronic alcoholics. It occurs due to insufficient production of ATP by the brain cells via the citric acid cycle as the PDHC is inactive.

Other options:

Option A: Pyruvate carboxylase facilitates the conversion of pyruvate to oxaloacetate by carboxylation.

Option C: Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase is involved in the decarboxylation and phosphorylation of oxaloacetate to form phosphoenolpyruvate seen in gluconeogenesis.

Option D: Transketolase with coenzyme thiamine pyrophosphate is an enzyme involved in the non-oxidative phase of the pentose phosphate pathway.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Cytochrome oxidase is inhibited in all of the following poisonings except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Methane

Cytochrome oxidase is a hemoprotein, which is the terminal component of the respiratory chain carriers (complex IV) in mitochondria. The action of cytochrome oxidase is inhibited in carbon monoxide, cyanide, and hydrogen sulfide poisoning, resulting in prevention of cellular respiration.

Hemoproteins are metalloproteins that have a typical heme prosthetic group. They are present in myoglobin, hemoglobin, and other cytochromes. Cytochrome oxidase contains two molecules of heme, each having one Fe atom that oscillates between Fe3+ and Fe2+ during oxidation and reduction. It also contains two atoms of copper, each associated with a heme unit.

Complexes  of ETC  :

Complex I: NADH-CoQ oxidoreductase
Contains - FeS, FMN, Coenzyme Q
Inhibitors – Rotenone

Complex II: Succinate-CoQ reductase
Contains - FeS, Coenzyme Q
Inhibitor - Carboxin

Complex III: CoQH2-cytochrome c oxidoreductase
Contains - cytochrome c, b, C1, and FeS
Inhibitor - Antimycin A

Complex IV: cytochrome oxidase
Contains - Cytochrome a, a3, and Copper
Inhibitor - Cyanide, Azide, Carbon monoxide

Complex V (informally): ATP Synthase
Inhibitor - Oligomycin

Note: MELAS (mitochondrial encephalopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke) is an inherited condition due to NADH-Q oxidoreductase (Complex I) or cytochrome oxidase (Complex IV) deficiency.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) is best measured using?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ion exchange chromatography

Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) is best measured using ion-exchange chromatography.

HbA1c is formed by non-enzymatic glycation of hemoglobin A present in RBCs. Normally this occurs to a small extent but is increased in diabetic patients with poor glycemic control. Since the half-life of RBCs is typically 60 days, HbA1c can be used to monitor mean blood glucose concentration over the past 6 to 8 weeks.

In ion-exchange chromatography:

• Proteins interact with the stationary phase by charge-charge interactions.
• Proteins with a net positive charge at a given pH will tightly adhere to beads with negatively charged functional groups such as carboxylates or sulfates (cation exchangers).
• Proteins with a net negative charge adhere to beads with positively charged functional groups, typically tertiary or quaternary amines (anion exchangers).
• Non-adherent proteins flow through the matrix and are washed away.
• Proteins elute in inverse order of the strength of their interactions with the stationary phase.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Identify the type of marked chromosome in the given karyotype.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acrocentric

The marked chromosome is chromosome 13 and the type is acrocentric.

Each chromatid has a long arm q and a short arm p. The two arms are separated by a centromere. In this image, the centromere is not midway between the two ends of the chromatids. It is seen towards one end with a marked difference in length between the p and q arms, hence it is an acrocentric chromosome.

Chromosomes are classified based on the position of the centromere as follows:

•

Metacentric: Centromere is centrally placed and the two arms are equal in length

•

Submetacentric: Centromere is slightly away from the center and the two arms are only slightly different in length

•

Acrocentric: Centromere is nearer to one end and the difference in length of arms is marked

•

Telocentric: Centromere lies at one end.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Insulin inhibits which of the following lipase enzymes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hormone sensitive lipase

Insulin has an inhibitory effect on lipolytic hormones like hormone sensitive lipase (HSL). In adipose tissues, the stored triglycerides are broken down (lipolysis) by hormone sensitive lipase (HSL) into free fatty acids (FFAs). Insulin inhibits HSL and thus reduces the release of FFAs and also glycerol.

In diabetic patients, low insulin level corresponds to an increase in HSL activity, promoting the breakdown of lipids and release of FFAs from adipose tissue. Hormone-sensitive lipase activity is accelerated by hormones like epinephrine, norepinephrine, glucagon, ACTH, TSH, GH, ADH, and Melanocyte stimulating hormones (MSH).

Insulin induces the activity of lipoprotein lipase (LPL) which is present on the walls of capillaries. LPL promotes hydrolysis of TGs and degradation of VLDL and chylomicrons. In diabetes, low insulin leads to decreased LPL activity resulting in increased VLDL and TGs levels.
