Defects in the synthesis of functional LDL receptors cause a significant elevation in plasma LDL-C. Patients with such deficiencies have type IIa hyperlipidemia /familial hypercholesterolemia (FH). This autosomal dominant condition predisposes individuals to premature atherosclerosis and coronary artery disease.

Patients with homozygous FH must be treated aggressively to delay the onset and progression of CVD. Two drugs that reduce the hepatic production of VLDL and thus LDL, a small-molecule inhibitor of the microsomal TG transfer protein (MTP) and an antisense oligonucleotide to apoB, and an antibody that inhibits ANGPLT3 are approved and should be considered in patients who have insufficient response to statins and PCSK9 inhibitors. LDL apheresis should be considered in patients who have persistently elevated LDL-C levels despite drug therapy.

Other options :

Option B - Defects in apo-E lead to type III hyperlipoproteinemia / familial dysbetalipoproteinemia.  It is characterized by defective clearance of chylomicron remnants and intermediate-density lipoproteins by the liver. This leads to hypercholesterolemia, xanthomas, and atherosclerosis.

Option C - Defective apo-C II results in type I hyperlipoproteinemia/ familial lipoprotein lipase deficiency. The resulting inactive lipoprotein lipase leads to slow clearance of chylomicrons and VLDL, and low levels of LDL and HDL. Patients present with eruptive xanthomas and acute pancreatitis.

Option D - Apo-B 48 is involved in the assembly of chylomicrons. Defects in this protein are not associated with familial hypercholesterolemia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: FISH technique helps to identify all except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Point mutation

Fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) is not useful in identifying point mutation. Point mutations are identified by other means like sequencing studies and restriction fragment length polymorphism.

FISH is a method of molecular analysis of genetic lesions involving large deletions, duplications, or more complex rearrangements that are not readily amenable to detection using polymerase chain reaction or DNA sequencing approaches.

FISH uses DNA probes that recognize sequences specific to particular chromosomal regions. To perform FISH, large fragments of cloned genomic DNA spanning up to 200 kb are labeled with fluorescent dyes and applied to metaphase chromosome preparations or interphase nuclei. The probe hybridizes to its homologous genomic sequence and thus labels a specific chromosomal region that can be visualized under a fluorescent microscope.

FISH can be performed on prenatal samples, peripheral blood cells, touch preparations from cancer biopsies, and even fixed archival tissue sections. It is used to detect numeric abnormalities of chromosomes (aneuploidy), subtle microdeletions and complex translocations that are not demonstrable by routine karyotyping, and gene amplification (e.g., HER2 in breast cancer or NMYC amplification in neuroblastomas).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In a patient with Diabetes Mellitus, the liver produces more TG and VLDL. What is the cause of the same?
options: Decreased action of LPL with increased action of HSL
Decreased action of LPL with Decreased action of HSL
Increased action of LPL with increased action of HSL
Increased action of LPL with decreased action of HSL
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Decreased action of LPL with increased action of HSL

In a patient with Diabetes Mellitus, the liver produces more TG and VLDL, due to decreased action of LPL with increased action of HSL.

• Lipoprotein lipase (LPL): Enzyme responsible for hydrolyzing triglycerides (TG) in VLDL and chylomicrons into free fatty acids (FFAs) for storage or energy use in tissues.
• Hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL): Enzyme that breaks down stored triglycerides in adipocytes into free fatty acids and glycerol.

Insulin has an inhibitory effect on hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL). In diabetes, low insulin corresponds to an increase in HSL activity. This promotes the breakdown of lipids and a release of TG and free fatty acids from the adipose tissue.

Insulin induces the activity of lipoprotein lipase (LPL) which is present on the capillary walls. LPL promotes hydrolysis of TG and the degradation of the transport proteins, VLDL and chylomicrons. In diabetes, low insulin leads to decreased LPL activity which corresponds to an increase in VLDL and TG.

This results in increased production of triglycerides and VLDL in the liver.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In the current scenario treatment for urea cycle disorder is available. Administration of amino acid phenylbutyrate can decrease ammonia formation. Which amino acid provides phenylbutyrate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glutamate

The amino acid that provides phenylbutyrate in the treatment of urea cycle disorders is glutamate.

Ammonia to Urea cycle: Ammonia gets converted to glutamate (non toxic form) through transamination.  Glutamate is transported to the liver as glutamine (by glutamine synthase). In the liver, ammonia is released from glutamine, converting it to alpha keto glutatamte. The released ammonia enters the urea cycle.

In acetylation therapy, Phenylbutyrate (a prodrug) which is metabolized to phenylacetate. Phenylacetate combines with glutamine (a nitrogen-rich amino acid) to form phenylacetylglutamine. Phenylacetylglutamine is water-soluble and is excreted in the urine. This process helps trap excess nitrogen, bypassing the urea cycle.

Other drugs that can be used to achieve the same outcome (ammonia scavengers) include:

• Phenylacetate
• Benzoate

Other Options:

Option A and C: Arginine and Aspartate do not play a role in this specific reaction.

Option D: Glycine: The combination of benzoate and glycine forms hippuric acid, a non-toxic compound. When Benzoate is administered to the body, it acts as a nitrogen-scavenging agent. Hippuric acid is water-soluble and is excreted in the urine, effectively removing one nitrogen molecule from the body per molecule of hippuric acid formed. This mechanism is similar to how phenylacetate acts as a scavenger for glutamate.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text:
Match the following conditions :

1) Glycogen accumulation in liver and renal cells and lactic acidemia, associated with hypoglycemia
a)Cori disease

2) Glycogen accumulation in lysosomes
b)McArdle disease

3) Exercise intolerance
c)Von Gierk disease

4) Accumulation of branched structures
d)Pompe disease
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 -c, 2 -d, 3 -b, 4 -a

The correct answer is option B: 1 -c, 2 -d, 3 -b, 4 -a

1) Glycogen accumulation in liver and renal cells and lactic acidemia, associated with hypoglycemia
c) Von Gierk disease

2) Glycogen accumulation in lysosomes
d)Pompe disease

3) Exercise intolerance
b)McArdle disease

4) Accumulation of branched structures
a)Cori disease

Von Gierke disease (type I glycogen storage disorder) occurs due to the deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase enzyme in the liver, kidney, and intestinal mucosa. Patients present commonly by 3-4 months of age with hypoglycemia (leading to seizures), lactic acidosis, and hepatomegaly. Affected children often have a doll-like face with fat cheeks, relatively thin extremities, short stature, and a protuberant abdomen due to massive hepatomegaly. The kidneys are also enlarged, whereas spleen and heart are not involved. Laboratory findings include hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, and hyperlipidemia.

Pompe's disease (type II glycogen storage disorder) occurs due to a mutation in alpha-1,4-glucosidase (also known as acid maltase), a lysosomal enzyme. A defect in this enzyme leads to the accumulation of glycogen in the lysosomes of peripheral, voluntary muscles and progresses to involve the cardiac muscle and diaphragm. Clinical features include hypotonia (floppy baby syndrome), cardiomyopathy, hepatomegaly, and failure to thrive. Myozyme can prevent worsening or can reverse cardiac and skeletal abnormalities.

Cori disease (type III glycogen storage disorder) occurs due to a deficiency of the glycogen debranching enzyme. The features of Cori disease include hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, and hyperlipidemia but with normal blood lactate and uric acid levels. Muscle weakness and atrophy can also occur in these patients. Liver biopsy shows the accumulation of glycogen in the form of limit-dextrins (branched structures).

McArdle disease (type V glycogen storage disorder) typically presents during late childhood or in the second decade of life. The muscle glycogen phosphorylase enzyme deficiency interferes with ATP generation by glycogenolysis in the muscles. This causes muscle glycogen accumulation. Symptoms are exercise intolerance associated with muscle cramps. This leads to severe muscle damage resulting in a massive release of myoglobin in the blood.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text:
Match the following with appropriate precursors

i. Melatonin
a. Tyrosine

ii. Histamine
b. Tryptophan

iii. Norepinephrine
c. Cystine

iv. Glutathione
d. Histidine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. i-b, ii-d, iii-a, iv-c

The correct matched sequence is : i-b, ii-d, iii-a, iv-c.

i. Melatonin
b. Tryptophan

ii. Histamine
d. Histidine

iii. Norepinephrine
a. Tyrosine

iv. Glutathione
c. Cystine

i. Melatonin – b. Tryptophan

Tryptophan is an essential amino acid and the precursor for the synthesis of melatonin, produced by the pineal gland. The process begins with tryptophan being converted into serotonin, and then serotonin is further converted into melatonin.

ii. Histamine – d. Histidine

Histamine is derived from the amino acid histidine. The conversion of histidine into histamine is catalyzed by the enzyme histidine decarboxylase. Histamine is involved in local immune responses, acts as a neurotransmitter, and plays a role in regulating gastric acid secretion.

iii. Norepinephrine – a. Tyrosine

Norepinephrine (noradrenaline) is synthesized from tyrosine. Tyrosine is first converted to L-DOPA by the enzyme tyrosine hydroxylase, and then L-DOPA is converted into dopamine. Finally, dopamine is hydroxylated to form norepinephrine. Norepinephrine is a neurotransmitter involved in the sympathetic nervous system's fight-or-flight response.

iv. Glutathione – c. Cystine

Glutathione is a tripeptide composed of glutamate, cystine, and glycine. The cystine component is crucial because it contains a thiol (-SH) group, which is responsible for the antioxidant properties of glutathione.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Nutritional deficiency of Copper, required by lysyl oxidase which is an importent key step for formation for covalent cross linking in collagen synthesis, gives rise to which of the following condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Menke's disease

Nutritional deficiency of copper, required by lysyl oxidase for formation for covalent cross linking in collagen synthesis, gives rise to Menke's disease.

Menke's disease is an X-linked recessive condition caused due to a mutation in the ATP7A gene on chromosome X. This causes impaired transport of dietary copper from the small intestine to the liver leading to low levels of copper-containing enzymes.

The final step of collagen synthesis involves the formation of covalent cross-links. This is done by the enzyme lysyl oxidase, a copper-containing protein. This is essential for the strength and rigidity of collagen. As a result of deficiency of copper in Menkes disease, this step of collagen synthesis is affected.

The patients presents with depigmented kinky hair, failure to thrive, neurodegenerative symptoms (loss of developmental milestones, truncal hypotonia, epilepsy), multiple fractures, anaemia due to ceruloplasmin deficiency, neutropenia, and recurrent infections.

Other Options:

Option B: Scurvy: Caused by vitamin C deficiency, leading to defective collagen synthesis due to impaired hydroxylation of proline and lysine.

Option C: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome: A group of genetic disorders affecting collagen structure or production.

Option D: Scoliosis: A structural deformity of the spine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The following Lineweaver-Burk plots depict enzymatic action in the presence of enzyme inhibitors. The enzyme action without inhibitor is represented by a blue line. What type of inhibitors are depicted in images 1 and 2?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1- Noncompetitive inhibition 2- Competitive inhibition

The Lineweaver-Burk plot in image 1 depicts non-competitive inhibition, and that in image 2 depicts competitive inhibition.

Important parameters in a reaction include:

• The affinity of the enzyme for its substrate, given by the Michaelis constant or Km. A low Km reflects a high affinity of the enzyme for substrate and vice versa. The value of Km is given by the substrate concentration at which the reaction velocity is equal to one-half Vmax. It does not change with changes in enzyme concentration.
• Vmax is the maximum velocity of a reaction.

Competitive inhibition is when the inhibitor binds reversibly to the substrate-binding site and competes with the substrate for the active enzyme-binding site. This effect can be overcome by increasing the substrate concentration by which maximum velocity can still be achieved. Therefore, Vmax is unaltered in this type of inhibition. However, the concentration of the substrate required to achieve half of the maximum velocity is increased. Therefore, Km is increased in this condition.

In a Lineweaver-Burk plot, the addition of a competitive inhibitor causes plots with the same y-intercept (Vmax is unaffected) but different x-intercepts (due to increased Km).

Noncompetitive inhibition is by binding of inhibitors to enzymes in locations remote from the active site. Increasing the concentration of the substrate does not overcome non-competitive inhibition. Thus, noncompetitive inhibitors decrease the Vmax of the reaction. They do not interfere with the binding of the substrate to the enzyme. Thus, the enzyme shows the same Km in the presence or absence of noncompetitive inhibitors.

In a Lineweaver-Burk plot, the addition of a non-competitive inhibitor causes plots with the same x-intercept (Km is unaffected) but different slopes and y-intercepts (due to decreased Vmax).

In uncompetitive inhibition, inhibitors bind with the enzyme-substrate intermediate complex and inhibit it. This leads to a decrease in both Vmax and Km.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text:
Which among the following are appropriate techniques for chromosomal aneuploidy?

i.  In situ hybridization

ii. Conventional cytogenetics

iii. Sanger sequencing

iv. Polymerase chain reaction
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. i,ii,iii,iv

In situ hybridization, Conventional cytogenetics, Sanger sequencing and Polymerase chain reaction are appropriate techniques for chromosomal aneuploidy.

Techniques to detect aneuploidy:

1. In situ hybridization: Fluorescent In Situ Hybridisation (FISH) helps in the detection of specific genetic information using fluorescent probes. FISH is used to detect chromosomal aneuploidy, subtle microdeletions and rearrangements, complex translocations, and gene amplification.
2. Conventional cytogenetics: This technique involves the study of chromosomes under a microscope, typically using methods like karyotyping, which arranges chromosomes by size, shape, and number. The analysis allows the identification of large chromosomal abnormalities, such as aneuploidy or structural changes.
3. Sanger sequencing: DNA sequencing that uses chain-termination to identify the exact sequence of nucleotides in a DNA molecule. Simple Senger sequencing can detect aneuploidy only with massive parallel sequencing.
4. Polymerase chain reaction: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is a rapid automated method for the amplification of specific DNA sequences (or genes). It can accurately quantify the target nucleic acid sequence within a sample. It is useful for determining somatic mutation with low allele frequency. Quantitative Fluorescence (QF) PCR is a method of rapid aneuploidy detection. It is less expensive and allows simultaneous processing of large number of samples of FISH.
5. Array Comparitive Genomic Hybridization: microarray based technique which can reveal imbalances across the genome.
6. Multiplex Ligation Probe Amplification: to detect gene dosage.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is not a heme breakdown product?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. ALA

Aminolevulinic acid (ALA) is not a product of heme breakdown; rather it is an intermediate in the synthesis of heme molecules.

The process of heme breakdown occurs over a series of reactions. In the reticuloendothelial system of the liver, spleen and bone marrow, heme is degraded by microsomal heme oxygenase. It requires NADPH and cytochrome c. In this process, the alpha methenyl bridge of the heme molecule is liberated as carbon monoxide. The Fe+ liberated is oxidized to Fe3+++ and taken up by transferrin.

The linear tetrapyrrole formed is biliverdin (green pigment), which is further reduced to bilirubin (red-yellow pigment) by an NADPH-dependent biliverdin reductase. The bilirubin is transported in the plasma bound to albumin and is taken up by the liver, where it is conjugated with glucuronic acid to make it water-soluble, which is finally excreted in the bile.

The intestinal bacteria deconjugate the bilirubin, which is reduced to urobilinogen. It is further reduced to stercobilinogen, which is excreted through feces.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is not a neurotransmitter derived from aminoacids ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Creatine

Creatine is not a neurotransmitter derived from amino acids.

Creatine is an intermediate product in the process of formation of creatinine. The steps involved in the formation are as follows:

• The amidino group of arginine is transferred to glycine to form guanidoacetic acid. This step occurs in the kidneys and pancreas.
• Guanido acetic acid is methylated by S-adenosyl methionine to form creatine. This step occurs in the liver.

Creatine is phosphorylated to creatine phosphate by the enzyme creatine kinase, which is present in the muscle, brain and liver. The reaction needs hydrolysis of ATP. The stored creatine phosphate in the muscle serves as an immediate store of energy in the muscle. During muscle contraction, the energy is first derived from ATP hydrolysis. Thereafter, the ATP is regenerated by the hydrolysis of creatine phosphate. This is called the Lohmann's reaction.

The creatine phosphate may be converted to its anhydride, creatinine, which is excreted in the urine. Creatinine level in the blood is an indicator of renal function.

Other options :

Option A - Gamma amino butyric acid (GABA) functions in brain tissue as an inhibitory neurotransmitter. It is formed by decarboxylation of glutamate by L-glutamate decarboxylase.

Option B - Dopa is a precursor in the formation of the neurotransmitters dopamine, norepinephrine and epinephrine. It is formed by the hydroxylation of tyrosine by tyrosine hydroxylase.

Option C - 5 Hydroxytryptamine is an important neurotransmitter in the brain, where it functions as an antidepressant. It is derived from the amino acid tryptophan, in a process of hydroxylation followed by decarboxylation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is not a post-transcriptional modification?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Glycosylation

Glycosylation is not a post-transcriptional modification; it is a post-translational modification.

A primary transcript is the initial, linear, RNA copy of a transcription unit. The collection of all the primary transcripts synthesized in the nucleus by RNA polymerase II is known as heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA). The pre-mRNA components of hnRNA undergo extensive co- and posttranscriptional modification in the nucleus and become mature mRNA. These modifications usually include the following :

• Addition of a 5′ cap - This is the first of the processing reactions for pre-mRNA. The cap is a 7-methylguanosine attached to the 5′ terminal end of the mRNA and is resistant to most nucleases. Creation of the cap requires the removal of the γ-phosphoryl group from the 5′ triphosphate of the pre-mRNA, followed by the addition of guanosine monophosphate. Methylation of this terminal G occurs in the cytosol and is catalyzed by guanine- 7-methyltransferase. Additional methylation steps may occur (options A and B).
• Addition of a 3′-poly-A tail - Most eukaryotic mRNA have a chain of 40 to 250 adenylates (adenosine monophosphates) attached to the 3′ end. This poly-A tail is added by the nuclear enzyme, polyadenylate polymerase. The poly-A tail terminates eukaryotic transcription. In addition, it helps stabilize the mRNA, facilitates its exit from the nucleus, and aids in translation.
• Splicing - Maturation of eukaryotic mRNA usually involves removal from the primary transcript of RNA sequences (introns) that do not code for protein (endonuclease cleavage). The remaining coding (expressed) sequences, the exons, are joined together to form the mature mRNA. The process of removing introns and joining exons is called splicing. The molecular complex that accomplishes these tasks is known as the spliceosome (option D).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text:
Which of the following is not associated with G6PD deficiency?

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD)
options: Equal incidence in males and females
Predisposes the patient to oxidative stress
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Equal incidence in males and females

G6PD Deficiency does not have an equal incidence in males and females. It is an X-linked recessive (XLR) disorder, hence males are more affected than females.

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency causes congenital hemolytic anemia due to enzyme deficiency. G6PD is required to generate NADPH while oxidizing glucose-6-phosphate in the hexose monophosphate pathway (HMP). G6PD deficiency leads to reduced NADPH levels (option B) which then reduces the level of reduced glutathione. Reduced glutathione is required to protect the cells against oxidative stress to RBCs and hemolysis.

Clinically, most patients are asymptomatic. When exposed to triggers like fava beans, infections, drugs such as primaquine, chloroquine, sulfonamides/sulfones, dapsone, and nitrofurantoin patient develops:

• Episodic hemolysis, both intravascular and extravascular
• Hemolytic anaemia
• Hemoglobinemia
• Hemoglobinuria

Increased oxidative damage to RBCs leads to the formation of denatured precipitates known as Heinz bodies. These bodies can damage the RBC membrane leading to intravascular hemolysis. Additionally, when such RBCs pass through the splenic cords, macrophages pluck out these precipitates, giving them the characteristic appearance of bite cells.

The images below show the presence of Heinz bodies and bite cells.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following methods is used to test the blood taken from a neonate for metabolic disease screening?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tandem Mass Spectrometry

Tandem mass spectrometry is used to screen a blood sample for metabolic diseases.

Mass spectrometry is a very sensitive quantitative analytical technique used to measure a wide range of clinically relevant analytes. It identifies molecules based on their mass or molecular size. A sample is vaporized such that a positive charge is produced on the molecule. An electric field is applied so that particles move. At the same time, a magnetic field is applied, so the cations are deflected and hit on the detector. For molecules of identical charge, the time required for the molecule to reach the detector is inversely proportional to the mass of the molecule.

In tandem mass spectrometry, two mass spectrometers (MS) are arranged sequentially. The first MS separates big peptides, based on their mass. From this observation, the parent ion can be directed into the second MS. Here the ions collide with argon gas molecules and are broken into smaller ions. These daughter ions are detected and quantified by their mass spectrum in the second instrument.

Tandem MS is used to screen blood samples from newborns for the presence and concentrations of amino acids, fatty acids and other metabolites. Abnormalities in metabolite levels can serve as diagnostic indicators for a variety of genetic disorders like phenylketonuria.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following micronutrients are associated with decreased sexual maturation and hypogonadism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Zinc

Zinc deficiency is associated with decreased sexual maturation and hypogonadism.

Zinc is the second most common trace element in the body after iron. As a component of zinc finger proteins, zinc regulates gene transcription and participates in nucleic acid metabolism, protein synthesis and thereby cell growth. Zinc is a major antioxidant being part of the enzyme superoxide dismutase.

Zinc is derived mainly from animal protein. Diets based on cereals, plants and legumes are associated with zinc deficiency due to dietary phytic acid decreasing the bioavailability of zinc.

Zinc is absorbed throughout the small intestine by a process of facilitated diffusion. Almost 90% of the total body zinc is localized in bone and skeletal muscle.

Deficiency -

• Poor physical growth is an important feature of zinc depletion in preschool and school-age children. Delayed sexual maturation and hypogonadism are prominent features of zinc deficiency in adolescents. Other features include anemia, anorexia, diarrhea, alopecia, impaired immune function and poor wound healing.
• Acrodermatitis enteropathica is an autosomal recessive disorder of severe zinc deficiency, caused by impaired intestinal absorption due to a defect in intestinal zinc transporter protein. It presents in early infancy with vesiculobullous, dry, scaly, or eczematous skin lesions chiefly in the periorificial and acral areas.

Normal requirements for children range between 3.5 and 5.0 mg/day. Acquired zinc deficiency stats can be treated with 0.5 to 1.0 mg/kg/day for several weeks. Malnourished children have much higher requirements of 2-4mg/kg/day.

Other options :

Option B - Copper deficiency results in microcytic, hypochromic anemia unresponsive to iron therapy, depigmentation of hair, neutropenia, neurological problems and osteoporosis. Disruption in copper transport is linked to Wilson's disease and Menke's disease.

Option C - Selenium deficiency is a cause of Keshan disease, a form of cardiomyopathy in young children seen in some regions of China. In combination with iodine deficiency, lack of selenium can result in myxedematous endemic cretinism.

Option D - Iron deficiency causes anemia, irritability, anorexia, pica, angular stomatitis, leg cramps and congestive heart failure.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which type of mutation results in the reversal to wild type of phenotype when the mutant gene is suppressed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mutations in tRNA

Mutations in tRNA are known to suppress the mutant gene and cause reversal to wild phenotype. Such mutations are called suppressor mutations.

Suppressor mutations are secondary mutations that alter the phenotypes caused by an existing mutation. This is not to be confused with reversion mutations in which the original mutation has been lost. Instead, suppressor mutations return the phenotype caused by the original mutation to a more wild-type phenotype despite the presence of the original mutation. The suppressor mutation’s effect on the phenotype can vary from partial restoration to full restoration of the wild-type phenotype.

In prokaryotic and lower eukaryotic organisms, abnormally functioning tRNA molecules have been discovered that are themselves the results of mutations. Some of these abnormal tRNA molecules are capable of binding to and decoding altered codons, thereby suppressing the effects of mutations in the structural genes.

These suppressor tRNA molecules, usually formed as a result of alterations in their anticodon regions, are capable of suppressing certain missense mutations, nonsense mutations, and frameshift mutations. An example of suppressor mutation is illustrated below.

A primary mutation occurs changing the original codon sequence from UGG (Trp) to UAG (Stop). A secondary mutation occurs in the gene for a glutamine tRNA leading to the anticodon switch from a GUC to AUC. This mutant tRNA can recognize the UAG stop codon and insert glutamine in place of the stop, allowing translation to continue past the stop and suppressing the original mutation.

In the laboratory context, such suppressor tRNAs, coupled with mutated variants of aminoacyl- tRNA synthetases, can be utilized to incorporate unnatural amino acids into defined locations within altered genes that carry engineered nonsense mutations. The resulting labeled proteins can be used for in vivo and in vitro cross-linking and biophysical studies.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 1-year-old child is brought with developmental delay, progressive abdominal distension, and recurrent respiratory infections. On examination, the child has coarse facial features, hepatosplenomegaly, corneal clouding, and skeletal abnormalities. Enzyme assay reveals deficiency of α-L-iduronidase, consistent with Hurler syndrome. Which of the following substances accumulates in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Heparan sulfate (HS) and Dermatan sulfate (DS)

The clinical picture—coarse facial features, organomegaly, corneal clouding, and intellectual disability—with deficiency of α-L-iduronidase is characteristic of Hurler syndrome (Mucopolysaccharidosis type I).

• α-L-iduronidase is required for degradation of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs)
• Deficiency leads to accumulation of:

o    Heparan sulfate (HS)

o    Dermatan sulfate (DS)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 6-month-old infant is brought with lethargy, vomiting, and poor feeding after a period of prolonged fasting. Labs show hypoglycemia with low ketone bodies (hypoketosis), suggesting a defect in fat metabolism. Which of the following is the most likely disorder?
options: Glycogen storage disease type I (Von Gierke disease)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Medium-chain acyl-Coa dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency

Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency is a fatty acid β-oxidation disorder in which the body cannot properly break down medium-chain fatty acids in mitochondria to generate energy during fasting.

In MCAD deficiency, impaired β-oxidation results in:

• Decreased energy production
• Reduced ketone body formation (hypoketosis)
• Hypoglycemia during fasting

This leads to symptoms such as lethargy, vomiting, poor feeding, and hypoketotic hypoglycemia, especially after prolonged fasting or illness.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Hers disease (GSD VI): Liver glycogen phosphorylase deficiency causing mild hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly, not hypoketotic hypoglycemia.
• Hereditary fructose intolerance: Presents after fructose ingestion with hypoglycemia and vomiting.
• Von Gierke disease (GSD I): Causes severe fasting hypoglycemia with hepatomegaly and lactic acidosis, but ketone production is not characteristically absent.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child presents with coarse facies, hypotonia, and seizures. Laboratory investigations reveal elevated very long-chain fatty acids. A defect in which of the following may be responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Peroxisomal biogenesis defect

This child most likely has Zellweger syndrome, a peroxisomal biogenesis disorder caused by mutations in PEX genes, leading to absent or defective peroxisomes. Peroxisomes are essential for β-oxidation of very long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs). Failure to metabolize VLCFAs results in their accumulation, causing hypotonia, seizures, developmental delay, coarse facies, hepatomegaly, and neurological dysfunction.

• Peroxisomal biogenesis defect → impaired β-oxidation of VLCFAs → ↑ VLCFAs (hallmark finding).

Why not the other options?

• A. Mitochondrial β-oxidation defect: Affects oxidation of long- and medium-chain fatty acids, not VLCFAs.
• C. Lysosomal hydrolase deficiency: Causes lysosomal storage disorders (e.g., Tay-Sachs, Gaucher), not VLCFA accumulation.
• D. Endoplasmic reticulum defect: Not associated with defective VLCFA oxidation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient came to the emergency room with severe pain in the abdomen. Serum triglyceride level was 1500 mg/dL. Identify the defect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Apo CII

Very high triglycerides (>1000 mg/dL) with acute abdominal pain suggests hypertriglyceridemia-induced pancreatitis, classically seen in familial chylomicronemia (Type I hyperlipoproteinemia).

• Deficiency of Apolipoprotein C-II (Apo C-II)
• Apo C-II is a cofactor for lipoprotein lipase (LPL)

Pathophysiology:

• Without Apo C-II → LPL cannot be activated
• Impaired breakdown of chylomicrons → massive accumulation of triglycerides
• Leads to pancreatitis, eruptive xanthomas, lipemia retinalis

Why other options are incorrect:

• Apo B-48: Needed for chylomicron formation (defect → abetalipoproteinemia)
• Apo B-100: Required for LDL/VLDL metabolism (familial hypercholesterolemia-like states)
• LDL receptor: Causes ↑ LDL (Type IIa), not severe triglyceridemia

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient has multiple tendon xanthomas. Serum cholesterol (398 mg/dL) and LDL 220 mg/dL were found to be raised. What is the defect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. LDL receptors defect

The presence of tendon xanthomas with markedly elevated total cholesterol and LDL is characteristic of familial hypercholesterolemia (Type IIa).

• Mutation in LDL receptor → impaired uptake of LDL by liver
• Leads to accumulation of LDL in plasma
• Normal triglycerides

Pathophysiology:

• Excess LDL deposits cholesterol in tissues → tendon xanthomas
•

Promotes atherosclerosis → premature coronary artery disease

Why other options are incorrect:

•

Lipoprotein lipase deficiency: ↑ triglycerides (chylomicrons), not LDL

• Apo E defect: Dysbetalipoproteinemia (↑ cholesterol + TG, palmar xanthomas)
• LCAT deficiency: HDL metabolism defect (fish-eye disease), not tendon xanthomas

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient is found to have accumulation of glucocerebroside within cells. Dysfunction of which intracellular organelle is most likely responsible for this finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lysosome

Glucocerebroside accumulation is the hallmark of Gaucher disease, a lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of β-glucocerebrosidase (β-glucosidase). Defective lysosomal degradation of glucocerebroside leads to its accumulation within macrophage lysosomes, forming characteristic Gaucher cells with wrinkled (“crumpled tissue paper”) cytoplasm.

Why not the other options?

• B. Peroxisome: Involved in β-oxidation of very long-chain fatty acids and α-oxidation of branched-chain fatty acids; disorders include Refsum disease, Zellweger syndrome, and X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy.
• C. Golgi apparatus: Responsible for protein modification, glycosylation, and sorting; not involved in degradation of sphingolipids.
• D. Mitochondria: Site of ATP production, oxidative phosphorylation, and apoptosis; not involved in lysosomal substrate degradation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presented with orange coloured tonsils, decreased HDL <5 mg/dl, triglyceride 140 mg/dl. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tangier disease

Tangier disease is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by a defect in the ABCA1 transporter, which is responsible for efflux of cholesterol from peripheral cells to HDL.

• Impaired cholesterol transport → failure of HDL formation
• Leads to extremely low HDL levels (<5 mg/dL)
• Cholesterol accumulates in tissues of the reticuloendothelial system

Characteristic clinical features:

• Orange-colored tonsils (pathognomonic clue)
• Very low HDL levels
• Peripheral neuropathy
• Hepatosplenomegaly (sometimes)

Why other options are incorrect:

• Abetalipoproteinemia: Absence of Apo B → fat malabsorption, acanthocytosis
• Familial hypercholesterolemia: ↑ LDL, tendon xanthomas
• Familial hyperchylomicronemia: ↑ triglycerides, pancreatitis

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presents with ataxia, ichthyosis, retinitis pigmentosa, and cardiac conduction abnormalities. Laboratory evaluation demonstrates elevated phytanic acid levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Refsum disease

Refsum disease is an autosomal recessive peroxisomal disorder caused by deficiency of phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase, resulting in defective α-oxidation of phytanic acid. The accumulation of phytanic acid causes the characteristic combination of retinitis pigmentosa, cerebellar ataxia, peripheral neuropathy, ichthyosis, hearing loss, and cardiac conduction defects.

Why not the other options?

• A. Zellweger disease: Peroxisome biogenesis disorder presenting in infancy with severe hypotonia, seizures, craniofacial abnormalities, hepatomegaly, and developmental delay.
• C. Adrenoleukodystrophy: X-linked disorder due to impaired peroxisomal β-oxidation of very long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs), causing adrenal insufficiency and progressive demyelination.
• D. Metachromatic leukodystrophy: Caused by arylsulfatase A deficiency, leading to sulfatide accumulation with progressive peripheral neuropathy and central demyelination.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presents with multiple eruptive xanthomas and markedly elevated chylomicron levels. Which of the following is most likely underlying defect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. LPL

Familial chylomicronemia syndrome (Type I hyperlipoproteinemia) is caused by lipoprotein lipase (LPL) deficiency or, less commonly, Apo C-II deficiency, resulting in impaired hydrolysis of triglycerides in chylomicrons. This leads to marked hypertriglyceridemia, persistent chylomicronemia, and the characteristic finding of eruptive xanthomas, often accompanied by recurrent acute pancreatitis.

Why not the other options?

• B. Apo E defect: Causes Type III hyperlipoproteinemia (Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia), characterized by accumulation of remnant lipoproteins, palmar xanthomas, and premature atherosclerosis.
• C. LDL receptor defect: Causes Familial hypercholesterolemia (Type IIa) with markedly elevated LDL, tendon xanthomas, and premature coronary artery disease.
• D. Apo B-100 defect: Results in impaired LDL receptor binding, leading to familial defective Apo B-100, which presents with elevated LDL cholesterol, not chylomicronemia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presents with seizures, a cherry-red spot on the macula, and no hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory investigations reveal a deficiency of hexosaminidase. Which compound is accumulated in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. GM2 ganglioside

The clinical triad of seizures, neurodegeneration, cherry-red spot on macula, and absence of hepatosplenomegaly is characteristic of Tay–Sachs disease.

• Deficiency of hexosaminidase A
• Leads to accumulation of GM2 ganglioside in neurons

Pathophysiology:

• GM2 accumulates in lysosomes of neurons → progressive neurodegeneration
• Retina becomes pale due to lipid accumulation, while the fovea appears as a cherry-red spot
• No organomegaly (important differentiating feature)

Why other options are incorrect:

• Galactosylceramide: Accumulates in Krabbe disease
• Sphingomyelin: Accumulates in Niemann–Pick disease (with hepatosplenomegaly)
• GM1 ganglioside: Accumulates in GM1 gangliosidosis

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presents with xanthomas and elevated cholesterol levels. Laboratory investigations show high LDL but normal triglyceride (TG) levels. There is also a family history of premature myocardial infarction (MI)—the patient’s father died due to MI. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hyperlipoproteinemia IIa

The clinical picture—tendon xanthomas, elevated LDL cholesterol with normal triglycerides, and family history of premature myocardial infarction—is characteristic of Type IIa hyperlipoproteinemia (familial hypercholesterolemia).

• Mutation in LDL receptor (most common) or ApoB-100
• Leads to reduced clearance of LDL from plasma

Lipid profile:

• ↑ LDL cholesterol
• Normal triglycerides

Clinical features:

• Tendon xanthomas (Achilles, extensor tendons)
• Xanthelasma
• Premature atherosclerosis → early MI

Why other options are incorrect:

• Type III (dysbetalipoproteinemia): ↑ cholesterol + ↑ triglycerides, palmar xanthomas
• Type I: ↑ chylomicrons → ↑ triglycerides (pancreatitis)
• Type IIb: ↑ LDL + ↑ VLDL → ↑ cholesterol + ↑ triglycerides

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presents with xanthomas on the Achilles tendon. Which of the following is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Familial hypercholesterolemia

Tendon xanthomas (classically over the Achilles tendon) are a hallmark of familial hypercholesterolemia (Type II hyperlipoproteinemia). This condition is caused by a defect in LDL receptors, leading to markedly elevated LDL cholesterol levels and deposition of cholesterol in tendons and skin.

It is associated with premature atherosclerosis and early coronary artery disease.

Key differentiation:

• Familial hypercholesterolemia: Tendon xanthomas
• Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia: Palmar xanthomas
• Hyperchylomicronemia: Eruptive xanthomas
• Tangier disease: Low HDL, orange tonsils

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient with family history presents with tendon xanthomas. Laboratory investigations reveal elevated cholesterol with normal triglyceride levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Familial hypercholesterolemia

Familial hypercholesterolemia (FH) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by defective or absent LDL receptors, leading to impaired clearance of low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol from the blood. This results in marked elevation of LDL cholesterol with normal triglyceride levels.

The excess cholesterol gets deposited in tissues, producing characteristic findings such as:

• Tendon xanthomas (commonly in Achilles tendon and extensor tendons)
• Xanthelasma
• Premature atherosclerosis and early coronary artery disease

Why other options are incorrect:

• Familial hyperlipidemia: A nonspecific term and not a defined disorder.
• Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia: Characterized by elevation of both cholesterol and triglycerides with palmar xanthomas.
• Familial hypertriglyceridemia: Mainly shows elevated triglycerides, not isolated high cholesterol.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Fatty acid transport through mitochondrial membrane is via?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Carnitine

Long-chain fatty acids cannot directly cross the inner mitochondrial membrane. Their transport into the mitochondrial matrix for β-oxidation requires the carnitine shuttle system.

Mechanism (Carnitine shuttle):

1.      Fatty acids are activated to fatty acyl-CoA in the cytosol.

2.      Carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT-I) converts acyl-CoA to acyl-carnitine (outer mitochondrial membrane).

3.      Acyl-carnitine is transported across the inner membrane via a translocase.

4.      CPT-II reconverts acyl-carnitine to acyl-CoA inside the mitochondria for β-oxidation.

Defects in the carnitine shuttle (e.g., CPT deficiency) lead to impaired fatty acid oxidation → hypoketotic hypoglycemia and muscle weakness.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Acyl carrier protein: Involved in fatty acid synthesis, not transport.
• Cholesterol transporter: Not related to fatty acid mitochondrial entry.
• LCAT (Lecithin–cholesterol acyltransferase): Involved in cholesterol metabolism (HDL function).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Hypertriglyceridemia is seen in all of the following conditions except:
options: High intake of fructose in diet
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Abetalipoproteinemia

Hypertriglyceridemia results from increased hepatic VLDL production or reduced triglyceride clearance. It is commonly seen in diabetes mellitus, high-fructose diets, and nephrotic syndrome. In contrast, abetalipoproteinemia is characterized by an inability to form apoB-containing lipoproteins (chylomicrons, VLDL, and LDL), resulting in very low plasma triglyceride and cholesterol levels.

• Abetalipoproteinemia (microsomal triglyceride transfer protein deficiency) → absent chylomicrons, VLDL, and LDL → low triglycerides, not hypertriglyceridemia.

Why not the other options?

• A. Diabetes mellitus: insulin deficiency/resistance increases lipolysis and hepatic VLDL synthesis, causing hypertriglyceridemia.
• C. High intake of fructose: promotes hepatic de novo lipogenesis and VLDL production, increasing triglycerides.
• D. Nephrotic syndrome: increased hepatic lipoprotein synthesis and reduced lipid clearance lead to hypertriglyceridemia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Patient with high triglycerides esterified with long chain fatty acid (LCFA) presents with fatigue and biopsy of muscle shows fat vacuoles. Which of the following is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Carnitine deficiency

Carnitine deficiency is a disorder of fatty acid oxidation in which long-chain fatty acids (LCFA) cannot be transported into mitochondria for β-oxidation. Carnitine is required for the carnitine shuttle

• LCFA cannot be utilized → accumulate as triglycerides in muscle
• Leads to lipid (fat) vacuoles in muscle biopsy
• ↓ energy production → especially during fasting/exercise

Clinical features:

• Muscle weakness & fatigue
• Hypoketotic hypoglycemia
• Myopathy with lipid accumulation

Why other options are incorrect:

• Fatty acid synthase defect: Affects synthesis, not oxidation
• Lipoprotein lipase (LPL) defect: Causes ↑ triglycerides in plasma (chylomicronemia), not muscle fat vacuoles
• LDL receptor defect: Causes hypercholesterolemia, not fatty acid oxidation defect

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Statement NOT true about β-oxidation of fatty acids:
options: CAT I and CAT II transport fatty acids
CoA released in cytosol during acyl-carnitine formation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. CoA released in cytosol during acyl-carnitine formation

β-oxidation of fatty acids occurs in the mitochondrial matrix, and long-chain fatty acids require the carnitine shuttle for mitochondrial transport.

Carnitine Shuttle Steps:

1. CPT-I (CAT-I): Converts fatty acyl-CoA → acyl-carnitine in the cytosol/outer mitochondrial membrane.
2. Acyl-carnitine is transported into mitochondria.
3. CPT-II (CAT-II): Converts acyl-carnitine → fatty acyl-CoA in the mitochondrial matrix, releasing carnitine.

Key points:

• ATP is used earlier for fatty acid activation to fatty acyl-CoA.
• Carnitine is released inside mitochondria after reconversion.
• CoA remains within the mitochondrial matrix, not released in the cytosol during acyl-carnitine formation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following are unsaturated fatty acids? 1. Lauric acid 2. Linoleic acid 3. Oleic acid 4. Palmitic acid Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2 and 3

Unsaturated fatty acids are generally liquid at room temperature and are considered healthier because they help reduce LDL cholesterol and lower cardiovascular risk.

• 1. Lauric acid ✗

• A saturated fatty acid (12:0).
• Commonly found in coconut oil and palm kernel oil.

• 2. Linoleic acid ✓

• A polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA, 18:2).
• An essential fatty acid (Omega-6) that must be obtained from the diet.

• 3. Oleic acid ✓

• A monounsaturated fatty acid (MUFA, 18:1).
• Major fatty acid in olive oil and groundnut oil.

• 4. Palmitic acid ✗

• A saturated fatty acid (16:0).
• Commonly found in palm oil, butter, and animal fats.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following defects causes familial hypercholesterolemia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. LDL receptor

Familial hypercholesterolemia (FH) is most commonly caused by a defect in the LDL receptor, which is responsible for removing low-density lipoprotein (LDL) particles from the bloodstream. When the LDL receptor is defective or absent, LDL cannot be efficiently taken up by the liver, leading to markedly elevated plasma LDL cholesterol levels.

This results in premature atherosclerosis, tendon xanthomas, and an increased risk of early coronary artery disease.

Other options are associated with different lipid disorders:

• Apo E defect → Type III hyperlipoproteinemia
• Apo CII defect → Impaired lipoprotein lipase activation (Type I hyperlipoproteinemia)
• Apo B48 → Involved in chylomicron formation, not FH.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which one of the following hereditary neuropathies is characterized by elevated serum ‘phytanic acid’ levels and manifests with the tetrad of peripheral neuropathy, retinitis pigmentosa, cerebellar ataxia and elevated protein concentration in cerebrospinal fluid?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Refsum’s disease

Refsum disease is an autosomal recessive peroxisomal disorder caused by impaired α-oxidation of phytanic acid, most commonly due to phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase deficiency. This results in accumulation of phytanic acid and produces the characteristic combination of peripheral neuropathy, retinitis pigmentosa, cerebellar ataxia, and elevated CSF protein.

Why not the other options?

• A. Krabbe disease: Deficiency of galactocerebrosidase → accumulation of galactocerebroside/psychosine; causes severe demyelination.
• B. Fabry disease: α-galactosidase A deficiency → accumulation of globotriaosylceramide; causes angiokeratomas, acroparesthesias, renal and cardiac disease.
• C. Tangier disease: ABCA1 mutation → markedly reduced HDL, enlarged orange tonsils, and peripheral neuropathy.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which protein, having structural homology with plasminogen, is responsible for myocardial infarction and stroke?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. LP(a)

LP(a) or Lipoprotein(a) consists of one mole of LDL attached to one mole of apo(a). The apo(a) component shows structural homologies to plasminogen, which is clinically significant. This similarity to plasminogen, a key protein in the fibrinolytic system, allows LP(a) to inhibit fibrinolysis (the normal breakdown of blood clots). Consequently, LP(a) promotes both atherosclerosis and thrombosis, significantly increasing the risk of premature coronary heart disease, myocardial infarction, and stroke.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 15-year-old boy presents with tremors, difficulty in speech, and behavioral changes. On examination, he has hepatomegaly and a golden-brown ring at the limbus of the cornea (Kayser–Fleischer ring). Wilson’s disease is suspected. Which of the following is the best investigation to support the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Liver biopsy for copper estimation

Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism caused by defective copper transport and impaired biliary excretion. This results in excess copper accumulation in the liver, brain (basal ganglia), and cornea, producing features such as hepatomegaly, neurological symptoms, behavioral changes, and Kayser–Fleischer rings.

The most definitive investigation to support the diagnosis is liver biopsy for quantitative copper estimation, which directly measures hepatic copper concentration. Markedly increased hepatic copper confirms abnormal copper accumulation.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Serum ceruloplasmin: Often decreased in Wilson disease but can be normal in some cases, so it is not definitive.
• Serum copper: Usually low due to reduced ceruloplasmin-bound copper and is not reliable for diagnosis.
• Urinary copper excretion: Increased in Wilson disease and useful for screening/monitoring but less definitive than hepatic copper estimation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 2-year-old child is brought with progressive pallor, recurrent infections, and failure to thrive. On examination, the child has hypopigmented skin and sparse, light-colored hair. Laboratory investigations reveal anemia and neutropenia. Which of the following micronutrient deficiencies best explains this clinical presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Copper

The combination of anemia + neutropenia + hypopigmentation of skin and hair is characteristic of copper deficiency. Copper is a cofactor for several important enzymes:

• Ceruloplasmin → involved in iron metabolism (Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺)
• Cytochrome c oxidase → energy production
• Tyrosinase → melanin synthesis

Pathophysiology:

• ↓ Ceruloplasmin → impaired iron mobilization → anemia
• Impaired immune function → neutropenia
• ↓ Tyrosinase activity → ↓ melanin → hypopigmentation

Clinical associations:

• Malnutrition
• Excess zinc intake (interferes with copper absorption)
• Menkes disease (genetic copper deficiency)

Why other options are incorrect:

• Zinc: Causes dermatitis, delayed wound healing
• Selenium: Cardiomyopathy (Keshan disease)
• Iron: Causes anemia only (no neutropenia or hypopigmentation)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 48-year-old male who has been working in a paint manufacturing factory for over 20 years presents with chronic abdominal pain, constipation, fatigue, headache, and joint pains. He also reports irritability and sleep disturbances. On examination, pallor is noted. Laboratory investigations reveal microcytic anemia. Peripheral smear shows basophilic stippling of RBCs. Which of the following enzymes is most likely inhibited in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ferrochelatase

Chronic exposure to lead (e.g., in paint factory workers) causes lead poisoning, which interferes with heme synthesis.

Lead inhibits two key enzymes in the heme pathway:

• Ferrochelatase → blocks incorporation of iron into protoporphyrin IX to form heme
• ALA dehydratase (ALAD) → inhibits conversion of ALA to porphobilinogen

Clinical features (classic):

• Abdominal pain (lead colic)
• Constipation
• Neuropathy (wrist/foot drop)
• Anemia
• Irritability, insomnia, headache

Why other options are incorrect:

• Uroporphyrinogen III synthase: Defect causes congenital erythropoietic porphyria
• Porphobilinogen deaminase: Defect causes acute intermittent porphyria
• ALA synthase: Rate-limiting enzyme; not inhibited by lead (actually regulated by heme)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child presents with erythematous scaly patches in the perioral region, mucosal ulcers, and impaired epithelial wound healing. What is the likely mineral deficiency associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Zinc deficiency

Zinc deficiency leads to characteristic periorificial dermatitis (around mouth, eyes, anus), mucosal ulcers, and impaired wound healing, as seen in this child. Zinc is a cofactor for numerous enzymes involved in:

• DNA & RNA synthesis
• Cell division and tissue repair
• Protein synthesis and epithelial integrity

Deficiency results in: Acrodermatitis enteropathica (genetic zinc malabsorption)

• Impaired epithelial regeneration → erythematous scaly lesions
• Poor wound healing
• Mucosal breakdown → ulcers

Other features of zinc deficiency:

• Alopecia
• Diarrhea
• Growth retardation
• Loss of taste (hypogeusia)

Why other options are incorrect:

• Iron deficiency: Causes anemia, not characteristic dermatitis
• Calcium deficiency: Affects bones (rickets/osteomalacia)
• Copper deficiency: Causes anemia and neurologic issues, not perioral dermatitis

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A Patient had dietary Cu deficiency, which is required by lysyl oxidase to cross link the collagen, what is the diagnosis of the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Menkes Disease

Copper is an essential cofactor for the enzyme lysyl oxidase, which catalyzes the oxidative deamination of lysine and hydroxylysine residues in collagen and elastin, allowing cross-linking of connective tissue fibers. Role of lysyl oxidase:

• Requires Cu²⁺ (copper) as a cofactor
• Forms cross-links between collagen and elastin fibers
• Provides tensile strength and structural stability to connective tissue

Menkes disease:

• X-linked recessive disorder
• Caused by mutation in ATP7A gene → defective copper transport
• Leads to systemic copper deficiency and reduced lysyl oxidase activity
• Weak connective tissue
• Kinky (steely) hair
• Neurodegeneration
• Failure to thrive
• Hypopigmentation

Differentiation from other options:

• Scurvy → Vitamin C deficiency → impaired hydroxylation of collagen
• Ehlers–Danlos syndrome → collagen structure/synthesis defects
• Scoliosis → spinal curvature disorder, not enzyme-related

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient's relatives sent a message on social media to the consulting doctor, unaware about the other investigations. But he mentioned that urinary coproporphyrin is positive. What is the probable cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lead poisoning

Lead poisoning interferes with heme synthesis, leading to accumulation of porphyrin precursors such as coproporphyrin in urine. Lead inhibits key enzymes in the heme pathway:

• ALA dehydratase (ALAD)
• Ferrochelatase

Consequences:

• ↑ ALA and coproporphyrin in urine
• ↓ heme synthesis → anemia

Clinical features:

• Abdominal pain (lead colic)
• Neurological symptoms (irritability, neuropathy)
• Anemia with basophilic stippling
• Wrist/foot drop

Why other options are incorrect:

• Asbestosis: Lung fibrosis (no effect on heme synthesis)
• Silicosis: Occupational lung disease
• Mercury poisoning: Neurological and renal toxicity, not porphyrin metabolism

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Acrodermatitis enteropathica is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder which affects the absorption of which one of the following micronutrients?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Zinc

Acrodermatitis enteropathica is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the SLC39A4 gene, resulting in defective intestinal absorption of zinc. Zinc deficiency leads to characteristic skin lesions, alopecia, diarrhea, and impaired immunity.

Symptoms usually begin after weaning from breast milk, as breast milk contains highly bioavailable zinc. Lifelong oral zinc supplementation results in dramatic clinical improvement.

Why not the other options?

• A. Iodine: Deficiency causes goiter and hypothyroidism, not acrodermatitis enteropathica.
• C. Iron: Deficiency causes microcytic hypochromic anemia.
• D. Selenium: Deficiency is associated with cardiomyopathy (Keshan disease) and myopathy, not the characteristic dermatitis of acrodermatitis enteropathica.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Heavy metal chelators are all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Oxime

Heavy metal chelators are agents that bind toxic metals and form stable complexes that can be excreted from the body, thereby reducing metal toxicity.

Examples include:

• Penicillamine – used in copper poisoning and Wilson disease.
• BAL (Dimercaprol) – used in arsenic, mercury, and gold poisoning.
• Trientine – another copper chelator used in Wilson disease.

Oximes (e.g., pralidoxime) are not heavy-metal chelators. They are used in organophosphate poisoning to reactivate acetylcholinesterase by removing the phosphate group from the inhibited enzyme.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following connective tissue degradation disorder is associated with aortic aneurysm?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Marfan's Syndrome

Marfan syndrome is a connective tissue disorder caused by mutation in the fibrillin-1 (FBN1) gene, leading to defective elastic fiber formation in connective tissues. Weakness of the aortic media predisposes to aortic root dilatation, aneurysm, and dissection, which is a major cause of mortality in these patients.

It is also characterized by tall stature, long limbs (arachnodactyly), lens dislocation, and skeletal abnormalities.

Why not other options:

• Ehlers–Danlos syndrome: Defect in collagen synthesis causing hyperextensible skin and joint hypermobility; vascular complications may occur in rare types but aortic aneurysm classically associated with Marfan syndrome.
• Atherosclerosis: Causes arterial narrowing and plaque formation, not primarily a connective-tissue degradation disorder.
• Scurvy: Vitamin C deficiency causing defective collagen synthesis leading to bleeding gums and poor wound healing, not aortic aneurysm.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following deficiencies is associated with sexual maturation defect and hypogonadism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Zn

Zinc deficiency is associated with delayed sexual maturation, hypogonadism, and impaired reproductive function. Zinc plays an important role in DNA synthesis, cell division, and hormone metabolism, including the normal function of the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis.

Deficiency of zinc can lead to delayed puberty, impaired spermatogenesis, decreased testosterone levels, growth retardation, poor wound healing, and decreased immunity.

Therefore, zinc is essential for normal sexual development and reproductive health, and its deficiency can result in hypogonadism and delayed sexual maturation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 58-year-old patient with a known malignancy undergoes molecular analysis of tumor cells. RNA sequencing reveals transcripts that are longer than normal, with inclusion of additional exon sequences not seen in healthy tissue. Which of the following mechanisms best explains this finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Alternative RNA splicing

Alternative RNA splicing allows a single gene to produce multiple mRNA transcripts with different exon combinations, leading to variation in transcript length and protein isoforms.

Role in Cancer:

• Cancer cells often exhibit abnormal alternative splicing.
• This can generate longer or altered mRNA transcripts.
• These variants may promote tumor growth, survival, and metastasis.

Why not other options:

A) Polyadenylation: Adds a poly-A tail at the 3′ end but does not significantly change transcript length of coding regions.

C) Gene amplification: Increases the number of gene copies, not the length of each RNA transcript.

D) Upstream promoter modification: Affects transcription initiation and expression level, not mRNA length.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 7-year-old child presents with severe photosensitivity, freckling over sun-exposed areas, and recurrent skin lesions since early childhood. There is a history of progressive neurological decline. On examination, multiple hyperpigmented macules and areas of skin atrophy are noted on the face and arms. The underlying defect involves impaired repair of UV-induced thymine dimers. Which DNA repair mechanism is primarily affected in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Nucleotide excision repair

UV radiation causes DNA damage in the form of pyrimidine (thymine) dimers, which distort the DNA helix. These lesions are repaired by the nucleotide excision repair (NER) pathway.

1.      Recognition of DNA distortion (thymine dimers)

2.      Excision of the damaged DNA segment

3.      DNA polymerase fills the gap

4.      DNA ligase seals the strand

Clinical relevance:

• Defect in NER → Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP)
• Presents with photosensitivity, exaggerated skin rash on sun exposure, and early skin cancers

Why other options are incorrect:

• Base excision repair: Repairs small base changes (oxidation, deamination)
• Double-strand break repair: Repairs DNA breaks (HR, NHEJ)
• Mismatch repair: Corrects replication errors (base mismatches)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child presents with multiple freckles, severe photosensitivity, and early-onset skin cancers. What is the primary underlying molecular defect responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nucleotide excision repair defect

The clinical features—multiple freckles, severe photosensitivity, and early-onset skin cancers—are characteristic of Xeroderma Pigmentosum (XP).

Underlying molecular defect:

• Defective nucleotide excision repair (NER) pathway
• This pathway normally repairs UV-induced DNA damage, especially pyrimidine (thymine) dimers

Pathophysiology:

• UV radiation → formation of thymine dimers
• NER defect → inability to remove damaged DNA
• Accumulation of mutations → high risk of skin cancers at an early age

Why other options are incorrect:

• Mismatch repair defect: Seen in Lynch syndrome (HNPCC)
• Base excision repair defect: Repairs small base damage (oxidation, deamination)
• Homologous recombination defect: Seen in BRCA mutations (breast/ovarian cancer)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child presents with recurrent self-mutilation, finger-biting, behavioral disturbances, and hyperuricemia. Which of the following enzyme deficiencies is the most likely cause if this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. HGPRT

Lesch–Nyhan syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT) deficiency, a key enzyme in the purine salvage pathway. Failure to salvage hypoxanthine and guanine leads to excess uric acid production, resulting in hyperuricemia, while the hallmark clinical feature is self-mutilating behavior (lip and finger biting) accompanied by neurological dysfunction.

Why not the other options?

• B. Sphingomyelinase deficiency: Causes Niemann–Pick disease, characterized by hepatosplenomegaly, neurodegeneration, foam cells, and a cherry-red macula.
• C. Glucocerebrosidase deficiency: Causes Gaucher disease, presenting with hepatosplenomegaly, bone crises, cytopenias, and Gaucher cells with “crumpled tissue paper” cytoplasm.
• D. α-Galactosidase A deficiency: Causes Fabry disease, an X-linked disorder characterized by angiokeratomas, acroparesthesias, hypohidrosis, and progressive renal and cardiac involvement.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A frameshift mutation occurs due to the insertion of a new nucleotide at the 4th position of an mRNA sequence containing 900 nucleotides. What is the most likely outcome of this mutation?
options: No change in the final protein
No change due to RNA editing
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Complete change in protein production

A frameshift mutation occurs when nucleotides are inserted or deleted in numbers not divisible by 3, altering the reading frame of the mRNA.

In this case, insertion of a nucleotide at the 4th position (early in the sequence) causes:

• Shift in the reading frame from that point onward
• All subsequent codons are altered
• Often leads to a premature stop codon
• Produces a completely abnormal (nonfunctional) protein

Why other options are incorrect:

• No change in protein: Seen in silent mutations, not frameshift
• Partial protein production: More typical of nonsense mutation (premature stop without frame shift)
• No change due to RNA editing: RNA editing does not correct frameshift mutations

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A mother brought her 14-year-old mentally retarded child with complaints of joint pain and an irresistible urge to bite his fingers and lips. On investigation, his serum uric acid level was found to be elevated. The child is likely suffering from which disorder?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lesch-Nyhan syndrome

The clinical features—intellectual disability, self-mutilation (biting lips/fingers), joint pain, and hyperuricemia—are characteristic of Lesch–Nyhan syndrome.

• Deficiency of HGPRT (Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase)
• A key enzyme in the purine salvage pathway
• Impaired salvage of hypoxanthine and guanine → increased degradation to uric acid
• ↑ PRPP and ↓ IMP/GMP → ↑ de novo purine synthesis → further uric acid production

Clinical features explained:

• Hyperuricemia → gout, joint pain
• Neurological dysfunction → intellectual disability
• Self-mutilation behavior (classic hallmark)

Why other options are incorrect:

• Xanthine oxidase deficiency: ↓ uric acid (xanthinuria), not hyperuricemia
• Thymidylate synthetase defect: Affects DNA synthesis
• CPS II defect: Affects pyrimidine synthesis

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presents with multiple colonic polyps and is diagnosed with colorectal carcinoma. There is a strong family history suggestive of Hereditary Non-Polyposis Colorectal Cancer (HNPCC). Which DNA repair mechanism is most likely defective in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mismatch repair

Hereditary Non-Polyposis Colorectal Cancer (HNPCC), also called Lynch syndrome, is caused by defects in the DNA mismatch repair (MMR) system. This repair mechanism normally corrects base–base mismatches and small insertion/deletion errors that occur during DNA replication.

Common genes involved:

• MLH1
• MSH2
• MSH6
• PMS2

Why other options are incorrect:

• Nucleotide excision repair: Repairs bulky DNA lesions such as thymine dimers caused by UV radiation (defective in xeroderma pigmentosum).
• Base excision repair: Corrects small base modifications such as deamination or oxidation.
• Double-strand break repair: Repairs DNA breaks through homologous recombination or non-homologous end joining.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A researcher treats cultured human cells with a histone acetyltransferase (HAT) inhibitor and observes rapid epigenetic changes. Within minutes, there is reduced transcriptional activity and chromatin appears more compact. Which of the following molecular changes is most likely to be seen immediately?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increased H3K9me2/3

• HAT inhibition → ↓ histone acetylation → chromatin condensation
• Associated with repressive marks (↑ H3K9 methylation)
• Acetylation = active chromatin; methylation (H3K9me2/3) = silenced chromatin

Histone acetylation relaxes chromatin and promotes gene transcription, whereas histone deacetylation leads to chromatin condensation and gene repression.

Effect of Histone Acetylase (HAT) Inhibition:

• ↓ Histone acetylation
• Chromatin becomes more condensed
• Leads to repressive histone marks, such as H3K9 methylation (H3K9me2/3)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A scientist is culturing a virus using the RT-PCR technique and performs 26 amplification cycles. After how many cycles would the DNA quantity be approximately half of what is present at the 26th cycle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 25

In PCR amplification, the amount of DNA doubles with each cycle (exponential amplification), the DNA quantity at 25 cycles is approximately half of that at 26 cycles.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: All are used in recombinant DNA technology (genetic engineering) except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Isomerases

Recombinant DNA technology (genetic engineering) involves cutting, modifying, and joining DNA molecules to produce recombinant DNA. This process requires enzymes that cut DNA, join DNA fragments, or modify DNA ends. Enzymes used in recombinant DNA technology:

1. Phosphatases

• Example: Alkaline phosphatase
• Removes 5′ phosphate groups from DNA ends.
• Prevents self-ligation of plasmid vectors, improving insertion of foreign DNA.

2. CRISPR–Cas9

• A gene-editing system derived from bacterial defense mechanisms.
• Cas9 nuclease cuts DNA at specific sequences guided by RNA.
• Used for precise genome editing.

3. Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (Terminal transferase)

• Adds nucleotides to the 3′ end of DNA without a template.
• Used in DNA labeling and cloning techniques.

Not used in recombinant DNA technology: Isomerases

• Catalyze rearrangement of molecules within the same molecule (e.g., glucose-6-phosphate ↔ fructose-6-phosphate).
• Function mainly in metabolic pathways, not in DNA cutting or joining.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: An 8-year-old boy is brought to the dermatology clinic because of severe sun sensitivity since infancy. His parents report that even brief exposure to sunlight causes blistering and persistent freckles over his face. Examination reveals multiple hyperpigmented macules on sun-exposed areas and a non-healing ulcer over the nose. Skin biopsy confirms basal cell carcinoma. The underlying genetic defect most likely involves failure of which of the following DNA repair mechanisms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Nucleotide excision repair

This child has xeroderma pigmentosum (XP), an autosomal recessive disorder caused by defective nucleotide excision repair (NER).

• NER normally removes UV-induced pyrimidine (thymine) dimers.
• Failure to repair these lesions leads to accumulation of DNA mutations, causing:

• Extreme photosensitivity
• Early freckling of sun-exposed skin
• Premature skin aging
• Early-onset basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and melanoma

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Base excision repair: Repairs small, non-helix-distorting DNA lesions (eg, oxidized, alkylated, or deaminated bases and uracil incorporation).
• B. Mismatch repair: Corrects replication errors such as base mismatches and insertion-deletion loops; defects cause Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) with microsatellite instability.
• D. Non-homologous end joining: Repairs double-stranded DNA breaks; defects impair V(D)J recombination, leading to immunodeficiency.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Consider the following statements with regard to point mutations: 1. If a purine is replaced by another purine, it is called ‘transition’. 2. If a purine is replaced by a pyrimidine, it is called ‘transversion’. 3. If a pyrimidine is replaced by another pyrimidine, it is called ‘transversion’. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 and 2 only

1. Purine → purine = Transition — Correct

• Purines are adenine A. and guanine (G).
• A ↔ G is a transition mutation.

2. Purine → pyrimidine = Transversion — Correct

• Pyrimidines are cytosine C. and thymine (T).
• A/G ↔ C/T is a transversion.

3. Pyrimidine → pyrimidine = Transversion — Incorrect

• C ↔ T is also a transition, not a transversion.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Disorders resulting from defects in nucleotide excision repair include all of the following, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ataxia Telangiectasia (AT)

Ataxia Telangiectasia is caused by defects in double-strand break repair, not by defects in nucleotide excision repair, which is the repair pathway affected in Xeroderma Pigmentosum, Cockayne syndrome, and Trichothiodystrophy.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: DNA packing is done by?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Histone

DNA packaging in eukaryotic cells is carried out by histone proteins, which help condense long DNA molecules into a compact, organized structure within the nucleus.

• DNA wraps around histone octamers (2 each of H2A, H2B, H3, H4) forming nucleosomes
• Nucleosomes further coil to form chromatin fibers and ultimately chromosomes

Functions of histones:

• DNA compaction (fits long DNA into nucleus)
• Regulation of gene expression (via histone modification like acetylation, methylation)

Why other options are incorrect:

• Glycoprotein: Not involved in DNA packaging
• Nucleic acid: DNA itself, not responsible for packing
• Helicases: Enzymes that unwind DNA during replication, not packaging

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: FISH is used to detect all of the following except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Point mutation

Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) is a cytogenetic technique that uses fluorescent DNA probes to detect large chromosomal abnormalities such as translocations, deletions, duplications, and gene amplifications.

However, FISH cannot detect point mutations because these involve single nucleotide changes, which are too small to be identified by probe-based chromosomal hybridization. Detection of point mutations requires molecular techniques such as PCR or DNA sequencing.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The number of Barr bodies in Klinefelter’s syndrome is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1

• In Klinefelter's syndrome, the genotype is XXY - there are two X chromosomes and one Y chromosome.
• The number of Barr bodies can be calculated using the formula: Number of Barr Bodies = Number of X chromosomes - 1.
• Since there are two X chromosomes in Klinefelter's syndrome, the number of Barr bodies is 2-1 = 1.
• Barr bodies represent the inactive, condensed X chromosome in cells, and only one X chromosome remains active in any cell regardless of how many X chromosomes are present.
• Klinefelter's syndrome (XXY) has one Barr body because there are two X chromosomes, and the formula for calculating Barr bodies is (number of X chromosomes - 1).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The sequence of the template DNA strand is 5'-GATATC-3'. What will be the sequence of RNA produced?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 5'-GAUAUC-3'

• RNA is synthesized complementary to the template strand of DNA, following base-pairing rules where A pairs with U (not T, as in RNA), G pairs with C, and C pairs with G.
• When transcribing DNA to RNA, these two strands are antiparallel.
• Given template DNA strand: 5'-GATATC-3'
• The RNA strand would be complementary and from 3' to 5' direction: CUAUAG
• When we write this sequence in (5' to 3') direction, the nucleotide sequence would be  5'-GAUAUC-3' so the answer is B.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The UGA codon signals:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Termination of protein synthesis

UGA is one of the three stop codons (along with UAA and UAG) in the standard genetic code. These stop codons signal the termination of protein synthesis by binding to release factors rather than tRNAs, causing the completed polypeptide chain to be released from the ribosome.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: True about telomeres is:
options: Gradually decreasing length of telomeres with ageing
Telomerase is found in somatic cells
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Gradually decreasing length of telomeres with ageing
