Telomeres are repetitive non-coding DNA sequences (TTAGGG repeats) present at the ends of chromosomes that protect them from degradation and fusion.

With each cell division, due to the end-replication problem, telomeres gradually shorten, leading to:

• Cellular aging (senescence)
• Limited replicative capacity of somatic cells

Telomerase is an enzyme that adds telomeric repeats to chromosome ends, thereby maintaining telomere length. However:

• It is active mainly in germ cells, stem cells, and cancer cells
• It is absent or very low in most somatic cells

Why other options are incorrect:

• Increased telomere length with ageing: Opposite is true.
• Telomeres have coding sequences: They are non-coding repetitive DNA.
• Telomerase is found in somatic cells: Generally absent or minimal in somatic cells.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: When a codon is changed to stop codon, then it is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Non-sense mutation

A nonsense mutation is a type of point mutation in which a codon for an amino acid is converted into a stop codon (UAA, UAG, or UGA). This results in premature termination of protein synthesis, producing a truncated and usually nonfunctional protein.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Stop codon mutation: Not a standard classification term used in genetics.
• Missense mutation: One amino acid is replaced by another (no stop codon formed).
• Silent mutation: Codon change does not alter the amino acid due to redundancy of the genetic code.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which Biochemical method is exploited for monoclonal antibody production by hybridoma technique?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Purine salvage pathway

The hybridoma technique for producing monoclonal antibodies uses HAT medium (Hypoxanthine-Aminopterin-Thymidine) for selection. In this medium, cells must use the purine salvage pathway to synthesize nucleotides because aminopterin blocks the de novo purine synthesis pathway.

Only hybridoma cells (fusion of antibody-producing B cells with myeloma cells) survive, as they possess the necessary enzymes (e.g., HGPRT) to utilize the purine salvage pathway, allowing selective growth and production of monoclonal antibodies.

Why not other options:

• Glycolytic pathway: Involved in glucose breakdown for ATP, not nucleotide synthesis or HAT selection.
• Pentose phosphate pathway: Produces NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate, but does not bypass the aminopterin block in HAT medium.
• Krebs cycle: Part of energy metabolism in mitochondria, unrelated to nucleotide salvage used in hybridoma selection.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following best represents the repeating cycles in sequence during PCR?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Denaturation → Annealing → Extension

PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) follows a specific sequence of steps that repeat in cycles. The first step is denaturation, where heat is used to separate the double-stranded DNA into single strands. The second step is annealing, where primers bind to their complementary sequences on the separated DNA strands at a lower temperature. The final step is extension, where Taq polymerase synthesizes new DNA strands using the primers as starting points.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following correctly depicts the sequence of steps in the PCR?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Denaturation → Annealing → Extension

Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) is a laboratory technique used to amplify a specific segment of DNA, producing millions of copies from a small DNA sample.

Sequence of steps in PCR

1. Denaturation (≈94–98°C)

• Double-stranded DNA separates into two single strands due to breaking of hydrogen bonds.

2. Annealing (≈50–65°C)

• Primers bind to complementary sequences on the single-stranded DNA template.

3. Extension / Elongation (≈72°C)

• DNA polymerase synthesizes new DNA strands by adding nucleotides complementary to the template.

These steps are repeated for multiple cycles, resulting in exponential amplification of the target DNA.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following enzyme is responsible for the synthesis of RNA primers during DNA replication?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Primase

Primase is an RNA polymerase that synthesizes short RNA primers, providing the free 3′-OH group required for DNA polymerases to initiate DNA synthesis. Since DNA polymerases cannot start DNA synthesis de novo, RNA primers are essential for replication of both the leading and lagging strands.

Why not the other options?

• A. Topoisomerase: Relieves torsional strain ahead of the replication fork by cutting and rejoining DNA; does not synthesize primers.
• C. DNA polymerase II: Involved mainly in DNA repair (in prokaryotes), not primer synthesis.
• D. DNA polymerase III: The principal prokaryotic DNA polymerase responsible for DNA chain elongation after the RNA primer has been synthesized.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is not an example of aneuploidy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Bloom syndrome

Aneuploidy refers to an abnormal number of chromosomes due to nondisjunction during meiosis, resulting in gain or loss of individual chromosomes.

Examples of Aneuploidy

• Down syndrome: Trisomy 21
• Patau syndrome: Trisomy 13
• Klinefelter syndrome: 47, XXY (sex chromosome aneuploidy)

Bloom syndrome is not an aneuploidy; it is a chromosomal instability disorder caused by mutation in the BLM gene (DNA helicase) leading to defective DNA repair and increased sister chromatid exchanges.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is not associated with post-transcriptional modification?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Glycosylation

Post-transcriptional modifications occur after RNA is synthesized from DNA and are essential for converting pre-mRNA into mature mRNA. The major modifications include:

• 5′ Capping: Addition of a 7-methylguanosine cap at the 5′ end, which protects mRNA from degradation and helps in ribosome binding.
• Endonuclease cleavage and splicing: Removal of introns and joining of exons to form mature mRNA.
• Methylation: Certain bases in RNA may be methylated during RNA processing.

Glycosylation is not a post-transcriptional modification. It is a post-translational modification of proteins that occurs in the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus, where carbohydrate groups are added to proteins.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is the best investigation for aneuploidy? A.In Situ Hybridization B.Conventional cytogenetics C.PCR D.Sanger sequencing
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A & B

Aneuploidy refers to an abnormal number of chromosomes (e.g., trisomy or monosomy). The most appropriate investigations are karyotyping (conventional cytogenetics) and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) because they directly evaluate chromosome number and structure.

• Conventional cytogenetics (karyotyping) visualizes the entire chromosome set and is the gold standard for detecting numerical abnormalities such as trisomy 21, trisomy 18, and monosomy X.
• In situ hybridization (FISH) uses fluorescent probes targeting specific chromosomes and provides rapid detection of aneuploidy, commonly used in prenatal and interphase cells.

PCR and Sanger sequencing are primarily used to detect gene-level mutations or small sequence variations, not whole-chromosome number abnormalities. Therefore, they are not ideal for detecting aneuploidy.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which one of the following statements regarding sex chromosomes in the human body is correct?
options: Chromosome X is included in Group C of the autosomal chromosomes
Chromosome Y is included in Group E of the autosomal chromosomes
Chromosome X is included in Group G of the autosomal chromosomes
Chromosome Y is included in Group F of the autosomal chromosomes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chromosome X is included in Group C of the autosomal chromosomes

According to the Denver classification of human chromosomes:

| Group | Chromosomes | Size | Centromere Position | Satellites

| ----- | ----------- | ---- | ------------------- | ----------

| A | 1, 2, 3 | Large | Metacentric/submetacentric | No

| B | 4, 5 | Large | Submetacentric | No

| C | 6–12 + X | Medium | Submetacentric | No

| D | 13, 14, 15 | Medium | Acrocentric | Yes

| E | 16, 17, 18 | Short | Submetacentric (16 is more metacentric) | No

| F | 19, 20 | Short | Metacentric | No

| G | 21, 22 + Y | Very short | Acrocentric | 21, 22 have satellites; Y does not

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which one of the following terms correctly denotes the mechanism and phenotypic changes that are not a result of variation in the underlying DNA sequence, but are caused by secondary modifications of DNA or histones in response to other heritable or environmental influences?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Epigenetics

Epigenetics refers to heritable changes in gene expression and phenotype that occur without alteration of the underlying DNA sequence. These changes can result from modifications such as:

• DNA methylation
• Histone modification
• Chromatin remodeling
• Regulatory non-coding RNAs

Why not other options?

• A. Pleiotropy: One gene produces multiple phenotypic effects.
• B. Epigenetics: Correct. Changes in gene expression without changing the DNA sequence.
• C. Co-dominance: Both alleles are expressed simultaneously in the heterozygous state.
• D. Epistasis: One gene masks or modifies the expression of another gene.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which PCR technique is considered the most appropriate method for syndromic diagnosis of pathogens causing meningitis?
questions.explanation: Correct answer: B. Multiplex PCR

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which technique is used to identify auto antibodies?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Indirect immunofluorescence

Indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) is commonly used to detect circulating autoantibodies in patient serum. In this technique, the patient’s serum is incubated with a substrate containing the target antigen (e.g., cells or tissue). If autoantibodies are present, they bind to the antigen. A fluorescent-labeled secondary antibody (anti-human IgG) is then added to detect these bound antibodies, producing fluorescence under a microscope.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Direct immunofluorescence: Detects antigen–antibody complexes deposited in tissues, not circulating autoantibodies in serum.
• ELISA: Can detect antibodies, but the classical and widely used screening method for many autoantibodies (e.g., ANA patterns) is indirect immunofluorescence.
• FISH (Fluorescence in situ hybridization): Used to detect DNA or chromosomal abnormalities, not antibodies.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which type of mutation results in the reversal to the wild type of phenotype when the mutant gene is suppressed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mutation of tRNA

A suppressor mutation can restore the wild-type phenotype of a mutant gene without correcting the original mutation. One common mechanism involves a mutation in tRNA that allows it to recognize altered codons (such as stop codons or frameshift codons) and insert an amino acid during translation.

These mutant tRNAs (suppressor tRNAs) compensate for the defective coding sequence, permitting translation to continue and partially or completely restoring protein function.

Thus, mutation of tRNA can suppress the effect of the original mutation and revert the phenotype toward wild type, even though the original DNA mutation remains present.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which type of PCR is suitable for identifying multiple causative agents?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Multiplex PCR

Multiplex PCR is used for simultaneous detection of multiple pathogens in a single reaction by using multiple sets of primers targeting different DNA sequences.

• Principle:

o    Multiple primer pairs → amplify different targets in one tube

o    Allows identification of multiple causative agents at once

• Advantages:

o    Saves time and cost

o    Requires smaller sample volume

o    Useful in syndromic diagnosis (e.g., respiratory, GI infections)

• Why not others:

o    Conventional PCR: detects single target per reaction

o    Real-time PCR: quantitative, but usually single target (unless multiplexed)

o    Nested PCR: increases sensitivity/specificity, not for multiple agents

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman with hypertriglyceridemia is considered for niacin therapy. She is a known diabetic managed adequately with sugars well under control. Why should niacin be used cautiously in this patient?
options: It can cause scleroderma which makes injecting insulin difficult.
It can increase the metabolism of oral hypoglyemic drugs.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It can cause hyperglycemia.

Niacin should be used cautiously in diabetics as it can cause hyperglycemia.

Niacin induces insulin resistance and also decreases glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, which may result in severe hyperglycemia. When niacin is prescribed for patients with known or suspected diabetes, blood glucose levels should be monitored at least once a week.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A newborn baby refuses breast milk since the 2nd day of birth but accepts glucose water. He develops vomiting and severe jaundice by the 5th day. Benedict's test was positive for urine and blood glucose was low. The most likely cause is due to the deficiency of
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase

The above clinical features on ingestion of breastmilk at birth suggest classical galactosemia, a disorder of galactose metabolism. Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase deficiency leads to classical galactosemia.

It is an autosomal recessive disorder. Clinical features include:

• Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in the liver causes liver damage & leads to hepatomegaly, vomiting, convulsions.
• Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate depletes the liver of inorganic phosphate leading to diminished ATP synthesis which affects gluconeogenesis resulting in hypoglycemia.
• Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in the nerves causes intellectual disability.
• Accumulation of galactitol in the lens causes an oil-drop cataract.

Urinary reducing sugar (Benedict's test) and the Mucic acid test are positive.

Treatment is a galactose-free diet.

The flowchart given below depicts galactose metabolism.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presents with recurrent kidney stones. Microscopic examination finding of the urine specimen is shown below. Which of the following is not seen in the urine of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Histidine

The image shows hexagonal, translucent and white crystals suggestive of cystinuria. Histidine is not seen in the urine of this patient.

Cystinuria is an autosomal-recessive disease due to a defect in renal PCT & intestinal amino acid transporter that is essential for reabsorptive transport of Cystine and the dibasic amino acids Ornithine, Lysine, and Arginine (COLA).

Diagnosis of cystinuria is by the cyanide–nitroprusside test. Initial treatment is with adequate hydration, alkalization of the urine with citrate supplementation or acetazolamide, and dietary modification to reduce salt and protein intake. If this fails then patients are usually started on chelation therapy with penicillamine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Defective fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase enzyme is associated with _____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Type 1 Tyrosinemia

Defective fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase enzyme is associated with type I tyrosinemia (tyrosinosis). It is the most common type of tyrosinemia.

There are three types of tyrosinemias:

• Type 1 (Hepatorenal tyrosinemia): Fumaryl acetoacetate hydrolase deficiency
• Type 2 (Oculocutaneous tyrosinemia/Richner-Hanhart syndrome): Tyrosine transaminase deficiency
• Type 3 (Neonatal tyrosinemia)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In which condition is excessive urinary excretion of 5- hydroxy indole acetic acid seen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Carcinoid syndrome

Excessive urinary excretion of 5-hydroxy indole acetic acid (5-HIAA) is seen in carcinoid syndrome.

Carcinoid syndrome is marked by symptoms of bronchospasm, cutaneous flushing, abdominal cramps, and diarrhea. It occurs due to excessive production of serotonin, a specialized product of tryptophan metabolism by tumors commonly in the small intestine, liver and lungs. It is then metabolized and excreted in urine as 5-HIAA.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Serotonin is also known as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 5 hydroxytryptamine

Serotonin is also known as 5 hydroxy-tryptamine, and it is a monoamine neurotransmitter. Serotonin is produced by hydroxylation of tryptophan and subsequent decarboxylation. It is a potent vasoconstrictor and stimulator of smooth muscle contraction.

Clinical correlation:

In carcinoid syndrome, excessive levels of serotonin is produced which causes flushing, diarrhea, wheezing, damage to the tricuspid valve, etc. The levels of 5-OH indole acetic acid (serotonin metabolite) is elevated in the urine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The flipped LDH ratio implies _______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. LDH 1 > LDH 2

The flipped lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) ratio is LDH 1 > LDH 2.

Under normal conditions, LDH 2 is predominantly present in the blood and LDH 1 is predominantly present in the heart. When cardiac tissue is damaged LDH 1 is released into the bloodstream.

LDH 1 > LDH 2 (flipped pattern) in the blood is suggestive of myocardial infarction.

LDH is a tetrameric enzyme with 4 subunits. It has four subunits with two isoforms: H isoform (heart) and M isoform (muscle)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Vanillyl mandelic acid is excreted in urine in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pheochromocytoma

• Vanillyl Mandelic Acid is the end product of catabolism of catecholamines and is excreted in urine in Pheochromocytoma.
• VMA is the urinary product of both epinephrine and norepinephrine.
• In pheochromocytoma and neuroblastoma, there is an excessive synthesis of catecholamines which causes enhanced synthesis of VMA and its excretion in the urine.
• It is a good screening test for pheochromocytoma and is also used to diagnose and follow up neuroblastoma and ganglioneuroma.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is responsible for the negative charge in fibrinopeptide A?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Aspartate and glutamate

Aspartate and glutamate are responsible for the negative charge in fibrinopeptide A and B of fibrinogen.

The negative charges contribute to the solubility of fibrinogen in plasma and importantly also serve to prevent aggregation by causing electrostatic repulsion between fibrinogen molecules.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common end-product of fatty acid synthesis pathway?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Palmitic acid

The most common end product of fatty acid synthesis is palmitic acid.

Palmitic acid is a 16 carbon saturated long chain fatty acid (LCFA). The substrate for its synthesis is acetyl CoA. Acetyl CoA is also the end product of fatty acid beta-oxidation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding an allosteric modifier?
options: Causes the enzyme to work faster only.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Participates in feedback regulation

An allosteric modifier of an enzyme usually participates in feedback regulation.

Allosteric regulations are a natural example of control loops, such as feedback from downstream products or feedforward from upstream substrates. Allosteric regulation is also particularly important in the cell's ability to adjust enzyme activity.

An allosteric modifier or effector binds to the allosteric site to induce a conformational change in the catalytic or active site. Those modifiers or effectors that enhance the protein's activity are referred to as allosteric activators, whereas those that decrease the protein's activity are called allosteric inhibitors.

Some examples of allosteric modifiers

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following should be avoided by a patient of fish odour syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Choline

A fishy odor is seen in trimethylaminuria. Consumption of food products with choline should be avoided in fish odor syndrome.

Fish odor syndrome (trimethylaminuria) is an autosomal recessive disease where TMA(trimethylamine) is not converted to the non-odorous TMAO (TMA-N-oxide) in the liver. This is due to the deficiency of flavin-containing mono oxygenase 3 (FMO3). TMA then builds up in the body and is released in sweat, urine, and breath, giving off a strong odor of rotting fish from the body.

Choline, lecithin, and TMAO are precursors of trimethylamine which are found in food products. These food products are eggs, liver, peanuts, meat, poultry, fish, dairy foods, pasta, and rice.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true about vitamin K?
options: Deficiency of vitamin K leads to hypercoagulability.
It is a water soluble vitamin.
Prolonged use of antibiotics leads to vitamin K deficiency.
Menaquinone is the dietary source of vitamin K found in green vegetables.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Prolonged use of antibiotics leads to vitamin K deficiency.

Prolonged use of antibiotics leads to vitamin K deficiency. This is due to the loss of normal bowel flora that synthesizes menaquinones (vitamin K2).

Vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin. The following are the vitamers of vitamin K:

• Phylloquinone (Vitamin K1) is the normal dietary source of Vitamin K that is found in green vegetables.
• Menaquinones (Vitamin K2) are synthesized by intestinal bacteria.
• Menadione (Vitamin K3) is a synthetic compound that is metabolized to phylloquinone.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: An infant presents with hypotonia and seizures. It was confirmed to be cerebrohepatorenal syndrome. Which of the following is accumulated in the brain in cerebrohepatorenal syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Long chain fatty acid

Cerebrohepatorenal syndrome or Zellweger's syndrome is characterized by the accumulation of very-long-chain fatty acid, abnormalities of synthesis of bile acids and a marked reduction of plasmalogens.

It occurs in individuals with a rare inherited absence of peroxisomes. It is due to mutations in genes encoding certain proteins called peroxins (involved in various steps of peroxisome biogenesis) in all tissues. They accumulate C26-C38 polyenoic acids in brain tissues and also exhibit a generalized loss of peroxisomal functions. It causes severe neurological symptoms and most patients die in the first year of life.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Common precursor amino acid for urea, creatine and nitric oxide is____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Arginine

Arginine is the common precursor for urea, creatine and nitric oxide.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Deficiency of which of the following causes increased glutamine in blood?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ornithine transcarbamoylase

Deficiency ornithine transcarbamoylase causes increased glutamine in blood

Ornithine transcarbamoylase catalyzes the condensation of carbamoyl phosphate with ornithine to form citrulline in the urea cycle. Its deficiency leads to the accumulation of carbamoyl phosphate. The carbamoyl phosphate is then shunted to pyrimidine biosynthesis, resulting in high ammonia and orotic acid levels in the blood. This condition is thus called hyperammonemia type 2.

As a compensatory mechanism, ammonia is then combined with glutamate to form glutamine (by the enzyme glutamine synthetase). The levels of glutamine are elevated in the blood, cerebrospinal fluid, and urine, probably as a result of this dysregulated glutamine synthesis.

Other options:

Option A: Deficiency of argininosuccinate lyase leads to argininosuccinic aciduria

Option C: Deficiency of alpha-galactosidase-A leads to Fabry’s disease and an accumulation of globotriaosylceramide.

Option D: Deficiency of arginase leads to hyperargininemia

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Excess ammonia reduces which of the following substrates of the Krebs cycle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Alpha ketoglutarate

Excess ammonia results in depletion of levels of alpha-ketoglutarate.

This happens because excess ammonia reacts with alpha-ketoglutarate to form glutamate, mainly in the CNS.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In a patient with lipoprotein lipase deficiency, which of the following is increased following a fatty meal?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chylomicron

After a fatty meal, chylomicrons are elevated in lipoprotein lipase deficiency.

Chylomicrons transport dietary lipids from the intestine to the peripheral tissues. They are synthesized in the intestine by assembling apo B-48 with lipids (mainly triacylglycerols). This is called a nascent chylomicron, which upon receiving apo C-II and apo E from HDL is remodelled into mature chylomicron.

Apo C-II activates lipoprotein lipase present on the endothelium. Lipoprotein lipase hydrolyzes the triacylglycerols into fatty acids and glycerol which are either used for storage or energy. Therefore, patients who are deficient in lipoprotein lipase or apo C-II (type I hyperlipoproteinemia) show increased levels of chylomicrons in the plasma after a fatty meal.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In a patient with Wilson's disease which of the following is decreased in urine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 3-methylhistidine

Urinary levels of 3-methylhistidine are decreased in patients with Wilson disease.

Amino acids in urine exist either in conjugated form (most) or in free form. In Wilson's disease the amount of conjugated amino acids far exceeds the amount of free amino acids. Methyl Histidine largely exists in free form and does not increase in amount on hydrolysis of acids in urine. Hence low amounts is seen in Wilson's disease.

Wilson disease is an autosomal-recessive disorder caused by mutation of the ATP7B gene located on chromosome 13. The ATP7B gene, encodes a transmembrane copper-transporting ATPase, expressed on the hepatocyte canalicular membrane.

Deficiency in the ATP7B protein causes a decrease in copper excretion into the bile, impairs its incorporation into ceruloplasmin, and inhibits ceruloplasmin secretion into the blood, leading to the accumulation of toxic levels of copper in the liver, brain, and eye.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In Menke’s disease, which of the following enzymes would be affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lysyl oxidase

Menke’s disease is due to defective lysyl oxidase.

It is an X‐linked recessive disorder caused by a mutation in ATP7A, which encodes for a copper-transporting ATPase‐α polypeptide.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: NADPH is used in ______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fatty acid synthesis

NADPH is the source of reducing equivalent for fatty acid synthesis.

This NADPH is derived from 3 sources:

• HMP shunt pathway (main source)
• Extramitochondrial isocitrate dehydrogenase (minor source)
• Malic enzyme

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: True regarding mitochondrial genome:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Maternal inheritance

Mitochondrial genome is maternally inherited.

Mitochondrial inheritance:

• Inherited exclusively from the affected mother (ovum) as an individual’s mitochondrial genome is entirely derived from the mother because sperms contain few mitochondria, which are typically shed upon fertilization.
• Both male and female children born to an affected mother will inherit the disease.

Pedigree shows mitochondrial inheritance.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following amino acid is necessary for the conversion of nor-epinephrine to epinephrine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Methionine

Methionine is necessary for the conversion of nor-epinephrine to epinephrine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following diseases have autosomal recessive inheritance?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Albinism

Albinism is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is autosomal dominant?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Achondroplasia

Achondroplasia is an autosomal dominant disorder.

It is caused by a mutation of the fibroblast growth factor receptor-3 (FGFR-3) gene.

The primary defect is abnormal chondrocyte proliferation at the growth plate that causes development of short and thick bones.

Clinical features:

• Short limbs
• Normal trunk
• Large head
• Saddle nose
• Exaggerated lumbar lordosis
• Severe spinal deformity may lead to cord compression

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 34-year-old male was on maize as a staple diet for a prolonged period. He presented with diarrhoea and lesion over his neck as shown in the image below. The condition occurs due to deficiency of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Niacin

The above history and clinical features suggest niacin/vitamin B3 deficiency.

Excessive consumption of maize-based diets can cause pellagra. Corn/Maize has low levels of niacin and tryptophan. Jowar has high leucine content which inhibits QPRTase, an enzyme in the synthesis of Niacin.

Niacin deficiency leads to a disease called pellagra which is characterized by

• Diarrhea
• Dermatitis
• Dementia

The lesion in the neck is characteristic Casal’s necklace pattern, seen in pellagra. The Casal collar or Casal necklace is a clinical sign in which there is an erythematous pigmented skin rash in the distribution of a broad collar (dermatomes C3 and C4).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient came to the hospital with complaint of abdominal pain. Routine investigations were unremarkable. On observation, the urine turned black on standing. Which of the following enzymes is likely to be defective in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Homogentisate oxidase

Urine turning black on exposure to air is suggestive of alkaptonuria which occurs due to the defect in homogentisate oxidase enzyme.

Alkaptonuria is a disorder of tyrosine metabolism, that develops due to the defect in homogentisate oxidase, which oxidizes homogentisate to maleylacetoacetate. The defect in this enzyme leads to the accumulation of homogentisate, which is then excreted in the urine. The excreted homogentisate gets oxidized when exposed to the air and causes the urine to turn black.

In some cases, the excessive homogentisate may get oxidized to benzoquinone acetate, which binds to the connective tissue. This leads to arthritis and pigmentation of the connective tissue, a condition called ochronosis.

Other options:

Option B: Xanthine oxidase deficiency results in hypouricemia, xanthinuria, and xanthine lithiasis.

Option C: Defects in phenylalanine hydroxylase can lead to phenylketonuria characterised by hyperreflexia, seizures, hypopigmentation, low IQ, hyperactivity, and tremors.

Option D: Defects in dihydroorotate dehydrogenase are rarely seen in clinical practice. Miller syndrome is associated with this defect.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presented with symptoms of peripheral neuropathy and macrocytic anemia. She was given folate 5mg and the blood picture improved. However, the neurologic manifestations were aggravated. What is the most likely cause?
options: Treatment with folate unmasking pyridoxine deficiency
Deficiency of folate reductase in CNS
Folate therapy using the B12 stores
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Folate therapy using the B12 stores

The most likely cause is folate therapy which used up the B12 stores, aggravating the symptoms.

Administration of folic acid for patients with macrocytic anemia can partially reverse the hematologic abnormalities associated with vitamin B12 deficiency. However, the neurologic manifestations of vitamin B12 deficiency are not treated by folic acid.

Administration of folic acid to an individual with vitamin B12 deficiency can potentially mask untreated vitamin B12 deficiency or even worsen the neurologic complications. Hence, testing for and/or treatment of vitamin B12 deficiency is required in all patients being treated with folic acid.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presents with a clinical scenario of obstructive jaundice. Which of the following results can be seen on Van den bergh's reaction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Direct positive

In a patient with obstructive jaundice , van der bergh reaction gives direct positive result due to conjugated  hyperbilirubinemia .

Van den Bergh reaction is used to determine the serum bilirubin level.

Van den Bergh reaction is a colorimetric method to measure serum bilirubin. It is based on the formation of red azodipyrroles when diazotised sulfanilic acid reacts with bilirubin.

Interpretation:

• In the absence of methanol, the water-soluble conjugated bilirubin reacts rapidly with the reagent and is called direct bilirubin.
• In the presence of methanol, both conjugated and unconjugated bilirubin react, providing the total bilirubin.
• Unconjugated (Indirect) bilirubin = Total-direct bilirubin

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Enzyme activated by a decrease in insulin: glucagon ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Glucose 6-phosphatase

Enzyme activated by a decrease in insulin: glucagon ratio is glucose 6-phosphatase.

A decrease in insulin: glucagon ratio is seen in fasting state, in which there is the activation of gluconeogenesis and inhibition of glycolysis.

Among the given options, only glucose 6-phosphatase is an enzyme of gluconeogenesis and therefore is activated. The enzymes mentioned as other options are irreversible enzymes of glycolysis and are inhibited in the fasting state.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: If the percentage of thymine residues in DNA is 28%. What is the percentage of cytosine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 22%

The percentage of cytosine in the DNA is 22%.

As per the Chargaff's rule, in the DNA molecules, the concentration of deoxyadenosine (A) equals that of thymidine (T), and the concentration of deoxyguanosine (G) equals that of deoxycytidine (C). Therefore, A=T and G=C.

In the question, the concentration of thymine is given as 28%, therefore the concentration of adenine is also 28%, both of which add up to 56%. The remaining 44% (100-56) of the DNA consists of G-C base pairs. Of which the guanine constitutes 22% and the cytosine constitutes another 22%.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Replacing alanine by which amino acid, will increase UV absorbance of protein at 280nm wavelength?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tryptophan

Replacing alanine with tryptophan will increase UV absorbance of protein at 280nm wavelength

The amino acids which absorb 250-290nm (maximum at 280nm) UV light are Tryptophan (Maximum Absorption), Tyrosine, Phenylalanine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The process of apolipoprotein B48 synthesis involves which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. RNA editing

The process of apolipoprotein B48 synthesis involves RNA editing.

RNA editing is the process by which the coding sequence of the mRNA is changed before translation. As a result, the mRNA template differs from the DNA from which it was transcribed. This leads to the formation of a different protein. This occurs by insertion of additional uracils at the 3’ end of the mRNA and proceeds in 3’ to 5’ direction.

RNA editing in apoB synthesis:

• In the liver, the apoB gene is transcribed to mRNA which is then translated to apoB 100.
• In the intestine, the same apoB gene is transcribed to the same mRNA. But now, the mRNA undergoes editing by an enzyme cytidine deaminase which converts the CAA codon in the mRNA to UAA at a single specific site. This edited mRNA translates to apoB 48.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Vitamin B12 is found maximum in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Animal products

Vitamin B12 is found maximum in animal products.

Vitamin B12 or cobalamin is synthesized only by microorganisms. Thus, the only source of cobalamin for humans is animal products. It is not found in plant sources. Therefore, individuals who are strict vegetarians are usually at the risk of developing vitamin B12 deficiency.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the function of the proteasome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Protein degradation

The proteasome takes part in protein degradation.

The proteasome is a cylindrical structure in the cytosol that degrades polyubiquitinated proteins. It has a central core with proteolytic enzymes. Proteins that are tagged by ubiquitin to be degraded enter the core through regulatory rings on either side of the cylinder.

Clinical relevance: It plays an important role in antigen presentation to T lymphocytes as it degrades viruses and other molecules to small peptides.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding non-competitive inhibition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Constant Km and decreased Vmax

Noncompetitive inhibition has constant Km and decreased Vmax.

Noncompetitive inhibition occurs when the inhibitor binds at a site different from the substrate-binding site. The structure of the inhibitor does not resemble that of the substrate and the inhibitor does not affect the binding of the substrate.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which vitamin, when infused in supraphysiological doses, causes macular edema and macular cysts?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vitamin B3

Macular cysts and edema may develop in patients due to the infusion of supraphysiological doses of vitamin B3 (niacin toxicity).

The toxic effects of niacin include:

• Flushing associated with skin dryness, itching, paresthesia, and headache is seen. These effects may be seen with even a low dose of 30mg/day. Pre-medication with aspirin alleviates these symptoms as these symptoms are mediated by prostaglandins.
• Macular edema and macular cysts
• Nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain.
• Hepatic toxicity presents as jaundice with elevated AST and ALT levels.
• Fulminant hepatitis requiring liver transplantation.
• Glucose intolerance
• Hyperuricemia

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy presented with easy fatigability, irritability and inability to concentrate. Labs revealed the following findings a and b (light and oil immersion respectively) on the bone marrow aspiration. Which of the following is the most likely enzyme deficient in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glucocerebrosidase

The given clinical scenario of a child with easy fatiguability, irritability, and inability to concentrate with the images showing a crumpled tissue paper appearance(Gaucher's cell) is suggestive of Gaucher's disease. The deficient enzyme is glucocerebrosidase (also known as beta-glucosidase). I

Gaucher's disease is an inborn error of metabolism caused due to a deficiency of beta glucocerebrosidase. It is the most common lysosomal storage disorder and the mode of inheritance is autosomal recessive. There is an accumulation of lipid-laden macrophages in the spleen, liver, and other tissues.

There are three clinical subtypes - type I (chronic non-neuronopathic), type II (acute neuronopathic), and type III (intermediate). Clinical features include anemia, thrombocytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, and neurological features depending on the subtype.

Gaucher's cells - These are formed as a result of the accumulation of massive amounts of glucocerebrosides within the phagocytes. The cells have a fibrillary cytoplasm and give a crumpled tissue paper appearance.

Option A: Deficiency of beta-hexosaminidase A is seen in Tay-Sachs disease. The deficiency of beta-hexosaminidase A and B causes Sandhoff's disease. Clinical features are seizures, macrocephaly, and hyperacusis.

Option C: Deficiency of sphingomyelinase leads to Niemann-Pick disease. It is characterized by the presence of foam cells in the bone marrow. There may be pulmonary infiltrates leading to lung failure.

Option D: Deficiency of N-acetylglucosaminidase leads to Sanfillipo's disease. It is a type of mucopolysaccharidosis (MPS - III). There is an accumulation of heparan sulfate leading to severe cognitive degeneration.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A farmer presented with loose stools and rashes over the sun-exposed areas. Careful diet history reveals a diet rich in maize. Which of the following deficiencies would you suspect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Niacin

History of a maize-rich diet along with loose stools and rashes over the sun-exposed areas is suggestive of niacin/vitamin B3 deficiency.

Niacin deficiency causes pellagra, found mostly among people eating corn/maize-based diets, which is low in niacin and tryptophan. Excess leucine in jowar and maize disrupts the conversion of tryptophan to niacin.

Niacin can be synthesized in the body from tryptophan. Two compounds- nicotinic acid, and nicotinamide have the biological activity of niacin. The nicotinamide ring of the coenzymes NAD ( nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) and NADP (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate) participate in oxidation/reduction reactions.

The initial symptoms of pellagra include loss of appetite, generalized weakness, irritability, abdominal pain, and vomiting. This is followed by bright red glossitis and a characteristic pigmented, scaly skin rash in sun-exposed areas. This rash is known as Casal’s necklace when it forms a ring around the neck.

The 4Ds of pellagra:

• Diarrhea
• Dermatitis
• Dementia, leading to
• Death

It is diagnosed by measuring urinary levels of 2-methyl nicotinamide and 2-pyridone.

It is treated by oral supplementation of 100–200 mg of nicotinamide or nicotinic acid three times daily for 5 days.

Casal’s necklace finding in niacin deficiency

Other options:

Option B: Dietary pyridoxine deficiency (vitamin B6) is rare but has been observed in alcoholics, newborn infants formulas low in vitamin B6, and women taking oral contraceptives. Isoniazid, an anti-TB drug, leads to pyridoxine deficiency resulting in peripheral neuropathy. Hence pyridoxine supplementation is included in ATT regimens.

Option C: Thiamine deficiency (vitamin B1) can manifest as wet beriberi (CVS features like heart failure and edema) or Shoshin beriberi, an acute and fulminant form of wet beriberi, dry beriberi (peripheral neuritis), or as Wernicke encephalopathy with Korsakoff psychosis (in alcoholics). Dietary deficiency of thiamine inhibits pyruvate dehydrogenase. Chronic alcoholics may develop potentially fatal pyruvic and lactic acidosis.

Option D: Dietary biotin deficiency is unknown but rarely, dermatitis, glossitis, loss of appetite, and nausea may occur after consumption of large amounts of uncooked egg white, which contains the protein avidin. It binds biotin and makes it unavailable for absorption.

Note: A similar image-based question on vitamin B3 deficiency was previously asked in NEET PG 2020. Vitamin deficiencies are a high-yield topic and are repeatedly tested every year.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presented with joint pain and on evaluation, urine turns black on standing. What is the likely enzyme deficiency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Homogentisic acid 1, 2 - dioxygenase

The urine turning black in color, on exposure to air, along with joint pain is suggestive of alkaptonuria. It occurs due to the defect in the homogentisic acid 1, 2 - dioxygenase enzyme.

Alkaptonuria is an autosomal recessive disorder of tyrosine metabolism, that develops due to the defect in homogentisate oxidase/homogentisic acid 1, 2 - dioxygenase, which oxidizes homogentisate to maleylacetoacetate. The defect in this enzyme leads to the accumulation of homogentisate, which is then excreted in the urine.

Alkaptonuria is characterized by homogentisic aciduria, ochronosis, and arthropathy (joint pain).

Homogentisic aciduria is the black discoloration of urine on prolonged exposure to air caused due to oxidation of the excreted homogentisate.

Ochronosis is the accumulation of oxidized homogentisic acid pigment (alkaptone bodies) in connective tissues leading to bluish-black discoloration of tissues mostly involving ear cartilage, ocular tissue, the skin of the eyelids, forehead, cheeks, and hands, nail beds, and intervertebral discs. The compound that accumulates in the tissues in ochronosis is benzoquinone acetate.

Painful arthritis (arthropathy) may be seen from the fourth or fifth decade.

Diagnosis: Blackish discoloration of urine on standing is diagnostic of alkaptonuria (shown below). The ferric chloride test will be positive.

The image further below shows Ochronosis.

Treatment:  No specific treatment is required. Symptomatic treatment with analgesics, spinal surgery, and arthroplasty along with ascorbic acid and protein restriction can be considered. Nitisinone (p-hydroxyphenylpyruvic acid (pHPPA) oxidase inhibitor) reduces urinary excretion of homogentisic acid.

Other options:

Option B: Tyrosine transaminase deficiency causes type II tyrosinemia (Richner-Hanhart syndrome). Patients present with painful corneal erosions with photophobia, learning disability, and palmoplantar keratosis.

Option C: Fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency causes type I tyrosinemia (Tyrosinosis). Patients generally present with failure to thrive, neuropathy, boiled-cabbage urine, and liver failure secondary to cirrhosis.

Option D:  4-hydroxy-phenyl pyruvate dioxygenase deficiency causes type III tyrosinemia (neonatal tyrosinemia). Patients might rarely have a mental disability. The liver function is generally normal.

The steps of tyrosine metabolism are shown below.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presented with symptoms of delayed adaptation to vision in dark places, gritty sensation in the eyes, dry eyes, and softening of the cornea. What is the likely deficiency in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Retinoic acid

The clinical picture of delayed adaptation to vision in dark places, gritty sensation in the eyes, dry eyes, and softening of the cornea is suggestive of vitamin A deficiency in the patient. Hence retinoic acid (the active form of vitamin A) is likely to be deficient.

Vitamin A is a fat-soluble vitamin that can occur as carotenoids (most common - beta carotene from plant sources) or retinoids (from animal sources).

3 forms of retinoids are:

• Retinal is required mainly for normal vision (present in the visual pigment rhodopsin).
• Retinol is important for the normal functioning of the reproductive system.
• Retinoic acid has a role in the regulation of gene expression and tissue differentiation.

Ocular manifestations of vitamin A deficiency include loss of sensitivity to green light (earliest to appear), nyctalopia (night blindness), xerophthalmia.

Xerophthalmia includes conjunctival xerosis (dryness) with Bitot’s spots (white patches of keratinized epithelium appearing on the sclera), corneal ulcers, and keratomalacia (softening of the cornea) that leads to corneal scarring and ultimately, blindness.

Other manifestations: General impairment of immunity, keratinization of skin (phrynoderma/toad skin).

Treatment: The WHO recommended schedule for all patients above the age of 1 year (except women of reproductive age): 200,000 IU of vitamin A orally or 100,000 IU by intramuscular injection should be given immediately on diagnosis (day 0) and repeated the following day (day 1) and 14 days later.
Dietary sources of vitamin A are liver, fish, eggs, dark green, and deeply colored fruits and vegetables.

Bitot's spots

The below image shows phrynoderma with multiple keratotic papules

Other options:

Option B: Ocular manifestations of riboflavin deficiency (vitamin B2) are photophobia, burning sensation, and vascularization of the cornea. Other features include cheilosis, magenta-colored tongue, glossitis, and seborrheic dermatitis.

Corneal vascularization. Seen in riboflavin (Vitamin B2) deficiency.

Option C: Niacin deficiency (vitamin B3) leads to pellagra. Dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia are its common features.

Casal’s necklace finding in niacin deficiency

Option D: Features of pantothenic acid deficiency (vitamin B5) are burning foot syndrome ( "nutritional melalgia"), dermatitis, enteritis, alopecia, ataxia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text:
A patient presented with tendon xanthomas. His lipid profile showed serum cholesterol levels to be 283 mg/dL and serum LDL to be 202 mg/dL. He was started on lovastatin. What is the likely diagnosis?

LDL - Low density lipoprotein
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Familial hypercholesterolemia

The clinical presentation with tendon xanthomas and elevated serum LDL (low-density lipoprotein) and elevated serum cholesterol points to a diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolemia (FH).

Familial hypercholesterolemia  (type IIa hyperlipoproteinemia) is an inherited disorder due to defects in LDL receptors. This defect causes a decrease in the uptake of LDL and cholesterol. As a result, the blood levels of both LDL and cholesterol are elevated. Such patients are at increased risk to develop atherosclerosis and coronary artery disease.

Features of FH:

• Painful polyarthritis and tendinitis are common.
• Physical findings seen are corneal arcus and tendon xanthomas over Achilles tendon and the dorsum of hands. Xanthomas are tumorous masses produced by foamy cell clusters (lipid-laden macrophages) found in the connective tissue of the skin and in tendons.

Diagnosis is done clinically based on hypercholesterolemia with

• LDL > 190 mg/dl,
• Family history of hypercholesterolemia and/or
• Premature coronary artery disease.

Treatment includes lifestyle changes, restriction of a fatty diet, and pharmacotherapy with statins in heterozygous FH patients.

Recent drugs for specific treatment of homozygous FH are:

• Lomitapide, a microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP) inhibitor, and
• Mipomersen, an antisense oligonucleotide against apoB.

The image below shows Achilles tendon xanthoma and a plain lateral radiograph of both ankles showing bilateral symmetrical swellings (arrows) superior to the calcaneum respectively.

Other options

Option B: Tangier’s disease is a hypolipoproteinemia caused by a mutation of the ABCA1 gene. Enlarged orange tonsils are pathognomonic. Low HDL levels are seen. There is an increased risk for atherosclerosis.

The image below shows enlarged yellow-orange colored tonsils in Tangier's disease.

Option C: Lipoprotein lipase (LPL) deficiency causes type I hyperlipoproteinemia due to defects in LPL or apo C-II. Eruptive xanthomas are seen. Chylomicrons and VLDL are elevated. LDL and HDL are low. There is no risk for coronary disease.

Option D: Familial hyperchylomicronemia syndrome is caused due to either LPL deficiency, ApoC-II deficiency, ApoA-V deficiency, or GPIHBP1 mutation. Clinically, patients present with recurrent episodes of severe abdominal pain due to acute pancreatitis. The retinal blood vessels may be opalescent and are called lipemia retinalis. Increased levels of triglycerides (mostly >1000 mg/dL) is seen. The risk of premature coronary heart disease is low.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient who has been diagnosed with multiple gastrointestinal polyps and carcinoma, with a positive family history/history of hereditary non-polyposis colon carcinoma has a defect in which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mismatch repair

Mismatch repair will be defective in a patient with multiple gastrointestinal polyps and carcinoma, with a positive family history/history of hereditary non-polyposis colon carcinoma (HNPCC)

Mismatch repair is a DNA repair mechanism that corrects single-nucleotide mismatches, insertions, and deletions introduced by the DNA polymerase during DNA replication.

HNPCC or Lynch syndrome is an autosomal dominant genetic condition. It occurs due to defects in DNA mismatch repair genes like MLH1 and MSH2. The genomes of these patients show microsatellite instability. HNPCC is associated with a high risk of colon cancer. It may also be associated with a risk of developing carcinomas of the endometrium, stomach, small bowel, ovary, pancreas, and transitional cell carcinoma of the ureter and renal pelvis.

The diagnostic criteria for HNPCC are referred to as the Amsterdam criteria or the 3-2-1-0 rule. It includes:

• Three or more relatives with HNPCC-associated cancer (colorectal cancer, endometrial cancer, cancer of the small bowel, ureter, or renal pelvis), one of whom is a first-degree relative of the other two.
• At least two successive generations affected
• At least one case diagnosed before age 50 years
• Familial adenomatous polyposis excluded
• Tumors verified by pathologic examination.

Other options:

Option B: Patients with xeroderma pigmentosum have a defect in the nucleotide excision repair pathway.

Option C: Defect in base excision repair pathway is seen in patients with MUTYH-associated polyposis.

Option D:  Sickle cell disease and beta-thalassemia are examples of diseases seen in patients with point mutations.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A person who had dinner at 8 pm the previous night, tested his blood glucose levels at 7 am the next morning. What is the source of blood glucose in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hepatic glycogenolysis

The source of blood glucose in a person fasting overnight for 11 hours (8 pm to 7 am) is hepatic glycogenolysis.

First stage of fasting: The fasting state begins two to four hours after the absorptive/well-fed state. In early fasting i.e; 4-18 hours after the well-fed state, the blood glucose level is maintained by hepatic glycogenolysis. The glycogen stores are sufficient for around 18 hours after a meal following which they start to deplete. So the source of blood glucose in a person fasting for 11 hours will be liver glycogenolysis.
Second stage of fasting: Gluconeogenesis begins 4–6 hours after the last meal but becomes fully active only after stores of liver glycogen are depleted (after 18 hours). They can serve as a source of glucose for up to 2 days.

Substrates for gluconeogenesis are:

• Glucogenic amino acids ( mainly alanine) from the muscle and
• Glycerol from adipose tissue

During fasting, the glucogenic amino acids are transported to the liver, transaminated into pyruvate, and converted to glucose.

Third stage of fasting:

• Lipolysis occurs in the adipose tissue due to the activity of hormone-sensitive lipase, stimulated by increased glucagon:insulin ratio.
• Free fatty acids are the source of energy in this stage and not glucose. Triacylglycerols will be hydrolyzed to fatty acids and glycerol.
• Beta oxidation of fatty acids takes place which provides acetyl CoA.
• In prolonged starvation (>3 days), acetyl CoA is converted to ketone bodies in the liver which will act as the main fuel source for skeletal and heart muscle and can meet up to 20% of the brain’s energy needs.

Final stage of fasting: After several weeks of starvation, ketone body synthesis will not take place due to depleted triacylglycerol stores. Proteins remain the only source of fuel. Protein degradation increases, and death results from a loss of heart, liver, or kidney function.

Role of insulin and glucagon:

When blood glucose falls during fasting, there is increased secretion of glucagon and decreased release of insulin. Hence glucagon:insulin ratio is increased.

Effects of increased glucagon:insulin ratio on enzymes of glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis:

1. It activates glycogen phosphorylase, the key enzyme of glycogenolysis, and deactivates glycogen synthase. This causes a rapid mobilization of liver glycogen stores to be utilized as fuel.
2. It favors the synthesis of glucose-6-phosphatase which converts glucose-6-phosphate to glucose. The resulting glucose is used by red blood cells (lack mitochondria) and the brain as they are largely dependant on glucose in the fasting state.
3. Phosphoenol pyruvate carboxykinase and fructose-1, 6-bisphosphatase are induced, leading to increased gluconeogenesis.

Metabolic process
Fasting state
Fed state

Glucagon: insulin
Increased
Decreased

Gluconeogenesis
Increased
Decreased

Glycogenolysis
Increased
Decreased

Ketogenesis
Increased
Decreased

Glycogen storage
Decreased
Increased

Other options:

Option C: Muscle glycogen cannot contribute directly to plasma glucose, since muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase. So glycogen cannot be converted to glucose to be used as fuel during starvation.

Option D: In the well-fed state/ absorptive state of two to four hours after a meal, dietary glucose is the main source of fuel.

The below image shows steps of glycolysis and gluconeogenesis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A young girl presented to the OPD for examination. She is tall and thin with slender fingers, and dislocated lenses. Workup revealed cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency. Which amino acid supplement is required in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cysteine

The clinical picture of a tall and thin young girl with slender fingers, dislocated lenses, and cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency is suggestive of classic homocystinuria. The amino acid supplement required in this scenario is cysteine.

Classic homocystinuria is a metabolic disorder of methionine metabolism, due to cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency. It is an autosomal recessive condition.

Cystathionine beta-synthase is a pyridoxal phosphate-dependent enzyme that condenses homocysteine with serine to form cystathionine. The absence of this enzyme will cause cysteine deficiency, hence cysteine needs to be supplemented in the diet.

Clinical features:

• Affected children are initially asymptomatic.
• Ectopia lentis (subluxation of the lens) is seen first, after 3 years of age.
• Intellectual disability and psychiatric and behavioral disorders.
• Thromboembolic episodes.
• Skeletal abnormalities resembling those of Marfan syndrome: They are tall and thin with elongated limbs and arachnodactyly (slender fingers).

Elevations of both methionine and homocysteine in body fluids are the diagnostic laboratory findings. The diagnosis is established by molecular analysis of cystathionine β-synthase (CBS) or by assay of the enzyme in cultured fibroblasts, phytohemagglutinin-stimulated lymphocytes, or liver biopsy specimens. Treatment includes restriction of methionine intake and supplementation with cysteine, betaine, vitamins B6, B12, and folate.

The image below shows arachnodactyly.

Methionine supplementation is required in non-classical homocystinuria. It is due to impaired re-methylation of homocysteine to methionine. This can be caused by defective methionine synthase or reduced availability of two essential cofactors, 5-methyltetrahydrofolate, and methylcobalamin.

Elevated homocysteine levels with low levels of methionine will be seen. Treatment includes methionine supplementation and administration of methyl folate, hydroxocobalamin, and betaine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: An alcoholic patient presented with itchy lesions as shown in the image, He also has a red-colored beefy tongue. Which of the following histories would you like to additionally ask/ elicit in this patient?
options: Ask for diarrhea and history of memory loss
Ask for diarrhea, thiamine deficiency features, and detailed dietary history
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ask for diarrhea and history of memory loss

An alcoholic patient with a red-colored beefy tongue, itching and the characteristic Casal's necklace, shown in the image, is suggestive of pellagra. It is caused by niacin/vitamin B3 deficiency. Hence, one should ask for a history of diarrhea and memory loss in this case.

Pellagra presents with 4 Ds: Diarrhea, Dermatitis, Dementia, and if untreated, Death. Early symptoms of pellagra are loss of appetite, generalized weakness and irritability, abdominal pain, and vomiting. Photosensitive dermatitis is seen over sun-exposed areas. Diarrhea occurs due to proctitis or malabsorption. Bright red glossitis (beefy tongue) and Casal’s necklace (a pigmented, scaly skin rash that forms a ring around the neck) follow. Depressive psychosis and dementia also commonly occur.

Corn/ maize/ jowar based diets are the main causes of niacin deficiency. Corn/maize lacks niacin and tryptophan. The excess leucine in jowar and maize disrupts the conversion of tryptophan to niacin. Niacin deficiency is also seen in alcoholism. Hence, additional histories of diarrhea and memory loss will aid in supporting the diagnosis of pellagra (along with dietary history).

Treatment includes oral supplementation with 100–200 mg of nicotinamide or nicotinic acid three times daily for 5 days.

Option B: Thiamine deficiency (vitamin B1) features include CVS manifestations like heart failure and edema (wet beriberi), peripheral neuritis (dry beriberi), and Wernicke encephalopathy (in alcoholics).

Option C: Dermatitis seen in pellagra is due to dietary deficiency of niacin and so allergy history is not relevant.

Option D: Conjunctivitis is not a feature of niacin deficiency.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The enzymes that convert pyruvate to acetyl CoA are given in the diagram. What are the enzymes marked as E1 and E2 respectively?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pyruvate dehydrogenase and dihydrolipoyl transacetylase

E1 is pyruvate dehydrogenase and E2 is dihydrolipoyl transacetylase in the image showing oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate. This is catalyzed by the pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex where E1, E2, and E3 are the three enzyme components of the complex.

The pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex is a multienzyme complex that is associated with the inner mitochondrial membrane. It catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA which enters the citric acid/Kreb’s cycle.

Enzyme components of PDH complex
Co-factors

Pyruvate dehydrogenase (E1)
Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP)

Dihydrolipoyl transacetylase (E2)

Lipoic acid

Coenzyme A

Dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase (E3)

Flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD)

Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+)

Steps of pyruvate decarboxylation:

• Pyruvate is transported into the mitochondria by a proton symporter.
• Pyruvate is decarboxylated by pyruvate dehydrogenase (E1). TPP is required for this step. The decarboxylated pyruvate remains bound to the enzyme, as hydroxyethyl thiamine pyrophosphate.
• The hydroxyethyl group is oxidized to form an acetyl group. It is then transferred from TPP to lipoamide to form acetyl lipoamide. This step is catalyzed by dihydrolipoyl transacetylase (E2).
• Acetyl lipoamide reacts with coenzyme A to form acetyl-CoA and reduced lipoamide.
• The reduced lipoamide is reoxidized by FAD-dependent dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase (E3).

The overall reaction is : Pyruvate + NAD+ + CoA → Acetyl-CoA + NADH + H+ + CO2

Clinical significance:

1. Dietary deficiency of thiamine inhibits PDH. Chronic alcoholics may develop potentially fatal pyruvic and lactic acidosis. Lactic acidosis is a common presentation in patients with inherited pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency too.
2. In arsenic and mercury poisoning, the heavy metal ions react with -SH groups of lipoic acid and inhibit pyruvate dehydrogenase.

Other multienzyme complexes include alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase. All the five coenzymes of PDH are common to these two complexes too.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) are responsible for corneal transparency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Keratan sulfate

The glycosaminoglycan (GAG) responsible for corneal transparency is keratan sulfate.

Glycosaminoglycans or mucopolysaccharides are complex carbohydrates made up of amino sugars and uronic acids. They may be attached to a protein molecule to form a proteoglycan.

Keratan sulfate is a mucopolysaccharide that does not contain uronic acid. It is constituted by repeating disaccharide units of N-acetyl glucosamine and galactose.

Keratan sulfate is present between the collagen fibrils in the cornea and plays a major role in corneal transparency.

2 types of keratan sulfate are seen:

• Keratan sulfate I is present in the cornea.
• Keratan sulfate II is mainly present in the cartilage.

Keratin sulfate I and II differ in their linkage to the core proteins. Keratan sulfate I links to a core protein L-asparagine via N-acetylglucosamine and Keratan sulfate II to  L-Serine (or L-Threonine) via N-acetylgalactosamine.

The chemical structure of Keratan sulfate is shown in the image below.

Other options:

Option B: In chondroitin sulfates (chondroitin 4-Sulfate & chondroitin 6-Sulfate), the repeating disaccharide units are glucuronic acid and N-acetylgalactosamine.  They maintain the structure of the extracellular matrix (ECM) and are located in endochondral bone and cartilage. They are also found in the ECM of the central nervous system. They act as signaling molecules in the prevention of the repair of nerve endings after injury.

Option C: Heparan sulfate is found on many extracellular cell surfaces and contains glucosamine with fewer N-sulfates than heparin. The predominant uronic acid is d-glucuronic acid. In the plasma membrane of cells, they act as receptors and mediate cell growth and cell-cell communication. It is also found in the basement membrane of the kidney along with type IV collagen and laminin, where it determines the charge selectiveness of glomerular filtration.

Option D: Hyaluronic acid is present in synovial fluid. It is also found in skin, bone, cartilage, vitreous humor, and embryonic tissues. It contains repeating units of N Acetyl Glucosamine and glucuronic acid. It plays a role in morphogenesis and wound repair. The high concentrations of hyaluronic acid along with chondroitin sulfates in cartilage contribute to its compressibility.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: You are conducting an experiment on mitochondrial respiration. You add malate/pyruvate and respiration is normal. You add succinate and respiration is normal. When you add another substance in the presence of pyruvate/succinate and malate, respiration is blocked. Which of the following substances is most likely added?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Oligomycin

In the experiment conducted on mitochondrial respiration, respiration will be blocked by the addition of oligomycin, an antibiotic, when added in the presence of pyruvate/ succinate and malate. Oligomycin inhibits oxidative phosphorylation in the mitochondria and hence blocks respiration.

Electron transport chain (ETC)/respiratory chain is the final pathway by which all the electrons derived from the oxidation of carbohydrates, fatty acids, and amino acids are directed towards the final reaction with oxygen, to form water and adenosine triphosphate (ATP).

The chemiosmotic theory states that the flow of electrons through the respiratory chain generates a proton motive force. This force drives the formation of ATP by the process of oxidative phosphorylation.

Complexes of ETC
Inhibitors

Complex I: NADH-CoQ oxidoreductase
Piericidin, amobarbital, rotenone

Complex II: Succinate-CoQ reductase
TTFA (thenoyltrifluoroacetone), carboxin, malonate

Complex III: CoQH2-cytochrome c oxidoreductase
BAL(British anti-lewisite), antimycin A

Complex IV: cytochrome oxidase
Hydrogen sulfide, carbon monoxide, cyanide

Complex V (informally): ATP Synthase
Atractyloside, oligomycin

In the given experiment, malate and pyruvate are electron donors (NADH) at complex I of the ETC, and succinate is the electron donor (FADH2) at complex II. Normal respiration is observed on the addition of substances at both complexes I and II i.e., both oxygen consumption and ATP synthesis from ADP (adenosine diphosphate) take place.

Oligomycin is a competitive inhibitor of the Fo (oligomycin-sensitive) complex of ATP synthase (complex V) and blocks oxidation and phosphorylation by stopping the flow of protons through the ATP synthase enzyme complex. Hence the addition of oligomycin will inhibit complex V and stop respiration.

Other options:

Options A and B: Rotenone (option A) if added, will inhibit complex I. Electron transfer before complex I will be blocked but not after. Hence, normal respiration will occur. Similarly, antimycin A (option B) inhibits complex III, and electron transfer prior to complex III will be blocked and not after. Hence, respiration will not be completely hindered.

Option C: 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP) is an uncoupler that dissociates oxidation in the respiratory chain from phosphorylation. Hence, respiration continues without ATP synthesis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child presents to you with anemia, thrombocytopenia, and bony pain. On examination, hepatosplenomegaly was noticed. If light microscopy of bone marrow aspirate reveals "crumpled tissue paper" appearance, what is the enzyme defect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Glucocerebrosidase

The clinical scenario points to a diagnosis of Gaucher's disease, where there is a defect in the enzyme glucocerebrosidase.

Gaucher's disease is a lysosomal storage disease with autosomal recessive inheritance. The condition results due to the deficiency of beta-glucocerebrosidase. This results in the accumulation of glucosylceramide (glycolipid substrate) in the reticuloendothelial cells. There is progressive infiltration of the liver, spleen, and bone marrow.

There are three clinical types:

• Type 1: Adult (non-neuronopathic) form
• Type 2: Infantile (acute neuronopathic) form
• Type 3: Juvenile (subacute neuronopathic) form

Type 1 is the most common. It presents with a myriad of symptoms, such as bruising secondary to thrombocytopenia, fatigue due to anemia, hepatosplenomegaly, and bone pain. Pathologic fractures and lytic lesions of the femur, ribs, and pelvis may also be seen. A few patients may have pulmonary involvement. Growth retardation may be observed in cases presenting in the first decade.

Type 2 is rare, and presents with hypertonia, strabismus, and organomegaly. Neurodegeneration is the characteristic feature. Stridor and failure to thrive can also be the presenting features. Ultimately, death can occur due to respiratory arrest.

Type 3 presents with intermediate symptoms, as seen in the other two types. By the age of 10–15 years, the child succumbs to death.

The Gaucher cells, which are the reticuloendothelial cells with glucosylceramide, have a wrinkled-paper appearance due to intracytoplasmic substrate inclusions. These cells stain strongly with periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain. This is characteristic of Gaucher's disease.

Other options:

Option B - Acid sphingomyelinase deficiency results in Niemann-Pick disease types A and B. Both are autosomal recessive conditions. Type A has a neurodegenerative course, while type B is non-neuronopathic. The former presents with hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and psychomotor retardation. Death occurs by the age of 3 years. Type B is associated with hepatosplenomegaly and mild pulmonary involvement.

Option C - Hexosaminidase deficiency causes Sandhoff disease. It has an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance. Clinical features include ataxia, dysarthria, and mental retardation.

Option D - Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency leads to von Gierke disease, which is a glycogen storage disorder.  It is an autosomal recessive condition. The affected children have characteristic doll-like facies. Hyperuricemia, lactic acidosis, and triglyceridemia can be seen. Hepatomegaly and renal enlargement is also associated.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient from a Mediterranean country visits Africa, where he develops malaria. He is treated with primaquine and later develops hemolytic anemia. Deficiency of an enzyme involved in which of the following pathways could be the cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hexose monophosphate (HMP) pathway

The deficiency of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) enzyme, which is involved in the hexose monophosphate (HMP) pathway, could be the cause behind this presentation.

G6PD is an enzyme that plays a critical role in redox reactions that occur in all aerobic cells. It is the only source of NADPH in erythrocytes, which helps in the formation of reduced glutathione. This reduced form protects erythrocytes against oxidative stress.

G6PD deficiency is an X-linked inheritance disorder. Most patients with this condition are asymptomatic. But when exposed to oxidative agents, they are prone to develop acute hemolytic anemia. The various oxidative triggers include:

• Fava beans
• Infections
• Drugs such as primaquine, dapsone, and nitrofurantoin

A hemolytic attack can present with weakness and abdominal/ lumbar pain. Later, the patient can develop jaundice, hemoglobinemia, and hemoglobinuria. Investigations will show elevated levels of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and low levels of plasma haptoglobin. Anisocytosis and spherocytes can be seen on peripheral smear. Acute renal failure is a complication seen in adults.

Other options:

Option A - Glycolysis, the main pathway of glucose, can occur either aerobically or anaerobically. A deficiency of the enzyme pyruvate kinase can present as hemolytic anemia. Fatigue can be the presentation when there is phosphofructokinase. Both these are enzymes of glycolysis.

Option B - Gluconeogenesis is the process by which non-carbohydrate precursors are used to synthesize glucose. Pyruvate carboxylase, phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase, and glucose-6-phosphatase are the enzymes in the pathway. Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency leads to von Gierke disease, which is a glycogen storage disorder. Defective gluconeogenesis results in hypoglycemia.

Option D - Luebering–Rapoport pathway is a shunt mechanism that generates and dephosphorylates 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG). 2,3-BPG mutase is the enzyme involved. A deficiency of this enzyme can cause erythrocytosis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A single mutation in a nucleotide base pair resulting in a termination codon is known as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nonsense mutation

A single mutation in a nucleotide base pair resulting in a termination codon is known as a nonsense mutation.

A codon is a sequence of three bases present on the mRNA (messenger RNA), and it codes for amino acids. Out of the 64 codons possible, only 61 code for the 20 amino acids. Three codons, UAA, UAG, and UGA  do not code for any of the 20 amino acids. These are known as nonsense/punctator/termination/stop codons and function as translation termination signals. The UGA codon is traditionally considered a stop codon, but it codes for selenocysteine (21st amino acid).

The tRNA (transfer RNA) contains the anticodon which recognizes specific codons present on the mRNA. The sequence of the anticodon is complementary to the codon. The pairing between the codon and anticodon can wobble at the third base. For example, GGU, GGC, and GGA all pair with the anticodon CCI. The wobble phenomenon along with degeneracy reduces the effect of mutations.

A mutation involving a single nucleotide base is known as a point mutation. A nonsense mutation is a type of point mutation where a codon previously coding for an amino acid is changed to a stop codon. This results in premature termination of translation and the formation of a truncated protein. mRNA containing premature stops are removed by the nonsense-mediated degradation pathway.

Other options:

Option A: A missense mutation is a type of point mutation where the new codon, formed by the changed base, codes for a different amino acid.

Option C: Stop mutation is a term that can be used interchangeably with nonsense mutation. Here, nonsense mutation is the best answer.

Option D: Silent mutations are point mutations where the new codon formed still codes for the same amino acid as the codon before the mutation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: An adolescent male patient presents to you with exercise intolerance. He gives a history of developing cramps on exertion. Which of the following enzyme deficiencies could be the cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Myophosphorylase

The clinical scenario points to a diagnosis of McArdle disease, which results due to a deficiency of the enzyme myophosphorylase (muscle glycogen phosphorylase).

McArdle disease, also known as type V glycogen storage disorder, is an autosomal recessive condition. It typically presents during late childhood or in the second decade of life. The muscle glycogen phosphorylase enzyme deficiency interferes with ATP generation by glycogenolysis in the muscles. This causes muscle glycogen accumulation.

Symptoms are exercise intolerance associated with muscle cramps. A second wind phenomenon, where the symptoms subside after a short period of rest, can also be seen. Myoglobinuria secondary to rhabdomyolysis leads to the passage of burgundy-colored urine in some patients.

Rarely, it can present during infancy as hypotonia, muscle weakness, and respiratory complications. It is generally fatal.

Muscle biopsy to measure glycogen content is the standard diagnosis. Avoiding strenuous exercise prevents symptoms. Glucose administration before exercise can improve tolerance. Vitamin B6 is also recommended.

Other options:

Option B - Hexokinase is a glycolytic enzyme. Its deficiency leads to hemolytic anemia. Splenomegaly may be another presenting feature.

Option C - Glucose-6-phosphatase is an enzyme involved in gluconeogenesis. Its deficiency leads to von Gierke disease also known as type I glycogen storage disease.

Option D - Hepatic glycogen phosphorylase deficiency results in type VI glycogen storage disease, also known as Hers disease.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: DNA packing is done by which of the following ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Histone

The proteins involved in DNA packing are histones.
