Chromatin contains double-stranded DNA molecules and small basic proteins known as histones. In addition, nonhistone proteins are present that are involved in DNA replication and repair, and RNA synthesis. Histones play a role in condensing the DNA.

Nucleosomes are the organizational unit of chromatin and contain an octamer of histones around which 150 base pairs of DNA are packed. There are various types of histone proteins. H2A, H2B, H3, and H4 groups are components of nucleosomes and are known as core histones. They undergo post-translational modifications such as acetylation and methylation. This plays a critical part in chromatin structure and function.

The DNA in the nucleosome is arranged in a left-handed helical configuration over the histone octamer.

Other options:

Option B - Glycoproteins are proteins with oligosaccharide chains (glycans) bound to amino acids. Certain plasma proteins, peptide hormones, and cell membrane proteins are examples. Structural changes in the glycoproteins present in cancer cells may play a role in metastasis.

Option C - Nucleic acids can be either DNA or RNA. DNA is thought to be arranged in a double-stranded helix model. RNA on the other hand exists as a single strand. There are different types of RNA such as mRNA (messenger RNA), tRNA (transfer RNA), and rRNA (ribosomal RNA).

Option D - Adenine is a purine base that when linked to ribose forms adenosine, a nucleoside. When a nucleoside is esterified with a phosphate group a nucleotide is formed. Guanine is the other purine base. Cytosine is the pyrimidine base common to DNA and RNA. Thymine is present only in DNA and Uracil in RNA.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The electron transport chain is a series of redox reactions that result in ATP synthesis. Which of the following is a cytochrome complex IV inhibitor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cyanide

Cyanide is an inhibitor of cytochrome complex IV or cytochrome a+a3 (cytochrome c oxidase). It is a component of the electron transport chain.

The electron transport chain (ETC) is a specialized set of electron carriers that can accept electrons. Energy-rich molecules like glucose are oxidized to produce water and carbon dioxide. The intermediate substrates in these reactions can pass on electrons to certain coenzymes such as nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) and flavin adenine dinucleotide (FADH2). The reduced forms can then donate electrons to the ETC by which they lose most of their free energy which is used to move H+ through the inner mitochondrial membrane. The H+ gradient thus produced results in the production of ATP. ATP synthesis together with electron transport is known as oxidative phosphorylation.

The reactions in oxidative phosphorylation and the arrangement of complexes that form the ETC are shown below.

These complexes can accept or donate electrons to coenzyme Q (CoQ) and cytochrome c, which are mobile electron carriers. Certain site-specific inhibitors can inhibit ATP synthesis.

Complexes of ETC
Inhibitors

Complex I
Piericidin A, amobarbital, rotenone

Complex II
TTFA (thenoyltrifluoroacetone), carboxin, malonate

Complex III
BAL(British anti-lewisite), antimycin A

Complex IV
Hydrogen sulfide, carbon monoxide, cyanide

Other options:

Option B - Carbon dioxide along with water is produced by the oxidation of energy-rich molecules in oxidative phosphorylation.

Option C - Oligomycin, an antibiotic, blocks the flow of protons through ATP synthase. This inhibits oxidative phosphorylation.

Option D - Ouabain is a cardiac drug that inhibits the Na+ - K+ ATPase of cell membranes by acting on the extracellular surface.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The following is due to the deficiency of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin A

The given image depicts Bitot's spots characteristically seen in deficiency of vitamin A. Bitot's spots are seen as white patches of keratinized epithelium on the sclera. It is more commonly bilateral and on the temporal side.

Vitamin A deficiency arises mostly due to the inadequate amounts of vitamin A in diet. It can present as night blindness, conjunctival xerosis, Bitot's spots, and keratomalacia. In later stages, it can lead to xerophthalmia. It also increases the risk of developing measles, diarrhea, and dysentery. Skin manifestations include xerosis, scaling, and dermomalacia. Phrynoderma may also be seen as keratotic follicular papules affecting the thighs and upper arms. It is shown in the image below.

In patients above the age of 1 year, vitamin A deficiency is treated with 200,000 IU of vitamin A orally or 100,000 IU by intramuscular route. It should be repeated the next day and two weeks later.

Vitamin A is a fat-soluble vitamin that plays an essential role in vision, reproduction, and maintenance of epithelial integrity. The various forms of vitamin A include retinol (storage form), retinal, retinoic acid, and beta-carotene. It is stored in the liver perisinusoidal stellate (Ito) cells as retinyl ester (retinyl palmitate).

Other options:

Option A - Vitamin C is a water-soluble vitamin that aids in iron absorption and collagen maturation. It cannot be synthesized in humans because of the absence of L-gulonolactone oxidase. Vitamin C deficiency results in scurvy.

Option C - Vitamin B deficiency has clinical manifestations pertaining to each type.

Option D - Vitamin E deficiency can present as posterior column and spinocerebellar symptoms. Peripheral neuropathy, ophthalmoplegia, and pigmented retinopathy are other features seen.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following disorders follows autosomal recessive inheritance pattern?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cystic fibrosis

Cystic fibrosis is a condition with an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance.

It results due to a defective mutation in the gene encoding for cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR gene). It functions as an epithelial anion channel. It plays an important role in mucociliary transport along the respiratory mucosa. It also helps regulate the amount of exocrine gland secretion.

The defect in the ion channel results in the production of hyper viscous, adherent secretions which can obstruct the airways. Organisms such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus can grow in the sputum. The exocrine pancreas can undergo fibrotic scarring, cyst formation, and acinar tissue loss. The viscid secretions can lead to pancreatic duct obstruction. The flow of digestive enzymes to the duodenum is hence impaired.

Symptoms include sinusitis, steatorrhea, and abdominal pain. Distal intestinal obstruction is a complication due to difficulty in excreting intestinal contents. In neonates, it can present as meconium ileus.

Detection of high levels of trypsinogen is used in newborn screening. Chloride level >60mEq/L in the sweat of affected patients is diagnostic. Hyponatremic hypochloremic alkalosis and hypokalemia may also be seen.

Postural drainage, short-term antibiotics, and inhaled bronchodilators can be used for medical management. The definitive treatment is lung transplantation.

In autosomal recessive inheritance, multiple affected members are seen in the same generation. Other generations are not affected. The following pedigree chart depicts an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance.

Other options:

Option A - Huntington's disease is a trinucleotide (CAG) repeat disorder with an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance. It is characterized by involuntary movements known as chorea.

Option B - Treacher Collins syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder that presents as mandibular and malar hypoplasia.

Option D - Achondroplasia has an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern and presents with short limbs, saddle nose, and spinal deformity.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following enzyme activities can be estimated in red blood cells to diagnose vitamin B2 deficiency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glutathione reductase

Glutathione reductase activity in red blood cells can be estimated to diagnose vitamin B2 deficiency.

Vitamin B2, also known as riboflavin, is a water-soluble vitamin. Its active forms are FMN (flavin mononucleotide) and FAD (flavin adenine dinucleotide). Glutathione reductase is a FAD-containing enzyme (flavoenzyme). Hence, riboflavin deficiency can be detected by measuring erythrocyte glutathione reductase activity. Red blood cell and urinary concentrations of riboflavin can also be estimated to detect a deficiency.

Deficiency of riboflavin can present as anemia, corneal vascularization, mucocutaneous lesions, and personality changes. Milk and other dairy products are important dietary sources.

Other options:

Option A - Transketolase contains thiamine diphosphate as a coenzyme. Estimation of erythrocyte apotransketolase (enzyme protein) after in vitro addition of thiamine diphosphate, can be used to assess thiamine nutritional status. Thiamine deficiency can result in peripheral neuritis, beriberi, and Wernicke encephalopathy with Korsakoff psychosis.

Option C - Kynureninase is an enzyme that requires pyridoxal phosphate as a coenzyme. It converts 3-hydroxykynurenine, a tryptophan metabolite, to 3-hydroxyanthranilate. In vitamin B6 deficiency, this is impaired and results in the formation and subsequent urinary excretion of xanthurenate. This can be used for diagnosis.

Option D - Pyruvate is decarboxylated by pyruvate dehydrogenase for which thiamine diphosphate acts as the cofactor. Therefore thiamine deficiency results in the accumulation of pyruvate. This leads to pyruvic and lactic acidosis, commonly seen in alcoholics.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following helps in the transport of fatty acids across the inner mitochondrial membrane?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Carnitine

Carnitine is responsible for the transport of fatty acids or long-chain acyl-CoA across the inner mitochondrial membrane.

Fatty acids are oxidized in the mitochondria to produce acetyl-CoA to produce energy. They must first be converted to acyl-CoA (active fatty acid) before they can be catabolized.

Carnitine palmitoyltransferase - I (CPT- I) transports acyl-CoA across the inner mitochondrial membrane only in the presence of carnitine. The acyl group of acyl-CoA is transferred to carnitine. The acylcarnitine so formed can penetrate the inner mitochondrial membrane via the carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase. This transporter transfers the acyl group back to CoA, restoring acyl-CoA and liberating carnitine, which is moved back to the intermembrane space. Carnitine palmitoyltransferase -II catalyzes this reaction. The deficiency of this enzyme is a common cause of recurrent myoglobinuria.

Carnitine deficiency can lead to hypoglycemia and restrictive or dilated cardiomyopathy. It can also cause hepatic steatosis.

Other options:

Option A - Acyl carrier protein is a component of the fatty acid synthase complex involved in the biosynthesis of fatty acids. It has vitamin pantothenic acid (vitamin B5).

Option C - Lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT) is present in the plasma and plays an important role in the esterification of cholesterol. Deficiency leads to low levels of lysolecithin and cholesteryl esters.

Option D - The long-chain fatty acids are bound to albumin in the plasma. But albumin does not transport fatty acids across the inner mitochondrial membrane. Albumin is a negative acute-phase reactant synthesized by the liver. It is a carrier for acidic drugs.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 4-year-old child presents with easy fatiguability. The mother also complains that the child has increased hunger between meals, which is relieved after food. Liver examination revealed no glycogen. The enzyme most likely deficient is _________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glycogen synthase

The most likely enzyme deficiency in a child with fatigue, excessive hunger between meals, and absent liver glycogen is glycogen synthase deficiency.

Glycogen is a storage carbohydrate synthesized from glucose (glycogenesis) and is stored in the liver, muscles, and brain. Glycogen synthase is a regulating enzyme for glycogenesis.

Glycogen synthase exists in both phosphorylated (inactive) and dephosphorylated (active) forms. Phosphorylation is stimulated by epinephrine, norepinephrine, and glucagon via cAMP. Dephosphorylation is stimulated by insulin via phosphodiesterase.

A deficiency of glycogen synthase leads to glycogen storage disorder and presents in infancy with early morning drowsiness and fatigue, fasting hypoglycemia, pallor, emesis, and hypoglycemic convulsions. It leads to a marked decrease in liver glycogen stores. Hepatomegaly is absent.

Laboratory investigations reveal prolonged hyperglycemia, glycosuria, ketosis, lactic acidosis, low alanine levels, and normal insulin levels after glucose administration. A liver biopsy is diagnostic.

Treatment involves protein-rich frequent meals, and nighttime supplementation with cornstarch to prevent hypoglycemia and hyperketonemia.

Other options:

Option A: Glycogen phosphorylase deficiency, also known as McArdle's disease or glycogen storage disease type V, primarily affects skeletal muscle glycogen metabolism. Affected individuals experience muscle weakness, cramps, and exercise intolerance, but it doesn't typically cause the symptoms mentioned in the question.

Option C: Debranching enzyme deficiency, also known as Cori's disease or glycogen storage disease type III, presents with hepatomegaly, hypoglycemia, and growth retardation. The liver would still contain glycogen, albeit with an abnormal structure.

Option D: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency, known as von Gierke's disease or glycogen storage disease type I, is characterized by severe fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, and hepatomegaly. In this case, glycogen is present in the liver but cannot be broken down efficiently into glucose.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child presents with bone pain and hepatosplenomegaly. A trephine biopsy and aspirate show the following finding. Which of the following is the most likely enzyme deficient in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glucocerebrosidase

The given clinical scenario of a child with bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly, and biopsy showing Gaucher's cell with a characteristic crumpled tissue paper appearance is suggestive of Gaucher's disease. The deficient enzyme is glucocerebrosidase (also known as beta-glucosidase).

Gaucher's disease is an inborn error of metabolism caused due to a deficiency of beta-glucocerebrosidase. It is the most common lysosomal storage disorder and the mode of inheritance is autosomal recessive. There is an accumulation of lipid-laden macrophages in the spleen, liver, and other tissues.

There are three clinical subtypes - type I (chronic non-neuronopathic), type II (acute neuronopathic), and type III (intermediate). Clinical features include anemia, thrombocytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, and neurological features depending on the subtype.

Gaucher's cells - These are formed as a result of the accumulation of massive amounts of glucocerebrosides within the phagocytes. The cells have a fibrillary cytoplasm and give a crumpled tissue paper appearance.

Option A: Deficiency of hexosaminidase A is seen in Tay-Sachs disease. The deficiency of beta-hexosaminidase A and B causes Sandhoff's disease. Clinical features are seizures, macrocephaly, and hyperacusis.

Option C: Deficiency of sphingomyelinase leads to Niemann-Pick disease. It is characterized by the presence of foam cells in the bone marrow. There may be pulmonary infiltrates leading to lung failure.

Option D: Pompe's disease (type 2 glycogen storage disease) occurs due to alpha 1,4-glucosidase (acid maltase) deficiency. It is the only glycogen storage disease that is a lysosomal storage disease and causes lysosomal glycogen accumulation in cardiac, skeletal, and smooth muscle cells. The clinical symptoms of Pompe disease are hypotonia (floppy infant), skeletal muscle weakness, hepatomegaly, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and macroglossia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child presents with erythematous scaly patches in the perioral region, mucosal ulcers, and impaired epithelial wound healing. The most likely mineral deficiency associated with this condition is ________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Zinc deficiency

The clinical features of periorificial dermatitis and stomatitis in a young child are suggestive of acrodermatitis enteropathica, seen in zinc deficiency.

Acrodermatitis enteropathica is a genetic disorder that results in the inability to absorb dietary zinc.

The clinical features develop after weaning and the infant presents with:

• Failure to thrive
• Skin manifestations such as symmetrical vesiculobullous dermatitis in the perioral, perianal, and acral regions
• Anorexia, diarrhea
• Recurrent infections due to T-cell immunodeficiency
• Alopecia with a reddish tint
• Impaired wound healing
• Male hypogonadism, growth retardation
• Neurological manifestations like tremors, nystagmus, photophobia, hypogeusia, irritability, and night blindness

Oral zinc supplementation is the treatment of choice.

Other options:

Option A- Iron deficiency is the most common micronutrient deficiency globally. It presents with iron-deficiency anemia and neurocognitive impairment. It presents clinically with pallor, fatigue, atrophic glossitis, and pica.

Option C- Calcium deficiency leads to rickets as a result of early weaning. It presents with typical symptoms of rickets, including failure to thrive; protruding abdomen; muscle weakness; fractures; craniotabes; delayed dentition; caries; enlargement of wrists and ankles; and hypocalcemic symptoms of tetany, stridor, and seizures.

Option D- Copper deficiency leads to anemia, growth retardation, defective keratinization and pigmentation of hair, hypothermia, degenerative changes in aortic elastin, osteopenia, and mental retardation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child presents with mental retardation, bone pain, and inability to walk. On funduscopy examination, a cherry red spot is seen. There is no organomegaly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tay-Sachs disease

The given clinical scenario, along with the fundoscopy image showing a macular cherry-red spot, indicates that the most likely diagnosis is Tay-Sachs disease.

Tay-Sachs disease is a lysosomal storage disease caused by the deficiency of β-hexosaminidase. It can present during infancy with macrocephaly, increased startle reaction, gradual loss of motor skills, and a macular cherry-red spot. Affected children usually die by the age of 10–15 years.

It is of two types—juvenile-onset and adult-onset. The symptoms of the juvenile-onset form include ataxia and dementia. Dysarthria, lower motor neuron signs, and psychiatric disorders are common in the adult-onset type.

Other options:

Options B - Niemann-Pick disease is an autosomal recessive inborn error of lipid metabolism. It results due to the deficiency of the sphingomyelinase enzyme. This results in the accumulation of sphingomyelin in the brain, lungs, liver, and spleen. The clinical features include a combination of hepatosplenomegaly, developmental delay, failure to thrive, severe psychomotor regression, interstitial lung disease, and a cherry-red spot in the macula.

Option C - Hurler syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis I) is an autosomal recessive condition that affects multiple organs. Presentation is usually at 6–24 months with corneal clouding, coarse facial features, joint stiffness, and skeletal dysplasia. Glaucoma, retinal degeneration, and nasal discharge are the other features. The condition is generally fatal.

Option D - Gaucher disease is a glycolipid storage disorder that can present with hepatosplenomegaly, mental retardation, and erosion of long bones. It is caused by the deficiency of β-glucosidase. The Gaucher cell has a wrinkled-paper appearance due to intracytoplasmic inclusions, which is a characteristic feature.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child presents with thinning of hair and scaling of the scalp. On taking further history, it is found that she consumes raw eggs in her diet regularly. The given manifestations are due to the deficiency of which of the following vitamins?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Biotin

The given clinical scenario of scaling and alopecia and the history of raw egg consumption are suggestive of biotin deficiency.

Raw egg white contains a glycoprotein known as avidin, which tightly binds to biotin and renders it unabsorbable from the intestine. Hence, there can be a biotin deficiency state.

Biotin deficiency may cause:

• Dermatitis, scaling, seborrheic, and erythematous rash
• Mental status changes (depression, hallucinations)
• Hyperesthesia
• Alopecia
• Atrophic glossitis

In infants, biotin deficiency presents as hypotonia, lethargy, and apathy. In addition, infants may develop alopecia and a characteristic rash that includes the ears.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child was brought with pedal edema and cheilosis. Cardiomegaly was present. What is the vitamin deficiency associated with this clinical presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thiamine

The given clinical presentation with pedal edema and cardiomegaly is suggestive of wet beriberi due to thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency.

Early symptoms of thiamine deficiency include peripheral neuropathy, irritability, loss of deep tendon reflexes and proprioception. As the disease progresses, increased intracranial pressure, meningismus and coma develop.

Wet beriberi results due to cardiac and renal dysfunction which leads to fluid accumulation. It is associated with tachycardia, cardiomegaly, cardiac failure, and edema. It is commonly seen in the refugee camps where people consume polished rice-based monotonous diets.

Dry beriberi is associated with neurological deficits such as peripheral neuropathy, optic atrophy, ataxia, and irritability. Complications include lactic acidosis and Wernicke encephalopathy in adults.

Diagnosis of thiamine deficiency can be established by erythrocyte transketolase activity assessment.

Other options:

Option A: Riboflavin deficiency can present with cheilosis, but it does not typically cause pedal edema and cardiomegaly.

Option C: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) deficiency can cause neurological symptoms, anemia, and dermatitis but is not associated with pedal edema, cardiomegaly, and cheilosis.

Option D: Niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency leads to pellagra, characterized by the triad of dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia. It is not associated with pedal edema, cardiomegaly, and cheilosis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A chronic alcoholic patient is diagnosed with gouty arthritis. What biochemical changes will be seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increased urate and lactate levels

This patient with chronic alcoholism and gouty arthritis will most likely have elevated levels of lactate and urate.

The oxidation of ethanol to acetate by alcohol dehydrogenase is accompanied by the reduction of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) to NADH. This results in a high concentration of NADH, leading to an increased NADH/NAD+ ratio (Option A).

Due to this, the following metabolic reactions that require NAD+ are inhibited:

1. Glycolysis
2. Citric acid cycle (ketogenesis favored)
3. Pyruvate dehydrogenase
4. Fatty acid oxidation

Decreased fatty acid oxidation leads to increased esterification and production of triacylglycerol, which causes fatty liver.

Also, there is an increase in two reactions:

• Pyruvate to lactate
• Oxaloacetate to malate

Increased lactate leads to hyper-lactic-acidemia, which leads to increased renal reabsorption of urate and decreased excretion of uric acid. This results in aggravation of gout. Alcoholics are deficient in thiamine which inhibits pyruvate dehydrogenase and leads to lactic acidosis.

A decrease in pyruvate and oxaloacetate levels, which are substrates for gluconeogenesis, leads to a decrease in blood glucose levels, causing symptoms of agitation, impaired judgment, and combativeness.

Other options:

Increased urea and urate levels are not specifically associated with alcoholism and gouty arthritis. While urate levels may be increased due to gout, urea levels are not directly related to the condition (Option B).

Increased levels of alkaline phosphatase can be seen in alcohol-induced hepatitis due to intrahepatic cholestasis but is not directly related to gouty arthritis in a chronic alcoholic patient. Therefore, this option is less relevant compared to increased urate and lactate levels (Option D).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A chronic alcoholic patient presented to the casualty with confusion, ataxia, and painful eye movements. What could be the vitamin deficiency seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vitamin B deficiency

The above clinical history is suggestive of Wernicke encephalopathy, which is caused by vitamin B1 (Thiamine) deficiency.

Vitamin B1/thiamine deficiency leads to following conditions:

1. Wernicke encephalopathy:

• An acute, neuropsychiatric syndrome characterized by nystagmus and ophthalmoplegia, mental status changes (confusion), and unsteadiness of stance and gait.
• Wernicke’s encephalopathy is a medical emergency, and thiamine should be initiated immediately, either intravenously or intramuscularly.
• The current standard of treatment for patients with symptoms of Wernicke's encephalopathy is to give thiamine 100 mg intravenously before administering glucose-containing IV fluids.

2. Korsakoff psychosis:

• Korsakoff syndrome is characterized by a pronounced anterograde and retrograde amnesia along with potential impairment in visuospatial, abstract, and other types of learning.
• Symptoms are similar to that of Wernicke encephalopathy, but also include memory loss and confabulation.
• Permanent in at least a partial form in about 50% of the people affected.

3. Beriberi: It can present with:

• Dry beriberi: sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy, muscle weakness
• Wet beriberi: tachycardia, cardiomegaly, high-output cardiac failure

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A family consumes only polished rice. Which of the following combination of vitamin deficiency and enzymatic defect will be present in this family?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thiamine-transketolase

The consumption of polished rice leads to thiamine deficiency which leads to defective transketolase activity.

Polished rice is rice that has had its husk, bran, and germ removed, leaving only the endosperm. This processing method results in a loss of nutrients, including thiamine.

Thiamine pyrophosphate (Vit B1) is the cofactor of transketolase. This reaction requires two cofactors:

• Mg2+
• Thiamine diphosphate (vitamin B1)

Transketolase and transaldolase are involved in the non-oxidative phase of the HMP pathway.

Thiamine deficiency can lead to beriberi, a condition characterized by peripheral neuropathy, weakness, and cardiovascular symptoms. In severe cases, it can also lead to Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, which is characterized by confusion, ataxia, and vision disturbances. Thiamine deficiency can be prevented by consuming a balanced diet that includes unprocessed grains, legumes, and other sources of thiamine. Diagnosis of thiamine deficiency can be established by erythrocyte transketolase activity assessment.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presented with diarrhea, dermatitis, and dementia. Which of the following vitamin deficiencies would you suspect in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vitamin B3 deficiency

The given clinical scenario of a patient with diarrhea, dermatitis, and dementia is suggestive of niacin/vitamin B3 deficiency.

Niacin deficiency causes pellagra, found mostly among people eating corn/maize-based diets, which are low in niacin and tryptophan. Excess leucine in jowar and maize disrupts the conversion of tryptophan to niacin.

Niacin can be synthesized in the body from tryptophan. Two compounds, nicotinic acid and nicotinamide, have the biological activity of niacin. The nicotinamide ring of the coenzymes nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP) participate in oxidation/reduction reactions.

The initial symptoms of pellagra include loss of appetite, generalized weakness, irritability, abdominal pain, and vomiting. This is followed by bright red glossitis and a characteristic pigmented, scaly skin rash in sun-exposed areas. This rash is known as Casal’s necklace when it forms a ring around the neck.

The 4Ds of pellagra:

• Diarrhea
• Dermatitis
• Dementia, leading to
• Death

It is diagnosed by measuring urinary levels of 2-methyl nicotinamide and 2-pyridone.

It is treated by oral supplementation of 100–200 mg of nicotinamide or nicotinic acid three times daily for 5 days.

Casal’s necklace finding in niacin deficiency:

Other options:

Option B: Vitamin B1/Thiamine deficiency can manifest as wet beriberi (CVS features like heart failure and edema) or Shoshin beriberi, an acute and fulminant form of wet beriberi, dry beriberi (peripheral neuritis), or as Wernicke encephalopathy with Korsakoff psychosis (in alcoholics). Dietary deficiency of thiamine inhibits pyruvate dehydrogenase. Chronic alcoholics may develop potentially fatal pyruvic and lactic acidosis.

Option C: Vitamin B6/Pyridoxine deficiency is rare but has been observed in alcoholics, newborns, formulas low in vitamin B6, and women taking oral contraceptives. Isoniazid, an anti-TB drug, leads to pyridoxine deficiency resulting in peripheral neuropathy. Hence pyridoxine supplementation is included in ATT regimens.

Option D: Vitamin B12/Cobalamin deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia, dementia, spinal cord degeneration, homocysteinemia, etc.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presenting with bleeding gums and easy bruisability was diagnosed with scurvy. This is due to ______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Defective collagen formation

Bleeding gums and easy bruisability seen in scurvy are due to defective collagen formation.

Scurvy results from the deficiency of vitamin C, which is required for the hydroxylation of prolyl and lysyl residues of collagen reactions. Hence, deficiency of vitamin C results in a defective prolyl hydroxylase activity, leading to defective collagen formation and resulting in generalized bleeding tendencies.

Hemorrhagic manifestations of scurvy include petechiae, purpura, ecchymoses at pressure points, epistaxis, gum bleeding, and characteristic perifollicular hemorrhages. Other manifestations are poor wound and fracture healing, hyperkeratosis of hair follicles, arthralgia, and muscle weakness. It also results in defective osteoid formation. Costo-chondral separation leads to the formation of tender nodules that are sharply angulated and are also known as the scorbutic rosary.

The cutaneous manifestations of scurvy include

• Phrynoderma over posterolateral arms which can then generalize over the back and thighs and legs.
• Corkscrew hairs -  fractured and coiled hairs due to impaired keratin cross‐links by disulfide bonds
• Perifollicular hemorrhage and purpura
• Lower limb edema
• Splinter hemorrhages

It is treated with vitamin C supplementation.

Other options:

Option A: Low calcium levels do not cause scurvy; they may contribute to other clinical conditions like osteoporosis or muscle cramps.

Option C: Inhibition of clotting factors is not responsible for scurvy. Vitamin K deficiency, however, can lead to the inhibition of clotting factors and cause bleeding tendencies.

Option D: Increased keratinization of epithelium is not the cause of scurvy. Vitamin A deficiency, on the other hand, can result in hyperkeratoses and epithelial changes, such as xerosis and Bitot's spots.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A young boy presents to the OPD with hypoglycemia and muscle cramps, on exertion or while playing. Then he becomes normal after resting for a while. These episodes are recurrent after a period of activity. He has decreased serum lactate and glucose levels. Which of the following diseases is he most likely to be suffering from?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. McArdle disease

A clinical scenario of a patient with muscle cramps, pain, weakness with exertion, myoglobinuria, and the muscle biopsy specimen showing vacuolar myopathy are suggestive of McArdle's disease, which is due to the deficiency of muscle glycogen phosphorylase.

McArdle disease, also known as type V glycogen storage disorder, is an autosomal recessive condition. It typically presents during late childhood or in the second decade of life. The muscle glycogen phosphorylase enzyme deficiency interferes with ATP generation by glycogenolysis in the muscles. This causes muscle glycogen accumulation.

Symptoms are exercise intolerance associated with muscle cramps. Due to high-intensity exercise, sudden persistent muscle contraction occurs. This leads to severe muscle damage resulting in a massive release of muscle proteins and myoglobin in the blood. Myoglobinuria secondary to rhabdomyolysis leads to the passage of burgundy-colored urine in some patients.

A unique feature associated with McArdle is the improvement in symptoms after rest for a few minutes. This is termed as the second wind phenomenon. This occurs due to the increased blood flow to the muscles and increased utilization of free fatty acids (FFAs) for energy production after resting for a few minutes. This compensates for the impaired ATP generation from glycogenolysis. Patients with McArdle disease can benefit from engaging in regular aerobic exercises, such as walking or cycling, which can help increase their exercise tolerance and cardiovascular fitness. However, they should avoid high-intensity exercises or activities that can trigger muscle cramps and rhabdomyolysis. Glucose administration before exercise can improve tolerance. Vitamin B6 is also recommended.

Standard diagnosis includes muscle biopsy, which shows periodic acid Schiff (PAS)-positive vacuoles (Shown in the image below) of high glycogen content due to lack of myophosphorylase and genetic testing (PYGM gene sequencing).

Other options:

Option B: Hers disease (type VI glycogen storage disorder) - It is caused by the deficiency of liver glycogen phosphorylase. Patients with Hers disease exhibit growth retardation, hepatomegaly, and mild hypoglycemia. They do not typically present with muscle cramps and myoglobinuria.

Option C: Cori's disease (type III glycogen storage disorder) - It is caused by a deficiency of glycogen debranching enzyme. Patients with Cori's disease present with hepatomegaly, growth retardation, and hypoglycemia. Muscle weakness may be present but not muscle cramps or myoglobinuria.

Option D: Andersen disease (type IV glycogen storage disorder) - It is caused by the deficiency of glycogen branching enzyme. This disease presents with hepatomegaly, cirrhosis, and liver failure. It does not cause muscle cramps or myoglobinuria.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: An infant is brought by his parents with complaints that his urine turns black on standing. Which of the following metabolic disorders is likely?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Alkaptonuria

Blackening of urine on standing is characteristic of alkaptonuria.

Alkaptonuria is an autosomal recessive disorder of tyrosine metabolism, that develops due to the defect in homogentisate oxidase/homogentisic acid 1, 2 - dioxygenase, which oxidizes homogentisate to maleylacetoacetate. The defect in this enzyme leads to the accumulation of homogentisate, which is then excreted in the urine.

Alkaptonuria is characterized by homogentisic aciduria, ochronosis, and arthropathy (joint pain).

Homogentisic aciduria is the black discoloration of urine on prolonged exposure to air caused due to oxidation of the excreted homogentisate.

Ochronosis, which is bluish-black pigmentation in connective tissue, generally occurs after the third decade of life, and it occurs due to the accumulation of homogentisic acid and its oxidation products like benzoquinone acetic acid in connective tissue.

Arthritis generally begins in the third decade. Arthritis often begins in the spine and resembles ankylosing spondylitis in its large-joint distribution. Radiographs of the spine showing flattened and calcified intervertebral discs are pathognomonic. Other findings include degeneration of the intervertebral discs, followed by disc calcification and eventually fusion of the vertebral bodies. Osteophyte formation and calcification of the intervertebral ligaments also occur.

Diagnosis: Blackish discoloration of urine on standing is diagnostic of alkaptonuria (shown below). The ferric chloride test will be positive. The blackening of urine occurs due to the excretion of homogentisic acid in the urine.

Image A - Normal urine
Image B - Alkaptonuria

Other options:

Option A: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is a metabolic disorder resulting from a deficiency of the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase. It does not lead to black urine. Patients with PKU have a musty or mousy odor due to phenylacetic acid accumulation.

Option C: Homocystinuria is an inborn error of methionine metabolism caused by a deficiency of the enzyme cystathionine β-synthase. It is characterized by tall stature, long limbs, dislocation of the lens of the eye, and predisposition to thromboembolism, but it does not lead to black urine.

Option D: Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) is an inherited metabolic disorder caused by a deficiency of branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase. It does not cause black urine. Patients with MSUD have urine with a characteristic sweet odor, resembling maple syrup.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is seen in low insulin:glucagon ratio?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Activation of hormone-sensitive lipase

Low insulin:glucagon ratio occurs in the fasting state. Since insulin has an inhibitory effect on hormone-sensitive lipase (lipolytic hormone), low insulin:glucagon ratio results in the activation of hormone-sensitive lipase.

In adipose tissues, decreased insulin results in the inhibition of lipogenesis and activation of intracellular hormone-sensitive lipase. The stored triglycerides are broken down (lipolysis) by hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) into free fatty acids (FFAs) and glycerol. In the fasting state, glucose is spared for the brain and glycerol is used as a substrate for gluconeogenesis.

In diabetic patients, low insulin level corresponds to an increase in HSL activity, promoting the breakdown of lipids and the release of FFAs from adipose tissue. HSL activity is accelerated by hormones like epinephrine, norepinephrine, glucagon, ACTH, TSH, GH, ADH, and melanocyte-stimulating hormones (MSH).

Well-fed state (Insulin)
During fasting (Glucagon)

Lipogenesis increased
Lipogenesis inhibited

Lipolysis inhibited
Lipolysis increased

Insulin inhibits HS-lipase
Glucagon activates HS-lipase

Lipoprotein lipase active
Lipoprotein lipase inactive

Other options:

Option A: Activation of lipoprotein lipase (LPL) is promoted by insulin, not low insulin: glucagon ratio. LPL is involved in the breakdown of triglycerides and is active in the well-fed state. In low insulin: glucagon ratio, lipoprotein lipase activity is reduced, leading to decreased hydrolysis of triglycerides.

Option B: Activation of glycogen synthase is promoted by insulin. In low insulin: glucagon ratio, glycogen synthase activity is reduced, leading to decreased glycogenesis. Instead, glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis are promoted to maintain blood glucose levels.

Option C: Activation of phosphofructokinase 1 (PFK1) is promoted by insulin. PFK1 is a rate-regulating enzyme in glycolysis. In low insulin: glucagon ratio, glycolysis is downregulated, and gluconeogenesis is upregulated to maintain blood glucose levels.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following zymogens requires gamma-glutamyl carboxylase?
options: Factors II, VII, IX, and X
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Factors II, VII, IX, and X

Clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X are zymogens of serine proteases that contain glutamic acid residues. These residues undergo vitamin-K-dependent carboxylation via gamma-glutamyl carboxylase to form gamma-carboxyglutamic acid residues. These residues chelate calcium ions, allowing the binding of clotting factors to the platelet surface.

Zymogens are the proprotein form of enzymes (proenzymes) that require proteolytic activation to carry out their function.

The reduced form of vitamin K acts as a cofactor in the post-synthetic modification of these zymogens and their activation. This reduced form of vitamin K is recycled back from its oxidized form by the enzyme vitamin K epoxide reductase, which is inhibited by warfarin.

The absence of vitamin K or the presence of warfarin inhibits carboxylation of the glutamate residues, leading to the release of abnormal precursors of clotting factors in the blood.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 10-year-old child from a southern Indian state, hailing from a poor family, presents with rough and scaly skin. The child’s diet lacks vegetables and fruits. After treatment with linseed oil, Vitamin A, and Vitamin B, the symptoms subsided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Phrynoderma

The cutaneous lesions with rough and scaly skin, with dietary history stating lack of vegetables and fruits is suggestive of phrynoderma.

Phrynoderma are keratotic follicular papules commonly present over the elbows and knees. They can also extend to the shoulders, neck, back, thighs, buttocks, and abdomen. It is also known as toad skin, due to the rough cone-shaped elevated papules. It can caused by deficiency of vitamins A, B complex, C, and E and essential fatty acids.

When it occurs due to vitamin A deficiency, it is associated with ophthalmic symptoms like xerophthalmia, night blindness, and Bitot's spots and cutaneous symptoms like xerosis, scaling, and acne.

Management includes nutritional improvement through diet, multivitamin supplementation, and treatment of the underlying cause.

Note: Linseed oil is rich in alpha-linolenic acid, which is an essential fatty acid.

The toad skin appearance of a child with phrynoderma is given below:

Other options:

Option A: Lichen planus is a papulosquamous lesion presenting as pruritic, purple, polygonal, planar, papules and plaques. These papules are often highlighted by white dots or lines called Wickham striae, which are created by areas of hypergranulosis. The characteristic lesions in lichen planus are shown below:

Option B: Erythroderma is a serious skin condition characterized by widespread redness (erythema) and scaling affecting more than 90% of the body's surface area. It is also known as exfoliative dermatitis and often results from underlying skin disorders, systemic diseases, or drug reactions.

Option D: Keratosis pilaris is an inherited abnormality of keratinization. It affects the follicular orifices leading to keratotic follicular plugging, perifollicular erythema, and follicular atrophy. It usually occurs during puberty. They present as small, keratotic papules on the extensor aspects of the limbs, particularly the arms which can lead to ingrowing of the hair. Treatment is purely reserved for cosmetic purposes.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 3-month-old child was brought to the clinic with a history of difficulty in feeding and failure to thrive. On examination, the child is floppy, 48 cm in length and weighs 2.8 kg. There is generalized hypotonia, macroglossia and hepatomegaly. The chest x-ray of the child is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pompe's disease

The child with a clinical history of difficulty feeding and failure to thrive with generalised hypotonia, macroglossia, hepatomegaly and chest x-ray findings of massive cardiomegaly suggest a diagnosis of Pompe's disease.

Pompe's disease is a glycogen storage disorder(type II) caused by a deficiency of lysosomal acid maltase (alpha-glucosidase) which leads to the accumulation of glycogen in the lysosomes of the liver (hepatomegaly), skeletal muscles in the form of large vacuoles (hypotonia and weakness), cardiac muscles (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy). The child generally dies by the age of 2 years due to cardiac failure. The adult form presents with muscle dystrophies.

Laboratory findings show elevated levels of serum creatine kinase (CK), aspartate transaminase (AST), alanine transaminase (ALT), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). Urine glucose tetrasaccharide, a glycogen breakdown metabolite, is a reliable biomarker for disease severity and treatment response. Treatment includes enzyme replacement therapy with recombinant enzyme a-glucosidase alfa (Myozyme).

Given below is the image of muscle biopsy showing glycogen-positive vacuoles.

Other options:

Option A- Ebstein's anomaly is the teratogenic effect of maternal lithium consumption which causes a cyanotic heart disease in the newborn with atrialization of the right ventricle and conduction defects. The chest X-ray will show a box-shaped enlargement of the right atrium and pulmonary oligemia.

Option C- Transposition of great vessels is cyanotic congenital heart disease where there is a switch in the position of two main arteries i.e. pulmonary artery and aorta. X-ray shows of egg-on-string appearance with pulmonary plethora.

Option D- Von Gierke disease occurs due to a deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase. Patients present commonly in 3-4 months of age with hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hepatomegaly, growth retardation, hyperuricemia, and hyperlipidemia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 3-year-old child is brought to the OPD with complaints of persistent delayed developmental milestones, and hyperpigmented macular lesions on the body which are more pronounced on exposure to sunlight. What is the error in DNA multiplication?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nucleotide excision repair

The history points to a diagnosis of xeroderma pigmentosum. It is characterized by defective nucleotide excision repair.

UV radiation leads to pyrimidine dimerization in DNA strands, preventing further replication by DNA polymerase. The nucleotide excision repair mechanism corrects the dimer formation in DNA. Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder characterized by an inability to repair DNA pyrimidine dimers caused by UV exposure. This leads to clinical and cellular hypersensitivity to ultraviolet (UV) radiation.

In XP the skin is normal at birth and has a three-stage progression:

• Diffuse erythema, scaling, and freckle-like areas over the sun-exposed regions of the body at around 6 months of age.
• The second stage is characterized by poikiloderma. This results in skin atrophy, telangiectasias with mottled hyperpigmentation, and hyperpigmentation.
• In the third stage appearance of cutaneous malignancies like squamous cell carcinomas, malignant melanoma, basal cell carcinoma, and fibrosarcoma.

Most of the cases with XP have ocular manifestations. Initially, it appears as photophobia, conjunctivitis, ectropion, and symblepharon with ulceration. Accumulation of pyrimidine dimer causes corneal opacification and neovascularization. Ocular malignancies are common in the lids, conjunctiva, and cornea as they are exposed to as much as facial skin. XP is ultimately fatal, and early detection of the skin lesions and their management with prevention of UV ray exposures prolong life.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 32-year-old lady comes with complaints of erythematous scaly rash, loose stools, and cognitive dysfunction. The rash involved her forearm, neck, and face. She seems to have difficulty remembering things from the recent past. Her electrolytes are within normal range. She admits to having shifted to a corn-based diet due to economic reasons. Which of the following would improve her symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Oral Nicotinamide supplementation

The given clinical features suggests the diagnosis of pellagra, due to her corn-based diet. Oral nicotinamide supplements can improve her symtpoms.

Niacin can be synthesized in the body from tryptophan. Two compounds, nicotinic acid and nicotinamide, have the biological activity of niacin. The nicotinamide ring of the coenzymes nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP) participate in oxidation/reduction reactions.

The initial symptoms of pellagra include loss of appetite, generalized weakness, irritability, abdominal pain, and vomiting. This is followed by bright red glossitis and a characteristic pigmented, scaly skin rash in sun-exposed areas. This rash is known as Casal’s necklace when it forms a ring around the neck.

The 4Ds of pellagra:

• Diarrhea
• Dermatitis
• Dementia, leading to
• Death

It is diagnosed by measuring urinary levels of 2-methyl nicotinamide and 2-pyridone.

Other options:

Option B: Thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency leads to conditions like beriberi and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, which are characterized by symptoms such as muscle weakness, peripheral neuropathy, cardiovascular issues, and confusion. While cognitive dysfunction can result from thiamine deficiency, rash and loose stools do not fit with thiamine deficiency. Therefore, thiamine would not address the full spectrum of this patient’s symptoms.

Option C: Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, which is associated with symptoms like bleeding gums, bruising, joint pain, and fatigue. Scurvy is not associated with a rash like the one described, nor does it typically cause cognitive dysfunction or diarrhea. Hence, high-dose vitamin C would not improve this patient’s symptoms.

Option D: Corn-based diets are low in niacin and tryptophan, leading to pellagra over time, especially if the diet is not balanced with other niacin-rich foods. While stopping the corn-based diet could prevent further niacin deficiency, it will not immediately address the existing deficiency and symptoms like rash, diarrhea, and cognitive dysfunction. The patient would still need niacin supplementation to resolve the current symptoms.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text:
A child presented to the OPD with complaints of fatigue and muscle weakness while exercising. Laboratory investigations found that LCFA oxidation was affected. A muscle biopsy was done which revealed the presence of fat vacuoles. What is the probable diagnosis?

LCFA- Long-chain fatty acid

LPL- Lipoprotein lipase

LDL- Low-density lipoprotein
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Carnitine deficiency

The clinical scenario of a child with fatigue and muscle weakness on exercise with laboratory findings of LCFA oxidation deficiency and fat vacuoles on muscle biopsy suggests a diagnosis of carnitine deficiency.

Carnitine deficiency is a defect in fatty acid oxidation that leads to hypoketotic hypoglycemia and hyperammonemia. Carnitine transports activated LCFA (long chain fatty acyl CoA) from the cytoplasm to the mitochondria for beta-oxidation (as they cannot cross the mitochondrial membrane), carnitine deficiency impairs this transport causing accumulation of lipids (skeletal muscle weakness). This excess fatty acid inhibits the urea cycle causing hyperammonemia. Since beta-oxidation cannot occur, energy production is reduced, and there is hypoglycemia without a corresponding increase in ketone bodies (hypoketotic) during times of glucose depletion such as exercise.

The role of carnitine in the metabolism of fatty acids is demonstrated in the image below:

Clinical features of carnitine deficiency begin in childhood and include poor feeding, lethargy, liver dysfunction and hepatomegaly, hypotonia, and dilated cardiomyopathy. Treatment involves oral supplementation of carnitine.

Other options:

Option A: An increase in LDL can cause hyperlipoproteinemia, and reduced LDL can cause defective absorption of fat-soluble vitamins.

Option B: LPL is involved in hydrolysis of lipoproteins in the blood to free fatty acid and glycerol which are then taken up by the tissues. A defective LPL can cause type 1 familial chylomicronemia syndrome presenting as pancreatitis.

Option C: Fatty acid synthase is a multienzyme complex involved in fatty acid synthesis in the cytosol which when defective may impair energy production, essential fatty acids, and affect metabolic pathways. There is no accumulation of fat vacuoles since fatty acids are not synthesised.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child presented with recurrent abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea following ingestion of milk-based products. Which enzyme is likely to be deficient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lactase

The given scenario indicates intolerance of milk-based products in this child, hence, the enzyme likely to be deficient is lactase.

Lactase is the enzyme that is responsible for breaking down lactose, a disaccharide found in milk and dairy products. When this enzyme is deficient, it can lead to the accumulation of lactose in the intestinal lumen where it is fermented by intestinal bacteria to lactate which produces symptoms of lactose intolerance, including recurrent abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea after consuming lactose-rich food items. Lactase and maltase are present in the intestinal brush border.

Other options:

Option A- Lipases are involved in the hydrolysis of dietary triglycerides to free fatty acids and glycerol. It is deficient in exocrine pancreatic deficiency states such as chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, and Crohn's. Although it might also present with abdominal pain and diarrhea, the stools are foul-smelling(due to gut bacteria) and greasy due to the presence of fat (steatorrhea) and are also associated with fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.

Option B- Maltase breaks down maltose which is a disaccharide intermediate of starch breakdown.

Option C- Amylase hydrolyses starch which is a glucose homopolymer and is present in germinating cereals, potatoes, legumes, and malt.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child presents to you with bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly, and pancytopenia. A trephine biopsy aspirate shows the following finding. Which of the following is the most likely enzyme deficient in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glucocerebrosidase

The given clinical scenario of a child with bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly, and trephine biopsy showing Gaucher's cell with a characteristic crumpled tissue paper appearance is suggestive of Gaucher's disease. The deficient enzyme is glucocerebrosidase (also known as beta-glucosidase).

Gaucher's disease is an inborn error of metabolism caused due to a deficiency of beta-glucocerebrosidase. It is the most common lysosomal storage disorder and the mode of inheritance is autosomal recessive. There is an accumulation of lipid-laden macrophages in the spleen, liver, and other tissues.

There are three clinical subtypes - type I (chronic non-neuronopathic), type II (acute neuronopathic), and type III (intermediate). Clinical features include anemia, thrombocytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, and neurological features depending on the subtype.

Gaucher's cells are formed as a result of the accumulation of massive amounts of glucocerebrosides within the phagocytes. The cells have a fibrillary cytoplasm and give a crumpled tissue paper appearance.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child suffering from phenylketonuria was started on necessary dietary modifications but the neurological symptoms persisted. Phenylalanine hydroxylase levels in the serum are normal. Which of the following enzymes is likely to be deficient in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tetrahydrobiopterin synthase

This child with phenylketonuria with neurological symptoms not improving despite dietary modifications and normal serum phenylalanine hydroxylase level is suggestive of tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) synthase deficiency.

A diet low in phenylalanine (eg: tapioca) is the mainstay of treatment for classic phenylketonuria but may not be sufficient in BH4 deficiency where supplementation with BH4 and deficient neurotransmitter precursors (L-dopa) is required to overcome the block.

Phenylketonuria (PKU) is an inborn error of metabolism seen due to a defect in the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase (classic phenylketonuria) and less commonly, due to a defect in BH4 synthase (non-classical). These defects result in the impaired conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine. The patient develops clinical features due to elevated levels of phenylalanine metabolites and decreased levels of tyrosine. The excess phenylalanine in the blood is metabolized to phenylpyruvate (positive ferric chloride) and phenylacetate (mousy odour) which are excreted in the urine. Infants appear normal at birth and gradually develop symptoms of hyperreflexia, seizures, hypopigmentation, low IQ, hyperactivity, and tremors.

Tandem mass spectroscopy is the investigation of choice. Guthrie test is a screening test that shows with absence of growth of Bacillus subtilis. The ferric chloride test is positive with the development of a transient blue-green colour.

Other options -

Option A: Tyrosine hydroxylase is the rate-limiting enzyme in the synthesis of epinephrine, converts tyrosine to DOPA, its deficiency does not cause phenylketonuria

Option B:  Homogentisic acid oxidase converts homogentisic acid to maleylacetoacetic acid in the tyrosine degradation pathway and its deficiency causes alkaptonuria with a dark colour of urine on standing, bluish-black pigmentation in connective tissue (ochronosis) and arthritis.

Option D: Dopa decarboxylase is another enzyme involved in the synthesis of epinephrine. It converts DOPA to dopamine in the presence of vitamin B6. While enzymes involved in epinephrine synthesis cause neurological dysfunction, they do not cause phenylketonuria as such.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A mother came back home to see her child suffering from difficulty breathing. The child had contact with rotenone while trying to bathe their pet. The child was taken to the emergency department and she later passed away. Inhibition of which of the following enzymes was the likely cause of her death?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. NADH-Q oxidoreductase

In the given clinical vignette, inhibition of NADH-Q oxidoreductase by rotenone was the likely cause of breathlessness, followed by death in this child.

Rotenone inhibits complex I, thereby inhibiting the respiratory chain, so electrons cannot be transferred to oxygen. This halts ATP production, leading to an energy deficit in the cells, eventually causing cell death. The ETC constitutes four enzyme complexes:

• Complex I: NADH-Q oxidoreductase
• Complex II: Succinate-Q reductase
• Complex III: Q-cytochrome c oxidoreductase
• Complex IV: cytochrome c oxidase

Components of complex I are FMN and Fe-S complex. NADH-Q oxidoreductase catalyses the transfer of electrons from NADH to coenzyme Q, along with the transfer of four H+ across the membrane.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient diagnosed with a rare homozygous recessive condition presented with ectopia lentis. In the peripheral smear, there was no megaloblastic anemia. Later, he was found to have elevated homocysteine levels in the blood. Which of the following supplementations will help the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pyridoxine

The vitamin that can be used as supplementation in this patient with homocystinuria is pyridoxine (vitamin B6).

Classical homocystinuria is an autosomal recessive disease most commonly caused by a deficiency of the cystathionine β-synthase. The deficiency of this enzyme leads to an accumulation of homocysteine in the blood and a clinical syndrome of intellectual disability, subluxated ocular lenses, long and slender extremities, arachnodactyly, and arterial and venous thrombi. The skeletal features of homocystinuria often mimic Marfan syndrome. Folic acid and vitamin B12 deficiency can also lead to homocystinuria with megaloblastic anemia.

Demonstration of elevated total homocysteine in the blood confirms the diagnosis. 50% of the cases of homocystinuria are termed pyridoxine-responsive because large doses of pyridoxine can enhance the activity of deficient enzymes in these patients. Administration of large doses of pyridoxine (vitamin B6) restores the activity of the deficient enzyme in half of all cases of homocystinuria.

Folate supplementation is also added to overcome any folate deficiency that might occur due to increased conversion of homocysteine to methionine. For the other 50% of the patients, the treatment consists of methionine restriction and cysteine supplementation. In addition, betaine (methyl group donor), folate and vitamin B12 may be added.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presented with multiple yellowish raised plaques on eyelids, xanthomas on the achilles tendon. What is the likely cause for the patient's presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Familial hypercholesterolemia

The clinical presentation with yellowish, raised plaques on eyelids, and tendon xanthomas points to a diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolemia (FH).

Familial hypercholesterolemia (type IIa hyperlipoproteinemia) is an inherited disorder due to defects in LDL receptors and Apo B100. This decreases the uptake of Low-density lipoprotein and cholesterol leading to their increased levels in the blood. The increased LDL accumulates in the blood vessels causing atherosclerosis (premature coronary artery disease)and in the Achilles tendon causing tendon xanthomas. Xanthomas are tumorous masses produced by foamy cell clusters (lipid-laden macrophages) found in the connective tissue of the skin and tendons. Patients can also have yellowish plaques around the eyes (Xanthelasma) and corneal arcus.

Treatment includes lifestyle changes, restriction of a fatty diet, and pharmacotherapy with statins in heterozygous FH patients.

The images below show Achilles tendon xanthoma and xanthelasma respectively:

Other options:

Option B: Tangier’s disease is a hypolipoproteinemia caused by a mutation of the ABCA1 gene. Enlarged orange tonsils are pathognomonic. Low HDL levels are seen. There is an increased risk for atherosclerosis.

The image below shows enlarged yellow-orange coloured tonsils in Tangier's disease.

Option C: Xanthomatosis is the deposition of lipids in various parts of the body like tendon xanthomas, xanthelasma, eruptive and tuberous xanthomas. This is a sign of underlying lipid metabolism disorders.

Option D: Fabry's disease is a lysosomal storage disorder with a defect in alpha-galactosidase. It causes angiokeratomas, hypohidrosis and characteristic Maltese cross deposits in urine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text:
A patient presents to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. The laboratory results show serum triglyceride levels > 2000 mg/dl. Which deficiency could be contributing to the patient's condition?

VLDL- very low density lipoprotein
LDL- low density lipoprotein
HDL- high density lipoprotein
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Apolipoprotein C II

The elevated triglyceride levels and symptoms of acute pancreatitis are likely related to a deficiency in apolipoprotein C II.

Apolipoprotein C2 is a lipoprotein lipase cofactor that catalyzes cleavage of chylomicrons. Defective apo C II results in type I hyperlipoproteinemia/ familial lipoprotein lipase deficiency. The resulting inactive lipoprotein lipase leads to slow clearance of chylomicrons and VLDL, and low levels of LDL and HDL. Patients present with eruptive xanthomas and acute pancreatitis.

Lipoprotein lipase is an extracellular enzyme that is present in the capillary walls of most tissues. It is chiefly synthesized by the adipose tissue, and cardiac and skeletal muscles. A deficiency of lipoprotein lipase or apo C-II leads to type 1 hyperlipoproteinemia or familial chylomicronemia which leads to an increased risk of acute pancreatitis.

Other options:

Option B: Apo B48 is involved in the assembly of chylomicrons. Defects in this protein are not associated with familial hypercholesterolemia.

Option C: Apo B100 binds low-density lipoprotein receptors. For the uptake of LDL, apo B100 acts as a ligand for the low-density lipoprotein receptor.

Option D: Apo A1 activates lecithin cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT). LCAT is the enzyme present in HDL, which is activated by apo A1. LCAT converts free cholesterol (amphipathic) in HDL to cholesterol ester(hydrophobic). The initial discoidal shape now becomes spherical. This facilitates reverse cholesterol transport.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient underwent gastrectomy for gastric adenocarcinoma. Which of the following vitamins needs to be supplemented in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vitamin B12

A patient who has undergone gastrectomy for gastric adenocarcinoma needs to be supplemented with vitamin B12.

Vitamin B12 absorption is a complex process that relies on several factors. Intrinsic factor, a glycoprotein secreted by the parietal cells in the stomach, is essential for this process. Gastric acid and pepsin release vitamin B12 from dietary proteins, allowing it to bind with cobalophilin in the saliva. In the jejunum, cobalophilin is broken down, freeing vitamin B12 to bind with intrinsic factor. This complex is then absorbed in the distal ileum through specific receptors.  Following gastrectomy, the production of intrinsic factor is impaired due to the removal of gastric tissue, making vitamin B12 absorption difficult. Therefore, vitamin B12 supplementation is necessary after gastrectomy to prevent deficiency.

Other complications of gastrectomy include:

• Nutritional deficiencies- Iron deficiency anemia (most common), Vitamin B12 deficiency, and osteoporosis
• Dumping syndrome: early and late
• Diarrhea
• Duodenal stump leak/blow out
• Bile reflux gastritis and esophagitis
• Gall stones
• Roux syndrome

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text:
A patient with a family history of coronary heart disease presented with tendon xanthomas. His lipid profile showed serum LDL to be 280 mg/dL and triglyceride levels was 398 mg/dl. What is the likely defect in this patient?

LDL - Low-density lipoprotein
VLDL - Very low-density lipoprotein
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. LDL receptor defect

The clinical presentation with tendon xanthomas, elevated serum LDL  and elevated serum triglycerides points to a diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolemia and is due to a defect in LDL receptors.

Familial hypercholesterolemia  (type IIa hyperlipoproteinemia) is an inherited disorder due to defects in LDL receptors. This defect causes a decrease in the uptake of LDL and cholesterol. As a result, the blood levels of both LDL and cholesterol are elevated. Such patients are at increased risk of developing atherosclerosis and coronary artery disease.

Features of FH:

• Painful polyarthritis and tendinitis are common.
• Physical findings seen are corneal arcus and tendon xanthomas over the Achilles tendon and the dorsum of the hands. Xanthomas are tumorous masses produced by foamy cell clusters (lipid-laden macrophages) found in the connective tissue of the skin and in tendons.

Diagnosis is done clinically based on hypercholesterolemia with

• LDL > 190 mg/dl,
• Family history of hypercholesterolemia and/or
• Premature coronary artery disease.

Treatment includes lifestyle changes, restriction of a fatty diet, and pharmacotherapy with statins in heterozygous FH patients.

Recent drugs for specific treatment of homozygous FH are:

• Lomitapide, a microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP) inhibitor, and
• Mipomersen, an antisense oligonucleotide against apoB.

The image below shows Achilles tendon xanthoma and a plain lateral radiograph of both ankles showing bilateral symmetrical swellings (arrows) superior to the calcaneum respectively.

Note: Lipoprotein lipase (LPL) deficiency causes type I hyperlipoproteinemia due to defects in LPL or apo C-II. Eruptive xanthomas are seen. Chylomicrons and VLDL are elevated. LDL and HDL are low. There is no risk for coronary disease.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A young female comes to the emergency department after ingesting 10 tablets of Phenobarbital. Which of the following components of the ETC is inhibited by this drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Complex I to Q

Phenobarbital is a barbiturate that inhibits complex I to Q of the electron transport chain.

Complex I of the electron transport chain is NADH-Q oxidoreductase. It oxidizes NADH and reduces coenzyme Q. Phenobarbital inhibits complex I to Q so that the electrons will not be able to be transferred from NADH to coenzyme Q, which is the first step in the electron transport chain. As a result, the rate of oxygen consumption will decrease.

The electron transport chain (ETC) represents the final pathway through which electrons, originating from the oxidation of carbohydrates, fatty acids, and amino acids, are channeled toward a final reaction with oxygen to produce water and ATP. The ETC complexes are embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane.

The oxidation of compounds by ETC complexes leads to the release of free energy. This is used to pump H+ to the intermembrane space. This results in the formation of a proton motive force that is used for the phosphorylation of ADP to ATP. Thus, oxidation is coupled with phosphorylation to generate ATP. NADH generates 2.5 ATP and FADH2 generates 1.5 ATP.

The table below summarizes the inhibitors of the electron transport chain.

Complexes of ETC
Inhibitors

Complex I:

NADH-Q oxidoreductase

Piericidin A, phenobarbital, rotenone

Complex II:

Succinate-Q reductase

TTFA (thenoyltrifluoroacetone), carboxin, malonate

Complex III:

Q- Cyt c oxidoreductase

BAL (British anti-lewisite), antimycin A

Complex IV:

Cyt c oxidase

Hydrogen sulfide, carbon monoxide, cyanide

Complex V:

ATP Synthase

Atractyloside, oligomycin

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: After the age of 12, the boy had an intellectual disability. On examination, fingernail abrasions, excessive biting of lips, and increased levels of serum uric acid were observed. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lesch-Nyhan disease

The above clinical scenario with findings showing self-mutilation and laboratory values of hyperuricemia is most likely suggestive of Lesch-Nyhan disease.

Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder due to a complete deficiency of the hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT). This deficiency results in an inability to salvage hypoxanthine or guanine leading to increased levels of phospho-ribosyl pyrophosphate (PRPP). Increased PRPP leads to increased purine synthesis, which is later degraded to uric acid. Increased hypoxanthine is also converted to uric acid.

The patients have intellectual disability, behaviors of self-injury like lip and finger biting, developmental delay, muscle dystonia, and extrapyramidal symptoms.

Diagnosis is made by the elevated levels of uric acid and by HGPRT enzyme assay.

The image given below shows the metabolism of hypoxanthine and guanine by HGPRT.

Orange diaper syndrome can be an early indicator of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. At birth, individuals with Lesch-Nyhan syndrome typically appear asymptomatic, with normal prenatal growth and development. The condition is often first detected through the presence of orange-coloured crystals in the diaper, resulting from hyperuricemia. Since hyperuricemia is a common feature across all variants of HGPRT deficiency, which causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, predicting associated neurodevelopmental abnormalities requires enzyme activity testing.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In the given Lineweaver-Burk plot, the blue line represents the action of an enzyme, and the red line represents the action of the same enzyme in the presence of an inhibitor. What is the type of inhibition shown here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Competitive inhibition

The given graph shows competitive inhibition, in which the value of Vmax remains constant and the Km value increases. The intercept on the y-axis remains unchanged while the intercept on the x-axis shifts close to zero forming a steeper slope.

Competitive inhibition is when the inhibitor binds reversibly to the substrate-binding site and competes with the substrate for the active enzyme-binding site. This effect of competitive inhibition can be overcome by increasing the substrate concentration by which maximum velocity can still be achieved. Therefore, Vmax (maximum velocity of the reaction) is unaltered in this type of inhibition. However, the concentration of the substrate required to achieve half of the maximum velocity is increased. Therefore, Km is increased in this condition.

The graph below shows the changes in Vmax and Km in competitive inhibition.

Other options:

Option B: Non-competitive inhibition is by binding inhibitors to enzymes in locations remote from the active site. Increasing the concentration of the substrate does not overcome non-competitive inhibition. Thus, noncompetitive inhibitors decrease the Vmax of the reaction. They do not interfere with the binding of the substrate to the enzyme. Thus, the enzyme shows the same Km in the presence or absence of noncompetitive inhibitors.

The graph shows the changes in Vmax and Km in non-competitive inhibition.

Option C: In uncompetitive inhibition, inhibitors bind with the enzyme-substrate intermediate complex, and inhibit it. This leads to a decrease in both Vmax and Km. An example is the inhibition of placental alkaline phosphate (ALP) by phenylalanine.

Option D: In Allosteric inhibition, inhibitors bind to a site other than the active site i.e. allosteric site, and induce a conformational change (change in the shape of the active site unlike in non-competitive inhibition) thus, inhibiting the enzyme. ATP is an allosteric inhibitor of Phosphofructokinase in glycolysis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which food item among these is the primary source of thiamine in Indians?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 4

Among the various food items given on the plate, the primary source of thiamine (vitamin B1) in the Indian diet is option 4 i.e. chapati and rice.

The thiamine content in various foods in decreasing order are as follows:

• Gingelly seeds
• Groundnut
• Bengal gram
• Whole wheat
• Rice

Gingelly (sesame) seeds have the highest content of thiamine.

Thiamine is lost from rice during the process of milling. As it is a water-soluble vitamin, washing, and cooking rice cause further losses. Hence, it is advisable to avoid highly polished rice and eat parboiled or under-milled rice.

Thiamine is essential for energy metabolism, particularly in carbohydrate processing. Its active form, thiamine diphosphate, acts as a coenzyme for three critical enzyme complexes: pyruvate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and branched-chain keto acid dehydrogenase. This coenzyme facilitates oxidative decarboxylation by forming a reactive carbanion that attaches to carbonyl groups like those in pyruvate, leading to the release of CO2. Thiamine diphosphate is also vital for transketolase in the pentose phosphate pathway.

Thiamine triphosphate, another form of thiamin, helps regulate nerve function by activating chloride channels in nerve membranes.

A thiamine deficiency can cause several conditions such as beriberi, characterized by peripheral neuritis, which can also involve heart failure and edema. Additionally, thiamine deficiency can lead to Wernicke's encephalopathy and Korsakoff's psychosis, commonly associated with alcohol or drug abuse. The lack of thiamine impairs the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, leading to increased levels of lactate and pyruvate in the blood, which can result in dangerous lactic acidosis, especially in those consuming high-carbohydrate diets.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which micronutrient is most likely deficient in a patient with the radiographic findings given below along with anemia, neutropenia, depigmented hair and skin?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Copper

The given clinical features of anaemia and neutropenia, along with depigmented hair and skin and the radiological findings suggestive of pelkan spurs, trummerfeld zone, Frenkel's line, and Wimberger's ring sign point to the diagnosis of Menke's disease. Patients with this condition have low serum levels of copper.

Menke's disease or Menke-Kinky hair syndrome is an X-linked recessive condition caused due to a mutation in the ATP7A gene on chromosome X. This causes impaired transport of dietary copper from the small intestine to the liver leading to low levels of copper-containing enzymes.

The final step of collagen synthesis involves the formation of covalent cross-links. This is done by the enzyme lysyl oxidase, a copper-containing protein. This is essential for the strength and rigidity of collagen. As a result of deficiency of copper in Menkes disease, this step of collagen synthesis is affected.

The patient presents with depigmented kinky hair, failure to thrive, neurodegenerative symptoms (loss of developmental milestones, truncal hypotonia, epilepsy), multiple fractures, anaemia due to ceruloplasmin and hephaestin deficiency (converts ferrous to ferric to be bound to transferrin), neutropenia, and recurrent infections.

Lab investigations show low serum copper (<65 μg/dL) and low ceruloplasmin(<20 mg/dl). The disease is fatal and has no curative treatment.

A variety of distinct anomalies that are representative of scurvy and acquired copper insufficiency can be seen on radiographs of people with menke's disease.

These include

Early administration of L-histidine and copper chloride injections may be beneficial.

Other options:

Option A: Iron deficiency causes iron deficiency anemia, and hair loss (telogen effluvium. It does not cause neutropenia, depigmentation of hair and skin, or bony abnormalities.

Option B: Zinc deficiency causes acrodermatitis enteropathica characterized by periorificial dermatitis, diarrhea, and alopecia.

Option D: Fluoride is essential for bone and teeth mineralization and its deficiency causes decreased bone-mineral density, osteoporosis, and tooth decay.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: You received a text message from your friend JOHN DOE about occupational exposure after he visited his doctor as shown below. What is the test used to diagnose?
questions.explanation:
