Correct answer: B. Lead poisoning

The test for coproporphyrinogen levels is used as a screening test to diagnose lead poisoning.

Lead inhibits the enzymes delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) dehydratase and ferrochelatase, which are involved in heme synthesis. ALA is converted to porphobilinogen by ALA dehydratase, inhibited by lead. So, serum porphobilinogen levels are decreased in lead poisoning.

Laboratory findings include the following:

• An elevated serum lead level
• An elevated level of protoporphyrin in blood and elevated ALA and coproporphyrinogen in urine
• Microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling in peripheral smear due to ineffective heme synthesis

Clinical features of chronic lead poisoning include facial pallor, anemia, basophilic stippling of red cells, blue lines in the gums, and retinal stippling. In the later phase, the findings are colic abdominal pain, constipation, nerve palsy, encephalopathy, and disturbance of the genito-urinary and cardiovascular systems.

Diagnosis of lead poisoning:

Laboratory parameter
Value
Remarks

Coproporphyrin in urine
>150 mcg/L
Screening test- indicates exposure

Aminolevulinic acid (ALA) in urine
>5 mg/L
Indicates lead absorption

Lead in blood
>70 mcg/dL
Clinical symptoms appear

Lead in urine
0.8 mg/L
Indicates lead absorption

Basophilic stippling of RBCs

Sensitive indicator

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 12-year-old girl with pigmented hair was noted. Which of the following amino acids is more likely to bind with keratin leading to this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cysteine

Cysteine is a sulfur-containing amino acid that is abundant in keratin, the principal structural protein of hair. During melanin synthesis, dopaquinone reacts with cysteine to form cysteinyldopa, which is the precursor of pheomelanin (yellow-red pigment). The incorporation of melanin into keratin gives hair its characteristic pigmentation.

Why not the other options?

• A. Methionine: A sulfur-containing essential amino acid involved in methylation reactions, but it is not the amino acid that directly combines with dopaquinone in melanin synthesis.
• B. Lysine: Important for collagen cross-linking and protein synthesis, but it has no specific role in hair pigmentation.
• D. Glycine: The most abundant amino acid in collagen, not keratin, and does not participate in melanin synthesis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 17-year-old tall male presents for a routine check-up. He has long limbs, arachnodactyly, hypermobile joints, a high-arched palate, and an increased arm span. Genetic testing reveals a defect in the FBN1 gene. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Marfan Syndrome

Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder caused by a mutation in the FBN1 gene, which encodes fibrillin-1, an important structural component of elastic fibers in connective tissue. Defective fibrillin leads to weakness of connective tissues, particularly affecting the skeletal system, eyes, and cardiovascular system.

• Tall stature with long limbs (dolichostenomelia)
• Arachnodactyly (long, slender fingers)
• Increased arm span compared to height
• Hypermobile joints and high-arched palate
• Ocular abnormalities such as ectopia lentis
• Cardiovascular complications such as aortic root dilation and aortic aneurysm

Why other options are incorrect:

• Ehlers–Danlos syndrome: Caused by defects in collagen, presenting mainly with hyperextensible skin and joint hypermobility.
• Osteogenesis imperfecta: Due to type I collagen defect, characterized by brittle bones and blue sclera.
• Heritable disorders of connective tissue: This is a broad category, not a specific diagnosis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child presented with a history of dark urine and dark pigmentation on the ear lobe. What is the most likely defect responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Homogentisate oxidase defect

The child most likely has Alkaptonuria, a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency of homogentisate oxidase (homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase) in the tyrosine degradation pathway. Accumulation of homogentisic acid (HGA) leads to dark-colored urine on standing due to oxidation of HGA and bluish-black pigmentation of connective tissues (ochronosis), particularly involving the ear cartilage, sclera, and nose.

Why not the other options?

• A. Phenylalanine hydroxylase defect: Causes Phenylketonuria (PKU), presenting with intellectual disability, seizures, fair skin, eczema, and a musty (mousy) odor, not dark urine or ochronosis.
• C. Pyruvate dehydrogenase defect: Causes lactic acidosis, developmental delay, and neurological dysfunction; it is unrelated to tyrosine metabolism.
• D. Fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase defect: Causes Tyrosinemia type I, characterized by liver failure, renal tubular dysfunction, rickets, and a cabbage-like odor, not dark urine with ear pigmentation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A neonate presents with seizures, low citrulline levels, hyperammonemia, normal orotic acid levels, and elevated glutamine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Type I hyperammonemia

Identify Type I hyperammonemia (CPS I deficiency) by the triad of hyperammonemia, low citrulline, and normal urinary orotic acid, which differentiates it from OTC deficiency (Type II hyperammonemia), where orotic acid is elevated.

Why not the other options?

• B. Type II hyperammonemia (OTC deficiency): Hyperammonemia with elevated urinary orotic acid.
• C. Citrullinemia: Elevated plasma citrulline due to argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency.
• D. Orotic aciduria: Elevated orotic acid with megaloblastic anemia, without hyperammonemia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient has markedly elevated plasma phenylalanine levels and low tyrosine levels. Phenylalanine hydroxylase enzyme assay is normal. Which of the following cofactor deficiencies is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Biopterin

Conversion of phenylalanine → tyrosine requires:

• Enzyme: Phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH)
• Cofactor: Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH₄, biopterin)

In this case, PAH is normal, so the defect lies in the cofactor (BH₄) deficiency, leading to:

• ↑ Phenylalanine
• ↓ Tyrosine

BH₄ is also required for synthesis of neurotransmitters:

• Dopamine (via tyrosine hydroxylase)
• Serotonin (via tryptophan hydroxylase)

Thus, deficiency leads to: Neurological symptoms more severe than classical PKU

Why other options are incorrect:

• DHFR: Involved in folate metabolism
• PLP (Vitamin B6): Cofactor for transamination reactions
• THF: Involved in one-carbon metabolism (DNA synthesis)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: An adult patient presents with tall stature, pigeon chest deformity, long arm span, lens dislocation, and cardiac defects. This patient is likely to have a defect in which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Fibrillin

The clinical features—tall stature, long arm span, pectus deformity (pigeon chest), lens dislocation, and cardiac abnormalities (aortic root dilation)—are classic for Marfan syndrome.

• Mutation in fibrillin-1 (FBN1 gene)
• Fibrillin is a key component of microfibrils in connective tissue

Clinical features explained:

• Skeletal: Tall, long limbs (arachnodactyly), pectus deformity
• Ocular: Lens dislocation (typically upward)
• Cardiac: Aortic root dilation → risk of aortic aneurysm/dissection

Why other options are incorrect:

• Elastase: Enzyme, not structural protein defect
• Collagen: Seen in Ehlers-Danlos or osteogenesis imperfecta
• Laminin: Basement membrane component

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Match the following amino acids with their respective derivatives: 1. Tyrosine 2. Tryptophan 3. Glycine 4. Cysteine a. Thyroxine b. Taurine c. Creatine d. Melatonin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1-a, 2-d, 3-c, 4-b

| Amino Acid | Important Derivative | Key Function

| ---------- | -------------------- | ------------

| Tyrosine | Thyroxine (T4) | Thyroid hormone involved in regulation of metabolism

| Tryptophan | Melatonin | Hormone regulating circadian rhythm and sleep

| Glycine | Creatine | Involved in energy storage in muscles (phosphocreatine system)

| Cysteine | Taurine | Important component of bile salts and antioxidant functions

• Tyrosine → Thyroid hormones (T3, T4), catecholamines, melanin
• Tryptophan → Serotonin → Melatonin
• Glycine + Arginine + Methionine → Creatine
• Cysteine → Taurine → Bile salts

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Respiratory distress syndrome is caused by the deficiency of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lecithin

Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS) in newborns is caused by deficiency of pulmonary surfactant, the most important component of which is lecithin (dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine, DPPC).

Function of lecithin (surfactant):

• Reduces alveolar surface tension
• Prevents alveolar collapse (atelectasis) during expiration
• Maintains lung compliance

Clinical correlation:

• Common in premature infants (immature type II pneumocytes)
• Assessed by Lecithin : Sphingomyelin (L/S) ratio in amniotic fluid

o    L/S ratio < 2 → high risk of RDS

Why other options are incorrect:

• Cephalin: Phospholipid involved in coagulation
• Sphingomyelin: Used as a reference in L/S ratio, not the main surfactant
• Cardiolipin: Found in mitochondrial membranes

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Sodium benzoate is given for urea cycle defects for scavenging ammonia. Which amino acid donates amino group to the scavengers?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glycine

In urea cycle disorders, toxic ammonia accumulates because the body cannot efficiently convert ammonia to urea. Nitrogen scavenger drugs such as sodium benzoate are used to remove excess nitrogen through alternative metabolic pathways.

Mechanism of Sodium Benzoate:

• Sodium benzoate conjugates with glycine in the liver.
• This reaction forms hippuric acid (benzoylglycine).
• Hippuric acid is then excreted in urine, removing one nitrogen atom from the body.

| Drug | Amino acid used | Product excreted

| ---- | --------------- | ----------------

| Sodium benzoate | Glycine | Hippurate

| Sodium phenylacetate / phenylbutyrate | Glutamine | Phenylacetylglutamine

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which diagnostic tool is preferred for metabolic disease screening in children?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tandem mass spectrometry

Tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) is the preferred screening tool for inborn errors of metabolism in newborns and children. It can simultaneously detect multiple metabolic disorders by measuring amino acids, organic acids, and acylcarnitines from a single dried blood spot.

This method is widely used in newborn screening programs to identify disorders such as phenylketonuria, maple syrup urine disease, fatty acid oxidation defects, and organic acidemias, allowing early diagnosis and treatment to prevent severe complications.

Why not other options:

• CBC: Evaluates blood cells (RBCs, WBCs, platelets); not useful for detecting metabolic enzyme defects.
• Urinalysis: May detect some metabolites but is not sensitive or comprehensive for screening multiple metabolic disorders.
• Genetic testing: Confirms specific mutations but is not practical for large-scale initial screening of many metabolic diseases.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which is not a product of heme catabolism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aminolaevulinic acid

During heme catabolism, heme is degraded by the enzyme heme oxygenase to produce biliverdin, ferrous iron (Fe²⁺), and carbon monoxide (CO). Biliverdin is subsequently reduced to bilirubin by biliverdin reductase.

Aminolevulinic acid (ALA) is not a product of heme breakdown; instead, it is an intermediate in heme synthesis, formed from glycine and succinyl-CoA by ALA synthase in mitochondria.

Therefore, aminolevulinic acid belongs to the heme biosynthesis pathway, not the catabolic pathway, making it the correct answer.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following amino acid classifications are correctly matched? 1. Uncharged amino acid – Cysteine 2. Nonpolar amino acid – Proline 3. Basic amino acid – Histidine 4. Basic amino acid – Lysine Choose the correct combination:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3, 4

Amino acids are classified based on the chemical properties of their side chains (R groups) into nonpolar, polar uncharged, acidic, and basic amino acids. Correct classification is fundamental for understanding protein structure and function.

Correct matches:

• 1. Cysteine → Polar uncharged amino acid ✓
• 2. Proline → Nonpolar amino acid ✓
• 3. Histidine → Basic amino acid ✓ (weakly basic; partially protonated at physiological pH)
• 4. Lysine → Basic amino acid ✓

Why are all correct?

• Cysteine contains a sulfhydryl (-SH) group, making it polar but uncharged and capable of forming disulfide bonds.
• Proline is a cyclic nonpolar amino acid that introduces bends in protein chains.
• Histidine contains an imidazole ring and is classified as a basic amino acid.
• Lysine has a positively charged ε-amino group and is a strongly basic amino acid.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following amino acids is likely to aggregate on the surface of a globular protein circulating in the plasma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lysine

Lysine would likely aggregate on the surface of a globular protein circulating in plasma because it is a hydrophilic amino acid with a positively charged side chain. In proteins that exist in aqueous environments like blood plasma, hydrophilic amino acids tend to orient toward the outside surface where they can interact favorably with water. This arrangement forms part of the tertiary structure of globular proteins, where hydrophilic residues face outward while hydrophobic residues cluster in the interior.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is deficient in a patient with phenylketonuria with normal phenylalanine hydroxylase levels?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dihydrobiopterin reductase

In a patient with hyperphenylalaninemia but normal phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH), the defect lies in the cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin (BH₄) metabolism.

Key enzyme involved: Dihydrobiopterin reductase (DHPR) Deficiency → ↓ BH₄ availability

• Impaired phenylalanine → tyrosine conversion → ↑ phenylalanine
• Also affects neurotransmitter synthesis:

o    ↓ dopamine (tyrosine pathway)

o    ↓ serotonin (tryptophan pathway)

Clinical importance:

• More severe than classical PKU
• Presents with neurological deficits due to neurotransmitter deficiency

Why other options are incorrect:

• Tyrosine transaminase: Involved in tyrosine metabolism (tyrosinemia)
• Dopa decarboxylase: Involved in dopamine synthesis, not primary cause here
• Tyrosine hydroxylase: Requires BH₄ but is not the defective enzyme in this condition

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 12-year-old adolescent presents with progressive joint pain, easy fatigability, and weakness. On examination, the patient has marfanoid habitus and mild developmental delay. Laboratory evaluation shows elevated homocysteine levels with decreased cysteine levels. Which vitamin supplementation is most appropriate in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vitamin B6 (Pyridoxine)

In homocystinuria, elevated homocysteine with low cysteine indicates a defect in the transsulfuration pathway, specifically the enzyme cystathionine β-synthase (CBS).

• Vitamin B6 (PLP) is a cofactor for CBS
• Required for conversion of:

Homocysteine → Cystathionine → Cysteine

• CBS deficiency → ↑ homocysteine and ↓ cysteine
• Leads to vascular damage, thrombosis, skeletal abnormalities

Giving Vitamin B6 enhances residual enzyme activity, reducing homocysteine levels

Clinical features of homocystinuria:

• Marfanoid habitus
• Lens subluxation (downward)
• Thromboembolism
• Intellectual disability

Why other options are incorrect:

• Vitamin B2: FAD-related enzymes
• Vitamin B1: Carbohydrate metabolism
• Vitamin B7 (Biotin): Carboxylation reactions

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 12-year-old boy presented to a health centre in Telangana along with his parents, with complaints of recurrent diarrhoea and skin changes on areas of the body exposed to sunlight. There is a history of progressive disorientation and increasing irritability. The child and his family ate sorghum cereal, there was very little consumption of milk and no consumption of foods of animal origin like meat, though the family is not strictly vegetarian by food habit. Consider the following plans of action: 1. Absolute avoidance of milk in the child’s diet 2. Encouraging shift of cereal consumption from sorghum to maize 3. Encouraging consumption of meat in the child’s diet, if the family can afford 4. Supplementation with nicotinic acid or nicotinamide Which of the plans of action given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 3 and 4 only

The child has the classic 3 Ds of pellagra:

• Diarrhea
• Dermatitis — photosensitive skin lesions
• Dementia — irritability, disorientation and neuropsychiatric changes

Why sorghum (jowar) causes pellagra:

Sorghum-based diets (common in parts of the Deccan plateau, including Telangana) are strongly associated with pellagra due to the "leucine excess theory" — sorghum is unusually rich in the amino acid leucine, which interferes with the enzymes involved in the tryptophan → niacin conversion pathway, precipitating niacin deficiency even when dietary intake isn't grossly inadequate. Lack of milk and animal-source foods (both good tryptophan/niacin sources) compounds the deficiency.

Evaluating the options:

1. Absolute avoidance of milk — Incorrect. Milk is actually a good source of tryptophan and should be encouraged, not avoided. Avoiding it would worsen the deficiency.
2. Shift from sorghum to maize — Incorrect. This is a classic distractor. Maize is equally, if not more strongly, associated with pellagra — its niacin is present in a biologically unavailable bound form (niacytin), and it too is deficient in tryptophan. Shifting from sorghum to maize does not solve the problem and may worsen it.
3. Encouraging meat consumption — Correct. Meat is rich in both tryptophan and preformed niacin, directly addressing the deficiency.
4. Supplementation with nicotinic acid/nicotinamide — Correct. This is the definitive treatment for established pellagra.

Exam pearl: Both sorghum and maize are classically linked to pellagra (via different mechanisms — leucine excess in sorghum vs. bound/unavailable niacin in maize) — so "switching cereals" is never the fix; the fix is adding tryptophan/niacin-rich foods (milk, eggs, meat, groundnuts) and direct niacin supplementation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 32-year-old man with chronic alcohol use presents with fatigue, irritability, and peripheral neuropathy. Laboratory evaluation shows impaired amino acid metabolism due to reduced activity of aminotransferase enzymes. Which of the following vitamins serves as the essential coenzyme for transamination reactions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)

Transamination is the transfer of an amino group from one amino acid to an α-keto acid. These reactions are catalyzed by aminotransferases (transaminases) such as AST and ALT.

• The essential coenzyme for all transamination reactions is pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), the active form of Vitamin B6 (Pyridoxine).
• PLP acts as a temporary carrier of amino groups during amino acid metabolism.

Other Options:

• Option A. Thiamine (Vitamin B1): Incorrect

• Functions as thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP).
• Required for oxidative decarboxylation of α-keto acids (e.g., pyruvate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase) and transketolase.

• Option C. Riboflavin (Vitamin B2; FAD): Incorrect

• Forms FAD and FMN.
• Participates in oxidation-reduction reactions, including the electron transport chain and succinate dehydrogenase.

• Option D. Niacin (Vitamin B3; NAD): Incorrect

• Forms NAD⁺ and NADP⁺.
• Serves as an electron carrier in numerous redox reactions, including glycolysis, the TCA cycle, and fatty acid metabolism.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 36-year-old man presents with decreased appetite, mouth soreness, diarrhoea and irritability. On examination he has a bright red tongue with a pigmented scaly rash around the neck. Which one of the following food items in his diet has a bearing on his disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Corn

This patient has pellagra, a disease caused by niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency or tryptophan deficiency. Pellagra is classically characterized by the “4 Ds”:

• Dermatitis
• Diarrhea
• Dementia (or neuropsychiatric symptoms such as irritability)
• Death (if untreated)

The pigmented scaly rash around the neck is known as Casal’s necklace, which is characteristic of pellagra.

• Corn (maize)-based diets are strongly associated with pellagra because:

• Niacin in untreated maize is bound (niacytin) and is poorly absorbed.
• Corn is deficient in tryptophan, the precursor of niacin. ⭐

• Populations consuming predominantly untreated maize are therefore at risk of niacin deficiency.

Why not the other options?

• A. Rice: Not specifically associated with pellagra (polished rice is associated with thiamine deficiency/beriberi).
• B. Wheat: Contains more available niacin and tryptophan than corn.
• D. Fish: Rich source of niacin and protein, helping prevent pellagra.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman presents with fatigue, pallor, and glossitis. Laboratory evaluation reveals macrocytic anemia. Serum studies show elevated homocysteine levels, while methylmalonic acid (MMA) levels are normal. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Folate deficiency

Folate deficiency causes megaloblastic (macrocytic) anemia due to impaired DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells such as erythroid precursors in the bone marrow.

Folate is required for one-carbon transfer reactions involved in thymidylate and purine synthesis, which are essential for DNA formation. When folate is deficient, DNA synthesis is impaired, leading to large, immature red blood cells (macrocytes/megaloblasts) and clinical features such as fatigue, pallor, and glossitis.

• Homocysteine: Increased (requires folate and vitamin B12 for metabolism)
• Methylmalonic acid (MMA): Normal in folate deficiency

This pattern helps differentiate folate deficiency from vitamin B12 deficiency.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Vitamin B12 deficiency: Causes elevated homocysteine and methylmalonic acid.
• Iron deficiency anemia: Produces microcytic hypochromic anemia, not macrocytic anemia.
• Thalassemia minor: Also causes microcytic anemia due to decreased globin chain synthesis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman with Rheumatoid arthritis is started on low-dose methotrexate therapy. After a few weeks, she develops oral ulcers and mild bone marrow suppression. Which of the following is most directly reduced due to this mechanism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Thymidine monophosphate (TMP)

Methotrexate is a folate antagonist that inhibits the enzyme dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR).

• Blocks conversion of dihydrofolate (DHF) → tetrahydrofolate (THF)
• THF is required for one-carbon transfer reactions
• Impaired synthesis of thymidylate (dTMP) from dUMP
• Leads to ↓ DNA synthesis, especially in rapidly dividing cells

Clinical relevance:

• Used in cancer chemotherapy, autoimmune diseases (RA)
• Causes megaloblastic anemia as a side effect

Why other options are incorrect:

• GMP, AMP: Purine synthesis also affected indirectly but main tested effect is dTMP inhibition
• CMP: Pyrimidine synthesis not directly dependent on folate in this step

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 52-year-old strict vegetarian presents with progressive numbness in feet, gait instability, and memory changes. Examination reveals loss of vibration and position sense with spasticity in lower limbs. Blood tests show macrocytic anemia. He is started on folic acid therapy, after which his anemia improves, but neurological symptoms worsen. What is the most likely mechanism for this deterioration?
options: Folate trap leading to methyl-THF accumulation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Folate trap leading to methyl-THF accumulation

In vitamin B₁₂ deficiency, folate becomes trapped as methyl-tetrahydrofolate (methyl-THF) due to impaired conversion of homocysteine to methionine, a reaction that requires vitamin B₁₂.

• Methionine synthase requires vitamin B₁₂
• Without B₁₂ → methyl-THF cannot convert to THF
• Leads to “folate trap” with accumulation of methyl-THF

Clinical Significance:

• Folate supplementation corrects anemia by providing folate for DNA synthesis
• But it does not correct B₁₂ deficiency
• Neurologic damage (due to impaired myelin synthesis) may worsen or continue

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 9-year-old boy presented with bleeding gums, recurrent poor wound healing, and pain in the lower extremities. Examination revealed corkscrew hairs and swollen spongy gums. X-ray showed a white line at the metaphysis. The underlying biochemical defect involves impaired hydroxylation of proline residues during collagen synthesis. Which vitamin deficiency is responsible?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin C

The child has scurvy, caused by vitamin C (ascorbic acid) deficiency. Vitamin C is an essential cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase, enzymes responsible for the hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues during collagen synthesis. Defective collagen formation leads to fragile blood vessels, impaired wound healing, bleeding gums, corkscrew hairs, bone pain, and characteristic White line at the metaphysis (Frankel’s white line) on X-ray

Why not the other options?

• A. Vitamin A: Deficiency causes night blindness, xerophthalmia, and keratinization of epithelium, not defective collagen synthesis.
• C. Vitamin D: Deficiency causes rickets in children with bowing of legs, widened wrists, and rachitic rosary, not bleeding gums or corkscrew hairs.
• D. Vitamin K: Deficiency impairs synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, causing bleeding, but does not impair collagen synthesis or produce corkscrew hairs.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child was brought with pedal edema and cheilosis. Further investigations revealed cardiomegaly. What is the vitamin deficiency associated with this clinical presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thiamine

Thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency leads to beriberi, which can present with both cardiac and peripheral manifestations. Types relevant here:

• Wet beriberi:

o    Cardiomegaly, high-output cardiac failure

o    Edema (pedal edema)

• Dry beriberi:

o    Peripheral neuropathy

Thiamine is a cofactor for key enzymes in energy metabolism:

• Pyruvate dehydrogenase
• α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase
• Transketolase

Cheilosis: Though classically seen in riboflavin deficiency, it can coexist in malnutrition, but the cardiomegaly + edema strongly points to thiamine deficiency.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Riboflavin: Causes cheilosis and glossitis but not cardiomegaly
• Pyridoxine: Causes neuropathy and sideroblastic anemia
• Niacin: Causes pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A family that consumes a diet predominantly consisting of polished rice develops symptoms of muscle weakness and difficulty in movement. Which of the following nutrients should be administered as prophylaxis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thiamine

A diet predominantly consisting of polished rice lacks thiamine (vitamin B1) because the polishing process removes the outer bran layer, which contains most of the thiamine. Deficiency of thiamine leads to beriberi, characterized by muscle weakness, neuropathy, and difficulty in movement due to impaired energy production in nerve and muscle cells.

Thiamine acts as an essential cofactor for enzymes involved in carbohydrate metabolism, including pyruvate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase. When thiamine is deficient, ATP production decreases, particularly affecting tissues with high energy demand such as nervous tissue and muscles, resulting in neuromuscular symptoms.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Calcium: Deficiency mainly causes bone disorders such as osteopenia or osteoporosis.
• Vitamin D: Deficiency leads to rickets or osteomalacia, not primarily neuromuscular weakness related to polished rice diets.
• Iron: Deficiency causes anemia rather than neuropathy or movement difficulty.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A known patient of tuberculosis, on INH for the past 3 months complains of numbness, tingling and burning sensation in all the extremities. What could be vitamin deficiency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vitamin B6

Isoniazid (INH) therapy in tuberculosis can cause vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) deficiency, leading to peripheral neuropathy (numbness, tingling, burning sensation).

• INH forms complexes with pyridoxine and increases its excretion
• This leads to ↓ availability of pyridoxal phosphate (active B6)
• Pyridoxal phosphate is required for neurotransmitter synthesis (e.g., GABA)

Deficiency results in:

• Peripheral neuropathy
• Paresthesia (glove and stocking pattern)

Prevention: Always give prophylactic vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) with INH therapy

Why other options are incorrect:

• Vitamin B12: Causes neuropathy but not specifically linked to INH
• Vitamin B1 (Thiamine): Causes beriberi/Wernicke’s
• Vitamin B3 (Niacin): Causes pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A non-alcoholic hypertensive patient on hydrochlorothiazide therapy presents with cerebellar ataxia, peripheral neuropathy, symmetrical tingling sensations, cardiac failure, and pedal edema. Deficiency of which of the following vitamins or nutrients can cause similar clinical features?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thiamine

The constellation of cerebellar ataxia, peripheral neuropathy, tingling, cardiac failure, and pedal edema is characteristic of thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency, which presents as a combination of dry beriberi (neuropathy) and wet beriberi (cardiac failure + edema).

Chronic diuretic use can increase urinary loss of thiamine, predisposing to deficiency

Thiamine (as TPP) is a cofactor for:

• Pyruvate dehydrogenase
• α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase
• Transketolase

Deficiency → impaired ATP production, especially affecting:

• Nervous system → neuropathy, ataxia
• Heart → cardiomyopathy, heart failure, edema

Why other options are incorrect:

• Selenium: Cardiomyopathy (Keshan disease) but no neuropathy triad
• Vitamin B12: Neuropathy without cardiac failure/edema
• Vitamin B2: Cheilosis, glossitis, dermatitis

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presented with follicular hyperkeratosis on the extensor aspect of the forearm. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Phrynoderma

Phrynoderma (“toad skin”) is characterized by follicular hyperkeratosis on extensor surfaces (arms, thighs), most commonly due to vitamin A deficiency.

• Vitamin A is essential for normal epithelial differentiation
• Deficiency → abnormal keratinization of hair follicles → rough, dry papules

Clinical features:

• Rough, keratotic papules over extensor surfaces
• Dry, coarse skin
• May be associated with night blindness

Why other options are incorrect:

• Darier’s disease: Genetic disorder with greasy papules (seborrheic areas)
• Eruptive xanthoma: Yellow papules due to hypertriglyceridemia
• Folliculitis: Infection of hair follicles (pus-filled lesions)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presented with megaloblastic anemia with neurological symptoms. Which vitamin is deficient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vitamin B12

Vitamin B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia with neurological manifestations, distinguishing it from folate deficiency, which causes megaloblastic anemia without neurological deficits. Vitamin B12 is required for:

• Methionine synthase (homocysteine → methionine)
• Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA)

Deficiency leads to impaired DNA synthesis, causing megaloblastic anemia, and accumulation of methylmalonic acid, resulting in demyelination of the posterior columns and lateral corticospinal tracts (subacute combined degeneration).

Why not the other options?

• B. Vitamin B1 (Thiamine): Deficiency causes beriberi and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, not megaloblastic anemia.
• C. Vitamin B2 (Riboflavin): Deficiency causes cheilosis, angular stomatitis, glossitis, and corneal vascularization, but not neurological deficits with megaloblastic anemia.
• D. Vitamin B3 (Niacin): Deficiency causes pellagra (3 Ds: Dermatitis, Diarrhea, Dementia), not megaloblastic anemia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presenting with bleeding gums and easy bruisability was diagnosed with scurvy. What is the biochemical basis of scurvy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Defective collagen formation

Scurvy is caused by vitamin C (ascorbic acid) deficiency, leading to defective collagen synthesis. Vitamin C is required for hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in collagen via prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase. This hydroxylation is essential for:

• Stabilization of collagen triple helix
• Proper cross-linking of collagen fibers

Clinical features explained:

• Bleeding gums & petechiae → weak vascular connective tissue
• Poor wound healing
• Bone pain (in children)

Why other options are incorrect:

• Low calcium: Causes bone disorders (rickets/osteomalacia)
• Inhibition of clotting factors: Seen in vitamin K deficiency
• Increased keratinization: Seen in vitamin A deficiency

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presents with clinical features suggestive of early vitamin A deficiency. What is the earliest manifestation involving the skin or the eyes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Night blindness

Night blindness (nyctalopia) is the earliest clinical manifestation of vitamin A deficiency. It occurs due to impaired regeneration of rhodopsin in the retinal rod cells, leading to poor vision in dim light.

WHO sequence of ocular manifestations (Xerophthalmia):

1. Night blindness (XN) ✔️ Earliest symptom
2. Conjunctival xerosis (X1A)
3. Bitot’s spots (X1B)
4. Corneal xerosis (X2)
5. Corneal ulceration/keratomalacia (X3A/X3B)
6. Corneal scar (XS)
7. Xerophthalmic fundus (XF)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presents with fatigue, gum bleeding, and multiple perifollicular hemorrhages on the lower limbs, along with a bleeding tendency. These findings are most consistent with a deficiency of which enzyme activity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Prolyl hydroxylase

The clinical features—bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhages, easy bruising, and fatigue—are classic for scurvy (vitamin C deficiency).

Vitamin C is required as a cofactor for:

• Prolyl hydroxylase
• Lysyl hydroxylase

These enzymes catalyze hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in collagen, which is essential for:

• Stability of the collagen triple helix
• Proper cross-linking of collagen fibers

Why other options are incorrect:

• Lysyl oxidase: Involved in collagen cross-linking but is copper-dependent, not vitamin C dependent
• Tyrosinase: Involved in melanin synthesis
• Alkaline phosphatase: Associated with bone metabolism

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient with chronic use of alcohol is brought to hospital with complaints of chronic liver disease. Which of the following you will add to the treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vitamin B1

Thiamine (Vitamin B1) supplementation is essential in patients with chronic alcohol use disorder, especially those with chronic liver disease or malnutrition, because alcoholism commonly causes thiamine deficiency due to poor nutritional intake, reduced intestinal absorption, impaired hepatic storage, and decreased utilization.

Thiamine supplementation prevents and treats Wernicke encephalopathy and Korsakoff syndrome, serious neurological complications of alcoholism.

Why not the other options?

• A. Vitamin A: Deficiency may occur in chronic liver disease, but supplementation is not routine because excess vitamin A can be hepatotoxic.
• B. Vitamin C: May be deficient in malnourished patients but is not routinely indicated as part of initial management.
• D. Vitamin D: Deficiency is common in chronic liver disease, but it is not the priority vitamin in patients with chronic alcohol use.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A woman on anti-depressants presents with bleeding. She gives a history of bulky stools which sticks to the pan. Which of the following vitamin deficiency can cause bleeding in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vitamin K

Bulky, foul-smelling stools that stick to the pan indicate fat malabsorption (steatorrhea). Since vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin (A, D, E, K), its absorption is impaired in conditions causing fat malabsorption.

Vitamin K is essential for γ-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, as well as proteins C and S. Deficiency leads to impaired coagulation and presents with bleeding tendencies.

Additionally, some antidepressants (e.g., SSRIs) can increase bleeding risk by affecting platelet function, further worsening the bleeding in vitamin K deficiency.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: An infant presents with bleeding from the umbilical cord. Which vitamin deficiency is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vit K

Vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB) is the most common cause of spontaneous bleeding in newborns. Bleeding from the umbilical stump, gastrointestinal tract, skin, or intracranial sites occurs due to deficiency of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, and X).

Why are newborns deficient in vitamin K?

• Poor placental transfer of vitamin K
• Sterile intestine (lack of vitamin K-producing gut flora)
• Low vitamin K content in breast milk

Key differentiating features:

• Vitamin K deficiency:

• Umbilical stump bleeding
• Prolonged PT/INR (earliest abnormality)
• May also prolong aPTT in severe deficiency
• Vitamin C deficiency: Gum bleeding, petechiae (older infants/children)
• Hemophilia: Deep tissue/joint bleeding with prolonged aPTT
• Thrombocytopenia: Petechiae and mucosal bleeding with low platelet count

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Casal’s Necklace is a characteristic erythema seen in deficiency of which one of the following vitamins?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Niacin

Casal’s necklace is a characteristic photosensitive dermatitis around the neck seen in niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency, classically as part of pellagra.

Niacin deficiency causes the classic 3 Ds:

• Dermatitis → photosensitive, including Casal’s necklace
• Diarrhea
• Dementia

Why not other options?

• A. Thiamine (B1): Deficiency causes beriberi and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.
• B. Riboflavin (B2): Causes cheilosis, angular stomatitis, glossitis and corneal vascularization.
• C. Niacin (B3) — Correct: Causes pellagra and Casal’s necklace.
• D. Pyridoxine (B6): Deficiency can cause sideroblastic anemia, dermatitis, neuropathy and seizures.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome: 1. It is a rare complication of chronic alcohol misuse characterised by ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and delirium. 2. There is damage to the mammillary bodies and dorsomedial nuclei of thalamus. 3. The underlying cause is deficiency of Vitamin B12 (Cobalamin). 4. The syndrome can also arise due to malabsorption or protracted vomiting. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome is a neuropsychiatric disorder caused by thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency, most commonly seen in chronic alcohol misuse, but it can also occur in malnutrition, malabsorption, hyperemesis, and prolonged vomiting. It consists of Wernicke encephalopathy (acute) and Korsakoff syndrome (chronic amnestic syndrome).

Why is B correct?

• 1. It is a rare complication of chronic alcohol misuse characterised by ophthalmoplegia\, ataxia and delirium✅: Wernicke encephalopathy classically presents with the triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and confusion (delirium).
• 2. There is damage to the mammillary bodies and dorsomedial nuclei of thalamus✅: These are the characteristic pathological lesions responsible for memory impairment.
• 4. The syndrome can also arise due to malabsorption or protracted vomiting✅: Any condition causing thiamine deficiency can precipitate Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome.

Incorrect statement:

• 3. The underlying cause is deficiency of Vitamin B12 (Cobalamin)❌: The disorder is caused by Vitamin B1 (Thiamine) deficiency, not Vitamin B12.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding Wernicke’s encephalopathy: I. It is caused by niacin deficiency. II. It is often seen in alcoholics. III. Ophthalmoplegia, polyneuritis and ataxia are some of its characteristic features. IV. It occurs occasionally in people who fast. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. II, III and IV

Wernicke’s encephalopathy is an acute neurological emergency caused by thiamine (Vitamin B₁) deficiency. It is most commonly seen in chronic alcoholics, but can also occur in prolonged fasting, starvation, hyperemesis gravidarum, and malnutrition. Early recognition and prompt intravenous thiamine administration are essential to prevent irreversible neurological damage.

• Cause: Thiamine (Vitamin B₁) deficiency, not niacin deficiency.
• Commonly associated with: Chronic alcoholism, prolonged fasting, starvation, hyperemesis gravidarum, bariatric surgery, prolonged TPN without thiamine.
• Classic triad:

• Confusion
• Ophthalmoplegia/Nystagmus
• Ataxia

• Peripheral neuropathy (polyneuritis) may also be present.
• Treatment: IV thiamine before glucose administration.
• Untreated cases may progress to Korsakoff syndrome, characterized by memory impairment, confabulation, and anterograde amnesia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Consider the following statements with regard to the treatment of vitamin A deficiency: I. Repeated high doses of retinol can cause liver damage and teratogenicity. II. Acute overdose of vitamin A may lead to increased intracranial pressure and skin desquamation. III. Regular vitamin A supplementation is also recommended for pregnant women even in countries where vitamin A deficiency is not endemic. IV. Excessive intake of carotene may cause harmless orange pigmentation of the skin. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. I, II and IV

Vitamin A (retinol) is a fat-soluble vitamin essential for vision, epithelial cell differentiation, immune function, reproduction, and growth. While supplementation is effective in treating deficiency, excessive intake can result in acute and chronic toxicity.

• I. Repeated high doses of retinol can cause liver damage and teratogenicity. ✅

• Chronic vitamin A toxicity causes hepatotoxicity, bone pain, alopecia, pseudotumor cerebri, and is teratogenic during pregnancy.

• II. Acute overdose of vitamin A may lead to increased intracranial pressure and skin desquamation. ✅

• Acute toxicity presents with headache, nausea, vomiting, raised intracranial pressure (pseudotumor cerebri), blurred vision, and skin peeling/desquamation.

• III. Regular vitamin A supplementation is also recommended for pregnant women even in countries where vitamin A deficiency is not endemic. ❌

• Routine vitamin A supplementation is not recommended during pregnancy in non-endemic regions because excess vitamin A is teratogenic. Supplementation is reserved for women with documented deficiency or specific public health indications.

• IV. Excessive intake of carotene may cause harmless orange pigmentation of the skin. ✅

• Excess β-carotene causes carotenemia, characterized by yellow-orange discoloration of the skin (especially palms and soles) without scleral icterus. It is benign and reversible.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: FAD status in body is determined by?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glutathione reductase

FAD (Flavin adenine dinucleotide) is derived from riboflavin (vitamin B2) and functions as a cofactor in various redox reactions.

The functional status of FAD in the body is assessed by measuring the activity of glutathione reductase in red blood cells. This enzyme requires FAD as a cofactor to convert oxidized glutathione (GSSG) to reduced glutathione (GSH).

• In riboflavin (FAD) deficiency, glutathione reductase activity decreases.
• When FAD is added in vitro, enzyme activity increases (activation coefficient), indicating deficiency.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Thiamine: Assessed by transketolase activity (not FAD).
• Hexokinase: Involved in glycolysis, not used for vitamin assessment.
• Transketolase: Used to assess thiamine (vitamin B1) status.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In folate deficiency, the False statement is:
options: High homocysteine and normal methylmalonic acid
B12 supplementation is recommended along with Folate
Purine and pyrimidine synthesis are affected
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hemolytic anemia is a feature

Folate deficiency causes impaired DNA synthesis due to defective purine and thymidylate (pyrimidine) synthesis, leading to megaloblastic anemia. It is characterized by elevated homocysteine levels with normal methylmalonic acid (unlike vitamin B₁₂ deficiency).

Hemolytic anemia is not a typical feature; instead, folate deficiency produces megaloblastic anemia due to ineffective erythropoiesis. Vitamin B₁₂ is often supplemented with folate to avoid masking an underlying B₁₂ deficiency and preventing neurological complications.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Korsakoff psychosis is true except? 1. Amnesia 2. Confabulation 3. Ophthalmoplegia 4. Ataxia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 3, 4

Korsakoff psychosis is a chronic neuropsychiatric disorder caused by thiamine (vitamin B₁) deficiency, most commonly seen in chronic alcoholism. It is characterized by anterograde and retrograde amnesia with confabulation (fabrication of stories to fill memory gaps).

Ophthalmoplegia and ataxia are features of Wernicke encephalopathy, the acute stage of thiamine deficiency.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Of the following ocular manifestations of Vitamin A deficiency, the first sign that can be clinically seen is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Conjunctival xerosis

Vitamin A deficiency (VAD) primarily affects the eyes (xerophthalmia) and is one of the leading preventable causes of childhood blindness. The first clinically visible sign is conjunctival xerosis, whereas the earliest symptom is night blindness (nyctalopia).

Progression of Xerophthalmia (WHO Classification)

• XN – Night blindness (earliest symptom)
• X1A – Conjunctival xerosis (first clinical sign)
• X1B – Bitot’s spots
• X2 – Corneal xerosis
• X3A – Corneal ulceration/keratomalacia (<1/3 cornea)
• X3B – Corneal ulceration/keratomalacia (>1/3 cornea)
• XS – Corneal scar
• XF – Xerophthalmic fundus

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The bony deformity of “pigeon chest” in children occurs due to deficiency of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin D

Vitamin D deficiency in children causes rickets, a disorder characterized by defective mineralization of the growing bones and growth plates. One of its characteristic skeletal deformities is pigeon chest (pectus carinatum), resulting from outward protrusion of the sternum due to abnormal development of the ribs and costochondral junctions.

• Vitamin D deficiency → Rickets (children), Osteomalacia (adults). ⭐
• Pigeon chest (pectus carinatum) is a classic chest deformity seen in rickets. ⭐
• Other skeletal features include:

• Rachitic rosary (enlarged costochondral junctions)
• Harrison’s sulcus
• Frontal bossing
• Craniotabes
• Widening of wrists and ankles
• Bow legs (genu varum) or knock knees (genu valgum)

• Biochemical findings: ↓ Vitamin D, ↓ phosphate, ↑ alkaline phosphatase, ↑ PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism).
• X-ray findings: Metaphyseal cupping, fraying, and widening.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The treatment given to the patient presenting with a history of binge alcohol intake and symptoms of convulsions, altered sensorium, and plasma glucose level of 45 mg/dL is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Thiamine followed by dextrose

In a chronic alcoholic with hypoglycemia (glucose 45 mg/dL) and altered sensorium, the correct management is thiamine administration before glucose.

• Chronic alcoholics are commonly thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficient
• Thiamine is required for glucose metabolism (pyruvate dehydrogenase, etc.)
• Giving glucose first increases metabolic demand and can precipitate or worsen Wernicke encephalopathy

Correct sequence: Thiamine first → then dextrose

• Thiamine deficiency → impaired cerebral energy metabolism
• Glucose without thiamine → accumulation of lactate → neuronal injury

Why other options are incorrect:

• 25% dextrose alone: Can worsen neurological damage
• Fomepizole: Used in methanol/ethylene glycol poisoning
• Thiamine alone: Does not correct hypoglycemia

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: True statement about Korsakoff syndrome is:
options: Anterograde amnesia and loss of recent memory
Anterograde amnesia with loss of personal identity and no residual deficit
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anterograde amnesia and loss of recent memory

Korsakoff syndrome is a chronic neuropsychiatric disorder caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, most commonly seen in chronic alcohol use. It is characterized by severe anterograde amnesia, impaired recent memory, variable retrograde amnesia, and confabulation, while consciousness and personal identity are usually preserved.

• The hallmark features of Korsakoff syndrome are:

• Anterograde amnesia (inability to form new memories)
• Loss of recent memory
• Confabulation

Why not the other options?

• B. Global confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia: These are features of Wernicke encephalopathy, the acute manifestation of thiamine deficiency.
• C. Anterograde amnesia with loss of personal identity and no residual deficit: Describes dissociative (psychogenic) amnesia, not Korsakoff syndrome.
• D. Implicit memory impaired: Implicit (procedural) memory is relatively preserved in Korsakoff syndrome; explicit (declarative) memory is impaired.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Vitamin leading to diversion of 3-hydroxykynurenine toward xanthurenic acid:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pyridoxine

Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) is required as a cofactor in the tryptophan–kynurenine pathway. It is necessary for the enzyme kynureninase, which converts 3-hydroxykynurenine → 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid.

When pyridoxine is deficient:

• The normal pathway is blocked.
• 3-hydroxykynurenine is diverted to form xanthurenic acid.
• Increased urinary excretion of xanthurenic acid occurs.

• Can occur with isoniazid therapy, which interferes with pyridoxine metabolism.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which amino acid will not be synthesized due to B12 deficiency in a patient with history of ileectomy with elevated homocysteine levels, increased methylmalonyl CoA and peripheral neuropathy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Methionine

Vitamin B12 deficiency (e.g., after ileectomy, where B12 is absorbed) leads to impairment of two key reactions:

1.      Homocysteine → Methionine (via methionine synthase, B12-dependent)

2.      Methylmalonyl-CoA → Succinyl-CoA (via methylmalonyl-CoA mutase)

Biochemical consequences:

• ↑ Homocysteine (cannot convert to methionine)
• ↓ Methionine synthesis
• ↑ Methylmalonyl-CoA → contributes to neurological damage

Clinical relevance:

• Peripheral neuropathy (due to myelin damage)
• Megaloblastic anemia
• Seen in ileal resection (ileectomy) due to impaired B12 absorption

Why other options are incorrect:

• Cysteine: Formed from homocysteine (via B6-dependent pathway), not directly dependent on B12
• Glutathione: Synthesized from glutamate, cysteine, glycine
• Tryptophan: Essential amino acid (not synthesized in body)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which micronutrient deficiency causes anemia, bleeding gums, and white line of Frenkel on X-ray?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin C

The triad of anemia, bleeding gums, and “white line of Frankel” on X-ray is characteristic of vitamin C (ascorbic acid) deficiency → scurvy.

Vitamin C is essential for hydroxylation of proline and lysine in collagen via:

• Prolyl hydroxylase
• Lysyl hydroxylase

Deficiency → defective collagen synthesis → weak connective tissue.

Clinical features explained:

• Bleeding gums & petechiae: Fragile capillaries due to weak collagen
• Anemia: Due to chronic bleeding + ↓ iron absorption (vitamin C enhances iron absorption)
• White line of Frankel (dense metaphyseal line): Due to defective osteoid formation in growing bones

Radiological signs in scurvy:

• White line of Frankel
• Pelkan spurs
• Scorbutic rosary

Why other options are incorrect:

• Copper: Causes anemia and neurological issues, not bleeding gums + Frankel line
• Iron: Causes anemia only
• Zinc: Causes dermatitis and poor wound healing

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding folate deficiency is FALSE?
options: High homocysteine and normal methyl malonic acid
If given at the diagnosis of pregnancy - can prevent neural tube defects
Folate supplementation is required in children with chronic hemolytic anemia
Vitamin B12 deficiency should be corrected before supplementing folate
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. If given at the diagnosis of pregnancy - can prevent neural tube defects

Neural tube closure occurs very early in embryonic development (between days 21–28 after conception, around the 4th week of gestation). By the time most women realize they are pregnant (usually 5–6 weeks gestation), neural tube closure has already occurred.

Therefore, folic acid must be taken before conception and continued through the first trimester to effectively reduce the risk of neural tube defects (NTDs).

• Recommended dose for low-risk women: 400 µg/day, beginning at least 1 month before conception.
• High-risk women (previous pregnancy with NTD, certain antiepileptic drugs, etc.): 4–5 mg/day before conception.

Why are the other options correct

A. High homocysteine with normal methylmalonic acid levels

Folate deficiency impairs the conversion of homocysteine → methionine, leading to:

• ↑ Homocysteine
• Normal methylmalonic acid (MMA)

In contrast:

| Deficiency | Homocysteine | Methylmalonic acid

| ---------- | ------------ | ------------------

| Folate deficiency | ↑ | Normal

| Vitamin B12 deficiency | ↑ | ↑

High-yield pearl: MMA differentiates vitamin B12 deficiency from folate deficiency.

C. Folate supplementation is required in children with chronic hemolytic anemia

Children with chronic hemolytic disorders (e.g., sickle cell disease, hereditary spherocytosis, thalassemia) have:

• Increased RBC destruction
• Increased bone marrow activity
• Increased DNA synthesis
• Increased folate requirement

Hence, routine folate supplementation is recommended to support erythropoiesis.

D. Vitamin B12 deficiency should be corrected before folate supplementation

This is an important clinical principle.

Giving folic acid alone to a patient with unrecognized vitamin B12 deficiency:

• Corrects the megaloblastic anemia
• Does not treat the neurological damage
• May allow neurological complications to progress unnoticed, sometimes irreversibly

Therefore:

• Always exclude or treat vitamin B12 deficiency first, or give both B12 and folate if both deficiencies are suspected.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following vitamin deficiencies is associated with cystic fibrosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin A

Patients with cystic fibrosis (CF) develop exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, leading to impaired digestion and absorption of dietary fats. As a result, they are prone to deficiencies of the fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K). Vitamin A deficiency is common and can cause night blindness, xerophthalmia, dry skin, and impaired immunity. In CF:

• Thick secretions obstruct pancreatic ducts.
• ↓ Pancreatic enzyme secretion → fat malabsorption.
• ↓ Absorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K).

Therefore, vitamin A deficiency is a common nutritional complication.

Why not the other options?

• A. Biotin (Vitamin B7): Water-soluble vitamin; deficiency is rare and usually associated with prolonged raw egg consumption or prolonged antibiotic use.
• C. Vitamin C: Water-soluble vitamin absorbed normally in CF; deficiency is uncommon.
• D. Riboflavin (Vitamin B2): Water-soluble vitamin and not characteristically deficient in cystic fibrosis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following vitamin deficiencies is most likely to cause lactic acidosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thiamine

Thiamine (Vitamin B1) is an essential cofactor for several enzymes involved in aerobic carbohydrate metabolism, particularly:

• Pyruvate dehydrogenase
• α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase
• Transketolase

When thiamine is deficient, the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction is impaired, preventing the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA. As a result, pyruvate is instead converted to lactate, leading to accumulation of lactic acid and lactic acidosis.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Niacin: Deficiency causes pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia).
• Vitamin C: Deficiency leads to scurvy due to impaired collagen synthesis.
• ·Riboflavin: Deficiency causes cheilosis, glossitis, and dermatitis, not lactic acidosis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which vitamin can be deficient in a patient who has undergone gastrectomy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin B12

Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency is common after gastrectomy due to loss of intrinsic factor (IF) production.

• Parietal cells of stomach produce intrinsic factor
• IF is essential for absorption of vitamin B12 in the terminal ileum
• Gastrectomy → ↓ intrinsic factor → impaired B12 absorption

Consequences:

• Megaloblastic anemia
• Neurological manifestations (subacute combined degeneration)

o    Paresthesia

o    Loss of vibration & position sense

o    UMN signs

Why other options are incorrect:

• Vitamin A: Fat-soluble, absorbed in intestine
• Vitamin C: Absorbed directly, not IF-dependent
• Vitamin D: Fat-soluble, not affected by intrinsic factor
